title: Bel review – a tearful, heartbreaking tribute to a spellbinding singer  | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: Beldina Odenyo was on the verge of stardom when she took her own life in 2021. In this beautiful documentary, her grief-stricken sister Leah attempts to finish her album – and her journey will make you cry again and again
Author: Chitra Ramaswamy
Headline: Beldina Odenyo was on the verge of stardom when she took her own life in 2021. In this beautiful documentary, her grief-stricken sister Leah attempts to finish her album – and her journey will make you cry again and again
Content: Beldina Odenyo in 2017.Photograph: BBC/Hopscotch Films/Andrew CawleyView image in fullscreenBeldina Odenyo in 2017.Photograph: BBC/Hopscotch Films/Andrew CawleyTV reviewTelevision & radioReviewBel review – a tearful, heartbreaking tribute to a spellbinding singerBeldina Odenyo was on the verge of stardom when she took her own life in 2021. In this beautiful documentary, her grief-stricken sister Leah attempts to finish her album – and her journey will make you cry again and againChitra RamaswamyTue 6 Oct 2026 18.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn 2021, the Kenyan-Scottish singer-songwriter Beldina Odenyo was on the brink of major stardom. That October, aged 31, she headlined a gig at Edinburgh’s Usher Hall, delivering an instantly legendary performance; barefoot, cloaked and bone-shaking in its intensity. Everyone in that concert hall knew they were witnessing something extraordinary that night. Two weeks later, Odenyo took her own life.This tender and grief-stricken documentary, which opens a year after her death, is directed with remarkable care by Louise Lockwood. What emerges is a sensitively drawn portrait of a visionary artist haunted by trauma, formed through her teenage video diaries, the words of those who loved her, the handful of exquisite songs she left behind – kept in a folder on her hard drive named “passable demos” – and the determination of her older sister, Leah McAleer, to keep her astonishing voice alive. A deeply painful venture that she understands is itself a product of her insurmountable grief.“All of this is a futile attempt to bring her back,” says McAleer while listening to Odenyo’s songs in the studio, her sparse guitar-playing sent through an amplifier to sound as though she’s in the room. Earlier, she put it even more starkly: “I need to finish her album.”View image in fullscreenExtraordinary … Bel’s last performance at  Edinburgh’s Usher Hall in 2021.Photograph: BBC/Hopscotch Films/Euan RobertsonAnd what an album it is, propelled by musical genius, the poles of suffering and survival between which Odenyo was buffeted, and her tremendous voice. “I love music,” says the often cocky, often crying 15-year-old at the start of Bel, in one of the charismatic video diaries delivered from her bedroom in the ex-mining village of Kirkconnel, Dumfries and Galloway, to her future fans. “I want to be a musician. I want to be famous, to show the world my skills …” she laughs, “and just rock their socks off.” In another video she notes: “I’m quite mad as a person. I don’t give a fuck, to be honest.”Odenyo was born in Kisumu, western Kenya, and for the first few years of her life lived with her mother and siblings. She met her father for the first time at around the age of six or seven. “A few weeks later,” she says in an interview, “I was in Scotland.” McAleer’s memory of what happened and why Odenyo was taken from her mother by her father is equally fractured – neither family spoke about the devastating loss that reverberated through her life. “My father came back [from Kenya] with a small child,” says McAleer. “I just remember the shock … and her pristine white dress. She didn’t cry. She didn’t speak for three days.” All this silence and shock was channelled into her music, and that once-in-a-generation voice.View image in fullscreenLeah and Bel circa 1998.Photograph: BBC/Hopscotch Films/Leah McAleerBel is also a close study of mental illness, its healing but also precarious relationship with creativity, and the devastating impacts of exile and racism. In Kirkconnel, where Odenyo was the only black kid in her school, “she was set on fire once,” says her best friend, Frances. “She had a chain wrapped around her neck … it was horrific physical abuse.” In Glasgow, during a mental health episode in which an ambulance was called by a friend because she was self-harming, the police arrived first. Odenyo said they broke down her door, threw her down the stairs, and demanded to know if she had HIV because “people from where you’re from do”. By the time lockdown hit she was living alone in Paisley, increasingly isolated, ill and vulnerable. It was then that she uploaded those “passable demos” to her computer.It’s a harrowing watch, which brings me to tears over and over again, brimming with voices traumatised by her suicide. The poet Jackie Kay was blown away by Odenyo’s self-possession: “Bel didn’t feel the need to smile or ingratiate herself with an audience.” Ex-boyfriend and fellow musician Lewis Semple remembers first hearing her sing in Glasgow: “Her voice fucking blew me away. I was shaking in my seat.” For venue booker Joe Rattray, she was “someone who makes a place cooler”. For Scottish singer-songwriter Kathryn Joseph whose sublime song The Bird was covered by Odenyo at that Usher Hall gig, “she was someone who understood humans … and pain.” At the end of Bel, footage from the Usher Hall gig plays again. Then Odenyo’s voice cuts out. A long, painfully apt silence ensues alongside stills of her flat, her musical equipment, her cables, her glasses. It’s beautifully done.In many ways Bel belongs to McAleer, a dignified and humane presence throughout. She was clearly a mother figure to Odenyo – they were “adultified children” who “grew up fast” is how she puts it – and speaks with incredible articulacy and self-awareness considering the immediacy of her grief. At Odenyo’s graveside in Kenya, where she wanted to be buried close to her mother and where the documentary ends, McAleer plays her album, which she’s worked tirelessly to release independently, and confesses: “I feel on a very deep level I let her down.” Which couldn’t be further from the truth: Bel is a memorial to her love.Ultimately, though, it’s Odenyo’s music that most powerfully tells her story. She performed as Heir of the Cursed, a name that came to her in a dream and turned out to be a translation of the Tetela name of the assassinated Congolese leader Patrice Lumumba. These few heartbreaking, sometimes foreshadowing songs, into which Odenyo poured all that she could not say, are played throughout the film. Watch it. Then go and listen to her phenomenal music.Bel aired on BBC Four and is on iPlayer now.In the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123, or emailjo@samaritans.orgorjo@samaritans.ie. In the US, you can call or text theNational Suicide Prevention Lifelineon 988, chat on988lifeline.org, ortext HOMEto 741741 to connect with a crisis counsellor. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. title: Don’t mention the Iron Dome: comedy genius Kemi on warpath at Tory conference  | John Crace | The Guardian
description: ‘It’s a Britannia Shield’ announcement proves no one does farcical improv better than the Conservative leader
Author: John Crace
Headline: ‘It’s a Britannia Shield’ announcement proves no one does farcical improv better than the Conservative leader
Content: Kemi Badenoch arriving for media interviews at the Tory conference. Or is it a remake of The Truman Show?Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PAView image in fullscreenKemi Badenoch arriving for media interviews at the Tory conference. Or is it a remake of The Truman Show?Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PAThe politics sketchConservative conference 2026Don’t mention the Iron Dome: comedy genius Kemi on warpath at Tory conferenceJohn Crace‘It’s a Britannia Shield’ announcement proves no one does farcical improv better than the Conservative leaderTue 6 Oct 2026 12.49 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 17.15 EDTShareJust another day in Crapland. It’s amazing what you can get used to. You can’t say the Tories haven’t put a lot of thought into their party conference. It takes some programming skill to make every day even more dismal than the last. You come expecting very little and get even less.Schopenhauer would be in dreamland. The very act of being has never felt so inconsequential. Yet there’s something very comforting about this. You leave the Birmingham theme park attraction feeling better about yourself than when you arrived. Who knew abject failure could be so much fun? You find yourself congratulating some members on being able to dress themselves. A curious hybrid of an endangered species and care in the community?You might find yourself wondering if you are being gaslit. Small pockets of people roaming around aimlessly with a smile on their face, insisting that it is very heaven in this dawn to be alive and repeatedly crossing themselves before images of the beatificKemi Badenoch. But then you realise that the people the Tories are really gaslighting are themselves. It’s almost painful to watch. Almost. But mostly it’s like a remake of The Truman Show. Everyone waking up each day and believing they are engaged in something meaningful. When the reality is nothing is happening. They are living in a Potemkin village. A series of distractions designed to look like a party conference.Badenoch denies ‘British Iron Dome’ plan – after Tories use phrase in press releaseRead moreThe breakout star is, of course, Kemi. She is the Tories’ chosen one. KULT KEMI. The leader who has rescued them from one black hole and is plunging them straight back into another. I’ve come to realise I’ve got Kemi wrong. Sure, she’s short-tempered and can’t tolerate dissent. But she’s actually a supremely gifted entertainer. A comedy genius. A woman whose one-liners often get mistaken for serious comment. A female Jack Dee. She would be far more successful taking her show to the Edinburgh fringe than Birmingham.View image in fullscreenKULT KEMI: Badenoch badges on sale at the Tory conference.Photograph: James McCauley/ShutterstockKemi’s act on the morning media round was one of her best yet. No one does improv better. Understandably, every interviewer wanted to ask her about the Tories’ overnight announcement of a £10bn Iron Dome to rival the Israelis’ that would protect the UK from any kind of drone or missile attack. Like, how did she imagine she was going to build the Iron Dome for about a tenth of the money that all the experts said it would cost? And wasn’t this just some bullshit nonsense designed to make the front pages of the Tory press that wouldn’t stand contact with reality?“Stop calling it an Iron Dome,” Kemi dead-panned. She really is a comedy pro. Even at 8.10am she’s still in role. “It isn’t an Iron Dome. I’ve never called it an Iron Dome. It’s a Britannia Shield.” Genius. She couldn’t think for the life of her why everyone was calling it an Iron Dome. Mmm. It might have been something to do with the Tory press office releasing a statement calling it an Iron Dome? And the opinion piece in the Sun, written by Kemi herself, calling it an Iron Dome? There are clearly a lot of replicant Kemis rushing around pretending to be the real one.OK, OK, we’ll call it a Britannia Shield, said the radio and TV presenters. Sometimes it’s easier to humour a guest. So when was it going to be operational, what would it look like and how much of the UK would it cover? Kemi laughed. She hadn’t a clue. She was just the one with the ideas. The details she left for others. But it definitely would be up and running before Penny Mordaunt returned to parliament to reprise her role in Sky’sThe War Game. As for the shield itself, that would be a few Sopwith Camel biplanes and barrage balloons that could be diverted to Scotland at a fortnight’s notice if required.Are you really just a one-woman band? Anna Foster asked on the Today programme. Your personal polls are higher than your party’s. A polite way of saying the Tories are tanking in third place. Not at all, Kemi ad-libbed. EvenJeffrey Archerwould have struggled to lie quite so shamelessly. Everyone knows who my shadow cabinet is. Er. I’m not sure I could name them all. I’m not even sure the shadow cabinet could. Just an array of nodding dogs on a dashboard. But maybe we’ve underestimated the public. They do know exactly who the shadow cabinet is. And that’s why the Tories are still bottom-lining.Back in the conference centre, those members who were still alive were struggling to find something to do. The morning’s entertainment was centred around the “Main Hall”, AKA the converted cupboard. For Laura Trott, the shadow education secretary, there were about 15 people in the room. The rest of the audience had disguised themselves as seats again. Still, not all bad news. Eight people were watching online. A figure that soon went down to one. For a while I wondered who this one poor sod was. Then I realised it was me.Laura looked close to tears by the time the session was over. She was met beside the stage by someone who I hope was a therapist. Quite where everyone else had got to was a mystery. There was also no one to hear Rebecca Paul – me neither – talk about £50k handbags with a woman called Plum. Self-selecting, I guess. Maybe there’s a separate hall for those experiencing extreme catatonia.By the afternoon we lucky few were stretched out into the much-reduced Symphony Hall to prepare for war with a Shahed drone hanging above our heads. First up was the shadow foreign secretary, Tom Tugendhat, a man who has sold his one-nation soul for a job in Kemi’s Kabinet. “I am coming back to serve,” SuperTug announced, matching the oratory skills of Andrew Griffith. He is a man who wakes up every day, and seems disappointed not to find himself at war. He rather died on his arse.Then we got the special guest. The rightwing historian Niall Ferguson. A more swivel-eyed, deranged Dr Strangelove. He had come to tell everyone that he too fancied a war, even if you didn’t want one. “A world war is coming,” he said, trying not to show if he had become sexually aroused. “And there is nothing we can do about it.” All of which made the later speeches of Kemi-come-latelies Helen Whately and James Cartlidge somewhat redundant. There’s no need to starve benefits claimants or build an Iron Dome when the apocalypse is upon us.Suddenly the Tory conference made sense. It wasn’t just a place where hope came to die. It was a place where we all came to die.Explore more on these topicsConservative conference 2026The politics sketchKemi BadenochConservative conferenceConservativesDefence policycommentShareReuse this content

title: How I Shop with Jonathan Van Ness: ‘The price you pay for impulsivity is years later’ | Celebrity | The Guardian
description: Always wondered what everyday stuff celebrities buy, where they shop for food and the basics they scrimp on? The Queer Eye legend talks handmade gifts, secondhand shopping and bag obsessions with the Filter
Author: Sarah Matthews
Headline: Always wondered what everyday stuff celebrities buy, where they shop for food and the basics they scrimp on? The Queer Eye legend talks handmade gifts, secondhand shopping and bag obsessions with the Filter
Content: Composite: Guardian Design/Jordan CarterView image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian Design/Jordan CarterGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.How I shopCelebrityInterviewHow I Shop with Jonathan Van Ness: ‘The price you pay for impulsivity is years later’As told toSarah MatthewsAlways wondered what everyday stuff celebrities buy, where they shop for food and the basics they scrimp on? The Queer Eye legend talks handmade gifts, secondhand shopping and bag obsessions with the FilterDon’t get the Filter delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereTue 6 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJonathan Van Ness rose to fame as the beauty and hair care expert on the multi-award-winning showQueer Eye. Their eight-year tenure as one of the “Fab Five” presenters ended when the show’s final season aired in January 2026. A hairstylist by trade, they have their own cruelty-free, vegan haircare brand, JVN Hair.Beyond TV and beauty work, Van Ness has continued a career as a comedian, writer and podcast presenter. They have written five books, including the New York Times bestselling memoirOver the Topand their latest young adult novel, which they wrote alongside Julie Murphy,Let Them Stare. Van Ness continues to be an advocate for the LGBTQIA+ community, working on campaigns withThe Trevor ProjectandPlanned Parenthood.What’s the last treat you bought for yourself?A spray tan at Sugared + Bronzed.Shop Sugared + BronzedWhere do you buy your food?View image in fullscreenBig Apple: fresh produce at a New York farmers’ market.Photograph: Boogich/GettyThe farmers’ market. I live two blocks away from it in New York and go there all the time.What’s the best present you’ve given?This obnoxiously hard-to-find twilly [narrow silk scarf] also from Hermès. The queen of my heart, my very best girl[friend], wanted one so bad that I went to 15 Hermès stores in like 15 cities and finally got it; it was the best Christmas present ever.View image in fullscreenShop scarves and more at Hermès… and the best present you’ve received?My mum made this stunning throw blanket with the nicest, thickest yarn, but I don’t want to use it because I have five cats who would slice it with their claws. I begged her to make me a duplicate, but she made me the world’s skinniest one – not as nice. I was like: “Mom, that’s not as big and chic as the first one.” She’s like: “Use the one I made you! I’m not knitting you another!” She’s a really crafty, fierce artist.What’s your favourite online store?EBay. I think resale is really interesting; I’m particularly obsessed with bags. It’s a little bit nerve-racking because who authenticated it? But I do like the prices, and I’ve seen so many gorgeous pieces on there that do check out.What’s your favourite bricks-and-mortar shop?In England, I’ve got to saySpace NK– I love to buy Skin Rocks by Caroline Hirons products there, especially the eye cream.View image in fullscreenSkin Rocks the eye cream, 15ml£70 at Space NKWhat’s the gadget you use most often?My Mophie portable phone charger.View image in fullscreenMophie PowerStation 5K£13.49 at Transparent CommunicationsWhat’s the purchase you regret the most?A house in Texas. I was in this era where I was like, “I must have more space”, but then it was way too much space – I bought at the top of the market, and then real estate in Austin tanked. It taught me that sometimes the price you pay for impulsivity is years later.What’s the thing(s) you get delivered?A grocery delivery service called Gopuff, for non-farmers’ market staples like Cinnamon Toast Crunch, milk, and kitty litter.Shop at GopuffWhere do you buy your underwear?I am obsessed with Hanro. It’s stupidly expensive, like $50 (about £38) for a pair of underwear, but those bitches hold up. I think I’ve had some of them for like five, six years, and they are very well made.View image in fullscreenHanro cotton essentials pants, two-pack£50 at HanroWhat would you buy with £20?JVN Hair notwithstanding, what I do like that’s under £20 is CeraVe body moisturiser. I suffer from psoriasis and, in a really bad flare, it is gentle, so nurturing and doesn’t sting.View image in fullscreenCeraVe moisturising cream, 454gskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion£13.13 at Lookfantastic£17.50 at Cult Beauty… and £200?For £200, fragrance from D’Orsay. Oh. My. God. One I would choose right now is Vanilla Affair.View image in fullscreenD’Orsay Vanilla Affair extrait de parfum, 90ml£217 at Nicchia Luxury£220 at LibertyWhat’s your ‘saved search’ on eBay/Vinted?My husband wants a 50cm Hermès Kelly Relax bag the soccer guys were carrying during the World Cup. He says he wants one that looks as if he filled it up with rocks and then threw it down the stairs, a bit [beaten up], but that’s kind of hard to find.What item do you buy on repeat?Protein Pop-Tarts. I’m so addicted to them, I can’t keep a box in my house for more than two days. (Though it says “protein” in huge letters, it’s just 5g per tart – or 10g per suggested serving of two tarts – instead of the regular 2g).View image in fullscreenProtein Pop-TartsSlammin’ Strawberry, box of eight£12.95 at AmazonAlso, the fizzy tail Percy Pigs. Target just started carrying them, so now my husband isn’t hiding them from me. Before, I would be like: “Why are there 40 packages of Percy Pigs in the back of my sock drawer?”View image in fullscreenPercy Pig Phizzy Pigtails, 170g£1.70 at OcadoHow do you make your coffee at home?In a Breville (marketed under the Sage brand in the UK) coffee machine – an americano with a splash of cold milk.View image in fullscreenSage Oracle Jet automatic bean-to-cup coffee machine£1,499.95 at Sage£1,529.95 at John LewisWhat’s your biggest splurge?Bags. Being socialised as a boy growing up, purses were for girls, so my mum let me carry around one of her bags in secret when my dad wasn’t around.Alongside Hermès, I love bags by the Row, and also Ikea shopping bags. Do I quit my life and start a bag resale business, where I just find people’s dream bags?View image in fullscreenSometimes an Ikea bag will do; other times it has to be designer, which you can shop below.Photograph: Courtesy of IkeaShop men’s bags at the RowShop women’s bags at the RowShop the Row bags at SelfridgesWhat everyday item do you scrimp on?View image in fullscreenThe wheel deal: Jonathan Van Ness prefers a Lime bike to a London taxi.Photograph: Mike Kemp/In Pictures/GettyTaxis: I ride my bike [instead], or use public transport. In London, I’m up on that tube or on Lime bikes. I was spending so much money on taxis, I was like, girl, I don’t need to do all that. I love to bike; I’ll just get a helmet.And what’s your greatest vintage find?My birthday present to myself this year. I found a black lizard Hermès Kelly Sellier from 1987, the year I was born, which has its original hardware, at Sotheby’s. It’s [so pristine] I think someone bought it in ’87, wore it twice, put it back in the box and thought: “I don’t like that thing.” In order for me to convince my business manager that this is OK, I had to sell however many bags it takes – which was seven – so it was not coming out of my income. I told myself the famous lie when I’m buying something too expensive: “This can be my everyday bag. I’m just gonna beat it up, it’s gonna be totally worth it.” But then I get it home, and I’m like: “I could never!”For more, read How I Shop withLaura JacksonandTom DaleyView image in fullscreenDon’t buy anything until you’ve read the Filter, the Guardian’s home for truly independent product reviews and recommendations. title: The west has a blinkered view of African music – and it’s hurting the whole continent’s culture | Pop and rock | The Guardian
description: The term Afrobeats is applied to all sorts of genres, flattening them into one. Artists, media and the music industry must do better at showing off the richness of African pop
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The term Afrobeats is applied to all sorts of genres, flattening them into one. Artists, media and the music industry must do better at showing off the richness of African pop
Content: Tyla at the 2026 MTV Video Music awards in Los Angeles last weekend.Photograph: JC Olivera/Variety/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTyla at the 2026 MTV Video Music awards in Los Angeles last weekend.Photograph: JC Olivera/Variety/Getty ImagesPop and rockThe west has a blinkered view of African music – and it’s hurting the whole continent’s cultureChibuzo EmmanuelThe term Afrobeats is applied to all sorts of genres, flattening them into one. Artists, media and the music industry must do better at showing off the richness of African popTue 6 Oct 2026 09.07 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 12.56 EDTShareIn 2024, South African pop star Tyla won the best Afrobeats award at the MTV VMAs. Beaming in a yellow dress, she began her acceptance speech in a celebratory tone. “This is such a big moment for African music. The global impact of Water,” – her hit single – “proves that African music can be pop music.” But as the audience’s cheers swelled, she became more sombre, describing the moment as bittersweet. “There’s a tendency to group all African music as Afrobeats,” she continued. “Even though Afrobeats has opened so many doors for us, African music is so diverse. I come from SouthAfrica, I represent amapiano”, referring to the country’s rolling, sensual dance subgenre. Her passionate entreaty notwithstanding, months later she’d reprise her win in the Afrobeats category of the American Music Awards.Tyla is hardly the only African artist to rail against the Afrobeats tag. Tems has spurned the term, describing her music as a cocktail of “Afro, R&B, soul and alternative elements”. Likewise, Burna Boy prefers to call his music Afrofusion, a fitting characterisation of the smorgasbord of sounds that converge in his music. Wizkid, Ckay, King Promise and Davido have also chafed at the term Afrobeats, yet it persists and holds back African music.The term emerged in the early 2010s as an umbrella label used to categorise contemporary dance music from west Africa, such as D’Banj’s Oliver Twist, spreading across European cities. London-based DJ Abrantee –per reporting in the Guardian– appended an “s” to Fela Kuti’s Afrobeat, creating a catch-all to market these sounds on radio and a burgeoning streaming marketplace. In recent years, however, as African music has exploded globally – underscored by hits like Water as well as Rema’s Calm Down or Moliy’s Shake It to the Max – Afrobeats has become the de facto label for all African pop, dance, rap, R&B, gospel, highlife and a sizeable amount of the continent’s alternative music scenes.This might come across as a minor quibble to be slugged out by music buffs, and “Afrobeats” has undoubtedly been successful as a brute marketing strategy – when the UK Official Charts Company introduced a chart for African pop in 2020, it was named Afrobeats. But what happens when a western description becomes the dominant way a culture understands itself? Grammy award-winning Nigerian producer and singer Bloody Civilian, who heads out on tour with Tyla in October, says the label is “deeply limiting” and finds it “confusing that westerners continue to box the numerous ways Africans experiment with sound”.Western popular music is allowed to exist across a wide spectrum of genres, while the music of an entire continent is routinely shoehorned into this single category. This does more than obscure its diversity; it flattens the nuances of distinct musical traditions and, in doing so, disconnects artists from those traditions. West African music, which has the biggest range of artists dubbed as Afrobeats, has also disproportionately felt the effects of the term: artists and producers from the region continue to synthesise new genres but these innovations are often treated as fodder for the larger Afrobeats machine, sustaining hype until they are discarded for the next shiny thing.Consider Mr Eazi’s “banku music”, a sound synthesised from Nigerian pop and Ghanaian highlife. Mr Eazi, a Nigerian who had attended university in neighbouring Ghana, vaulted to continental fame in 2015. It is difficult to overstate how much his languid, yearning music riveted west Africa, and banku music had many of the characteristics of a genre in its own right: its laid-back tempo and distinctive four-stroke kick-drum pattern engendered a vibrant culture around the sound. Artists such as Runtown and Tekno adopted its sonic vocabulary and put their own spins on it, while university students across the region embraced Mr Eazi’s distinctive style of dress: a straw hat and dashiki.View image in fullscreenMr Eazi.Photograph: Michael Oliver LoveIn another world, banku music, like South Africa’s amapiano (which emerged around the same time), blossoms into a cultural force and perhaps spawns other genres. Instead, it wasn’t marketed to the west or contextualised locally as a distinct sound, so it faded into obscurity rather than developing into a culturally specific musical form. Countless other genres and styles have faced a similar fate: azonto, zanku, cruise, afropiano. Culture journalist Tiléwa Kazeem explains that international publications often find these nascent genres and styles to be “esoteric”. Afrobeats, he argues, “has not just obscured other genres but also affected their documentation”.The west seems increasingly unwilling to engage with the richness of African music: the Afrobeats category was dropped from the MTV VMAs this year, but not on the grounds that the term was limiting, and now there is no African music category at all. But Kazeem adds that west African publications, used to the Afrobeats label, also hesitate to substantially document new genres and styles, similarly viewing them as esoteric.New styles continue to emerge, ranging from the spiritually mindedafro adurato mara, an explosive fusion of street pop and electronic music. But for them to take hold in the way, say, grunge or hyperpop have done in the west, “there has to be enough documentation, enough lore, enough intentionality around them,” says Dolapo Amusat, founder of Nigerian music and creative network WeTalkSound. “Mara is a good example of what that can look like when people who genuinely care about the sound start building substantial identities so these sounds can stand on their own.”That responsibility falls on those marketing this music in the west, but also on the artists, and those in the African music and media industries. “There’s a tension between culture and commerce,” culture writer Dennis Ade Peter says. “Afrobeats artists and stakeholders routinely rail against the term, but still market their music as Afrobeats and validate awards and events where their music is described as such; it’s paradoxical.” As bell hooks noted in her essay collection Art on My Mind, Black people “must be held accountable when we do not make needed critical interventions” required to correct insular views around Black art.Burna Boy, Wizkid, Tyla and more took African pop global. So why don’t they tour Africa itself?Read moreJust as stalwarts like Kuti and King Sunny Adé were allowed to float new genres that continue to define contemporary African culture today, a new generation – who have proved themselves just as charismatic and musically adept – must be given the same opportunity.Explore more on these topicsPop and rockAfricacommentShareReuse this content

title: Who owns ‘brain rot’? Inside the international legal drama over a beloved meme  | Technology | The Guardian
description: Copyright law in the US only applies to human-made creations, but AI characters like Tung Tung Tung Sahur are challenging that
Author: Kari Paul
Headline: Copyright law in the US only applies to human-made creations, but AI characters like Tung Tung Tung Sahur are challenging that
Content: Viral internet character Tung Tung Tung Sahur was created in 2025 by an Indonesian teen who goes by the username Noxa, using OpenAI’s image-generation tool.Illustration: Guardian DesignView image in fullscreenViral internet character Tung Tung Tung Sahur was created in 2025 by an Indonesian teen who goes by the username Noxa, using OpenAI’s image-generation tool.Illustration: Guardian DesignTechnologyWho owns ‘brain rot’? Inside the international legal drama over a beloved memeCopyright law in the US only applies to human-made creations, but AI characters like Tung Tung Tung Sahur are challenging thatKari PaulTue 6 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 21.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne of the most beloved characters in anabsurdist genre of online video contenthas become the center of an international legal battle that could determine where human creativity ends and artificial intelligence begins.Tung Tung Tung Sahur, also known as Triple T, was created in 2025 by an Indonesian teen who goes by the username Noxa, using OpenAI’s image-generation tool. Based on a kentongan– a type of drum used to wake south-east Asian Muslims for their pre-dawn meal during Ramadan – the character is an anthropomorphized version of the instrument with a broad smile and a vacant stare. Hesits under the umbrella of“Italian brain rot”internet videos.Since his creation, Triple T has become a global sensation: YouTube and TikTok host dozens of videos withhundreds of millions of viewsstarring the character. People dress like Triple T at cosplay conventions and lovingly createfan artandanimationsof the stick-like creature, and hislikeness appears on plushies, perfume and stickers.The character has generated a great deal of money and stands to create much more – he will soon bejoining Fortniteas a skin. But who should benefit from this virality?That question is at the heart of a lawsuit filed in the US district court’s northern district of California, where a games company is suing the French creative agency Mementum, which represents Noxa, over the right to use Triple T as a character in a popular Roblox game.Eben Jeda, co-founder of Mementum Lab, said he started the agency with the goal of modernizing economic infrastructure around internet-native works, the creators of which are often completely cut out of any resulting profit.“Brain rot is one of the first highly visible manifestations of a much larger transformation: internet native creativity can now become global almost instantly, while the people who originate it can remain economically invisible,” he said.Opponents argue no one person should own a meme whose ultimate value has been amplified by the online collective. Fabian Mosele, a self-described “Italian brain rot expert” who has made several Tung Tung Tung Sahur videos, said they see brain rot as collectively owned.“There are a ton of creators who made these characters come to life,” Mosele said. “Before, they were really just images. Having been part of making the virality of these characters, to gatekeep it to the original prompter of this character doesn’t seem right.”What constitutes ‘human authorship’ in the age of generative AI?Tung Tung Tung Sahur is one of many characters that have emerged as part of the Italian brain rot genre of meme – a universe of strange, AI-generated characters beloved by generation Alpha and younger members of gen Z. These include the likes of Ballerina Cappuccina (a ballet dancer with a coffee cup for a head), Tralalero Tralala (a shark wearing sneakers), and a variety of other intentionally bizarre creations.Capitalizing on the virality of these mascot-esque characters, video game company Do Big Studios released a game populated by recognizable personae in May 2025 called “Steal a Brainrot”, which quickly became one of the most-played games within Roblox, where users can create minigames.But in September 2025, Spyder Games LLC and Speedy Simulator Gaming LLC – the owners of Do Big – received a cease and desist letter from Mementum regarding the use of Tung Tung Tung Sahur in the game. Do Big initially pulled the character and attempted to negotiate a resolution with Mementum, but ultimately Spyder and Speedy sued the company instead, statingin a complaint: “Mementum’s claimed rights do not exist. Under established law, copyright protection requires human authorship, and AI-generated material does not qualify.”Copyright law in the United States applies only to human-made creations – but AI is challenging the interpretation of that rule. A 2025 report from the United States Copyright Officedeclaredthat copyright protects “original expression” in work created “by a human author” even if the work also includes AI-generated material, but that it “does not extend to purely AI-generated material, or material where there is insufficient human control over the expressive elements”.The copyright office’s report does not offer a clear standard for ownership of creations that involve AI: “Whether human contributions to AI-generated outputs are sufficient to constitute authorship must be analyzed on a case-by-case basis.”Do Big argues that, in the case of Tung Tung Tung Sahur, the level of human intervention in the character’s creation is not sufficient to claim ownership. Court documents filed by Mementum in a separate trademark-related dispute in France show that Tung Tung Tung Sahur was created over the course of 15 minutes using seven prompts before he achieved his final form. The prompts included basic instructions like, “draw a pentungan sahur with a face and legs”, then “human face”, and “no hands, legs like a human, and a human face”.“We are not claiming in this case that AI-assisted work can never be owned by anybody,” said Aaron Moss, a copyright lawyer representing Do Big through the firm Mitchell Silberberg & Knupp LLP. “In a case where somebody makes real creative choices, there is human authorship that is subject to protection. But it’s our position that sparse prompts – typing in a few words and picking [the image] you like – does not constitute human authorship.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionItalian brain rot, global consequencesThe blurry nature of authorship in the age of AI is not the only complicating factor in the case – the global reach of online content also makes enforcement difficult. An Italian brain rot character that was created by aTikTokuser in Indonesia and largely popularized in Latin America is being claimed by a French company in a California courthouse. Jeda said that as a French company, Mementum does not “view this question exclusively through an American legal lens”.Case in point: Mementum issued a takedown request under the EU’s Digital Services Act, requesting the removal of Tung Tung Tung Sahur from Do Big’s Steal a Brainrot game, which was successful. Mementum then countersued in the United States for trademark infringement. The company does not yet hold a trademark for Triple T in the United States, but in some cases trademark infringement can be argued before registration.“Our client is pursuing a global strategy on all of this,” said Steven Stein, a partner at Greenberg Glusker, the US law firm representing Mementum Lab. “It is less about approaching it from a copyright law standpoint, and more about approaching it from the standpoint of – in this new wild west, where works are created with the involvement of AI, what can you do to make it so they are protectable under intellectual property law?”How the lawsuit plays out will come down to a complicated, international web of legal dealings surrounding intellectual property laws – one that could have major implications moving forward, said James Grimmelmann, a professor at Cornell Tech and Cornell law school.“This is the kind of case that could do one of two things: we could get a court decision that tells us, in a concrete setting, what is copyrightable and what isn’t when AI is involved,” he said. “It could also start establishing best practices and widespread norms on how people use AI.”Such best practices could include better documenting creation processes, including what prompts are used to create characters. The prompt used to create Tung Tung Tung Sahur is at the center of this story – both in the legal case, where documentation of the process was revealed in pre-trial discovery – and online,where speculationover how Triple T was created has repeatedly gone viral.Adam Aleksic, a content creator who has made multiple videos on the topic, said the frenzy over trying to back-solve the origin of the character reflects the mythological status and quasi-religiosity of brain rot characters.“There’s this idea of origination when it comes to Tung Tung Tung Sahur – somehow out of the void, some memes are able to emerge into the cultural forefront, into our collective mainstream discourse,” he said.The collective creation of such characters, which made brain rot popular in the first place, is exactly what makes it difficult to claim an origin for Tung Tung Tung Sahur, legally and culturally. When it comes to Tung Tung Tung Sahur, even speaking the name of the character has now come to inherently reference the absurdity central to brain rot,similar to how“skibidi toilet” became shorthand for “being really online”.It is perhaps fitting, then, that of all of the Italian brain rot characters, the hero who has most come to represent virality itself has become a lightning rod for this kind of copyright battle.“That’s the thing about archetypes – they are empty vehicles for you to project your expectations, desires, or narratives on to,” Aleksic said. “Triple T is a tool for you to tell your narrative, broadly, across the entire internet. That’s what memes do – they are a way for us to create our own stories in a time when it feels like our stories are meaningless.”Explore more on these topicsTechnologyAI (artificial intelligence)Intellectual propertyDigital artControversyGamesTikTokfeaturesShareReuse this content
