title: Chancellor plans major intervention to help poorer UK households with rising energy bills | Energy bills | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Officials working on further radical changes that would change how much energy companies could charge customers
Author: Kiran Stacey
Headline: Exclusive: Officials working on further radical changes that would change how much energy companies could charge customers
Content: The bulk of the £1bn the chancellor is planning to spend helping energy consumers will likely to go towards increasing the discount given to households on certain benefits.Photograph: Danny Lawson/PAView image in fullscreenThe bulk of the £1bn the chancellor is planning to spend helping energy consumers will likely to go towards increasing the discount given to households on certain benefits.Photograph: Danny Lawson/PAEnergy billsChancellor plans major intervention to help poorer UK households with rising energy billsExclusive: Officials working on further radical changes that would change how much energy companies could charge customersKiran StaceyandJessica ElgotTue 6 Oct 2026 15.27 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJohn Healey is planning a major intervention to cut energy bills for poorer households in this month’s budget, after ministers became alarmed atforecasts that showbills rising by hundreds of pounds in January.The chancellor is working on plans to spend more than £1bn to help energy consumers, the bulk of which is likely to go towards increasing the discount given to households on certain benefits.Sources say final decisions have not been made, but Healey is set to rebuff a call from the energy secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh to spend billions more on removing levies from bills altogether.Energy officials are working up more radical changes to bills, however, which could be implemented after the budget and would change how much companies could charge customers, rather than subsidising their bills.If approved, the energy discount will form a major plank of the budget, which government sources say will be low-key but focused on reducing voters’ cost of living.Labour figures uneasy about Healey’s ‘underpowered’ approach to budgetRead moreThe chancellor is facing a cash crunch as he looks for money to fund an additional £4.7bn in defence spending and rebuild his fiscal buffer, which has been eroded by higher borrowing costs.He is likely to raise taxes to pay for the additional spending, and is rumoured to be looking at higher bank taxes in particular.Government sources had previously insisted the VAT cut to electricity bills which Andy Burnham announced soon after becoming prime minister would be the last support to be offered this year.View image in fullscreenChancellor John Healey has been considering submissions from the energy department for how to ease the pressures on households in the coming months.Photograph: Ian Davidson/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.But they have become increasingly concerned byforecasts showingthat the Iran war will push the energy price cap up by as much as £442 in January – entirely eroding the impact of the VAT cut.As a result Healey has been considering submissions from the energy department on how to ease the pressures on households in the coming months.The most likely solution is understood to be increasing the warm homes discount – a £150 discount to energy bills offered to households on certain benefits.Healey is understood to be considering increasing this by a further £100, which would be funded by taxpayers, rather than bill-payers as the existing discount is.Fahnbulleh, meanwhile, has been pushing for more sweeping action to reduce bills for all consumers by as much as £120 by removing all levies.Under the energy secretary’s proposals, the levies, which fund renewable energy and efficiency schemes, would be paid for through taxation instead.Shetold the Guardianlast week: “If we want a system that is resilient, if we want a system that can cope, if we want a system that ultimately can deliver the diversity of energy that we want, what is the fairest way in which we pay for it?“That is both across the exchequer versus our bill-payers, and then within our bill-payers. So we have to ask that question. Every other country is asking that question, and ultimately we’ve got to come to a fair deal.”Removing levies from bills would reduce inflation, but would cost as much as £3.2bn and would be difficult for the government to unwind should energy costs come down in the future.Officials in the energy department are working on more radical proposals for after the budget, meanwhile, including proposals to reduce tariffs for poorer households or those that use less energy.Burnham told the Labour conference last week: “British businesses and bill-payers pay some of the highest energy costs in Europe. Within 10 years, I want those costs to be in line with our neighbours.“This means reforming a broken energy market so it better serves the public interest.”A so-called “social tariff” would force energy companies to charge poorer households less for each unit of electricity they consume than richer ones.Creating such a scheme, however, would involve a large amount of data collection from tax authorities, the Treasury and energy companies – an exercise likely to take far longer than the next few weeks.An alternative plan, known as a “rising block tariff”, would also vary the tariffs that energy companies can charge, but by consumption levels rather than income.The idea,which was proposedby the New Economics Foundation (NEF) thinktank when Fahnbulleh ran it, would charge consumers less for a set amount of “essential” use and more once their consumption crossed that level.Healey urged to offer energy support in budget as bills rise 4%Read moreAlex Chapman, head of economic and environmental policy at NEF, said: “A serious price spike is coming, and without action, bills will exceed the peak of the last crisis. The government must use the budget to put in place both targeted support for the most vulnerable and, critically, a safety net for all.”He added: “Repeated crises have exposed the flaws in our privatised energy system – these can only be fixed by fundamental reform. This means capturing the benefits of cheap renewables and offering every household a ‘block’ of essential energy at a truly protected and affordable price.”Alfie Stirling, economist and director of policy at the Joseph Rowntree Foundation, said: “Energy support for this winter needs to tick three boxes. It needs to support the majority of households; within this, it needs to target the most support towards those in greatest need; and – as far as possible – it needs to actually lower the price, thereby bringing down inflation.“The UK does not yet have the right toolkit to respond effectively to energy price shocks – building better tools is now a critical priority for our future security and living standards.”A spokesperson for the Treasury said: “As has always been the case, decisions on tax are a matter for the chancellor to set out at fiscal events, rather than routinely commenting on rumour, speculation or proposals.”Explore more on these topicsEnergy billsEnergy industryConsumer affairsHousehold billsUK cost of living crisisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Labour figures rule out working with Greens after ‘Zionism is racism’ vote | Labour | The Guardian
description: Minister says they could not see parties cooperating, while official says coalition should be formally ruled out
Author: Aletha Adu
Headline: Minister says they could not see parties cooperating, while official says coalition should be formally ruled out
Content: Green party leader Zack Polanski stopped short of endorsing or criticising the motion.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAView image in fullscreenGreen party leader Zack Polanski stopped short of endorsing or criticising the motion.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPALabourLabour figures rule out working with Greens after ‘Zionism is racism’ voteMinister says they could not see parties cooperating, while official says coalition should be formally ruled outAletha AduandPeter WalkerTue 6 Oct 2026 14.26 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSenior Labour party figures said it was very unlikely their party would cooperate with the Greens in the future after theyadopted a policytreating Zionism as a form of racism.OneLabourminister said they could not foresee how the two parties could work together, while a government official said Labour should formally rule out a future coalition or other arrangement.There is also pressure within theLiberal Democratsfor them to end existing arrangements with Zack Polanski’s party, with some senior Lib Dems calling on the party to end its coalition with the Greens in Southwark, south London.Green members voted at the party’s conference on Sunday to adopt a binding policy that says Zionism should be treated by the party as racism, and which calls for a single Palestinian state in place of Israel.After the vote, Bridget Phillipson, the Labour chair, called the move “shameful”, saying it highlighted how vital it had been for her party to tackle antisemitismunder the leadershipof Jeremy Corbyn.While Phillipson’s statement was backed by her fellow ministers, there was debate as to whether Labour should go further and formally rule out any ties with the Greens, for example if a future general election delivered a hung parliament.A source linked to the Jewish labour movement said Labour should “absolutely” rule out governing with the Greens, arguing the policy raised serious questions about whether its treatment of Jewish members could breach equality law.It follows months of speculation of possible cooperation between the parties. Polanski said earlier this year that the Greens could consider an electoral pact with Labour under Andy Burnham or Angela Rayner, while ruling out one under the former prime minister Keir Starmer.Labour views the Zionism motion, and the criticism that has followed, as a means to simplify its political argument against the Greens at a time when Polanski’s party has increasingly sought to attract disillusioned Labour voters on the party’s left.A big test of this will come on Thursday, with voting in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, where Polanski is seeking to win Starmer’s former seat from Labour.The Greens have poured huge resources into the contest, with Polanski telling the Guardian that it is “really on a knife-edge”. Despite the Greens’ campaigning efforts, helped by their massively increased membership, Labour is considered the favourite to win.The Lib Dems and Greens already govern together in Southwark after May’s local elections, with the Greens as the senior partner.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFollowing the Zionism motion, both Southwark partiesreleased a“joint administration statement against antisemitism”. Without mentioning the new Green policy, it said they would “continue to work with Jewish community organisations to make sure they know they have a place in Southwark”.It brought a scathing response from some senior Lib Dems. Tagging Victor Chamberlain, the Lib Dem deputy leader of Southwark, Sarah Ludford, a peer and former MEP for the party,wrote on Xthat she did not understand “how you think this greenwash is an adequate response to the Greens’ antisemitic ‘Zionism is racism’ motion, from which I believe you should entirely distance yourselves”.Another Lib Dem peer, Lynne Featherstone, who was formerly an MP, replied to a post by Chamberlainto say: “I would ditch them. Grow a pair!”The policy was adopted at theGreen partyconference in Brighton on Sunday by 1,022 votes to 813, despite being opposed by four of the party’s five MPs.Polanski, who left the Green conference early on Friday to campaign, stopped short of endorsing or criticising the motion. In a statement on Monday night after the European Greens and German Greens distanced themselves from the policy, Polanski said antisemitism and criticism of the Israeli state “are and must always be completely distinct”. Polanski said he remained proud of the party’s stance on Palestinian rights.Explore more on these topicsLabourZack PolanskiGreen partyLiberal DemocratsAntisemitismJudaismnewsShareReuse this content

title: Israeli settlers beat press photographer as soldiers watch in West Bank | West Bank | The Guardian
description: Jaafar Ashtiyeh was covering violence against olive farmers when settlers set upon him with the butts of their rifles
Author: William Christou
Headline: Jaafar Ashtiyeh was covering violence against olive farmers when settlers set upon him with the butts of their rifles
Content: Agence France-Presse photographer Jaafar Ashtiyeh being carried by Palestinian first responders to get medical attention after being beaten.Photograph: John Wessels/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAgence France-Presse photographer Jaafar Ashtiyeh being carried by Palestinian first responders to get medical attention after being beaten.Photograph: John Wessels/AFP/Getty ImagesWest BankIsraeli settlers beat press photographer as soldiers watch in West BankJaafar Ashtiyeh was covering violence against olive farmers when settlers set upon him with the butts of their riflesWilliam Christouin Jerusalem and agenciesTue 6 Oct 2026 17.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 17.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleArmed Israeli settlers beat a photographer in the presence of Israeli soldiers, hospitalising him, as he covered worsening settler violence against olive farmers in the occupiedWest Bank.Jaafar Ashtiyeh, a 58-year-old veteran photographer for Agence France-Presse inPalestine, was assaulted by a group of settlers, who beat him with the butts of their rifles, despite him being marked as press. He was assaulted in view of about a dozen armed Israeli soldiers.Ashtiyeh suffered bruises to his head and torso and was taken to hospital, according to witnesses, his family and fellow journalists.Israeli forces overwhelmed by violent settlers in ‘terrorist attack’ on Palestinian familyRead moreHis assault came amid a worsening wave of Israeli settler violence in the West Bank. Every year, settlers attack Palestinian farmers trying to harvest their olives – an economic lifeline for the beleaguered Palestinian economy – with few legal consequences.This harvest season has been particularly violent as the Israeli elections approach at the end of the month.Ashtiyeh and another AFP photographer, John Wessels, were near the northern village of Aqraba when they noticed an Israeli soldier detaining a man as local Palestinians picked olives.A quad bike suddenly raced towards the AFP journalists on top of a hill and a man on it opened live fire, with one Palestinian dropping to the ground. He was also hospitalised, with a gunshot to the foot, according to the Palestine Red Crescent Society.At least six other people then rushed towards the AFP journalists firing guns. As Ashtiyeh attempted to enter a car, which was clearly marked “Press”, two men jumped on him and beat him repeatedly with the butts of their rifles.A group of at least a dozen Israeli soldiers were about 500 metres away at the time of the attack, according to Wessels.“I could hear his screams,” said Wessels, who was also threatened at gunpoint. The assailants also took Ashtiyeh’s camera equipment.Ashtiyeh, who is Palestinian, was conscious in a hospital in Nablus. He underwent X-rays which did not detect broken bones but he will remain in hospital for round-the-clock observation, his son, Zain Jaafar, said.The man who initially fired the gun was wearing a long white shirt as well as military fatigue trousers and boots, which are commonly worn by soldiers, Wessels said.UN adds 61 firms to settlements blacklist over alleged human rights violations against PalestiniansRead moreAFP has asked the Israeli military for comment. Settlers are rarely arrested or charged for their attacks against Palestinians.“We strongly condemn yet another serious attack on journalists trying to report on events in the West Bank and demand a full investigation. It is unacceptable that journalists can be beaten and robbed by armed settlers in front of Israeli security forces who made no attempt to intervene,” said Phil Chetwynd, AFP’s global news director.The Foreign Press Association, which represents international media in Israel and the Palestinian territories, said it was “deeply alarmed”.“Israeli authorities must investigate why soldiers present in the area did not intervene in this attack against clearly identified journalists,” it said.“This attack is a blatant attempt to intimidate the press and obstruct accurate reporting from the West Bank. International media have a responsibility to tell all sides of the story and will not be deterred by physical assaults or threats.”Israel was the world’s leading killer of journalists in 2025, and has killed at least 225 journalists in Lebanon and Gaza, according to the UN Human Rights Office.Violence has flared in recent months in the West Bank with near-daily attacks, thefts or vandalism by Israeli settlers against Palestinians.There have also been attacks against Israelis, with a Palestinian shooting dead a settler last month.Extremist Israeli settlers have been seizing olive groves owned by Palestinians, who consider the trees a cultural symbol.About 500,000 Israeli settlers live in the West Bank – which Israel captured in 1967 – among 3 million Palestinians. Settlements in occupied territory are illegal under international law.Media rights groups say Israeli settlers have increasingly targeted journalists and that authorities have imposed growing impediments to coverage.Israeli authorities have detained 19 journalists in the West Bank, including one AFP contributor, in the three years since the 7 October, 2023 Hamas-led attack on Israel, according to Paris-based Reporters Without Borders.Agence France-Presse contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsWest BankMiddle East and north AfricaJournalist safetyPress freedomNews photographyIsraelPalestinenewsShareReuse this content

title: Riot police fire teargas as 250,000 take part in schools protests across France | France | The Guardian
description: Officers also carry out baton charges as students, staff and parents march in cities including Paris, Marseille and Lyon
Author: Jon Henley
Headline: Officers also carry out baton charges as students, staff and parents march in cities including Paris, Marseille and Lyon
Content: A student signals their defiance after riot police fire teargas to break up a protest in the southern city of Bordeaux.Photograph: Philippe Lopez/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA student signals their defiance after riot police fire teargas to break up a protest in the southern city of Bordeaux.Photograph: Philippe Lopez/AFP/Getty ImagesFranceRiot police fire teargas as 250,000 take part in schools protests across FranceOfficers also carry out baton charges as students, staff and parents march in cities including Paris, Marseille and LyonEurope live – latest updatesJon Henleyin ParisTue 6 Oct 2026 13.39 EDTFirst published on Tue 6 Oct 2026 08.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePolice have fired teargas at ⁠protesters as more than 250,000 pupils, teachers and parents demonstrated acrossFranceon the biggest day yet of a campaign for better high school conditions that has been marred by often violent clashes with police.‘This is state violence’: Paris students rage at politicians and heavy-handed policingRead moreThe French prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, said at least 215 teenagers and 85 school staff had been injured since the protests began more than a fortnight ago, calling the figures “the heaviest ⁠toll in decades paid by the school system”.The country’s president, Emmanuel Macron, called key ministers to the Élysée Palace for talks on Tuesday night, French media reported.The interior ministry said 200,000 people had taken part in mainly peaceful marches in cities including Marseille, Nantes ⁠and Lyon on Tuesday, with 56,000 more joining the biggest demonstration inParis. Organisers put the total at 450,000.Most passed off without serious incident, but some – including in Paris – ended in sporadic vandalism and running skirmishes with riot police, with officers firing teargas and carrying out baton charges to disperse protesters.Nearly 500 people were arrested on Tuesday, according to figures from the Interior Ministry reported by newspaper Liberation. The ministry also said 43 police officers were injured.Trade unions and rights groups have accused the police of using unnecessary force against the young protesters in recent days, with Amnesty International saying French authorities should “put an end to the disproportionate police repression”.View image in fullscreenProtesters marching in Marseille.Photograph: Sener Yilmaz Aslan/Getty ImagesBut interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said the police response had been proportionate in “almost all cases” and that the protests had at times turned into riots, requiring police intervention.At Tuesday’s demonstration in Paris, students held aloft smoke flares and placards with slogans including “under our text books, anger” – a nod toa celebrated “under the paving stones, the beach” slogan from the May 1968 student riots. Other slogans included “schools with no money = country with no future”.One student, Anna, told reporters at the capital’s Place de la Nation: “Our demands are simple: better study conditions, enough teachers, decent school buildings. The authorities’ response has been catastrophic. There’s enough violence already.”Tuesday’s marches came after two weeks of protests that ⁠began in the northern suburbs of Paris and have snowballed nationwide. Besides the injuries to protesters and staff, 715 police officers have been wounded in the clashes, Lecornu’s office said.View image in fullscreenProtesters marching in Paris.Photograph: Sener Yilmaz Aslan/Getty ImagesDemonstrators have set dustbins on fire outside their schools, destroyed bus shelters and hurled projectiles at riot police, who have responded with batons, teargas and riot-control rounds.Twenty-four schools have been burned or ransacked since mid-September, while more than 6,100 people have ​been arrested, almost all of them minors. More than 1,800 are being prosecuted, nearly 1,500 of them under 18, the justice ministry said.The education ministry said more than 900 of the country’s 3,700 high schools were blockaded or had been closed for the day on Tuesday, although student groups put the number at 1,800. Some local education authorities moved classes ‌online.View image in fullscreenProtesters in Bordeaux hold a placard depicting a caricature of Emmanuel Macron.Photograph: Christophe Archambault/AFP/Getty ImagesOcéanne, 18, was among the marchers in Marseille. “We just want to save our education and be educated,” she said, adding that she had suffered from absent teachers who were replaced either by “pointless substitutes” or not at all.Many teachers were also demonstrating. In the western city of Rennes, Romain Dubourg said he and “about 30 colleagues” had “talked about the police brutality that we’ve witnessed, and decided to be there for our students if they need us”.Trade unionists were also on the marches, with the head of the CGT union, Sophie Binet, urging members to “protect high school students”. The Green party leader, Marine Tondelier, urged local officials and parents to wear white and “go and protect our children during demonstrations”.A chart comparing class sizes across the world.Anne Savinel-Barras, the president of Amnesty France, said: “The images and testimonies widely circulated over the past week raise alarming concerns about the dangerous use of teargas, batons and policing techniques by the police.” Nuñez, said police had launched 10 internal investigations into allegations of brutality since the protests started.On Monday, a 15-year-old’s hand was blown off as protesters battled riot police in northern France.A 16-year-old lost the use of his right eye after he was seriously injured in the head on Wednesday during the blockade of a high school in Tours. The local prosecutor, Catherine Sorita-Minard, said the wounds were “compatible with the impact of a defensive bullet of the blast ball type”.A chart showing France’s declining Pisa scores.In another incident, a 14-year-old lost most of his teeth on Monday when a police officer appeared to fire a grenade at him at close range during a protest north-west of Paris. “His jaw is sealed shut, he can no longer speak and he eats through a straw,” his mother told reporters.Lecornu has ordered his ministers to tackle the students’ core demands, which include ensuring absent teachers are replaced, reviewing the length of the 8am to 6pm school day and repairing ‌ageing buildings.He denied accusations of routine excess force by police, saying officers had mostly acted proportionately. He told MPs on Tuesday that“extreme violence” had come “knocking on high-school doors, and must be condemned”.View image in fullscreenProtesters face off with riot police at Place de la Nation in Paris.Photograph: Abdul Saboor/Reuters“Setting fire to a school will not help repair it. Attacking a teacher will not help replace missing staff,” he said.The protests, seven months before crucial presidential elections to choose a successor to Macron, have piled pressure on a government trying to reduce a ballooning budget deficit amid mounting investor concern over France’s ​mountainous debt and weak economic growth.The government has accused the radical-left La France Insoumise party of encouraging and even orchestrating the movement after numerous LFI MPs attended school blockades. The party’s veteran leader and presidential candidate, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, has strongly supported the protests, while urging non-violence.Explore more on these topicsFranceProtestParisYoung peopleSchoolsEuropeShareReuse this content

title: Christa Pike is conscious and speaking after botched execution attempt, lawyers say | Tennessee | The Guardian
description: The prisoner received two doses of pentobarbital as authorities tried to put her to death on 30 September
Author: Maya Yang
Headline: The prisoner received two doses of pentobarbital as authorities tried to put her to death on 30 September
Content: Christa Pike in a Knoxville, Tennessee, courtroom in December 2007.Photograph: J Miles Cary/ReutersView image in fullscreenChrista Pike in a Knoxville, Tennessee, courtroom in December 2007.Photograph: J Miles Cary/ReutersTennesseeChrista Pike is conscious and speaking after botched execution attempt, lawyers sayThe prisoner received two doses of pentobarbital as authorities tried to put her to death on 30 SeptemberMaya Yangand agenciesTue 6 Oct 2026 19.35 EDTFirst published on Tue 6 Oct 2026 17.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleChrista Pike, aTennesseeprisoner who survived the state’s attempt to execute her, is awake and speaking as she receives treatment at a hospital, her attorneys said on Tuesday.Pike, 50, survived two doses of pentobarbital, a sedative, asTennesseeofficials attempted to put her to death last Wednesdayin a case that shocked many in America and created headlines around the world. She was set to be the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years.“Against all odds, Christa Pike is conscious, speaking and continues to receive critical medical care. Despite the severe damage she endured to her arms, she is still handcuffed and shackled to the bed. Her recovery is medically unprecedented. Her prognosis remains unclear but, at a minimum, we expect a long recovery,” attorneys for Pike said in a statement.Her attorneys said they are grateful for the first responders and the medical team at the hospital “who treated Christa like a human and have provided exceptional care to her”.Christa Pike’s lawyers had warned execution would be ‘difficult and perhaps cruel’ due to her veinsRead more“She is the only person known to have survived a complete execution attempt in the US. Christa is a survivor and will take recovery one day at a time. We continue to ask the Governor of Tennessee to commute Christa Pike’s sentence to life imprisonment without the possibility of parole,” Pike’s attorneys added.The statement was the first indication that Pike has improved since an ambulance carried her away from a Nashville prison on the night of 30 September.Witnesses to the attempt to executePike described how they heard she was choking and struggling for an hour after receiving the first injection. She was then hospitalized after a second dose failed to kill her. In hospital, she was put on a ventilator and had been in critical condition.Following the botched execution attempt, one of Pike’s lawyers, Randy Spivey,calledthe process “cruel and torturous”, adding that he had counted seven needles in Pike’s left arm, “one of which appeared to be bent when it was pulled from her”. Her lawyers hadwarnedbefore the execution that officials might struggle to locate veins and cause her suffering in the process, but the state had pushed to proceed and the US supreme court allowed the prison to move forward.The disastrous attempt sparked widespread condemnation across the political spectrum and among advocates for banning the death penalty. Tennessee’s prison chief, Frank Strada, alsoresignedin the aftermath. Strada was facing intensifying scrutiny, with lawyerssayingPike’s case was the fifth “botched” execution under his leadership across two states.Pike and her boyfriend, who was 17 at the time, killed 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, one of their classmates at Knoxville Job Corps, in 1995. The case garnered nationwide headlines due to the ages of those involved and the brutality of the murder.According to prosecutors, Pike was worried Slemmer was trying to take her then boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, away from her. Together, they lured Slemmer into a wooded area behind the agriculture campus steam plant at the University of Tennessee on 12 January 1995. Pike cut Slemmer’s stomach and throat with a box cutter before smashing her head with a rock.Shipp carved a pentagram into Slemmer’s chest and Pike later showed a friend a fragment of Slemmer’s skull.Shipp was convicted of first-degree murder in 1997 and was given a life sentence with the possibility of parole.Pike has never denied her involvement in Slemmer’s killing. She was later diagnosed with bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder.“I was a mentally ill 18-year-old kid. It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I’d done. Even more to accept how many lives I affected. I took the life of someone’s child, sister, friend. It sickens me now to think I had the ability to commit such a crime,” Pike said in a statement that was included in her clemency petition.As a child,Pike had been subject to various abuse, including multiple rapes by different men, as well as beatings by her relatives.Pike later underwent nearly 30 years of solitary confinement while on death row.In the wake of the botched execution attempt Helen Prejean, a Catholic nun who is perhaps the best-known advocate for abolition of the death penalty in America,told the Guardian: “This is the essence of cruelty. Take a conscious, imaginative human being, give her a date for her death, have her anticipate it over and over again, and then take her out and try and kill her.“She was rendered defenceless as they deliberately attempted to kill her – what greater mental torture for a human being is there?”Sam Levin and the Associated Press contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsTennesseeCapital punishmentUS crimeUS justice systemnewsShareReuse this content

title: Senior academics set out key questions Cambridge must answer over Jason Arday’s death | University of Cambridge | The Guardian
description: Letter from more than 40 signatories says university has backed away from promised thorough review of events before death
Author: Richard Adams
Headline: Letter from more than 40 signatories says university has backed away from promised thorough review of events before death
Content: Academics say it is not clear how Cambridge’s proposed review will answer difficult questions about its involvement in events leading up to Arday’s death.Photograph: Chris Radburn/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAcademics say it is not clear how Cambridge’s proposed review will answer difficult questions about its involvement in events leading up to Arday’s death.Photograph: Chris Radburn/AFP/Getty ImagesUniversity of CambridgeSenior academics set out key questions Cambridge must answer over Jason Arday’s deathLetter from more than 40 signatories says university has backed away from promised thorough review of events before deathRichard AdamsEducation editorTue 6 Oct 2026 14.44 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 17.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSenior Cambridge academics have criticised the university’s plans to investigate Prof Jason Arday’s death as inadequate, and said those responsible for “serious failures of leadership” should face consequences.In a letter to Chris Smith, Cambridge’s chancellor, the academics said “it is not yet clear” how the proposed review will answer difficult questions about the university’s involvement in the events leading up to Arday’s death, including its handling of the criticism Arday suffered after his appointment as professor of sociology of education in 2023.Ardaydied at his home in Londonon 14 August, nine days after he resigned amid allegations of plagiarism and inconsistencies in statements about his career.Cambridge University asks former chief crown prosecutor to open Arday reviewRead moreAninquest will be heldto determine the cause of death.Arday’s family said he was subjected to a campaign of sustained abuse for more than three years.Now, a letter signed by more than 40 professors, associate professors and fellows raises concern that Cambridge has backed away from initial promises by Deborah Prentice, the university’s vice-chancellor, to carry out a “thorough and transparent” examination of the circumstances that led to Arday’s appointment and treatment.Rather than reviewing the “lessons learned”, the group wants the investigation to pinpoint the crucial advice given and decisions made during Arday’s hiring and subsequent career.“The investigation must establish who authorised and directed the university’s public promotion of Professor Arday; what assessment was made of the risks that accompanied it; who authorised any legal or other communications with journalists investigating the story; what the university knew as racist and ableist abuse and media hounding escalated; and how responsibility for Professor Arday’s protection was allocated and exercised across the university,” the letter says.View image in fullscreenJason Arday’s family have said he was subjected to a campaign of sustained abuse for more than three years.Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianThe signatories included Cahir O’Kane, a professor of genetics; Caroline Bassett, a professor of digital humanities; Clair Wills, the King Edward VII professor of English literature; and Clément Mouhot, a professor of mathematical sciences.Cambridge last monthannounced a two-part review, with part one to beled by Nazir Afzal, a former chief crown prosecutor for north-west England, focusing on the support given to Arday immediately before his death.The university has not yet named a chair for part two of the review, which it said would be “a broader review of institutional processes and practice” and only consider “the wider context” of Arday’s period at Cambridge, including general appraisals of recruitment and support available to academics facing media scrutiny.Jason Arday accuser given three-month teaching ban but can continue researchRead moreThe group behind the letter, which was also sent to Cambridge’s governing council, said the “scope and investigative character” of the second part of the review would be crucial in settling the decisions, structures and processes involved.They wrote: “To this end, it is vital that the university establishes a clear chain of responsibility for the institutional decisions made in the period following Professor Arday’s appointment, through the events leading to his death and the university’s subsequent responses.“The university should state clearly how responsibility will be acted upon if the review establishes serious failures of leadership or responsibility … Serious findings must have consequences for the individuals and offices responsible.“At the same time, individual accountability cannot substitute for the institutional changes required where failures arose from structures of decision-making, scrutiny or governance.”TheUniversity of Cambridgewas approached for its response to the letter.Cambridgepublicised Arday’s appointmentat the age of 37 as the youngest black person ever appointed to a professorship at the university, saying he would “inspire more people from under-represented backgrounds into higher education, building on the university’s many initiatives in this area”.Arday denied the accusations of plagiarism but on 5 August Cambridge said it would open an investigation into his academic qualifications. Arday resigned hours later.Explore more on these topicsUniversity of CambridgeJason ArdayUniversity administrationUniversitiesHigher educationAcademicsUniversity leadershipnewsShareReuse this content

title: Dolly Parton’s estate alleges her nephew used barbed wire to avoid being served | Dolly Parton | The Guardian
description: Court filing alleges Bryan Seaver, star’s ex-security head, had also posted no trespassing signs to thwart serving of lawsuit
Author: Victoria Bekiempis
Headline: Court filing alleges Bryan Seaver, star’s ex-security head, had also posted no trespassing signs to thwart serving of lawsuit
Content: Dolly Parton poses at the Carnegie Medal of Philanthropy ceremony in New York on 13 October 2022.Photograph: Andrés Kudacki/APView image in fullscreenDolly Parton poses at the Carnegie Medal of Philanthropy ceremony in New York on 13 October 2022.Photograph: Andrés Kudacki/APDolly PartonDolly Parton’s estate alleges her nephew used barbed wire to avoid being servedCourt filing alleges Bryan Seaver, star’s ex-security head, had also posted no trespassing signs to thwart serving of lawsuitVictoria BekiempisTue 6 Oct 2026 17.07 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 18.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDolly Parton’s estate has alleged that her nephew and former security head used barbed wire and a no trespassing sign to avoid being served in a lawsuit,according to a court filingconfirmed by the Guardian.The country star’s company has filed suit against her nephew, Bryan Seaver, claiming that he menaced and attempted to strong-arm Parton’s estate after she died on 25 August. Seaver announced Parton’s death in a video and previously said this was “something Dolly asked of me years ago”.A process server who attempted to deliver lawsuit documents to Seaver saw that his home featured a “no-trespassing sign in the front yard and barbed wire draped across the handrails leading to the front door”, according to the document.“Mr Seaver attempted to evade service of process, and this court should not reward that behavior,” the court filing states, also claiming that a process server tried delivering the lawsuit three times.The filing was first reported by ABC News.Seaver could not immediately be reached for comment. An attorney listed as representing Parton’s company did not immediately respond to a request for comment.Parton’s estate was granted arestraining orderagainst Seaver in September. Following Parton’s death her business manager, Danny Nozell, reportedly terminated Seaver from his security position.Nozell has alleged that Seaver engaged in “relentless” threats. Alawsuitalleged: “These were not ordinary workplace disputes or heated words; they were deliberate threats from a self-proclaimed heavily armed, former security operative with a military-contractor background. Many of [Parton’s staff members] are now afraid to come to work or have resigned entirely because they do not feel safe.”The judge who granted the restraining order considered the threats cited in the civil complaint as well as Seaver’s alleged prior claim to have “access to weapons, experience with violence and intention to retaliate”.Under the restraining order, Seaver and his security concern, Squadron Augmented Protection Services, are mandated to refrain from being within 1,000ft (300 meters) of staffers, lawyers and business associates of She’s Alive, the company founded to handle Parton’s estate. The order is reportedly intended to prevent Seaver from interfering with her estate’s business dealings.Seaver is reportedly accused of telling one of Parton’s lawyers that “I’m a killer.” He also is accused of separately saying to Nozell: “I’m literally an international arms dealer and mercenary. All I do is warfare. Everyone needs to be worried about what I might do.”According to a docket in the litigation, a hearing is scheduled for 20 October.Explore more on these topicsDolly PartonLaw (US)newsShareReuse this content

title: Eva Marie Saint, star of North by Northwest and On the Waterfront, dies aged 102 | Movies | The Guardian
description: Landmark roles were in 50s classics directed by Elia Kazan and Alfred Hitchcock, before going on to play Superman’s adoptive mother in later life
Author: Andrew Pulver
Headline: Landmark roles were in 50s classics directed by Elia Kazan and Alfred Hitchcock, before going on to play Superman’s adoptive mother in later life
Content: Golden age legend … Eva Marie Saint in 1955.Photograph: Hulton Archive/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGolden age legend … Eva Marie Saint in 1955.Photograph: Hulton Archive/Getty ImagesMoviesEva Marie Saint, star of North by Northwest and On the Waterfront, dies aged 102Landmark roles were in 50s classics directed by Elia Kazan and Alfred Hitchcock, before going on to play Superman’s adoptive mother in later lifeEva Marie Saint – a life in picturesHer best films – rankedAndrew PulverTue 6 Oct 2026 17.24 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 17.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEva Marie Saint, one of the last survivors of Hollywood’s golden age of the 1940s and 50s, has died aged 102. Her screen work spanned six decades: Saint made her screen debut opposite Marlon Brando in On the Waterfront, starred in Alfred Hitchcock’s celebrated thriller North by Northwest, and in one of her last screen appearances played Superman’s adoptive mother Martha Kent in the 2006 superhero filmSuperman Returns.A family spokesman said on Tuesday that Saint had died of natural causes at her home in Los Angeles.Eva Marie Saint – a life in picturesRead moreBorn in 1924 in New Jersey to a Quaker family, Saint had an early career as a jobbing radio and TV performer that was chronicled ina 1949 feature in Life magazinewhich started with the prophetic words: “The name of Eva Marie Saint may someday be a household word” – it followed her struggles to gain a foothold in the entertainment industry. By the early 50s she was making some headway, appearing in 1953 in both the original telecast and the premiere Broadway production of the Horton Foote play The Trip to Bountiful.Saint told the Santa Barbara Independentthat On the Waterfront director Elia Kazan spotted her in The Trip to Bountiful and invited her to audition by improvising a scene with Marlon Brando. Saint said she found the experience difficult, but was offered the role of Edie Doyle, Brando’s love interest, in the hardhitting drama about mob union activities; she would go on to win the Oscar for best supporting actress in 1955.Eva Marie Saint’s best films – rankedRead moreAfter this meteoric success, Saint quickly began securing a wide variety of leading roles. She starred opposite Bob Hope in That Certain Feeling, played a woman married to a secret drug addict in the Fred Zinnemann-directed issue picture A Hatful of Rain and co-starred with Elizabeth Taylor in the period western Raintree County. Saint then achieved the highly coveted role opposite Cary Grant in Alfred Hitchcock’s 1959 spy classic North by Northwest: secret agent Eve Kendall, “a blond who has all the answers”.She said in a TCM interviewthat she got her career-defining role – partly – by wearing beige and white gloves to a lunch appointment with Hitchcock.Saint kicked off the 1960s by playing American nurse Kitty Fremont in Exodus, the hit adaptation of Leon Uris’s novel about the creation of the state of Israel, but subsequently eased up on her workload to prioritise her young family. In 1962 she appeared opposite Warren Beatty in All Fall Down as a woman infatuated with Beatty’s drifter, starred as Richard Burton’s wife in The Sandpiper in 1965 alongside Elizabeth Taylor and played a journalist who has an affair with Yves Montand’s race driver in Grand Prix in 1966.View image in fullscreenWith Cary Grant in North by Northwest.Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Ltd/AlamyDespite critical acclaim for her role in the 1970 infidelity drama Loving alongside George Segal, Saint’s film parts largely dried up in the 70s and 80s, with the actor instead turning to TV movies and guest appearances.Sporadic film appearances ensued after a “comeback” in the 1986 Tom Hanks/Jackie Gleason comedy Nothing in Common; later appearances included as Sam Shepard’s mother in the Wim Wenders-directed western Don’t Come Knocking in 2005, and a year later she was cast in Superman Returns – where she was “reunited” with On the Waterfront star Brando, whose estate gave permission for 1978 footage to be used in the film after his death in 2004.Saint worked more consistently in TV, winning a best supporting actress Emmy award for the 1990 mini-series People Like Us, adapted from Dominick Dunne’s novel. Her final onscreen role was in Winter’s Tale as the sister of the seemingly immortal Colin Farrell.Saint married Jeffrey Hayden in 1951 and had two children; they remained together until his death in 2016.Explore more on these topicsFilmNorth by NorthwestAlfred HitchcockThrillersComedy filmsFilm adaptationsComedynewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘All I want to do is cry’: trauma of 7 October survivors three years after the attacks | Israel | The Guardian
description: Israeli communities shattered by Hamas massacres are torn between rebuilding their lives and remembering lost friends and relatives
Author: Emma Graham-Harrison
Headline: Israeli communities shattered by Hamas massacres are torn between rebuilding their lives and remembering lost friends and relatives
Content: Pictures on a blackened wall in Nir Oz commemorate victims of the 7 October attacks. The sign says Benjamin Netanyahu has blood on his hands.Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPictures on a blackened wall in Nir Oz commemorate victims of the 7 October attacks. The sign says Benjamin Netanyahu has blood on his hands.Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The GuardianIsrael‘All I want to do is cry’: trauma of 7 October survivors three years after the attacksIsraeli communities shattered by Hamas massacres are torn between rebuilding their lives and remembering lost friends and relativesEmma Graham-HarrisonandQuique Kierszenbaumin Nir OzTue 6 Oct 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKeith Siegel spent many of his long hours in Hamas captivity inGazaetching everything that happened after 7 October 2023 into his memory. For 484 days, he recited to himself every place he was held, the dates he was moved and every attack or humiliation he endured or witnessed.He aimed to store intelligence that could help Israeli forces free other hostages if he was released, to keep track of time as the days slid by and be able to tell his family what happened to him. Now his body is free, but he cannot loosen those memories.“I’m living a kind of dual life,” he said in an interview in Tel Aviv. “I’m here for some of the time, and I’m in Gaza some of time. It’s very challenging to convey in words what it was like.”View image in fullscreenAviva and Keith Siegel were abducted from their home in Kfar Aza in southern Israel by Hamas on 7 October 2023.Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The GuardianSiegel and his wife, Aviva, were among 251 people taken captive to Gaza on the deadliest day in Israel’s history, when Hamas militants broke across the border to launch a wave of attacks on kibbutzim, border towns, military bases and music festivals.Israel’s security forces were caught by surprise, and by the time they regained control of the area, 1,209 people had been killed, the majority of them civilians,including36 children, according torecordskept by the IsraelinewspaperHaaretz.The cemetery at Nir Oz contains two lines of fresh headstones, marking lives that all ended on that same date. A shared plot for a family of five – a mother, father and their three young children – has been made into a garden with space left for their still-living grandparents.Caretaker Shlomo Margalit, who will soon turn 89, points to the graves of three of his oldest friends, founding members of the kibbutz who came to Nir Oz from Haifa with him in the 1950s.“This is my life project, as well as my home,” Margalit said, explaining why he has come back to a place of such loss. He is waiting for a new house but, for now, staying in the former home of Gadi Moses, 82, who survived 482 days as a hostage.View image in fullscreenShlomo Margalit, a founder of Kibbutz Nir Oz, survived the Hamas attack in his safe room together with his wife, Hanna.Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The GuardianThe graves he tends are a silent testament to the brutality of the attacks and the scale of the state’s failure, which in Nir Oz was staggering, even on a day of terrible failures.A five-person volunteer defence force held Hamas at bay for at least two hours, Margalit said. When they had all been shot, the kibbutz was taken over and sacked, homes burned, families slaughtered and kidnapped.Then, before the first Israeli soldier arrived, the Hamas forces, other Palestinian gunmen and civilian looters all left. Nir Oz had beenforgotten by the armyand ripped apart without the military firing a single shot to defend it.In total, 47 people were killed and 76 taken to Gaza, includingShiri Bibas, her 10-month-old baby Kfir and four-year-old Ariel, who were killed in Gaza. The dead and hostages represented more than a quarter of the small community.View image in fullscreenShlomo Margalit tends to the graves in the Nir Oz cemetery, a silent testimony to the 7 October attacks.Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The GuardianRevisiting that terrible day, and the trauma that followed, is painful and exhausting for Margalit, but he still accepts interviews for a simple reason. “I want people to know what really happened here,” the 89-year-old said.The third anniversary of the 7 October attacks falls a few weeks before national elections, and much of the country is caught up in a furious debate about responsibility for the deadliest day in Israel’s history and the conduct of the war that followed.Survivors and bereaved relatives are avoiding the political fray, still grappling with the trauma and the struggle to rebuild something like normality.In Nir Oz, there is a terrible, almost irreconcilable struggle between re-establishing the kibbutz as a living community, and preserving physical testimony of the attack.Freed Israeli hostage Aviva Siegel on Netanyahu’s unbearable strategy and waiting for her husband to come homeRead moreThe cemetery echoes with the sound of construction and families have already moved into several rows of new houses near the kibbutz entrance.But on the other side of the compound, paths still lead between blackened ruins and memorials to the dead. Some bereaved survivors want the homes of loved ones preserved this way as permanent monuments to mark their loss.“There are families that can’t [bear to] live here, but want a memorial place to come to visit,” Margalit said. “On the other hand, can you build a new kibbutz where children grow up running around between burnt houses?”He is on the remembrance committee and, two years on, they are struggling to reach a decision on this impossible choice. “Is there right or wrong here? No,” he said. “We are dealing with that, trying to find an answer.”One compromise might be a memorial garden on the border of the kibbutz. For now, there are plaques with the stories of families attacked on that day and a memorial house to remember the dead and kidnapped.When the kibbutz took a collective decision to return and rebuild, Margalit and his wife, Hanna, knew they wanted to join. His only concession to the trauma was asking for a new home that did not face Gaza.View image in fullscreenAbout 60% of the houses in Nir Oz were destroyed on 7 October and some families have decided not to return.Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The Guardian“I’ve found myself building this place for the second time,” he said. “I know when I’m gone, I will have done something with my life. I took part in putting this spot on the map.”The Siegels, who lived in the nearby kibbutz of Kfar Aza, also among the worst hit, have decided not to return as they focus on mental and physical recovery. Aviva was 62 when she was kidnapped. Keith was 64.“What happened to me in Gaza, what happened with Keith in Gaza, it’s there all the time,” said Aviva.“I understand that it’s going to be a process of healing. There’s always things that remind me, and if I don’t remember, then he reminds me. If I’m cooking lunch or making a cup of tea and I turn around and see Keith with tears in his eyes, because he just read something or let himself feel.”The days approaching the anniversary have been particularly difficult, she said. Last year, at this time, she was still campaigning for the release of other hostages, her own emotions held at bay by the urgency of that campaign.For a time, she tried to deal with the trauma by telling herself, over and over again “I must feel lucky,” simply because she had made it back alive.Now she has allowed herself to feel again, and as 7 October approached, she has realised how raw the wounds still are. “Getting ready [for the anniversary] has been very very painful,” she said. “The last couple of weeks all I want to do is cry. Now I’m feeling things I didn’t feel before.”View image in fullscreenAviva Siegel has written a book about her ordeal, saying it was therapy and an act of celebration.Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The Guardian“When I hear my grandson say he is afraid of being kidnapped in the middle of the night, it breaks my heart.”She has written a book,Survived to Tell, about the ordeal, which she describes as therapy and an act of celebration. She wrote so her grandchildren could read about what she and Keith endured, for other hostages who couldn’t tell their own stories and to inspire a broader audience in Israel and beyond.After the exhausting campaign to get Keith and other hostages home, she said she had struggled to concentrate on the election. Keith’s political focus is an independent inquiry into 7 October to prevent other families suffering as his has.He said: “There needs to be an investigation to understand how this happened, in order to do everything possible that it won’t happen again. So many people were killed, injured, traumatised.”Benjamin Netanyahu, the prime minister, has fiercely opposed an independent state commission of inquiry. Critics say he is afraid it would expose his own failings.In the immediate aftermath of the attacks, few people inside or outside Israel expected him to stay in power long, particularly as the country’s coalition governments have rarely served out their full terms.Netanyahu had for years championed a foreign and security policy based on the premise that Hamas was “contained” in Gaza, behind unbreachable layers of fortifications.The security officials who were in command that day have all stepped down yet, three years on, Netanyahu is still in power, having deflected all demands for his resignation.Yaakov Godo, a bereaved father, interrupted Netanyahu’s speech at the official commemoration event this year to accuse him of negligence.“You did not protect my son on 7 October, you did not protect 1,200 people murdered in one day. Shame!” he shouted, before being ushered away.View image in fullscreenThe back of Yocheved Lifshitz’s home in Nir Oz. She has become a vocal critic of Benjamin Netanyahu.Photograph: The GuardianBoth US and Israeli officials have said Netanyahu rejected ceasefire deals that could have halted the war in Gaza and brought many Israeli hostages home sooner. But criticising the prime minister means venturing into a vicious political debate where age and loss offer little protection.Yocheved Lifshitz, 88, was taken hostage from Nir Oz with her husband Oded, whose magnificent cactus garden blooms at the heart of the kibbutz. He died in Gaza, she survived and since her return she has been a vocal critic of Netanyahu.A candidate for Netanyahu’s Likud party, Itzik Bonzel, said last month that he wished he could turn back the clock and return her to Hamas captivity. He later apologised, blaming grief for his son who died fighting in Gaza, but Lifshitz denounced it as a proxy attack driven by the prime minister.Netanyahu, who is battling a corruption trial and could be more vulnerable legally if he loses power, is pushing to intensify Israeli attacks on Gaza and his coalition partners are calling for ethnic cleansing and annexation ofPalestine.View image in fullscreenThe graves of Oded Lifshitz and Alex (Alexander) Dancyg, who were abducted by Hamas on 7 October.Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The GuardianThe war Israel launched in response to 7 October has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, the majority of them civilians, including about 20,000 children.Netanyahu has also waged a years-long campaign to dismantle institutions protecting democracy inside Israel’s 1967 borders. Palestinians under Israeli military rule in the occupied West Bank do not have the rights of Israeli citizens.Many Israelis opposed to this rightwing vision of perpetual war in a state with diminished institutions consider this election the most critical since Israel was founded in 1948, among them Margalit.Nir Oz, like many communities targeted by Hamas, had its roots in the leftwing Zionist movement, and although the brutality of 7 October pushed some to the right, others saw their pain as bitter proof that war alone cannot offer long-term security.“I don’t believe we can ignore the fact that Palestinians live here,” Margalit said. “We have to find a way we can live here with them and be secure. I don’t have an answer, I just know we are here to stay and they are here to stay. Maybe we need someone from the outside.”Explore more on these topicsIsraelGazaPalestineBenjamin NetanyahuMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: The Register that shatters the myth of Britain’s role in profiting from enslavement | Slavery | The Guardian
description: In this month’s newsletter: for Caribbean scholars, the evidence of how deeply slavery shaped Britain’s wealth has never been in doubt. Plus, heritage walks in Manchester
Author: Ahmed Reid
Headline: In this month’s newsletter: for Caribbean scholars, the evidence of how deeply slavery shaped Britain’s wealth has never been in doubt. Plus, heritage walks in Manchester
Content: Composite: GuardianView image in fullscreenComposite: GuardianCotton Capital: ongoing seriesSlaveryThe Register that shatters the myth of Britain’s role in profiting from enslavementIn this month’s newsletter: for Caribbean scholars, the evidence of how deeply slavery shaped Britain’s wealth has never been in doubt. Plus, heritage walks in ManchesterDon’t get Cotton Capital delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereAhmed ReidTue 6 Oct 2026 11.10 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 12.30 EDTShareWelcome to this month’s Cotton Capital newsletter. I’m Ahmed Reid, coming to you from Jamaica, where I am programme manager for the Guardian’s Legacies of Enslavement team.The recently published Register of British Slave-Traders,reported exclusivelyin the Guardian, lists 13,000 men and women who invested in and profited from the trafficking of more than three million enslaved Africans between 1563 and 1807.TheRegistercaptures a broad range of investors, from ordinary men and women in provincial towns tothe monarchy. Queen Elizabeth I and many in her court invested in John Hawkins’s 1563 and subsequent missions. They provided Hawkins with money and ships, including the royal shipJesus of Lübeck, which trafficked 359 Africans to the Americas in 1568. Elizabeth I’s successors – including James I, Charles I, Charles II, James II, William III, Queen Anne, George I, and George II – were major investors, shareholders, and directors in the state-sponsored Company of Royal Adventurers Trading in Africa, the Royal African Company, and the South Sea Company.Other investors included famed philosopher John Locke (who ironically championed the concept of natural rights) and Tobias Rustat a University of Cambridge benefactor whose bust is stilldisplayed in the Chapel at Jesus Collegedespite the college’s attempts to seek permission from an ecclesiastical court to remove it). Forty-five vicars from the Church of England and 24 directors and governors of the Bank of England were also investors. As the project’s lead researcher, William Pettigrew,has stated, slavery was not a footnote in British history – it helped shape the country.Some have expressed surprise at the extent of the involvement. The question worth asking is this: why, 193 years after emancipation, is the true scale of Britain’s role in chattel slavery still not fully understood in Britain?Pre-existing evidenceView image in fullscreenUnpalatable truths … Dr Eric Williams, author of Capitalism and Slavery.Photograph: Val Wilmer/Getty ImagesThe findings are not surprising to scholars in the Caribbean and the wider diaspora. Eighty-two years ago, Eric Williams, the Trinidadian scholar who later became prime minister, argued inCapitalism and Slaverythat profits from chattel enslavement “financed the Industrial Revolution” in Britain. Williams, showed how manufacturing towns and industries, including banking, shipbuilding, insurance and warehousing, were integrated into colonial trade, as were some families.The Nigerian scholar Joseph Inikori, inAfricans and the Industrial Revolution in England, has shown that these linkages provided the scaffolding for Britain’s industrial advancement. During the 2007 Commons debate marking the Bicentenary of the Abolition of the Slave Trade, William Hague pointedlystatedthat: “William Pitt, when he was prime minister, said 80% of British overseas income was derived from our West Indian colonies.” Pitt should know.Caribbean scholars, among them Williams, Sir Arthur Lewis, CLR James, Walter Rodney, Elsa Goveia, Kamau Brathwaite, Hilary Beckles, Orlando Patterson, George Beckford and Verene Shepherd, have spent their professional careers exposing the magnitude of Britain’s involvement in the trafficking of enslaved Africans and its impact across theCaribbeanarchipelago. Plantation ledgers, deeds, wills and probate inventories, whether in repositories in the Caribbean, Britain, or across Europe, show the accumulation and transfer of mind-numbing wealth to Britain.Ship records document the names of ship captains and owners as well as the sadistic violence inflicted on enslaved men, women and children. Those of us who have worked in these archives have spent our careers seeing the names of these monarchs, merchants, vicars, bankers, absentee owners and institutions written alongside the names of the enslaved men, women, and children they owned as “property”. The evidence is not new.Wall of silenceView image in fullscreenNot an accident … forgetting a nation’s violent past is an active process.Composite: GuardianThe reception of the Register reveals much aboutBritish attitudes towards chattel slaveryand how it is taught inschools (pdf)as well as raising questions about why Britain’s role in chattel slavery has not been fully realised.The reason,Catherine Hall has argued, is the conscious effort to occlude the archives. Hall argued that forgetting a nation’s violent past is an active process, not an accident, and Britain’s began as soon as the trafficking in enslaved people was outlawed in 1807.Thomas Clarkson’s history of the abolition campaign celebrated white humanitarian men and omitted Black and women abolitionists and the horrors of trafficking in enslaved people. Abolition of the trafficking in 1807 and emancipation of chattel slavery in 1833 were recast as proof of British liberty and virtue. At the same time, the newly freed people were forced into an unpaid “apprenticeship” while the government paid £20m – or 40% of Britain’s public expenditure – in compensation to the owners of enslaved people. What emerged was an amalgamation of institutions and social and cultural forces to create a wall of silence around the period of chattel enslavement, colonialism and its harmful legacies.The reaction to the Register shows that what Hall described 13 years ago remains true today. The real strength of the Register is that it will help break the wall of silence around Britain’s trafficking in enslaved Africans and “undo the forgetting”.Editor’s picksNearly 4m records of enslaved people searchable online | Aamna MohdinMonarchs, MPs and merchants: the register laying bare Britain’s slave trading past | David ConnCaribbean nations draft action plan to push UK to redress reparations over slavery | Natricia DuncanGiving voice to a lost history: retracing the steps of the Black lives that shaped Manchester | Chris OsuhKing Charles III to acknowledge ‘darkest days’ of Britain’s colonial rule during Caribbean tourRegional spotlightView image in fullscreenHistory on the streets … a Cotton Capital Heritage Walk in Manchester.Photograph: Ruby RamelizeManchester| Did you know that 7 October is World Cotton Day? Created in 2019 by representatives from Benin, Burkina Faso, Chad and Mali, it aims to address the issues facing the cotton industry today while acknowledging its history. This year, the Legacies programme is co-hosting an event at theScience and History Museumincluding talks, workshops and live textile demonstrations.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |MonthlySign up toCotton CapitalStarting with the Guardian’s own history, Guardian journalists explore the legacies of enslavement and reparative justice around the worldEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn the evening there will be a panel discussion featuring Duncan Ivison, the vice-chancellor of University of Manchester, Cleo Lake, the first black female lord mayor of Bristol, Adeola Adelakun, the co-founder of Black Creative Trailblazers, and artist Liam Hopkins, to discuss how World Cotton Day can help us work together to reflect on Manchester’s interwoven history. You can book free tickets forthe evening event here. Across the city there will also beheritage trailslooking at how Manchester’s history is woven into the streets.Keisha Thompson, Legacies of Enslavement programme managerSea Islands| October is Gullah Geechee Cultural Heritage Awareness Month, a time to honour the culture and history of the descendants of enslaved West Africans in the south-east US who retained their unique heritage. Started in 2014, the heritage month includes conferences, festivals, workshops, and film showings in the four states that encompass the Gullah Geechee Cultural Heritage Corridor: Georgia, Florida, North and South Carolina. Visitors come from all over the world to attend celebrations throughout the month.Theeventskicked off with theLowcountry Fish and Grits music festivalon Hilton Head Island on 3 October with performers including Latrese Bush, a Gullah Geechee woman from Bluffton, who sung the jazz, soul and gospel music that defined her upbringing. The Georgia-based Gullah Geechee Ring Shouters also displayed the ring shout, a traditional ritual rooted in West African culture and Christianity. While moving counterclockwise in a circle, the performers stomp their feet, clap their hands and sing in call and response. The month will culminate withCharleston’s Grand Gullah-Geechee Hoodoo Ballin Mount Pleasant, South Carolina, on 31 October, where guests will be treated to Gullah Geechee cuisine, live music, spirituality and dance performances.Melissa Hellmann, US race and equity senior reporterJamaica| The global reparations movement has been gaining phenomenal pace, shifting from the fringes of international debate to the centre of diplomatic discussions. Caribbean governments have managed to push reparations on to the agendas of the Commonwealth, the UN, and in the parliaments and public domains of countries in the region, as well in the UK.But within this broader push, one of the often overlooked elements is the call for repatriation – the right of people of African descent to return to the continent from which their ancestors were taken. For decades, repatriation was dismissed as symbolic or utopian. But African governments including Ghana, Sierra Leone and Liberia are nowdeveloping concrete pathwaysto residency and citizenship for diaspora Africans.As the Commonwealth leaders summit approaches in November, repatriation is likely to become a prominent part of the conversation about what meaningful repair should look like, and how the Caribbean envisions its relationship with Africa.Natricia Duncan, Caribbean correspondentWhat we’re enjoyingView image in fullscreenMultitalented … Author and actor Phoebe McIntosh.Photograph: Orion PoulterI really enjoyed readingDominoesby London-based actor, playwright and novelist Phoebe McIntosh. It’s a smart and witty romance that offers a powerful reflection on the legacies of enslavement. The story follows Layla as she prepares to marry her sweetheart Andy, with whom she happens to share the same surname. Thanks to some sleuthing from Layla’s best friend, it emerges the couple also share a complex, unsettling history – threatening to derail their upcoming nuptials.Angela Foster, assistant editorDominoes by Phoebe McIntosh (Vintage Publishing, £9.99). To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Looking aheadManchester will host Barack Obama as part of Black History Month celebrations. The former US president will appear at Co-op Live on 15 October for an eagerly anticipatedevening of conversation.Meanwhile, the Booker prize-winning author Bernardine Evaristo will join acclaimed screenwriter Russell T Davies on 11 October at Manchester Literature Festival.Chris Osuh, community affairs correspondentWe want to hear from youWhat would you like to see covered in Cotton Capital?Let us know by emailingcottoncapital@theguardian.com. We’ll be back next month.Explore more on these topicsSlaveryCotton Capital: ongoing seriesReparations and reparative justiceAfricaCaribbeanMonarchyColonialismnewslettersShareReuse this content
