title: Lord Archer of Weston-super-Mare obituary | Jeffrey Archer | The Guardian
description: Bestselling author and Conservative politician whose scandal-ridden career ended with a prison sentence
Author: Stuart Jeffries
Headline: Bestselling author and Conservative politician whose scandal-ridden career ended with a prison sentence
Content: Jeffrey Archer in his London apartment overlooking the River Thames in 1999.Photograph: Andy Hall/The ObserverView image in fullscreenJeffrey Archer in his London apartment overlooking the River Thames in 1999.Photograph: Andy Hall/The ObserverJeffrey ArcherObituaryLord Archer of Weston-super-Mare obituaryBestselling author and Conservative politician whose scandal-ridden career ended with a prison sentenceStuart JeffriesTue 6 Oct 2026 13.05 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 19.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJeffrey Archer, who has died aged 86, was irrepressible, though not necessarily in a good way. Ordinary humans would be sunk by the allegations of lies, thefts, frauds, gussied-up CVs, expenses fiddles, charity swindles, plagiarisms, insider trading deals, funding illicit coups and – perhaps most unforgivable of all – unpleasantness to underlings that dogged Archer’s life. But Lord Archer of Weston-super-Mare – bestselling novelist, disgraced politician, one-time athlete and convicted liar – was not ordinary: he was what the Titanic was designed to be, unsinkable.One morning in September 2000, for instance, Archer emerged from Wimbledon police station. He had just beencharged with perjuryfor persuading a friend to lie for him during his1987 libel action against the Daily Starnewspaper, which had claimed he had paid a sex worker to buy her silence.That morning, Archer’s life had started to unravel: the following July he would bejailed at the Old Baileyfor this crime. But instead of returning to his sumptuous Thameside apartment overlooking parliament to consult with lawyers or have a good cry, he smiled for the media, climbed into a chauffeur-driven BMW and went on to his next appointment. The Archer show had to go on. That evening he made his senior stage debut in a production of his own play at the Theatre Royal, Windsor.The Accusedwas, if nothing else, strikingly topical. In it, Archer played Patrick Sherwood, a GP accused of poisoning his wife. Posters for the play read: “See You in Court”.The stage was a simulacrum of the Old Bailey courtroom where he would later stand in the dock. Critics noted that it was a good job Agatha Christie was no longer alive to add the charge of plagiarism to the list he was soon to face. The Accused, they pointed out, bore a striking resemblance to her play Witness for the Prosecution. This was not the first time he faced allegations of plagiarism:Archer once judged a short story competitionand duplicated many of the features of the winning entry in one of his own.View image in fullscreenJeffrey Archer and his wife Mary after his victorious libel case in the high court against the Daily Star in 1987.Photograph: Frank Martin/The GuardianThe theatre audience was the jury, giving their verdict on keypad. Most nights, Archer got off. In the real world, he was not so fortunate. But Archer’s comeuppance was not fatal. In jail, he wrote the three-volume memoirA Prison Diaryand was regularly visited there by literary editors, eager to work up the raw copy of Britain’s most bankable novelist into publishable form in time to capitalise on the Christmas market.Born in London, two weeks later Jeffrey moved with his family to Weston-super-Mare, in Somerset. He was the third child ofLola (nee Cook)and William Archer. The first two of Lola’s children, including another Jeffrey, were born outside marriage and given up for adoption. His father, a convicted fraudster and bigamist who was 64 when Archer was born, left the family home not long after and died in 1956, when his son was 15.His doting mother spoiled him in compensation for that loss. She wrote a column for the local paper called Over the Teacups, about her scamp of a son who featured as “Tuppence”. He attended Wellington school, in Somerset – though he later implied he had attended the grander Wellington college, in Berkshire – where weedy Jeffrey was nicknamed The Pune, for his puny skin-and-bones physique, and bullied. He took up bodybuilding and athletics in response and was so successful at the latter that he became a blue at Oxford and later ran for Britain.He left school with three O-levels (English literature, art and history), trained for the army and the police, and then found a niche at private schools as that rare thing, a popular PE teacher.Then he went to Oxford, where he studied for three years at Brasenose College, though he was never registered there as an undergraduate. Rather, he studied for a teaching qualification on a course based at the college.At Oxford, Archer also raised money for Oxfam, and succeeded in inviting the Beatles to visit Brasenose to sign a cheque and mingle with the dons in the senior common room. During that February 1963 soiree, undergraduate Sheridan Morley and Beatles drummer Ringo Starr found themselves at adjacent urinals. “[Ringo] asked if I knew this Jeffrey Archer bloke,” theatre criticMorley later told the Guardian. “I said everyone in Oxford was trying to work out who he was. Ringo said: ‘He strikes me as a nice enough fella, but he’s the kind of bloke who would bottle your piss and sell it.’”While at Oxford, Archer wooed the student Mary Weeden, who in 1966 became his wife and latera chemistry lecturer at Cambridge University. Despite her husband’s shaming bankruptcies and his reported infidelities, Mary Archer justified standing by her man with more imaginative verve than, say, Tammy Wynette. She said much later: “I think I would find it a little monochrome, a little grey, to have a sort of a more conventional life with a more conventional husband.”View image in fullscreenArcher in 1990 during a provincial tour of his play Beyond Reasonable Doubt.Photograph: Jeff Overs/BBC News & Current Affairs/Getty ImagesAfter leaving Oxford, he continued as a charity fundraiser, working for a medical charity and for the United Nations Association, whose chairman, the former Conservative MP Humphry Berkeley,alleged that Archer fiddled his expenses. He also served as a Conservative councillor on the Greater London council from 1967 to 1970, during which time he was accused of fiddling other councillors’ expenses. Despite these allegations, and despite Berkeley striving to convince Conservative central office that Archer was an unsuitable parliamentary candidate, he beat the future Tory ministerIan Gowto become Conservative candidate for Louth in Lincolnshire. He took the seat in a byelection on 4 December 1969, becoming – or so his book blurbs repeatedly claimed – the youngest MP in the House of Commons, aged 29. In fact, as Michael Crick points out in his biography, there were four younger MPs already in the Commons.In 1974, he became one of the youngest MPs to relinquish his seat. That year, as a result of a complicated speculation he was involved in, Archer lost £500,000 in a fraudulent Canadian company called Aquablast. At the edge of bankruptcy, he resigned from parliament. In terms of fulfilling his ambitions, he may have been prudent: “I realised there would never be a career for me there,” he said of the Commons later.Facing bankruptcy, he told his wife, then pregnant with their second child: “The only way I can get out of this is to write my way out of it.” Friends were sceptical that Archer could make capital from novel writing, having failed to do so from property deals. “Jeffrey, you can barely spell,” his friend Adrian Metcalfe told him, “let alone write.” “No, but I can tell stories,” Archer is said to have replied.He was right. His first novel, Not a Penny More, Not a Penny Less, published in 1976, became a bestseller, as did many of the more than 50 novels, prison journals, children’s books and short story collections that followed.That fictional debut was something of a roman a clef, since it told the story of four men swindled out of $1m – roughly what Archer lost in business deals. The novel’s denouement though, in which the men revenge themselves on their swindlers, was part wish fulfilment and partly cribbed from the then popular movie, The Sting. His wife reportedlyhelped him edit it, correcting his spelling and grammar.View image in fullscreenArcher’s novel Kane and Abel was a huge international bestseller.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianLater, teams of editors worked on making his novels publishable. They were impressed by his capacity for work: he would address the task in blocks of two hours at a time, then wrote as many as 17 further drafts at their behest.Jonathan Coleman, one of four editors who worked on Archer’s international bestseller Kane and Abel (1979), said that, though the book was heavily edited, “he did the rewriting ... I mean, he wasn’t trying to write a literary masterpiece.”He was, rather, trying to make money – and he did. Much came from TV adaptations, but he was a publishing phenomenon whose books were bought at the rate of 25,000 a month at the peak of his literary bankability, resulting in overall sales of around 300m copies.By the mid-70s, then, the disgraced ex-MP was back. Yes, there was a report that he had stolen some suits from a Toronto store when he was giving evidence at the Aquablast trial in Canada in 1977, but that was never proved. And yes, some did complain that he trod on the little people as he rose again (“The sales people at HarperCollins loathed him – absolutely loathed him – because he was so awful to booksellers,” one company manager told Crick, referring to the sales rep as a “waste of space, being very abusive and unpleasant”), but none of this would stop him becoming rich and famous.In 1979, Archer bought the Old Vicarage, Grantchester, a house associated with the poet Rupert Brooke. He also began to hold shepherd’s pie and Krug parties for politicians, business people and even journalists at his Thames-side apartment. He loved to give directions to the toilet: “Past the Picasso and left at the Matisse.”View image in fullscreenArcher, when he was deputy party chairman, with Margaret Thatcher at the 1986  Conservative party conference in BournemouthPhotograph: PA Images/AlamyHe even returned to politics. Margaret Thatcher made him Conservative deputy chairman in 1985 – despite the misgivings of the senior Tories Norman Tebbit, Edward Heath and Willie Whitelaw – partly in gratitude for the sums he had funnelled into Tory party coffers.The political return was shortlived. The following year he resigned because of newspaper allegations that he had paid Monica Coghlan, a sex worker, £2,000 through an intermediary at Victoria station to go abroad. In 1987, he sued the Daily Star for claiming he had slept with her.In one of the case’s more memorable moments,Mr Justice Caulfield spoke to the jury: “Remember Mary Archer in the witness box. Your vision of her probably will never disappear. Has she elegance? Has she fragrance? Would she have, without the strain of this trial, radiance? How would she appeal? Has she had a happy married life? Has she been able to enjoy, rather than endure, her husband Jeffrey?” He said of Jeffrey Archer, “Is he in need of cold, unloving, rubber-insulated sex in a seedy hotel round about quarter to one on a Tuesday morning after an evening at the Caprice?” The judge’s questions, counterintuitively, were rhetorical. Archer won and was awarded £500,000 damages.In 1992, thanks to the prime minister, John Major, Archer was politically rehabilitated again. Major made him a life peer, Lord Archer of Weston-super-Mare, chiefly because of his role in the previous year’s fundraising concert for Kurds. Archer, with the Red Cross, set up the charity Simple Truth.But once more his philanthropy was questioned. Archer had claimed to have raisedmore than £57m for Kurdish refugees. Kurdish disaster relief groups claimed only £250,000 had been received by groups in Iraq. Years later, Scotland Yard investigated these discrepancies, but Archer was never prosecuted.In 1994, Archer was back in trouble overalleged insider dealing involving shares in Anglian Television, of which his wife was a director. An inquiry by the Department of Trade and Industry concluded that Archer would not be prosecuted.In 1999, aged 59, Archer was poised to fulfil one of his ambitions – to hold high political office – when he was selected as Conservative candidate for the London mayoral election of 2000. But that ambition was thwarted when the News of the World reported that he had perjured himself in the 1987 libel case.His former friend, theTV producer Ted Francis, and his former personal assistant, Angela Peppiatt, decided to reveal that he fabricated an alibi at the trial because they thought he was an unsuitable mayoral candidate.He withdrew his candidacy the next dayand was, in February 2000, expelled from the Conservative party for five years. The then party leader William Hague, who had hailed Archer’s “probity and integrity”, said: “This is the end of politics for Jeffrey Archer. I will not tolerate such behaviour in my party.”Archer’s trial for perjury began in May 2001. Once more, his wife Mary gave evidence. Archer did not, though he had to hear his former secretary, Peppiatt, detail alleged marital infidelities with a former employee. During the judge’s summing up, his mother died. As a result, she missed seeing her sonsentenced to four years’ imprisonmentby Mr Justice Potts. He served only two years in jail and retained his life peerage.Archer’s scandals were not over yet. A year after his release, he wasaccused by Equatorial Guinea’s governmentof co-financing the failed 2004 coup d’etat attempt.double quotation markHe will dive over a cliff and then be amazed that he’s fallingHe continued writing after his release. In 2007, he collaborated with the Catholic scholar Francis J Moloney in a book entitledThe Gospel According to Judas. In this version of the story, Judas did not betray Jesus. The treatment of the story must have appealed to the disgraced peer, since in it he rehabilitated Judas. Perhaps in his mind, Archer – similarly maligned though more fairly – hoped for a similar rehabiliation.Archer’s life was lived, if not told, in heroic denial of what he was. “He will dive over a cliff and then be amazed that he’s falling,” said his college friend Morley who, like many politicians in the party that Archer disgraced, remained supportive. “He thinks he’s Peter Pan, that he’ll never die. Everything he does he thinks is going to be all right in the end.”In fiction, if not reality, Archer was rehabilitated. The maligned Judas became a national hero when in 2002 the writer Guy Jenkin wrote a TV comedy calledJeffrey Archer: The Truth. It told the version of the Archer story that never gets told (least of all in the newspapers) – about a misunderstood man who took the blame selflessly, suffered abuse, disgrace and imprisonment for the nation’s good.“My Jeffrey Archer is the man who has frequently saved Britain over the last 30 years,” said Jenkin. “He’s beloved of all women he comes across, all men, all dogs – he’s a superhero.” If only the real Jeffrey Archer had been like that. But his life did not imitate art because it could not: it was rather, in the title of Crick’s biography, Stranger ThanFiction.Archer retired from the Lords in 2024, and said that his final novel would be Adam and Eve. His death came unexpectedly, on the day before its publication.He is survived by Mary, and his sons, William and James.Jeffrey Howard Archer, Lord Archer of Weston-super-Mare, author and politician, born 15 April 1940; died 5 October 2026Explore more on these topicsJeffrey ArcherConservativesFictionobituariesShareReuse this content

title: Artificial review – Luca Guadagnino takes on OpenAI in muddled tech satire | New York film festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: The origin story of Sam Altman’s company is reimagined as a campy comedy starring Andrew Garfield
Author: Owen Myers
Headline: The origin story of Sam Altman’s company is reimagined as a campy comedy starring Andrew Garfield
Content: Andrew Garfield as Sam Altman and Yura Borisov as Ilya Sutskever in Artificial.Photograph: Courtesy of NeonView image in fullscreenAndrew Garfield as Sam Altman and Yura Borisov as Ilya Sutskever in Artificial.Photograph: Courtesy of NeonFirst look reviewNew York film festival 2026ReviewArtificial review – Luca Guadagnino takes on OpenAI in muddled tech satireNew York film festival:The origin story of Sam Altman’s company is reimagined as a campy comedy starring Andrew GarfieldOwen MyersTue 6 Oct 2026 12.58 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 13.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn the day thatLuca Guadagnino’s film aboutSam AltmanandOpenAIpremiered, Vanity Fair released acover storyon Altman. Alongside glossy portraits from Annie Leibovitz, the world’s pre-eminent portrait photographer, the story describes him as the Oppenheimer of his day, evoking the image of a man leading humanity towards its own inevitable demise at the hands of sentient robots. Altman doesn’t seem to be grappling with much existential angst about the whole thing though: in aninterviewalso released this week, he said that we should be prepared to accept “bad things” in return for the benefits of AI.Club Kid review – Jordan Firstman’s heartfelt comedy is irresistibleRead moreHow much worse can things get? AI agents have alreadygone rogue, hacking into government systems and “bruteforcing” UN databases.Last year, a young woman usedChatGPTas a therapist before she killed herself (the software helped her write her suicide note). Studies show that using AI is probably leading us all towards something called cognitive surrender, which does not seem like the best use of your one wild and precious life.Artificial is a stylish and blunt satire that is unambiguous in its perspective: that Sam Altman is an amoral manipulator who might be dead inside. That goes some way towards explaining why Amazon MGM Studiospulled outof distributing the film in June (Jeff Bezos’s company has a $50bn investment in OpenAI). I found it to be more of an op-ed than a movie, with little insight into what makes Altman and the tech elite tick. Neither does it have much to say about the world – glossy magazines included – that has welcomed them with open arms.In 2003, a young math prodigy named Ilya Sutskever (Yura Borisov, the heartbeat of the film) visits Prof Geoff Hinton (Mark Rylance) in his office hoping for a job with the man known as the godfather of AI. “Have you ever considered the link between knowledge and patience?” Hinton serenely asks his young charge. You can almost feel Guadagnino is turning to the audience and giving us a big stage wink.Nine years later, Sutskever and Hinton’s technology is starting to work “much the way your mind does”, with an ability to differentiate between cats and dogs, but Sutskever is growing increasingly impatient with what he sees as Hinton’s conservative ambitions for the technology. It’s at this point that Elon Musk (Ike Barinholtz) introduces Sutskever to Sam Altman (Andrew Garfield), who is fresh from selling his Loopt app, a kind of proto-Find My Friends, for $40m.You Can See Everything review – Nathan Fielder’s Elizabeth Holmes doc is a modern masterpiece of deceitRead moreThese guys are total dweebs, peppering each other with puerile jokes while doing shots in upscale restaurants as servers grimace and pray for a tip. Everyone is starting to want what these guys are selling, and one prospective investor speculates that AI will soon be able to reverse climate change and cure cancer. When talking about the technology, Sutskever’s eyes light up. “All pain, all loneliness will cease,” he says, as knowingly over-the-top haunted house music plays. “We will be free.”The film’s dramatic tension rests in the opposing poles of thought represented by Sutskever, a delusional optimist, and the self-motivated hubris of Altman. As we move into the recent past, cracks and fissures appear in their partnership as OpenAI’s self-learning technology begins to first outsmart humans at video games, and then becomes a different beast entirely. Garfield is brilliantly slimy, nailing Altman’s evolution from demon twink to a narcissistic grifter with a victim complex that climaxes with him being fired as the CEO ofOpenAIand then rehired five days later. “They’re being very mean to me,” he pouts in one scene after his board airs one of its many legitimate concerns over the ethics of his product.View image in fullscreenYura Borisov, Luca Guadagnino, Andrew Garfield and Ike Barinholtz at the Artificial premiere at the New York film festival on Monday.Photograph: Michael Loccisano/Getty Images for FLCArtificial is the most outwardly comedic Guadagnino film to date, with a script by the New Yorker essayist Simon Rich. The humor can be frustratingly broad, and it often feels like Barinholtz is impersonating Mike Myers doing Musk on Saturday Night Live than the Tesla founder himself (Rich is a former writer on SNL). Garfield seems to be playing Altman, who is an out gay man, as more effete than he actually is, which is strange as there are plenty of reasons to laugh at the tech oligarch that don’t involve him being light in his loafers. At other times, the script is satisfyingly savage. After being questioned over safety concerns by his associate Mira Murati (Monica Barbaro), Altman snaps, “I didn’t invent teen suicide, Mira.”A Statement review – outstanding climate change dramedy about a 1980 meetingRead moreI could have done without some Artificial’s clangingly obvious visual metaphors, such as a random shot of a unhoused person wearing VR goggles, or the sudden plunge into a simulator-like sequence of a car accelerating over a foggy Golden Gate Bridge (we get it, we’re taking a reckless leap into the unknown). The film comes with a score by Damon Albarn, and the Blur frontman contributes one original composition that an ASPCA advert would reject for being too on-the-nose with lyrics like, “In a corrupt world, we’ll sing the saddest song.”It’s tech oligarch season at the movies, with films aboutElon Musk, Elizabeth Holmes and Mark Zuckerberg also due for release over the next few months as film-makers try to respond to the zeitgeist in real time. “We opened Pandora’s box,” Altman says in a standout monologue towards the end of the film. “Countries will fall, industries will collapse, and we get to be the ones to usher people into this new world.”It’s a grim prophecy that gets lost in Guadanigno’s tonal jumble of a film, which has a certain self-satisfaction in telling us that dystopia is upon us. I couldn’t help but crave a leaner, meaner version of this movie. Despite some genuinely chilling moments, Artificial shows the limits of holding up a mirror to the world.Artificial is screening at the New York film festival and wil be released in the US on 25 December, in Australia on 21 January and in the UK on 27 JanuaryExplore more on these topicsNew York film festival 2026First look reviewSam AltmanOpenAIAI (artificial intelligence)ComputingElon MuskLuca GuadagninoreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘We live in grief-phobic societies’: experts on how to get more comfortable with death | Well actually | The Guardian
description: We are all going to die, and so is everyone we know. So how can you not be terrified?
Author: Madeleine Aggeler
Headline: We are all going to die, and so is everyone we know. So how can you not be terrified?
Content: Illustration: Ibrahim Rayintakath/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Ibrahim Rayintakath/The GuardianMemento mori: a series about deathWell actually‘We live in grief-phobic societies’: experts on how to get more comfortable with deathWe are all going to die, and so is everyone we know. So how can you not be terrified?Madeleine AggelerTue 6 Oct 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 12.53 EDTShareFor most people, death is not a standard conversation topic. Once, at lunch, a friend began talking about her mother’s death several years earlier. Her voice caught occasionally, but she spoke about it plainly – like a simple fact of life. As we talked, I noticed another friend was shifting uncomfortably in his seat; he didn’t say much.Afterwards, I asked him what was wrong. “I really don’t like talking about death,” he said, his hands twitching anxiously. “I don’t even like thinking about it. It freaks me out.”His discomfort struck me as silly – and also the most normal thing in the world. We are all going to die, and so is everyone we know. So why be terrified? And how can you not be terrified?My friend is far from alone in his discomfort. “We live in grief-illiterate and grief-phobic societies,” says Dr Lucy Hone, a resilience and grief researcher and author of the book How Will I Get Ever Through This?: A Practical Guide to Navigating Life’s Toughest Times.Hone began researching grief over a decade ago, after the sudden death of her daughter, Abi. On our video call, she wears one of Abi’s old hats, an orange and white beanie with polka dots and a big orange pouf on top. It’s ridiculous, Hone says, but it makes her laugh.For someone who has experienced such intense loss and spends so much of her time talking to people about their grief, Hone is remarkably cheerful and bubbly. This is in part because of her work, she argues. Hone and several other experts I spoke with said that thinking and being around death was “life-affirming”.Below, experts share why so many of us are so scared of death, and how we can learn to get a little more comfortable with it.Why we are so uncomfortable with deathDeath disrupts the usual orientation of our lives, argues Dr Todd May, instructor of philosophy at Warren Wilson College.“People in the west and elsewhere are forward-looking,” May says. We do not just exist in the moment – we engage in projects and relationships that we see unfolding over time. “The thought of our lives ending violates this future orientation we all have,” he explains.The typically western, individualistic approach to life affects how we feel about death, says Sister Chȃn Trì Nghiȇm, an Australian-born Zen Buddhist nun. In the Judeo-Christian tradition, “there is a strongly shared belief that God created individuals separate from each other … we have a certain lifespan, and we die at a certain time”. This view causes fear and anxiety, argues Trì Nghiȇm.In the Buddhist tradition, beginnings and endings are far less defined. Take a question as simple as when you first began to exist: was it when you were born? The nine months you were in your mother’s belly? When you were just a precursor cell within your unborn mother? “In Buddhism, we have always existed and there was no time when we didn’t exist,” says Trì Nghiȇm. Seen through this lens, death is less of an ending and more of a continuation.The idea of finitude can bruise our fragile egos, saysAlua Arthur, author and death doula. “We have no control at all, and that’s very disquieting,” she says. “We think we’re infallible, and death reminds us how small we are, and that’s uncomfortable.”And the thought of death brings about big feelings that most people would prefer to avoid, says Dr Luyi Kathy Zhang, a hospice and palliative care doctor.“So many of us are ill-equipped to deal with uncomfortable emotions, and death is probably one of the peak uncomfortable experiences,” she says. “It is easier for us to say that death is an eventuality that we will deal with when it comes rather than to face the feelings now.”Finally, dying increasingly happens out of sight, says Hone – in hospitals or care homes. But it wasn’t always this way.“Throughout human history, we had death around us,” Hone says. “We’d care for the sick and dying at home, so we were forced to talk about it and think about it.”This shift accelerated in the mid-20th century. “In Boston in 1912, about two-thirds of residents died at home,” theNew York Timesreported in 2019. “By the 1950s, the majority of Americans died in hospitals and by the 1970s, at least two-thirds did.”Removed from our immediate surroundings, for many death became something more distant and abstract.Why it is important to think about deathNot talking or thinking about death “doesn’t mean that it’s not coming, it just means that you’re going to be ill-prepared when it does come”, says Arthur.Thinking about and planning forthe logistics of deathcan also make things easier for the people around us. “That way, they’re not in grief and also trying to figure out where your social security card is,” says Arthur.Planning for how we’d ideally like to spend our last days gives us agency, says Zhang. “You can choose to be involved in it rather than [experience] the overwhelm and stress of being forced to deal with it,” she explains.‘Death is not a mystery’: what happens to your body when you’re dying?Read moreThere are more immediate benefits too. I spoke to over a dozen experts on death, and they raised the same point again and again: thinking about death helps us live better lives.“Accepting that we’re going to die allows us to live more purposefully,” says Hone. For her, losing Abi and confronting grief in her work clarified the brevity and fragility of life. Given that, she says, “I need to know who and what matters most to me now and focus my attention on them.”Reflecting on our mortality can be a good way to keep things in perspective, says Zhang. For example: will this frustrating traffic jam matter to you on your deathbed? And if you are nervous about asking someone out, or applying for a job, ask yourself how you might feel at the end of your life if you didn’t go after what you wanted. “That might be enough of a perspective shift for us to overcome fear or hesitation,” Zhang says.It can also help us appreciate our life now. “If we ask ourselves, ‘What if this is the last time I get to have dinner with my family?’ that is a very different way of experiencing something that feels ordinary and mundane,” Zhang says.How to get more comfortable with deathOften, familiarity with death is something we don’t have much of a say about – the loss of a friend, family member or even beloved pet forces us to confront it, whether we’re ready or not.But experts say there are certain practices that can help one begin to “tolerate” the thought of death, as Hone puts it. “I’m not at peace with the fact that I’m going to die and all the people I love are going to die,” she admits. “But I can tolerate it, because I can tolerate difficult things.”I’m a death expert. I designed eight questions to help you think about dyingRead moreDon’t feel ashamed of your fear.Fear of death is natural, and often a big part of what keeps us alive, says Arthur. “It’s the thing that tells you to stop walking when you get to the edge of that cliff, and to drink water when you’re in the desert,” she says. The goal, Arthur argues, is not to completely eliminate the fear of death, but to understand where and why it might be holding us back.Start planning.Whether it’s writing your will or anadvance directive– a document outlining who you want making your financial and medical decisions for you if you can’t – thinking about the practicalities of death can be a helpful, less emotionally fraught way to approach it, Arthur says.Ask yourself some big questions.Questions like, “What will I regret not doing in 10 or 15 years?” and “Will I care about this on my deathbed?” help put the current moment and emotions into perspective, says Zhang.Think about someone you know who died. Even if it’s just for five minutes, Hone says, reflect on what you learned from that person, and how you might want to live differently because of what they taught you. “That’s quite a nice, constructive way to think about death,” she says.Think about your relationships.Reflect on the important people in your life and whether you’re holding anything back from them, Arthur says. “Who do you need to say sorry to? Who do you need to say thank you to? Who do you need to forgive?” she asks.Learn how to balance the present and the future.As important as it is to be present in our lives, we cannot only live in the moment, says May. “We need to keep our engagement in activities with a future,” he says. But because we could die at any moment, “living solely for the future sacrifices the riches of our present”. The aim is to exist in a balance of both, May says, which is “difficult, but perhaps achievable to some degree.”

title: Is this the end of the British school photo? | Parents and parenting | The Guardian
description: For generations, professional photographers have captured the country’s pupils in all their awkward glory. But an increasing number of parents are using AI to avoid paying them
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: For generations, professional photographers have captured the country’s pupils in all their awkward glory. But an increasing number of parents are using AI to avoid paying them
Content: But are you willing to pay full price?Photograph: South_agency/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBut are you willing to pay full price?Photograph: South_agency/Getty ImagesPass notesParents and parentingIs this the end of the British school photo?For generations, professional photographers have captured the country’s pupils in all their awkward glory. But an increasing number of parents are using AI to avoid paying themTue 6 Oct 2026 09.54 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 17.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleName:School photos.Age:Around since Victorian times.Future:Uncertain.Surely not. The school photo is a grand British tradition, and one that shall not be given up without a fight.Yes, but have you seen the price of them recently?No.My kids just had theirs done. It’s £20 for one photo, but if you want extras – for the shot to be turned into a magnet, keyring or snow globe, say – then prices can run up to about £100.Changed my mind. No fighting. Let it end.Well, you could let it end, or you could just do what some parents have been doing.Which is what?Getting the low-res preview shots from the photographer’s website, then using AI to upscale them and remove all the watermarks, as theTimes reports.Are people actually doing that?Oh yes, and apparently in such numbers that the photographers are starting to notice.Or could it be that photos are so expensive that parents just aren’t buying them any more?Possibly, but the AI hack is everywhere too.Those poor photographers.Well, yes and no. The average spend on these things is £25. A big primary school with two classes of 30 kids a year group could pull in £10,500, which does sound like a fortune. But once you knock off expenses such as printing, mounting, shipping, the cost of cameras and lights – and the school’s commission, don’t forget – the net take will be a lot less. And that’s before you get to wages …And isn’t it immoral to take something without paying?That too. And besides, the school photograph is an important document of your youth. Where else are you going to keep a record of all your bad haircuts and adolescent skin complaints?I dunno. Selfies?Yes, but they don’t have the hallmarks of a school photo. There’s no self-consciousness with a selfie, no sense of being trapped within an oppressive institution.So we’re agreed that using AI is bad.Of course we’re agreed. Using AI for anything is bad, especially makingposters for restaurants. Nobody wants to look at unconvincingly rendered AI images of plasticky-looking sausages. It isn’t appetising. When will people learn?You’ve strayed from the subject a little.Fine. But the same goes for school photos. Using AI to remove watermarks is bad and will put people out of work, but next you’ll be using it to make your child’s teeth whiter and their hair shinier, and soon you’ll have a row of pictures of grinning deathless mannequins on your mantelpiece. Avoid it altogether, I say.Do say:“Watch the birdie.”Don’t say:“Say ‘ChatGPT’.”Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: ‘It could knock a whole street down’: the art of defusing a second world war bomb | Defence policy | The Guardian
description: The long read: On 14 January this year, army and navy squads faced an unprecedented challenge: one bomb on a Plymouth building site, another floating on a dredger in Exmouth. That afternoon, the clock started ticking
Author: Samira Shackle
Headline: The long read: On 14 January this year, army and navy squads faced an unprecedented challenge: one bomb on a Plymouth building site, another floating on a dredger in Exmouth. That afternoon, the clock started ticking
Content: Capt Liam Kidman and Maj Andrew Boyce of the 11 Explosive Ordnance Disposal and Search Regiment (11EOD).Photograph: Sam Frost/The GuardianView image in fullscreenCapt Liam Kidman and Maj Andrew Boyce of the 11 Explosive Ordnance Disposal and Search Regiment (11EOD).Photograph: Sam Frost/The GuardianThe long readDefence policy‘It could knock a whole street down’: the art of defusing a second world war bombOn 14 January this year, army and navy squads faced an unprecedented challenge: one bomb on a Plymouth building site, another floating on a dredger in Exmouth. That afternoon, the clock started tickingSamira ShackleTue 6 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTShareEveryone at Exmouth Marina knew there was an unexploded German bomb in the water. Old hands at the dock had been saying so since the end of the second world war. But the marina had been dredged and re-dredged and nothing had ever come up. It had started to sound like an old wives’ tale. The marina is a busy stretch of water: a commercial port until the late 1990s that had since been converted into a home to private yachts. A bomb, you’d think, would have a hard time staying hidden. But in the middle of the afternoon on Wednesday 14 January 2026, 81 years after the end of the second world war, Steve Hockings-Thompson, the manager of Exmouth Marina, got a call from the crew of a dredging vessel telling him he’d better come out to the boat. “I thought: ‘Oh crikey. We’ve got a bit of an issue here,’” Hockings-Thompson told me recently.He went out to the dredger, a squat barge that hauls silt and other debris from the marina floor on to a flat deck that resembles a steel sieve. Sitting on the deck was a huge hunk of metal, caked in mud and stones. As Hockings-Thompson got closer and saw its distinctive conical shape, he knew it was a bomb – a big one. The dredger was loaded with 20,000 litres of diesel fuel, so if the bomb detonated, it would be disastrous. He called the police, who quickly came to the scene. “And then,” he said, “all hell broke loose.”To deal with the explosives, they called in the army. The call was picked up at the control centre at Vauxhall Barracks in Didcot, a small town in Oxfordshire. This is the headquarters of the 11 Explosive Ordnance Disposal and Search Regiment (11EOD), a specialist army division responsible for all kinds of bomb disposal – from improvised devices planted by terrorist groups to second world war-era munitions.When the Exmouth bomb was called in, Maj Andrew Boyce, who was managing operations for the regiment, was confused. “We were talking about ‘the bomb’, which I’d been told was a 50kg,” he recalled. “And then somebody on the phone tells me it’s a 250kg. I’m like, how have you confused a 50kg bomb, which is the size of a fire extinguisher, with a 250kg bomb, which is the size of a hot water tank?”The reason for the confusion soon became clear: the Exmouth Marina bomb was not the first to be discovered that day. Another second world war bomb had been unearthed a few hours earlier at a building site in Plymouth, 50 miles away.In Plymouth that morning, Luke Templeton, director of S.I UXO, a private contractor that goes in ahead of construction companies to look for unexploded bombs, had known what he was looking for. His company’s historians had already spent a fortnight doing a detailed risk assessment of the site, drawing on historical documents showing the Luftwaffe’s flight paths and local records of airstrikes. From this, they’d worked out that it was highly likely there were two bombs buried somewhere on the building site. Using specialist equipment, they had found a 50kg bomb buried more than four metres down. After inspecting the bomb up close, Templeton called the police.As far as Boyce knew, this was the first time since the immediate postwar period that two unexploded bombs had been discovered on the same day. The two bombs were in the same part of the country, and had been reported to the same police force,Devonand Cornwall. “We’re used to having confusion with location or devices. We’re not used to having two devices,” said Brig Darren Fisher, who at the time was a colonel overseeing the operations. Once the confusion had been straightened out – it was a 50kg bomb at the building site in Plymouth, and a 250kg bomb floating on the dredger in Exmouth – the response began.When most people think of bomb disposal, they imagine a lone figure in a bomb suit carefully approaching an improvised device as bullets fly overhead, holding steady as they unpick wires, knowing that one wrong move will kill them. This image was forged in Belfast during the Troubles and Helmand province during the invasion of Afghanistan, and it is not unwarranted; bomb disposal is commonly described as the most dangerous job in the military. But, in Britain in 2026, the daily reality of the job is quite different.Although the same team deals with terrorist incidents, such as the 2017 Manchester attack on an Ariana Grande concert, it is unexploded second world war munitions that make up the core work of the UK’s bomb-disposal teams. The Luftwaffe dropped more than 60,000 tonnes of bombs on Britain over the course of the war, and the Ministry of Defence estimates that roughly one in 10 of these failed to explode on impact. The reasons range from the grim – poor manufacturing quality due to a reliance on forced labour in concentration camps – to the prosaic: a bomb might have landed at an odd angle, or on soft ground that absorbed the impact before the fuze could fire. (“Fuse” is the general spelling for electrical safety devices and burning cords, while “fuze” refers to engineered explosive detonators.) Britain also dropped munitions on its own land during training exercises and deliberately buried surplus after the war in an effort at disposal. Eight decades on, the physical remnants of the war still account for about 2,000 of the 2,500 incidents that military bomb-disposal teams respond to in an average year.The calls often come in from metal detectorists and magnet fishers, hobbyists who throw strong magnets into waterways to see what comes up. They surge on bank holidays, when people are out walking and notice things underfoot, or catching up on tasks such as clearing out a grandparent’s home. Not long ago, the bomb-disposal unit was called to deal with a 2in mortar that had been used for 20 years as a paperweight. Increasingly, calls come from construction sites, as buildings get taller and companies dig deeper, which has led to a growing industry of private contractors actively searching for unexploded bombs. “We’re expanding cities, building new homes, and an accident could happen,” said Templeton. “If a 250kg bomb went off in a city, it could knock a whole street down.”The passage of time has not rendered these explosives less dangerous. In June 2010, three bomb-disposal experts in Göttingen, Germany, werekilled by a 500kg American bombfound beneath the site of a new sports arena. In 2020, a 250kg bombexploded beneath a crab boat off the Norfolk coast, seriously injuring five of its seven crew. In 2021, another bomb exploded beneath a drilling rig near Munich’s main railway station, injuring four. Because it was a global war, this is a global problem.This year, a second world war bomb beneath a stilt house in Indonesia detonated, killing five people and injuring 20.These decades-old devices are difficult to read or predict. “You don’t really know why [a particular bomb] didn’t function, which is part of the problem,” said Lt Col Andy Hambley, the commanding officer of 11EOD. Years of corrosion, shifting ground and rust make the fuzes less predictable, the machinery harder to read.That was exactly the issue facing two teams in two different corners of Devon on the afternoon of 14 January.At about 1pm, PO Scott Dooley, a diver and bomb-disposal operator with the Royal Navy’s Diving and Threat Exploitation Group, arrived at the building site in Plymouth. Dooley, a tall man with a neatly trimmed beard and a soft Devon accent, grew up in the military; his father was in the Royal Engineers, doing bomb disposal. In recent years, he had acquired the nickname “the Doom Watch”, because every time he was on duty, the phone didn’t stop ringing (his record was 11 call-outs in a single week). In Plymouth, Dooley scanned the area for risk: there was a school nearby, as well as a glass-fronted hotel that could shatter if the worst happened.Policewere already at work establishing a cordon and evacuating the area around the bomb.When an operator approaches a bomb for the first time, they do not know what they are walking towards. The most important thing is to assess the fuze, a metal cylinder screwed into the side of the bomb. It is the first link in a chain. The fuze contains explosives, which fire a tiny, highly sensitive detonator, which sets off a booster charge, which sets off the main filling of the bomb, a comparatively stable “secondary” explosive. Most German fuzes were electrical, charged from the aircraft as the bomb was released. After 80 years, there is no charge left in them. But some German bombs were fitted with a mechanical delayed-action fuze, constructed from gears and springs, like a watch. Once triggered, this fuze ticks down before detonating between two and 72 hours later. The Luftwaffe deliberately fitted these fuzes to maximise disruption; hospitals, roads and factories were cleared for days at a time because the bombs could detonate long after impact.Everything, therefore, turns on the fuze. If the fuze is judged to be sensitive, that usually means it is too dangerous to move the device. The safest option is to surround it with sandbags and detonate it where it is. If the fuze is stable, then it can be moved somewhere safer, such as out to sea.Dooley had two things working in his favour: a 50kg bomb was less likely to have a ticker, and it was still half-buried, which suggested it hadn’t been badly jolted. On the other hand, the fuze was submerged in mud and he couldn’t see it. Bomb-disposal operators try to avoid moving a device until they’ve assessed the fuze, lest they trigger a ticker, but Dooley had no choice. Down in the pit, he and a colleague built a stable platform on a ledge of mud, surrounding it with sandbags, and set to work painstakingly unearthing it. Once it was out, he placed a listening device on it called a microphone stethoscope, or mic steth. He listened for ticking.Silence. A moment of relief, quickly followed by further investigation. Silence only means that at that moment, no mechanical fuze has been triggered. Was there one in the bomb at all? Dooley needed to physically examine it. The bomb had been lodged more than four metres underground for decades and was caked in thick clay. Still listening for ticking on the mic steth in case his movements triggered anything, he poured water on the fuze to wash away the mud. “The fuze was absolutely more than gone,” he said. It was so degraded that none of the markings were visible. No markings, no information. They would have to X-ray it.While this was unfolding in Plymouth, Capt Liam Kidman was anticipating a quiet couple of days at home. Kidman had just come off a gruelling week that ended in rural west Wales, cutting open a safe packed with explosives at the bottom of a dead man’s garden. (The man had apparently used the explosives for felling trees, and nobody knew where he kept the key.) Then, shortly after he had completed that job, the control centre rang to say two bombs had been discovered in Devon. The local team in Plymouth was already occupied with one of them. Could he go to Exmouth? Kidman was back on the road within the hour.An energetic man from south Wales, Kidman ended up in bomb disposal almost by accident – when he joined the army more than 20 years ago, there was a shortage of ammunition technicians. As he climbed the ranks, dealing with improvised explosive devices (IEDs) in Afghanistan and second world war jobs in the UK, he came to love the problem-solving aspect of the work.A map of Exmouth showing the site of the unexploded bomb, and 400m and 600m exclusion zones.A map of Exmouth showing the site of the unexploded bomb, and 400m and 600m exclusion zones.It was past 7pm when Kidman reached Exmouth Marina from his base in Gloucestershire. The closer he got to the marina, the emptier the roads got. The bomb was sitting out in the middle of the harbour, bobbing on the open deck of the dredger. It was so big that if detonated it could flatten the marina’s waterfront. The bomb was only accessible by sea, and the nearest naval team was tied up with the other bomb in Plymouth that night. Usually, the army handles incidents on land and the navy anything at sea, but the unexpected nature of two bombs being found on the same day had turned everything on its head.The bomb had been handled roughly – hauled off the seabed and dumped unceremoniously on to a metal deck. “If there’s a mechanical fuze on there, that’s enough for it to be ticking down,” said Kidman. They had to get ears on it. Harry Griffin, the marina compliance manager, stepped up. Griffin knew there was a chance the bomb could go off, but reassured himself that it had been in the water for 80 years without incident. He ferried a sergeant from Kidman’s team over to the bomb to get a mic steth on to the device. “That’s the bit that gets the operator’s heart going,” said Kidman.It was not ticking. But nobody relaxed. Just as in Plymouth, they did not know what kind of fuze they were dealing with.On a bright day in June, I visited RAF Northolt, a base on the outskirts of London, to observe a training exercise on airdropped weapons. Learning how to correctly assess an old, rusting bomb takes time and practice. Bomb disposal is a dangerous job but, Hambley told me: “Knowledge dispels fear.”Bomb disposal as a specialism was created in the second world war. Britain wasn’t ready for the blitz, and the early assumption was that police or air raid wardens could simply deal with any bomb that failed to go off. But as delayed-action mechanical fuzes – those ticking timebombs – became more common, it was clear that targeted intervention was needed. As the historian James Owen details in his 2010 book Danger UXB, in May 1940, the War Office handed the problem to the Royal Engineers, who formed 25 bomb-disposal sections armed with little more than picks, shovels and stethoscopes. By September 1940, they were dealing with more than 3,000 bombs a month. By some estimates, the average life expectancy of a bomb-disposal operator in this period was 10 weeks.View image in fullscreenMunitions on display in 11EOD’s museum at their base at MOD Ashchurch.Photograph: Sam Frost/The GuardianThose early teams mapped every bomb they dealt with, and the maps are still in use. Matt Fuller, a researcher at S.I UXO, the contractor that found the bomb in Plymouth, works through wartime bomb censuses and Home Office daily intelligence reports. Studying the bomb maps, he found that the Plymouth bomb most likely fell on the night of 21–22 March 1941. (The Exmouth bomb he puts at 24-25 February 1941.) Conducting risk assessments, Fuller is struck by the sheer number of places that were targeted, some of them small towns with tiny populations. “The last person to die from an unexploded bomb dropped in world war two probably hasn’t been born yet,” he told me. Fuller also marvels at the detailed records local wardens kept. They saw the danger that unexploded bombs would pose for future generations. In keeping those records, they reached out a helping hand from past to present.In contrast to their second world war counterparts, modern bomb-disposal teams come armed with robot-mounted cameras, mic steths that can be operated from a distance, and X-ray machines that can penetrate thick layers of steel to examine the explosive content inside. “Risk to life comes above everything – for the public, but also for us – and risk to property comes second,” Hambley told me. But when a bomb is 80 years old, even this equipment can be unreliable.At RAF Northolt, a 500kg German bomb was perched on a grassy verge. The bomb, which was inert, had been placed there, at an awkward angle, for bomb-disposal technicians to assess in pairs: what type of bomb is it? Which fuze? What action can be taken? I approached the bomb with Maj Matt Walker, the squadron duty officer. It was roughly the length of a two-seat sofa: a long, thin hunk of dull metal, its surface rough and textured with rust. Walker told me that a device this size would have a blast radius of “a few hundred to a thousand metres”.Without clear markings, trainees would have to use their knowledge to work out whether the fuze had a mechanical timer, or an additional anti-handling fuze: a booby-trap built into the bomb that detonates it if anyone tries to move it or remove the main fuze. The trainees had to work out what to do next. “It’s extreme problem solving,” said Walker. “Someone described it to me the other day as – you start by juggling five books, then someone throws a glass ball and you have to keep that juggling as well. They then throw a ball of fire.” If you drop one of the balls, you and those nearby will probably die.We left the 500kg bomb where it was and walked into the “museum”, a grand name for a few long, dusty shelves inside a garage that acts as a visual reference library. “Anything and everything will turn up here,” said Walker. He picked up a tapered, hollow metal tube. “This one is actually a kid’s baseball bat. But it got called in.” They’d hung on to this and other red herrings so that trainees could see, in practice, how easy it is to mistake something for a bomb. The other miscellanea included an internal part from the Citroën 2CV car that looks so much like a bomb that people regularly call 999 after finding it in a scrapyard. Until I looked at the items in the museum, I hadn’t fully grasped how little there is to go on: the munitions are not just rusted but distorted, sometimes missing pieces, completely blank. Translating these rusted lumps of metal into something legible requires an expert eye: a cylindrical shape with a curved end means it could be a German SC50, particular fuze pocket positioning can identify a British SAP250.There is a generational difference between bomb-disposal technicians in the UK. People who qualified before 2012 cut their teeth in Afghanistan, where the Taliban laid an extraordinary number of IEDs. In 2011 alone, US-led forces recorded 16,800 IED incidents, roughly 46 a day. Those who qualified after 2012 tend to have mainly worked on second world war munitions. Hambley’s own career has mapped this change. His first job as a bomb-disposal officer was in Helmand in 2012, walking toward a buried device while live rounds tore past his ear. These days, the problems are different: orchestrating large-scale evacuations of civilians, trying to avoid property damage. “You’ve got a lot more latitude than when you’re deployed in Afghanistan,” Hambley told me. “In the UK, we own the ground, no one is going to shoot at us, we’ve got time, so we can afford to be as safe as we possibly can be.” Caution, though, is slow – and the moment a bomb is discovered, the clock is ticking to get people back into their homes.Sitting at her desk overlooking Exmouth Marina, Fiona Bolt, a chartered financial planner in her 60s, could see the bomb on the dredger. At about 3pm on Wednesday 14 January, police knocked on the office door and told Bolt and her four colleagues to pack up and leave. “It was really quite scary,” she told me. By 8pm, the safety cordon had expanded from 100 to 400 metres and police started knocking on doors on streets near the marina. Some people went to stay with family members nearby, others in hotels. One of the Bolts’ neighbours ended up sleeping in their car.View image in fullscreenWO Sarah Rowland of 11EOD.Photograph: Sam Frost/The GuardianAs the night set in, Kidman’s team was out on the water, trying to see inside the bomb. The first X-ray images of the fuze were unusable: the steel casing, thickened and blistered by rust, defeated the beam. They spent seven hours cycling through different X-ray equipment, trying to get a clear image. As Kidman worked through the night, he could see lights going on and off at the far end of Exmouth harbour, in flats that would ideally be empty. Police can’t force anyone to leave. When someone refuses, police hand them a letter saying they’re staying at their own risk, and the regiment has to work around them. InGreat Yarmouththree years ago, Hambley worked to render a 250kg bomb safe with a resident “teeth-chatteringly close” – less than 50 metres away.When Bolt got up the next morning, she noticed her street, close to the marina, was eerily empty. When Bolt left the house she saw how far the exclusion zone had expanded along the seafront: it now encompassed 400 metres, and 2,000 properties. She didn’t have an office to go to. “I felt really lost, like a rabbit in headlights,” she said. “It was all just so out of my control.” The council had hastily assembled makeshift shelters out of a leisure centre and retirement home. When Bolt stopped by the leisure centre that day, she saw that camp beds and bedding had been brought in during the night, and Tesco had donated food. “If we’d been in wartime,” she said, “I imagine that’s what the community spirit was like.”By about 5pm, it was clear Bolt would not be going home that night. Her house was deep within the cordon. She stuffed essentials into a rucksack and walked across town to her son’s house. By 9pm the cordon had crept up to 600 metres, encompassing a further 500 homes, cleared block by block by police officers. This was a big operation, but in Germany, where far more unexploded ordnance lies buried, even larger scale evacuations are common. In September 2017, 60,000 peoplewere cleared from central Frankfurt, including two hospitals, so that a 1.8-tonne British “blockbuster” bomb could be defused. In 2025, the city of Cologne alone carried out 19 evacuations for wartime bombs, affecting almost 70,000 residents.At their respective sites, Dooley and Kidman were both acutely aware of the disruption around them, which adds an intense time pressure to their work. In Plymouth, all the buildings within a 100-metre radius of the building site had been evacuated on Wednesday, including the school. Dooley’s first X-rays, taken with the standard equipment, had come out completely black. At around 4pm on Thursday, high-sensitivity X-ray plates arrived from elsewhere in the country. Finally, a readable answer. The bomb had no mechanical fuze, and no anti-handling device. Dooley breathed a sigh of relief. “People could just calm down a little bit,” he said. “It wasn’t going to tick if you knocked it.”Soon afterwards, in the late afternoon, the high-sensitivity X-ray machine arrived in Exmouth. It went out on to the dredger. The team started scanning, and kept going for hours. Still nothing. Kidman reported back to the operations team: they couldn’t identify the fuze.The forward base in Exmouth was the lifeboat station, and over the course of Thursday it filled up with marina staff, police, coastguard and emergency planning officers from the council. Briefings and strategy meetings took place every few hours. The position of the bomb severely limited the normal mitigation procedures. The regiment’s standard protection for a 250kg bomb is a sand-filled fortification weighing about 350 tonnes. This could not be built on a barge. Abrasive cutting, an advanced technique for cutting out the fuze, was not deemed appropriate. The next option was towing the dredger out to sea and blowing the whole thing up. Griffin, the marina’s compliance manager, phoned its insurers to ask whether this would be covered. Most marine policies carry an act-of-war exclusion, which raises a difficult question: after 80 years, is a Luftwaffe bomb still an act of war? “We went round in circles, really,” said Griffin.This is a sensitive subject for 11EOD. In February 2021, a 1,000kg German bomb – one of the heaviest in the Luftwaffe’s arsenal – was discovered on a construction site next to Exeter University’s halls of residence. The team could not establish if the bomb was booby-trapped so it decided to do a controlled detonation where it was, with 400 tonnes of sand around it to absorb the blast. It was not enough. The explosion, which was heard for miles, left a crater the size of a double-decker bus in the ground and threw debris at least 250 metres, shattering windows of nearby buildings. The university claimed on its all-risks policy; the insurer, Allianz, declined, citing a clause excluding damage “occasioned by war”. The high court found in favour of the insurer. The military was not financially liable for this, but the experience of having every step of its process picked over in court made the unit even more cautious. “We are very aware that everything could end up in court and everything could be questioned,” said Hambley.0:33Exeter: WW2 bomb detonated after homes evacuated – videoCaution pulled one way and time pressure – the need to get people back into their homes in Exmouth and kids back to school in Plymouth – pulled another. The idea of exploding the entire dredger was ruled out due to the risk of environmental pollution from the 20,000 litres of fuel on board and fragmentation of the vessel itself. That left only one option: get the bomb into the water and tow it away to detonate safely at sea. But this left a question: how to remove it?By 11pm on Thursday 15 January, there was a plan for the smaller bomb in Plymouth: lift it out, place it in a 4x4 packed with sandbags, drive it 1km to the water’s edge, take it out to sea and blow it up there. By 12.30am, police and fire crews were going door-to-door to evacuate everyone who lived within 150 metres of the route. At about 2.30am, Dooley and another bomb operator lifted the 50kg bomb out of the pit with their hands, climbing up on a makeshift staircase they had built out of sandbags. The bomb, slick with mud, was cold and heavy. It was dark, and the steps, wedged deep in a muddy pit, were slippery. They placed the bomb carefully into the back of the waiting vehicle. The convoy slowly moved off, at walking pace. As the vehicles passed by, the police released the cordon, letting people back into their houses while the bomb was still crawling towards the sea.Once it was at the water’s edge, the bomb was carried down on to a boat and lowered over the side, where a buoyancy device was waiting so that it could be dragged along underwater at a safe distance from the boat. Dooley was aboard the navy boat, which lowered the bomb into the water as it got further away from the harbour. He’d had two hours sleep in the preceding 36 hours.The King’s Harbour Master, which controls shipping in Plymouth Sound, had given permission for the bomb to be detonated in a specific patch of sea, and they sailed out four nautical miles towards this spot. At the drop point, Dooley fixed an explosive charge to the bomb and had it lowered down to the seabed. A navy diver followed the rope down in the dark. It was pitch black and the water was thick with silt, rendering a torch useless. Working by touch, the diver undid the bolts, let the air out of the float and brought it to the surface.Map of Plymouth, showing the route taken as the bomb was driven to the water’s edge for disposal at sea.Map of Plymouth, showing the route taken as the bomb was driven to the water’s edge for disposal at sea.When the diver came back up, Dooley took the boat back a hundred metres. From there, the only thing showing the location of the bomb was a small lit float attached with a line, bobbing on the surface of the water. The swell of the waves kept hiding it. Police drones confirmed nobody on shore was in danger. The navy confirmed there was nothing on radar at sea. The charge was initiated. Dooley counted down.At 5.13am on Friday 16 January, the sea briefly lit in the dark. A plume of white water rose above the surface, then nothing. Eight decades after it was dropped, the bomb had been detonated.As this unfolded in Plymouth on Thursday night and into Friday morning, Exmouth Marina was empty except for the military bomb-disposal team and the two marina staffers. “It was quite eerie,” said Hockings-Thompson, the marina manager. “It was like going back to Covid times.” They were all focused on how to get the bomb off the dredger. Someone suggested bringing the dredger in closer, but moving the boat meant moving the bomb, and nobody wanted to risk it.Griffin went back into the office and called a local crane hire company, who agreed to bring a 55-tonne crane. The next problem was who would drive it. Senior officers including Fisher scrambled to find a military crane operator qualified to drive a 55-tonne crane, available at short notice. They could not. The civilian crane driver who had brought it over offered to do it himself. “I can’t own the risk of him driving that crane,” said Fisher, who held the military liability. That passed the question to the police, who had to decide whether to authorise a civilian to handle an unexploded bomb – and whose financial responsibility it would be if the crane was destroyed. “If the worst happens,” Fisher said, “we’ve got much bigger problems than losing the crane.” Eventually, they let him go ahead. (The crane driver declined to speak to me for this article.)After midnight, in the early hours of Friday 16 January, bomb-disposal operator Lt Matt Bowden attached straps around the bomb casing and added a buoyancy device. He left the dredger and the crane lifted the bomb. As the 250kg lifted from the deck, the barge rose in the water. They had discussed this in advance: whether the dredger, suddenly lighter, would bob up hard enough to bump into the bomb and trigger something. The dredger heaved. The bomb swung out to the side and missed the steel vessel entirely. It was lowered into the water and attached to a navy boat.Everything now depended on the tides. There was a fixed window in which it could be towed out and detonated. At about 4.30am, the boat picked its way through moored yachts with the bomb submerged and trailing 100 metres behind. By 6.30am, the bomb was so far out and deep underwater that residents were allowed back to their homes.Hockings-Thompson and Griffin, who had been mostly awake for the preceding 48 hours, went aboard the dredger to bring it back into the marina. Then they walked up to a coffee shop on the seafront. They were in the queue at 8.13am when the bomb went off, a mile and a half out. “The whole seafront was full of people expecting to see a massive bang and a splash,” said Griffin. “All we got was a bit of a plop.” The sea had done its job and neutralised the blast.By 11am, businesses around the marina were open again. Kidman was exhilarated. “No one died, there was no injury, no damage to infrastructure,” he said. After working for 36 hours straight, everyone went home to sleep. For Dooley, after his own successful operation in Plymouth, it was only a few hours later, when he was sitting with his family, that the magnitude of what had happened hit him. “You’re just doing your job,” he said. “Then you sit there and think, what have I done here? A 50kg could kill you as much as a 1,000kg.”In late summer, about six months after the double bomb discovery, I sat in the bar at Vauxhall Barracks with Dooley, Kidman, Fisher, Boyce and others who had worked on the two operations. It was a wood-panelled room with a blue patterned carpet, the wall adorned with regiment photos and a framed Private Eye cover of the Queen meeting Martin McGuinness in a bomb-disposal suit. As I pressed for details, they found their recollections blurring. Was a particular memory from 14 January? Or was it the 250kg Plymouth bomb that was found in April outside an Aldi? The one found in June at a business park in Coventry? “So much has happened since then,” said Boyce. In fact, WO Sarah Rowland, who had worked with Dooley on the bomb in Plymouth, was unable to join the meeting as that morning she’d been called out to Staffordshire, where a 500kg bomb had been found in a quarry. (She texted Dooley to say she was collecting them all, “like Pokémon cards”.)It came from outer space: the meteorite that landed in a Cotswolds cul-de-sacRead moreThey are getting busier. Ten years ago, one or two large airdropped weapons were found each year. This year there have already been six. The latest was on 21 September, when a 115kg American bomb was found in the water off Pendennis headland, at the mouth of Falmouth’s harbour. The call went to Dooley, but he was already on another job. Kidman was assigned to it and drove down to Cornwall, where he spent almost all of the next three days awake, problem solving. The job was complicated. Blowing it up where it lay risked rupturing waste tanks 40 metres away and pouring sewage into the Channel. Instead, more than 300 households were evacuated while the navy lifted the bomb and towed it out to deep water. It was too dangerous to send a navy diver down, so the bomb was left on the seabed, far from anyone, while the regiment counted down the hours.On 27 September, with the clock on the Falmouth bomb still running, another call came in: three white vans near RAF Fairford, a Gloucestershire base used by American bombers. A major counter-terror operation began. Kidman and Rowland drove to the scene. A robot searched the vans. X-rays followed. They helped each other out, catching some sleep in the car when possible. Kidman was still overseeing the bomb in Falmouth. On 28 September, they found that there were no explosives in the white vans. Kidman went home to sleep. At 2.25pm on 29 September, the timer was up on the bomb in Falmouth, so the team went back to detonate it at sea. “And then,” Kidman said, “we’re ready for the next bomb, I guess.”Listen to our podcastshereand sign up to the long read weekly emailhere.

title: Kemi Badenoch is the most rightwing leader in Tory history. Isn’t it time she got some actual scrutiny? | Owen Jones | The Guardian
description: Farage’s scandals have allowed Badenoch to get her party back in the race. But her programme would be no less ruinous for our country, says Guardian columnist Owen Jones
Author: Owen Jones
Headline: Farage’s scandals have allowed Badenoch to get her party back in the race. But her programme would be no less ruinous for our country, says Guardian columnist Owen Jones
Content: Kemi Badenoch prepares to give an interview at the Conservative party conference in Birmingham on Tuesday.Photograph: Oli Scarff/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenKemi Badenoch prepares to give an interview at the Conservative party conference in Birmingham on Tuesday.Photograph: Oli Scarff/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionKemi BadenochKemi Badenoch is the most rightwing leader in Tory history. Isn’t it time she got some actual scrutiny?Owen JonesFarage’s scandals have allowed Badenoch to get her party back in the race. But her programme would be no less ruinous for our countryTue 6 Oct 2026 14.04 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 19.57 EDTShareThe Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, will march on to the conference stage in Birmingham feeling buoyed. “Kemi’s soaring,”coos the Sun, and that sums up the prevailing wisdom. More than four in 10 Britonsthink she is doing wellas Tory leader, compared with a third who think otherwise. As Nigel Farage’s stock has plummeted thanks to scandals over a £5m personal gift anddonations from crypto billionaires, the polling suggests that the Conservatives could regain the mantle of Britain’s main rightwing force.Yet Badenoch has been the beneficiary of circumstance. Her tenure as opposition leader has been defined by Keir Starmer’s project imploding almost as soon as it gained power. When Reform UK enjoyed its seismic polling lead, the Tory plight was double-edged: they were starved of attention, but that inevitably resulted in a lack of scrutiny, too. It has been easy for Badenoch to appear formidable while her opponents have disintegrated.With the Conservatives now back in the race, the spotlight falls on Badenoch. Let us consider the absurdity of her proposed air defence system. Our would-be prime ministerdenied comparing it to Israel’s Iron Dome, despite the term appearing in both a press release and a newspaper article under her own name. This amateurishness is one thing, but even on its own terms, her proposal is a mess. It will “protect the whole United Kingdom, our sovereign territories and British bases overseas”, she claims, which would be impossible for the £10bn over 10 years she is proposing to spend on it.The former British general Richard Barrons suggestssuch a systemwould cost more than £100bn.What does this say about Badenoch’s sense of priorities? The actual urgent national security threat Britain faces is not volleys of missile attacks, but the climate emergency. There were estimated to be thousands of excess deaths from heatwaves this summer, while ourintelligence serviceswarn of serious disruption to our food supply from 2030. YetBadenoch has committed to repealing the Climate Change Actand claimed that net zero by 2050 is “impossible” without bankrupting Britain. This not onlycontradicts the conclusionof the government’s statutory climate scientific advisers, but Badenoch herself. As a Treasury minister in 2021,she told parliamentthat it would cost less than 2% of GDP, largely from “increased investment in growth markets of the future”. Even three former Tory prime ministers have criticised Badenoch’s shift against net zero –including the former rightwing pin-upBoris Johnson.Then there’s her economic agenda.A year ago, Badenoch declared that she sought to become Britain’s version of Argentina’s far-right president, Javier Milei. His government has imposed devastating cuts to pensions,universitiesandpublic healthcare, while poverty isonce more surging. Badenoch proposes welfare cuts worth £23bn, and misleads the public as she does so. In May,she declared: “For the first time ever, the total welfare bill is now higher than total receipts from income tax.” This has been the case since 2011, and as the UK Statistics Authority notedin a letterrebuking her, this was misleading for other reasons: the gap had actually narrowed in recent years, and most of the welfare bill goes to pensioner benefits, including the state pension.What would £23bn in cuts mean? They would includestripping workers with indefinite leave to remainof social security – people who have lived here for years, worked and paid taxes. That would not only be an injustice to them – consider that there isalready a staffing crisisin sectors such as social care that immigration restrictions are worsening. She wouldreinstate a two-child benefit capthat would drive hundreds of thousands of children into poverty. Most of the rest would fall on the shoulders of sick and disabled people, including those receiving support while they work.Consider this too: while we still live with the consequences of the 2008 financial crash,Badenoch proposes endingthe ringfence for big banks separating retail and investment activities, and reducing their capital requirements.What of her authoritarianism? Badenoch hasdeclared free speechto be “the birthright of every citizen”, yet has advocated a blanket ban on pro-Palestinian protests. The justification is conflating opposition to genocide with threats to Jewish people, but this is a Tory leader who, when asked about Gaza,said that“Israel is fighting a proxy war on behalf of the UK”. Withdrawal from the European convention on human rights and repealing the Human Rights Act would strip citizens of crucial protections against an overbearing executive and abuses of state power. Badenochadvocates an ICE-style mass deportationapparatus with sweeping powers of surveillance – directly mimicking an institution across the Atlantic that snatches people from the street and kills migrants and US citizens alike.Her attitude to the rights of minorities, meanwhile, is underlined by her commitment toscrap the public sector equality dutyin its entirety. As a minister in 2021, shebacked it, saying it helped ensure “that fairness is at the heart of everything we do”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionYet the average punter knows little about Badenoch. The increasing extremism and scandals of Farageism have allowed her to appear somehow more reasonable and stable in comparison. But Badenoch is easily the most rightwing Tory leader in the party’s history. Her programme is a wishlist of rightwing zealots – one which would be ruinous to our social fabric. Yet few have bothered to look under the bonnet. The danger is that Britain discovers what Badenoch really stands for only when she is close enough to power to put it into practice.Owen Jones is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
