title: Morrisons is not a must-do deal for Sainsbury’s | Nils Pratley | The Guardian
description: Odds are good the CMA would approve of a supermarket merger. But does Sainsbury’s need Morrisons?
Author: Nils Pratley
Headline: Odds are good the CMA would approve of a supermarket merger. But does Sainsbury’s need Morrisons?
Content: Morrisons and Sainbury’s are in merger talks.Composite: AlamyView image in fullscreenMorrisons and Sainbury’s are in merger talks.Composite: AlamyNils Pratley on financeJ SainsburyMorrisons is not a must-do deal for Sainsbury’sNils PratleyOdds are good the CMA would approve of a supermarket merger. But does Sainsbury’s need Morrisons?Tue 6 Oct 2026 14.10 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTShareWould competition regulators really smile upon a combination of Sainsbury’s and Morrisons? One must assume the two companies believed the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) would give a thumbs up if asked, otherwise they would not have initiatedtheir now-aborted merger talks.It’s easy to list the arguments the duo could make. First, the combined market share of Sainsbury’s (15.2%, on the latest numbers from Worldpanel analysts) and Morrisons (8.4%) would still be less than that of mighty Tesco (27.8%). It would not be a case of leap-frogging the market leader, which was Sainsbury’s big idea back in 2018 whenAsda was in its sights.Second, Aldi and Lidl are a stronger force in the land. Together, the German discounters represent almost a fifth of the UK market and, since they’re backed by serious international buying muscle, their role as the country’s grocery price police might not be affected one jot.Sainsbury’s and Morrisons ‘held talks this year’ on multibillion-pound mergerRead moreThird, since Morrisons has already sold its petrol stations, the CMA needn’t worry about the touchy issue of fuel. Fourth, at a push, Sainsbury’s and Morrisons could argue that the UK’s food security (a growing political worry) would improve if the latter’s 18 food-processing factories were housed within a stronger company that could boost local production.So, yes, one would probably bet that the CMA would ultimately approve some version of a deal. But what version? How many store disposals would be demanded?The CMA, as in 2018, would presumably conduct a site-by-site analysis of drive-times to judge local competition. The regulatory instinct, one suspects, would be to err on the side of intervention in light of the overall national picture. Never mind Tesco’s size, it would still not be a simple decision for a competition regulator to sanction a supermarket setup in which half the trade, or thereabouts, would be in the hands of just two companies.Would a deal still make sense after the CMA’s remedies? It’s impossible for Sainsbury’s andMorrisonsto know until they go through the process. That’s the distraction factor for Sainsbury’s. Does its chief executive, Simon Roberts, really want to spend a year bogged down in regulatory back-and-forth? In the Asda episode, the effort sucked the life out of his predecessor’s reign.It’s not as if Sainsbury’s is struggling today. The group is winning market share, profit margins are stable, there’s enough spare cash for share buy-backs and the strategic headaches of itsbankand Argos have been solved byselling both. While it would be preferable to square up to Tesco’s buyers on more equal terms, life ain’t bad.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRound at private equity-owned Morrisons, the calculation will be different. Five years afterbuying the chain for £7bn, owners Clayton, Dubilier & Rice’s thoughts will be turning to how to exit a tricky investment. A disposal will surely look easier than a stock market flotation and the list of potential suitors is short: Sainsbury’s is indeed the obvious candidate.All of which says Sainsbury’s can afford to do nothing, or wait for the terms of any deal to improve. It was the party that walked away from the talks, reported the FT. That’s not a surprise. If a relative bargain is possible, the hassle of a CMA process might be worthwhile. But this is not a must-do deal for Sainsbury’s.Explore more on these topicsJ SainsburyNils Pratley on financeMorrisonsRetail industrySupermarketsMergers and acquisitionsCompetition and Markets AuthorityRegulatorscommentShareReuse this content

title: Pedro Sánchez is a master of the political comeback. But calling a snap election in Spain may be a gamble too far | Paolo Gerbaudo | The Guardian
description: A thriving economy, a model green transition, social advances – Spain’s PM shouldn’t be in trouble. Yet he is, and it’s a lesson for progressives everywhere, says sociologist Paolo Gerbaudo
Author: Paolo Gerbaudo
Headline: A thriving economy, a model green transition, social advances – Spain’s PM shouldn’t be in trouble. Yet he is, and it’s a lesson for progressives everywhere, says sociologist Paolo Gerbaudo
Content: Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, attends a press conference at the Moncloa palace, Madrid, on Tuesday.Photograph: Juan Medina/ReutersView image in fullscreenSpain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, attends a press conference at the Moncloa palace, Madrid, on Tuesday.Photograph: Juan Medina/ReutersOpinionSpainPedro Sánchez is a master of the political comeback. But calling a snap election in Spain may be a gamble too farPaolo GerbaudoA thriving economy, a model green transition, social advances – Spain’s PM shouldn’t be in trouble. Yet he is, and it’s a lesson for progressives everywhereTue 6 Oct 2026 10.57 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 12.48 EDTShareTo progressives across the west, Spain has been arare glimmer of hopein a world where far-right parties are increasingly entering government. Under Pedro Sánchez, who became prime minister in 2018, the country has combined a post-Covid economic boom with a bold green energy transition programme, anda pro-immigration stance with a principled opposition to the war agenda of Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu. Yet, at the end of next month, this rare beacon of democratic progress could fall.OnMondaySánchez called asnap generalelection, set for 29 November, after two decrees to address the country’s housing crisiswere voted downin the lower chamber by politicians from rightwing parties. Speaking from the staircase of the Moncloa palace,Sánchez admittedthat his government had not achieved all it had set out to do. “Many injustices remain to be corrected … particularly regarding inequality in public services and access to housing,” he said, adding: “To do more, we need to renew and expand public support.”Sánchez attempted to pass the legislation after tens of thousands took to the streets to protest against the housing crisis,setting up camps reminiscent of thecountry’s 15-M anti-austerity movementand the global Occupy movement of 2011. But this explosion of popular anger has been long in the making. According to Spain’s national public opinion research institute Centro de Investigaciones Sociológicas (CIS), housing has been thecountry’s top preoccupationsince the end of 2024, as a growing number of people struggle to pay rent.It shouldn’t take the eviction of an 87-year-old to get Spain’s housing crisis fixed | María RamírezRead moreIn the latest gamble of his long career as master of the political comeback, Sánchez hopes to ride the wave of popular mobilisation to turn public attention away from theCeuta immigration crisisof July, which rightwing opponents exploited as a demonstration of the government’s failures, and focus attention on the housing crisis, an issue where the left holds stronger political ground.But this time it will be hard to convince Spaniards that with a new lease of life, the progressive coalitiongovernment will solve an issue it had promised to address a long time ago.Sánchez’s troubles provide useful lessons for progressives all over the world about the difficulties of translating policy achievements into a solid base of political support.They are also a reminder that – as championed by New York’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani – addressing the affordability crisis rather than promising abstract economic growth is of more significance to voters.In the US midterm election campaign, Republicans are struggling because ofrising prices at the gas pump, while in Brazil, rightwing challengerFlávio Bolsonaro justrode to an impressive resultin the first round of the presidential elections partly due to discontent with living conditions and household pressures. In Spain, Sánchez’s government is facing similar concerns about affordability, which are obfuscating an otherwise impressive macro-economic performance.Indeed, seen from the outside, Sánchez’s Spain may appear to be a dazzling political success. The country, which in the 2010s was derided as part of theEuropean Piigs– a term coined to mock Portugal, Ireland, Italy, Greece and Spain as the eurozone’s weakest economies –has become an economic powerhouse. In the years after the Covid pandemic, Spain’s GDPgrew at a rate of around 3%, while France, Germany, the UK and Italy grew at a miserly 1% or less.Spain is also held up as a model of successful green transition, with renewables now generating close to60% of the country’s power, which has also kept energy bills low and helped insulate the country from the energy shocks caused by international crises. Spain, enabled by significant Chinese investment, is also surprisingly becoming the leading European hub for electric car production, to thedismay of some of the country’s traditional allies.To these economic and environmental achievements add the significant social improvements achieved under Sánchez, exemplified by the rise in the minimum wage from€736 to €1,184 per month since 2018.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionYet despite these measurable successes, Sánchez’s centre-left coalition is nowtrailing the right by about 7 percentage pointsin national polling. That’s partly because while minimum wages have increased, median wages have remained relatively stagnant. But it is real estate that Sánchez’s government has been judged as failing to deliver: during its eight years in power, house prices have risenby an estimated 50%, with rents rising by over 40%.As climbing the housing ladder becomes prohibitive, a growing number of young people in Spain are forced to pay extortionate rents. This is acutely felt in large urban areas, where the presence of tourists and digital nomads further increases rents, forcing out local residents; this is enabled by private equity firms, who purchase entire blocks to expel local inhabitants in orderto create Airbnbs. Sánchez’s government has repeatedly promised to take action on these issues, but its measures have been thwarted by political gridlock or otherwiseproven indecisive, partly due to fear of alienating homeowners and antagonising international finance.If Spain’s centre-left coalition falls, the country could be left with an alliance of the mainstream conservative Partido Popular and the far-right party Vox. It would be the most rightwing Spanish government since Francisco Franco’s dictatorship.The lesson for progressives everywhere is clear: economic growth and ambitious reform will count for little unless working people feel the benefits in their daily lives.Paolo Gerbaudo is a senior researcher at the faculty of political science and sociology of Complutense University in Madrid and a lead researcher at the Alameda InstituteExplore more on these topicsSpainOpinionPedro SánchezThe far rightEuropecommentShareReuse this content

title: Stop worrying about my AI, says multibillionaire Sam Altman. So we bear the risks and he keeps the money | Chris Stokel-Walker | The Guardian
description: OpenAI’s CEO seems to want to privatise his company’s huge financial gains while making all of us pay for any negative consequences, says author Chris Stokel-Walker
Author: Chris Stokel-Walker
Headline: OpenAI’s CEO seems to want to privatise his company’s huge financial gains while making all of us pay for any negative consequences, says author Chris Stokel-Walker
Content: Sam Altman at an OpenAI developers conference in San Francisco on 29 September 2026.Photograph: Heather Diehl/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSam Altman at an OpenAI developers conference in San Francisco on 29 September 2026.Photograph: Heather Diehl/Getty ImagesOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)Stop worrying about my AI, says multibillionaire Sam Altman. So we bear the risks and he keeps the moneyChris Stokel-WalkerOpenAI’s CEO seems to want to privatise his company’s huge financial gains while making all of us pay for any negative consequencesTue 6 Oct 2026 11.30 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 12.49 EDTShareTech bros’ messianic streaks can show up in subtle ways. But one of Sam Altman’s flaws is that he often lacks that subtlety. “We believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology,” said the OpenAI chief executivein an interview with Politicolast weekend.That’s easy for Altman to say. But it’s pretty galling to hear for the rest of us. Lest we forget, we didn’t ask for OpenAI to unleash AI agents that went rogue andweaselled their way into government IT systemsand private businesses around the world. Nobody voted for ChatGPT to be released, but the company put it out into the world as a test product that happened to catch the zeitgeist. That kickstarted an arms race among AI companies to push the frontier of the technology ever further and faster, resulting in the mess we now find ourselves in.OpenAI’s competitors, including Anthropic, have started to step back from the brink – as has OpenAI itself, decidingnot to release its latest modelbecause it’s purportedly too dangerous. Anthropic’s CEO, Dario Amodei, hastalked about needing to “pace the frontier”: tech-bro jargon for pumping the brakes to bring down the speed at which the runaway vehicle is skidding out of control.Yet we’re expected to take these incidents – and the harm they cause – as the natural consequences of OpenAI’s continued march towards an IPO that would bring its investors millions. It’s hard to escape the idea that Altman wants to privatise his company’s gains while socialising the risks of untrammelled AI development.Every useful technology – and AI is a useful technology, despite the holdouts and occasional users’ carping – carries risk. Cars can and do crash, while medicines that save us often have harmful side effects. Very rarely, aircraft fall from the sky. But we accept those risks because the benefits are substantial, and we build rules to limit the harm. We also make companies liable. And most importantly, we get some say in deciding what level of risk is and isn’t acceptable.Altman seems to suggest that his company’s messes are our problem to sort out – or worse, that the consequences of his tech are ours to tolerate. But Altman would do well to think about this differently. OpenAI gets to decide how fast it develops its technology and when it releases it. Its investors benefit financially if those bets pay off. But it feels as if he’s suggesting that when the tech creates problems outside OpenAI’s own walls, the costs of cleaning up are ours to bear, not his company’s.The idea that private companies profit while we’re left to deal with the consequences becomes even harder to defend as AI stops being something we opt into using as a chatbot, and becomes something that acts on and changes the world around us. If I ask ChatGPT something and it gives me a bad answer, I chose to expose myself to that risk, so should share that burden. But the same isn’t true for a government department that suddenly finds an OpenAI agent lurking in its files and rooting around. It didn’t opt in; it became an unwilling participant in someones experiment.That’s why Altman’s argument sounds so disingenuous. OpenAI shouldn’t be able to decide for all of us what is and isn’t an acceptable level of failure, then ask everyone to live with the result. The burden ought to be on it to prove its technology can be trusted – and to pick up the bill if it can’t.It’s no wonder that OpenAI wants to travel quickly. The company isseeking $30bn in new funding, and a valuation of $1.4tn ahead of a public listing likely next year. There’s money to be made – never mind at whose expense.To his credit, Altman also acknowledged in the Politico interview that there will need to be a liability framework for companies offering models such as OpenAI’s, and that the company will have to take responsibility for at least some of what goes wrong during training. But that “some” is doing a lot of work.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIf Altman believes some bad things are an acceptable price for AI’s progress, OpenAI can dig into its deep pockets to pay that price itself – for instance if its agents go rogue and do damage to government or private company systems, or compromise user data. It can’t, and shouldn’t, get the financial upside when everything goes right, then ask the rest of us to accept the consequences when things go wrong. That’s especially the case when we never agreed to the unregulated experiment in the first place.Chris Stokel-Walker is the author of TikTok Boom: The Inside Story of the World’s Favourite AppExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionSam AltmanOpenAIComputingcommentShareReuse this content

title: JD Vance and Ted Cruz are fighting for control of the GOP. The problem? Neither is called Trump | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: Having seemingly written off the midterms, the Republican bigwigs are making their pitches for 2028. But the current commander-in-chief could be looking closer to home, writes Arwa Mahdawi
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: Having seemingly written off the midterms, the Republican bigwigs are making their pitches for 2028. But the current commander-in-chief could be looking closer to home, writes Arwa Mahdawi
Content: Best of enemies … Ted Cruz and JD Vance at a conservative conference in 2023.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBest of enemies … Ted Cruz and JD Vance at a conservative conference in 2023.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesOpinionUS midterm elections 2026JD Vance and Ted Cruz are fighting for control of the GOP. The problem? Neither is called TrumpArwa MahdawiHaving seemingly written off the midterms, the Republican bigwigs are making their pitches for 2028. But the current commander-in-chief could be looking closer to homeTue 6 Oct 2026 10.46 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 17.15 EDTShareThe US midterm elections are a month away and it’s looking rough for the Republicans. I wouldn’t discountdevious schemesbehind the scenes, but, on the face of it, the president and his entourage seem to be flailing. Donald Trump is desperatelydangling moneyin front of voters andpromising “a big surprise”. Meanwhile, the vice-president, JD Vance, and the GOP senator Ted Cruz seem more concerned with fighting over who will be Trump’s heir than with the midterms.If the polls are to be believed,Vance is the frontrunnerfor the Republican presidential nomination in 2028. But while he may have great name recognition, Vance is also unlikable. According to theCNN analyst Harry Enten, he is one of the least popular vice-presidents in history. He’s also apparentlymade enemies within his own party, largely because of his scepticism about the Iran war. His detractors include Cruz, who toldMS Nowin August that Vance wasn’t a shoo-in for the nomination. The party, Cruz said, was still figuring out the best candidate and needed “to decide who we are, what do we believe”.These remarks did not go unnoticed by the ever-observant vice-president. “It is really obvious to me that, at this very moment, Ted Cruz is running for president,” Vance said in an interview with NBC Newson Friday. “At this moment, I’m not. I’m trying to help elect Republicans.”Cruz, in turn, denied he was thinking about 2028 yet and suggested Vance may have a chip on his shoulder. “In my experience, people engage in political bomb-throwing when they’re feeling insecure,” Cruztold Politicoon Saturday. “So he’s welcome to make whatever comments he likes.”Yes, please continue making whatever comments you like, JD! In fact, I’d strongly suggest you take it up a notch and remind people of Cruz’s greatest hits. There was the time he fled to Cancún on holiday when his state, Texas, was facingdeadly, record-breaking freezing temperatures, for example. And the time his official Twitter account “liked” apornographic tweet(apparently it was “a staffing issue, and it was inadvertent”). And there’s the longstanding joke, which started with a meme in 2013, that Cruz is theZodiac killer. Obviously, this was baseless, but it went viral because apparently it is believable. Indeed, a2016 pollfound that 10% of voters in Florida thought Cruz was the Zodiac killer and an additional 28% said they were not sure.That said, Vance should be careful about what he dishes out: he’s been the subject of a few memes himself. Who can forget the (completely unfounded) viral rumours about the vice-presidenthaving sexual relations with a couch?While Vance and Cruz may be butting heads now, I suspect they’ll eventually kiss and make up. They are pragmatists, which is a polite way to say soulless opportunists. They had similar journeys when it comes to Trump, for example. In 2016,Cruz called Trump, who nicknamed him Lyin’ Ted, a “serial philanderer” and a “pathological liar”. Around the same time, Vance wondered if Trump was“America’s Hitler”andcalled him“the most-raw expression of a massive finger pointed at other people”. Now, of course, it’s a very different story. Vance is veep and Cruz has become such a staunch Trump ally that the president calls himBeautiful Ted.With the news as grim as it is, you’ve got to find satisfaction where you can. And it’s certainly satisfying to watch Vance (who absolutely does not fornicate with furniture) and Cruz (who is definitely not the Zodiac killer) feud. Ultimately, though, it may turn out that we don’t have to worry about either man come 2028. MS Now’s Rachel Maddow thinks the president may follow the authoritarian playbook and install a family member as his successor.“If he wants [his family] to not end up in jail or prosecuted or having their … gains investigated … he’s got to make sure that the next president is also a Trump,” Maddow opined on arecent podcast. Potus himselfhas said“there could be” a Trump dynasty and seemed to suggest his daughter-in-law Lara may be his successor. Take a seat on a comfy couch for this one, JD: you’re going to have a tough time trumping a Trump.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines USGet the most important US headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionArwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on the French school protests: the political class needs to heed the voice of students | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: A generation facing unprecedented challenges deserves better than an underfunded education system
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: A generation facing unprecedented challenges deserves better than an underfunded education system
Content: High school students and the unions supporting them gather in Reforme Square and begin marching toward Porte d'Aix on 6 October in Marseille, France.Photograph: Sener Yilmaz Aslan/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenHigh school students and the unions supporting them gather in Reforme Square and begin marching toward Porte d'Aix on 6 October in Marseille, France.Photograph: Sener Yilmaz Aslan/Getty ImagesOpinionFranceThe Guardian view on the French school protests: the political class needs to heed the voice of studentsEditorialA generation facing unprecedented challenges deserves better than an underfunded education systemTue 6 Oct 2026 14.31 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 18.48 EDTShareOne of the most famousslogansin France’s May 1968 student protests declared “L’imagination au pouvoir” (Power to the imagination). In a postwar context of steady growth, the ’68ers dreamed of shaping an egalitarian society, freed from the social constraints of their parents’ generation. Nearly five decades on, in a very different economic climate, the goal for most of the tens of thousands of pupilsdisruptingschools across the country is more modest. As one placard on display had it: “I’d like to be worrying about my maths exam, not my future”.A hugeturnoutof hundreds of thousands of protesters on Tuesday – a number that included many parents and teachers – confirmed the depth of resentment at years of budget cuts leading to crumbling school buildings, overcrowded classes and chronic staff shortages. Other complaints point to a lack of resources to deal with the now frequent heatwaves that make classrooms intolerable in May and June, and the unfairness of an opaque, algorithmically driven selection process for universities.Confronted by the anxieties of a generation facing challenges ranging from the climate emergency to the impact of AI on future job opportunities, the response of Emmanuel Macron’s government has been disastrously heavy-handed. Instead of being instructed to show maximum restraint, given the age of most of those involved, security forces wereurgedto intervene to break up the school “blockades”. The result has been heightened confrontation and unacceptable violence on both sides. More than 200 students have been injured, as well as over 700 police officers and a number of teachers. One 15-year-old boyhadhis hand blown off during a protest in Lens, another lost an eye, and more than 4,000 minors were taken into custody, with nearly 1,500 facing prosecution.At a political level, the eruption of anger over the underfunding of education has underlined the folly of Mr Macron’s ongoing attempt to balance France’s books by taking an axe to social spending. During his chaotic second term as president, five prime ministers have attempted to force through austerity budgets in order to cut the deficit and satisfy increasingly restive bond markets. The latest, Sébastien Lecornu, has belatedly said that the students’ core demands should be addressed. But last month heproposedcuts worth €54bn, including a real-terms reduction in schools funding. A credible approach would require more resources, not less.Six months out from a presidential election in which Marine Le Pen is the frontrunner, the spectacle of burned-out schools, baton rounds and teargassed protesters feels ominous. As French politics polarises amid a crisis of faith in mainstream leaders, Ms Le Pen has accused the hard left of fomenting the school protests and called for a toughening up of “anti-riot” legislation. Public sector workers were on the streets on Tuesday, demonstrating against wage freezes. The major unions are jointlyplanningfurther demonstrations for November. An autumn of discontent now seems possible, as a lame-duck government enters its final months.Mass protest in the streets is hardly an unknown phenomenon in France. But as calls mount for government spending to be furthercutto appease market sentiment, the scale and intensity of the school protests should be heeded by the political class. As the social contract in France comes under increasing strain, the voice of its protesting students needs to be heard.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on the Green party and Palestine: rejecting two states is no shortcut to peace | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Zack Polanski must defend Palestinian freedom while reassuring Jewish members and showing that his party can handle disagreements
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Zack Polanski must defend Palestinian freedom while reassuring Jewish members and showing that his party can handle disagreements
Content: Zack Polanski delivering his speech on day one of the Green party conference in Brighton on 2 October 2026.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAView image in fullscreenZack Polanski delivering his speech on day one of the Green party conference in Brighton on 2 October 2026.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAOpinionGreen partyThe Guardian view on the Green party and Palestine: rejecting two states is no shortcut to peaceEditorialZack Polanski must defend Palestinian freedom while reassuring Jewish members and showing that his party can handle disagreementsTue 6 Oct 2026 14.34 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTShareLast year, the UN general assembly endorsed theNew York Declarationsupporting two states in the Holy Land by 142 votes to 10. Those voting against included the US and Israel. The wider international diplomatic consensus rests on a2002 UN security council resolution, which explicitly affirmed a two-state vision for Israel and Palestine. Saudi Arabia’s then crown princesaidpeace required “two equal parties” and could not survive “oppression and humiliation”. His words remain as relevant now as then.The Green party has nowrejectedthat two-state framework in favour of a one-state solution. The Guardian strongly disagrees with this move. Peace needs to acknowledge reality: the latestpollsin Gaza and the West Bank suggest that a majority support a two-state formula based on the 1967 borders compared with just 10% who back a single democratic state with equal rights. The European Greens alsodisagreewith the new direction of their English and Welsh sister party. The EU-wide representatives argue that the policy is incompatible with previously agreed positions. Europe’s Greens – which include the centrist German party – condemn “the genocide against Palestinians” and call for sanctions against Israel’s government.Political scientistssaythat currently, west of the Jordan River, one system under Israeli control enforces unequal laws and relegates Palestinians to a “lower caste”. The international consensus has plainly failed to deliver Palestinian statehood, or indeed prevent the near-total destruction of Gaza by Israel. But a “single democratic” entity in Palestine seems even more remote. There may need to be fresh future thinking about peace, includingconfederationmodels being considered as the crisis deepens in theoccupied Palestinian territories. The ultimate test of any solution to the Israel-Palestine conflict is whether it ends domination by any one group and provides equal rights so both peoples have a secure political future.The vote at the Green party conference to adopt acontroversialset of policies was decided by about 200 votes – less than one-thousandth of the membership. The Greens’ leader, Zack Polanski, who is himself Jewish, has become embroiled in a row over antisemitism around the third anniversary of the 7 October attacks, at a time when he is fighting a parliamentary byelection in London. Themotiondefines Zionism as being “to the exclusion and/or domination of the non-Jewish population” in historic Palestine. Most in the Jewish community disagree, seeing it solely in terms ofJewish self-determination. The anger is real and understandable. There could be real-world consequences. The policy declares that an ideology that most Jewish people identify with is racist and raises the question of whether someone who identifies as a Zionist can remain in the Greens.Green delegates rejected safeguards against disciplining members for affiliation with Jewish institutions identifying as Zionist. Lawyers warn that Zionist beliefs may qualify for protection under equality legislation. On Monday, Mr Polanskiruled out“exclusion, or refusal to engage with anyone” in the Greens because of religious or communal affiliation. The test is whether the party honours this in practice. Whatever the motion’s eventual impact, it is clear that Green party structures urgently need to be reformed for a mass membership base. Mr Polanski, a London assembly member, wants to join the five Green MPs in parliament. He will need to show a surer political touch to get there.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Why a PR voting system is the best bet for Britain | Electoral reform | The Guardian
description: Letters: Tom Walker responds to a letter that said first past the post is the lesser of two evils for voters. Plus letters from Susanna Dammann and Steve Smart
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Tom Walker responds to a letter that said first past the post is the lesser of two evils for voters. Plus letters from Susanna Dammann and Steve Smart
Content: ‘The fundamental problem with first past the post is that millions of votes have little bearing on parliament.’Photograph: Matthew Horwood/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘The fundamental problem with first past the post is that millions of votes have little bearing on parliament.’Photograph: Matthew Horwood/Getty ImagesElectoral reformLettersWhy a PR voting system is the best bet for BritainTom Walkerresponds to a letter that said first past the post is the lesser of two evils for voters. Plus letters fromSusanna DammannandSteve SmartTue 6 Oct 2026 12.56 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 14.05 EDTShareIt is common in the argument against proportional representation (PR) to reach for Italy as a cautionary tale, as Gian Lorenzo Spisso does in his letter (A proportional representation voting system could spell disaster for Labour, 30 September). The irony is that Italy does not actually have a proportional system: it has a mixed system. If we want to assess PR, we should look at countries that actually use it – Germany, Sweden, the Netherlands, Denmark – hardly synonymous with political instability.Also, small parties or weak local representation are not unique to PR. The tiny Democratic Unionist party held the balance of power at Westminster less than a decade ago under first past the post (FPTP), while the Scottish National party and Plaid Cymru wield influence disproportionate to their UK-wide vote because their support is geographically concentrated.Germany limits fragmentation with a minimum electoral threshold. And systems such as Germany’s combine PR with constituency MPs, while Ireland’s single transferable vote system retains a strong geographical link between voters and representatives.Gian’s letter does raise a more interesting point: FPTP encourages major parties to contain competing tendencies within broad internal coalitions rather than allowing them to form separate parties. But is it preferable for those coalitions to be internal and opaque, forcing voters into tactical choices, rather than external and explicit, requiring parties to negotiate and find common ground?The fundamental problem with FPTP is that millions of votes have little bearing on parliament. If your preferred candidate has no realistic chance of winning, voting for them does not translate into representation. In 2024, Labourwon33.7% of votes cast but 63.2% of the seats. That distortion is not a minor technical flaw. Who wields power depends heavily on where votes are cast rather than who people vote for. This disconnect is precisely why Britain needs electoral reform.The question isn’t whether PR is perfect, but whether we can design a system in which parliament reflects the votes people actually cast. Other stable democracies do so. Britain can too.Tom WalkerLondonRe Gian Lorenzo Spisso’s letter and Zoe Williams’ article (Electoral reform could be a gamble too far for Burnham, 30 September), there are several reasons for the UK to adopt a more proportional voting system of which the most important is the moral one: it’s fairer.In the last general election, the current system gave us a government that only about 20% of the electorate had voted for. No wonder the public has been hostile since the start of this administration: almost 80% of us didn’t vote for it.There are other, more pragmatic reasons, particularly for those of us on the centre/soft left: if we are anxious to avoid having an extreme party in power, we need to ditch first past the post – and fast. Reform UK may be lagging a little in the polls at the moment, but with £76m behind them, they may be able to mount a campaign of mis- and disinformation that could persuade 30% of the electorate to vote for them – and they might win. If we don’t want an extreme right (or left) party in power, we need a way to elect MPs that reflects that view. We need proportional representation.Of course, not all PR systems are the same. Italy uses a mixed system similar to the one used in Scotland for elections to Holyrood. However, as a report published byMake Votes Matteron possible future electoral systems points out, the Italian system “tilts the playing field rather than levelling it”. Its results do not reflect the views of the Italian population accurately.The crucial effect of any proportional system that meets the criteria of the “good systems agreement” (which sets out the standards that a system should meet to be considered by the proposed national commission) is to encourage cross-party collaboration and cooperation. It undermines the tit-for-tat squabbling so typical of our House of Commons and reduces the policy flip-flop of right-left-right administrations that makes it so hard for businesses, and individuals, to plan long term. It is precisely that collaborative, creative approach to policy that would encourage the stability and prosperity our people are longing for.Susanna DammannLondonGian Lorenzo Spisso’s letter arguing against proportional representation voting in the UK is superficial and wrong-headed. Up and down the country there are huge numbers of voters like me whose entire lifetime has been spent thoroughly fed up with our unfair system. I am 79 now, and my vote has never elected an MP since I lived in an urban area private rental in my early 20s.As a middle-class, left-leaning voter living in mainly middle-class towns and suburbs, my vote has been wasted in a succession of places. Of course PR could elect a rightwing government; it could also lock the right wing out of power for a long time, and as a democratic socialist I would be happy to live with the prospect of a long-term progressive coalition. PR would also give the Greens the scale of representation in parliament that their increasing national support deserves.Steve SmartMalvern, WorcestershireHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Unemployment and the rise of the Nazis | Nazism | The Guardian
description: Letter: John Plowright reflects on how unemployment was viewed by Germans and the fear the KPD sparked
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: John Plowright reflects on how unemployment was viewed by Germans and the fear the KPD sparked
Content: Adolf Hitler giving a speech, circa 1925.Photograph: Brandstaetter Images/GettyView image in fullscreenAdolf Hitler giving a speech, circa 1925.Photograph: Brandstaetter Images/GettyNazismLettersUnemployment and the rise of the NazisJohn Plowrightreflects onhow unemployment was viewed by Germans and the fear the KPD sparkedTue 6 Oct 2026 12.55 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 13.56 EDTSharePhilipp Ruch believes that the impact of the 1929 Wall Street crash cannot explain the Nazi breakthrough at the 1930 Reichstag election, as the full effects of Black Thursday “didn’t fully arrive in Germany until July 1931” (‘Hitler was a lazy criminal who slept in until noon’: why most of what we think we know about the rise of the Nazis is wrong, 1 October). But unemployment more than doubled between 1928 and the 1930 election, and that fact alone might be thought sufficient to explain the change in Nazi fortunes. Not so, says Ruch, for “in regions where unemployment was high, the Nazi party performed relatively poorly. If anything, unemployment was a factor contributing to anti-fascist resilience.”This, however, marks a failure to appreciate how rising unemployment was seen by most Germans at the time. Not only did they see it as signifying one aspect of the failure of the coalition parties in government to manage the economy competently, but they also rightly regarded it as fuelling the rise of the Communist party ofGermany(KPD) – with it being the other great political beneficiary of the Wall Street crash along with the National Socialist German Workers’ party. As the KPD grew, so the Nazi party grew – as it was perceived as the only party with the resolve and the numbers (thanks to the brownshirts) to stop the communists seizing power on the streets.The fact that the KPD proved a damp squib should not blind us to the fact that the party once inspired genuine, strong and very widespread fear.John PlowrightRepton, DerbyshireHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Medical dramas on television and in real life | Medical drama | The Guardian
description: Letter: John Fisher recalls meeting a Casualty actor offering medical assistance to a passenger on a plane
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: John Fisher recalls meeting a Casualty actor offering medical assistance to a passenger on a plane
Content: All the drama: (clockwise from top left) ER, St Elsewhere, Casualty and The Pitt.Composite: NBC/Everett/BBC/HBOView image in fullscreenAll the drama: (clockwise from top left) ER, St Elsewhere, Casualty and The Pitt.Composite: NBC/Everett/BBC/HBOMedical dramaLettersMedical dramas on television and in real lifeJohn Fisherrecalls meeting a Casualty actor offering medical assistance to a passenger on a planeTue 6 Oct 2026 12.56 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 14.07 EDTShareRe Adrian Chiles’s article on TV medical dramas (I have a new favourite medical drama – and now I want to have a nasty accident in Pittsburgh, 30 September), my wife (a nurse) and I were on a flight back from Malta when the pilot called for any doctor or nurse on board to assist the cabin crew. My wife went to the back of the plane and found a hysterical woman freaking out on one of the seats. Standing over her were a cabin crew member and another woman, “attending” her. My wife said: “Oh, are you a doctor or a nurse?” She said: “No, I’m an actress, but I’ve been in several episodes of Casualty.”The cabin crew member told her to clear off, and my wife looked after the hysterical woman. Some of these actors really get lost in their parts.John FisherEastleigh, HampshireHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Is regulation enough to stop AI systems killing us all? | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Letter: Martyn Thomas wonders how any rational person can argue that independent oversight and regulation will be sufficient
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: Martyn Thomas wonders how any rational person can argue that independent oversight and regulation will be sufficient
Content: Sam Altman, the CEO of OpenAI, speaking at the OpenAI DevDay 2026 conference.Photograph: Jeff Chiu/APView image in fullscreenSam Altman, the CEO of OpenAI, speaking at the OpenAI DevDay 2026 conference.Photograph: Jeff Chiu/APAI (artificial intelligence)LettersIs regulation enough to stop AI systems killing us all?Martyn Thomaswonders how any rational person can argue that independent oversight and regulation will be sufficientTue 6 Oct 2026 12.56 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 14.05 EDTShareOnce again a frontier AI model has been withdrawn because it fails safety tests (OpenAI scraps release of new model over safety concerns in internal testing, 28 September). There is the usual call for “independent oversight and regulation”, though never any explanation of how this would work or, most importantly, what evidence should persuade a regulator that an AI system is adequately safe.There is a long engineering tradition of regulating safety-critical software systems, such as those controlling aircraft or nuclear power stations; international standards require “safety cases” – rigorous analyses that show that the possible hazards have been identified and controlled and that the probability of an accident is extremely low.Typically, the safety case should show, with a probability of at least 99%, that an accident that could cause multiple fatalities will not occur more often than once in 1,000 years. It is extremely hard to provide evidence for such low probabilities, even for aircraft that at worst might kill 1,000 people in a single accident. The developers of frontier AI systems tell us that their systems might kill the whole of humanity, yet they have provided no detailed risk analyses, no safety cases that could be independently assessed, and no evidence that such safety cases couldeverbe produced for frontier AI systems.How, then, can any rational person argue that independent oversight and regulation will be sufficient? Policy must be based on rigorous analysis of the facts, not on fantasy.Martyn ThomasFellow and emeritus professor of IT, Gresham CollegeHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Harry Kane doubles up on landmark night as England cruise past Czechia | Nations League | The Guardian
description: England won 3-0 against Czechia in the Nations League at Wembley, Harry Kane scoring twice to mark his record-equalling 125th cap
Author: David Hytner
Headline: England won 3-0 against Czechia in the Nations League at Wembley, Harry Kane scoring twice to mark his record-equalling 125th cap
Content: Harry Kane jumps for joy after doubling England’s lead on his 125th senior appearance.Photograph: Adam Davy/PAView image in fullscreenHarry Kane jumps for joy after doubling England’s lead on his 125th senior appearance.Photograph: Adam Davy/PANations LeagueHarry Kane doubles up on landmark night as England cruise past CzechiaDavid Hytnerat WembleyTue 6 Oct 2026 16.50 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 18.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was a night that belonged to Harry Kane. Yet another one. It began with him being shown a replay of his first England goal during a pre-match interview with ITV – the header against Lithuania in 2015, just 79 seconds after he came on as a substitute for his debut. It ended with him reflecting on two more in what was a supremely comfortableNations Leaguevictory over Czechia. Some things never change.It remains a numbers game for Kane. They are getting bigger and ever more impressive. On the occasion of his 125th cap, the one that took him level with Peter Shilton at the top of the all-timeEnglandlist, he moved to an astonishing 91 goals. Nobody will be surprised if he reaches the century. The only question appears to be when.England know how to beat the game’s smaller fry. Under Thomas Tuchel, they have played 16 matches against teams ranked outside the world’s top 20. They have won 15 and drawn one – against Ghana at the World Cup. They have conceded only once – against the Democratic Republic of the Congo, also at the World Cup.Czechia, who are ranked No 50, were never in the contest.Harry Kane wins record-equalling 125th England cap, drawing level with Peter ShiltonRead moreKane is similarly inevitable. The captain even claimed the assist for the breakthrough goal with a cross into the corridor of uncertainty that spooked Vladimir Coufal so severely he shot into his own net. Kane’s passing was very good. When he was withdrawn in the 82nd minute, he left to a great ovation.The victory meant that England virtually guaranteed their progress into the Nations League quarter-finals and, perhaps more importantly, saw them close out this elongated window with plenty of optimism. One of the main goals was to put as much distance as possible between themselves and the World Cup semi-final defeat against Argentina. It was mission accomplished.Kane will break the caps record when England host Croatia in November and that will be the night when he is truly feted. As an aside, he would want to do it at Wembley rather than in Madrid against Spain where England’s next-but-one game will be staged. Was that why he was so keen to play in all four of the matches during this window? It might have been a part of it.Then again, Kane always wants to play. He was one of only three England players to start each of the matches in this series. The others were Manchester City’s Marc Guéhi and Elliot Anderson. Was the City manager, Enzo Maresca, happy about that? Probably not. Does he have bigger problems at the moment? Yes.Kane’s act of drawing level with Shilton was the box-office detail. His name was on everybody’s lips; his face on the big screen before kick-off. He was pictured alongside Shilton when his name was read out with the teams. The Wembley crowd roared.Kane was at the heart of the opening goal, providing the teasing cross from the right and it was some finish from the player just inside the six-yard box. One that Kane would have been happy to call his own. The problem from a Czechia point of view was that it came from their right-back. Coufal could feel Eberechi Eze at his back as he faced towards his own goal, albeit the England winger was not that close. Coufal stretched and everybody had the time to have the same thought: you do not have to do this. Coufal did it. He could not check his momentum and steered firmly past his goalkeeper.View image in fullscreenCzechia’s Vladimir Coufal scores an own goal to put England ahead.Photograph: Adam Davy/PATrent Alexander-Arnold, who Tuchel recalled at right-back, was involved in the buildup and he caught the eye, especially when surging up and inside. He repeatedly got into advanced areas and there was one moment in the first half when he stormed into the No 9 position on to an Anderson pass. He just could not bring it under his spell. Alexander-Arnold had extended Lukas Hornicek with a whipped free-kick at the outset.Jude Bellingham was excellent. Of course he was. There were fizzed passes from him that took the breath, getting England into dangerous positions, including one for Morgan Rogers in the 25th minute that the Chelsea attacker wasted. There were those strutting runs and it was Bellingham, as much as anybody, who advertised the fact that England were going to break through.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnderson should have made it 2-0 after a Bellingham lay-off; Kane sparked the move and Alexander-Arnold’s cross drove it. The second goal arrived before half-time and it had to be Kane. It would have been all about the buildup were it not for the identity of the scorer. Anderson’s lofted ball up the inside right was a beauty and Rogers’ first-time cross on the half-volley was even better, cut unerringly towards you-know-who in the middle. Kane was unmarked. Hornicek was helpless.Kane wanted more. As usual. He got it. As usual. There was the moment shortly after the restart when he unloaded from the edge of the area and watched the shot kiss the top of the crossbar. Hornicek was beaten. Then he was for real.View image in fullscreenHarry Kane’s header puts England 3-0 up at Wembley.Photograph: Adam Davy/PAIt was Lewis Hall – impressive at left-back – who swung over the corner, which came after Hornicek kept out an audacious Bellingham flick. Only Jiri Slama knows why he gave Kane so much room in front of goal. It was always going to end badly for the Czechia defender. Kane rose and the header had too much power for Hornicek.There was the minor irritation for Tuchel when Myles Lewis-Skelly got himself booked in the 53rd minute for pulling back Pavel Sulc. The midfielder will be suspended for England’s next game and it was certainly not a great idea for him to get in the face of Michal Sadilek shortly afterwards. Sadilek had fouled Rogers and was booked. It was a needless risk from Lewis-Skelly.England toyed with Czechia in the second half with Eze running through some of his party tricks. It was Kane who provided the substance.Explore more on these topicsNations LeagueEnglandCzechiaHarry Kanematch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Sturm warning rocks Pocognoli as abject Scotland turned over by Slovenia | Nations League | The Guardian
description: Sébastian Pocognoli’s start as Scotland manager took a turn for the worse as Slovenia completed a 2-1 comeback win at Hampden Park
Author: Ewan Murray
Headline: Sébastian Pocognoli’s start as Scotland manager took a turn for the worse as Slovenia completed a 2-1 comeback win at Hampden Park
Content: Danijel Sturm completes Slovenia’s second-half comeback at Hampden Park.Photograph: Ian MacNicol/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDanijel Sturm completes Slovenia’s second-half comeback at Hampden Park.Photograph: Ian MacNicol/Getty ImagesNations LeagueSturm warning rocks Pocognoli as abject Scotland turned over by SloveniaEwan Murrayat Hampden ParkTue 6 Oct 2026 16.50 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe nature of this Scotland defeat felt far more significant than the fact it arrived at all. Sébastien Pocognoli is already in tricky territory, just four games into his tenure as Scotland head coach. Slovenia comprehensively outplayed the fragile hosts at Hampden Park, which leaves Pocognoli staring at a third-placed finish in a softNations Leaguesection. Brave new dawn or beginning of an error?Scotland were defensively disorganised. Their attacking play was timid. Long before full time, the 39-year-old Belgian had the look of a coach throwing darts blindly at a board. And missing. Wastefulness fromSloveniaprevented Scottish embarrassment.Cristiano Ronaldo accuses Portugal coach Jorge Jesus of broken promisesRead moreA scathing assessment arrived from theScotlandcaptain, Andy Robertson, who admitted his team were “outfought”. Robertson added: “They looked a lot fresher, a lot more hungry.”Pocognoli was more circumspect. “We didn’t play the game we wanted to,” he said. “We were not at the level we expect to be. I will not say everything is perfect or everything is bad but we need to improve many things. We have enough quality.”A pre-match presentation to Robertson, who reached the 100-cap mark duringScotland’s win in North Macedoniaon Saturday, carried wider meaning. Gordon Strachan and Alex McLeish, Robertson’s first two Scotland managers, were joined on the Hampden pitch by Steve Clarke. This marked a swift and welcome return to the national stadium for Clarke, who departed the Scotland job in unsatisfactory circumstances following failings at the World Cup. Clarke, bashful by nature, took as significant a bow as was ever likely before supporters.Scotland find themselves in a post-Clarke state of flux. He was the manager who made this country relevant on the wider stage once again. There was, however, widespread criticism that Clarke’s team lacked ambition. Pocognoli has been charged with not only maintaining at least decent results but also delivering an alternative brand of football. It is a fanciful quest, perhaps.The first quarter mirrored the opening half whenthese teams met in Ljubljana. Scotland looked uncertain. Slovenia were perfectly comfortable, not only in a defensive sense but when springing into attack. Adam Gnezda Cerin should have afforded the visitors a 13th-minute lead but failed to connect with appropriate force, allowing Jack Hendry to boot clear when just three yards from his own goal. This venue, which should be an asset to Scotland, was eerily quiet.Ryan Christie raised the mood. That the goal was horribly ugly mattered not a jot to the Scottish contingent. A short free-kick was played wide to Ben Gannon-Doak, whose deflected cross was headed on to a post by Hendry. Modern football’s madness means Oli McBurnie will be credited with an assist for the header with which he was undoubtedly trying to score. The ball instead landed at the feet of Christie, who tapped home from close range.View image in fullscreenRyan Christie gives Scotland the lead from close range.Photograph: Robert Perry/EPARobertson demonstrated his ongoing value before the break. Zan Vipotnik seemed certain to equalise before the Tottenham full-back’s rescue act, courtesy of a sliding block. Ominously for Scotland, Danijel Sturm had totally bamboozled their three-man defence when supplying Vipotnik.It was impossible to argue Slovenia were not worthy of their equaliser, which arrived 11 minutes after half-time. It came from a Scotland throw-in, where possession was cheaply conceded. Sturm played through the centre and towards Aljosa Matko, who brushed Luis Binks aside as if the Brøndby defender was not even there. The Scotland goalkeeper Angus Gunn, as is something of a theme, was weak in trying to deal with Matko’s shot. Sturm should have sent Slovenia in front two minutes later but saved the blushes of a hilariously open Scotland defence by shooting over. This had to be alarming for Pocognoli.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSlovenia were swaggering around their hosts. Pocognoli switched to a back four for the first time in this elongated international window shortly before Matko was denied his second goal of the night by an offside flag. The decision was not at all debatable.View image in fullscreenScotland’s Sébastian Pocognoli looks away in horror on the touchline.Photograph: Ian MacNicol/Getty ImagesNeither was the goal which took Slovenia ahead. This time Matko turned supplier, having rampaged down the right flank and crossed for the onrushing Sturm. Gunn was left with no chance as Sturm slammed the ball past him. Pocognoli was now subjected to Tartan Army boos.Findlay Curtis and Josh McPake had penalty claims rejected for Scotland. Desperation had indeed become the order of the day. McPake was at least lively, having stepped from the bench. Too many of his teammates either underperformed or are not cut out for this level. It is up to Pocognoli to source answers, and sharply. This is no patient football domain.Explore more on these topicsNations LeagueScotlandSloveniamatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: F1 drivers face ‘unhealthy’ Singapore air as ‘super’ El Niño fuels wildfire haze | Formula One 2026 | The Guardian
description: Most intense wildfire season for ‘over a decade’ could make conditions difficult for drivers at this weekend’s Singapore Grand Prix
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Most intense wildfire season for ‘over a decade’ could make conditions difficult for drivers at this weekend’s Singapore Grand Prix
Content: People walk along the boulevard at Marina Bay as buildings are seen shrouded with haze.Photograph: Roslan Rahman/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPeople walk along the boulevard at Marina Bay as buildings are seen shrouded with haze.Photograph: Roslan Rahman/AFP/Getty ImagesFormula One 2026F1 drivers face ‘unhealthy’ Singapore air as ‘super’ El Niño fuels wildfire hazeF1 circus greeted by smoky skies before this Sunday’s GPPollution affects reaction times like ‘alcoholic beverage’Adam Hancock in SingaporeTue 6 Oct 2026 09.57 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 17.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSingapore’s Formula One night race is an annual opportunity for the city-state to showcase its dazzling, illuminated skyline. But this year the lights of the country’s many skyscrapers will shine a little less brightly.The south-east Asian nation is shrouded in a thick haze that has drifted from huge wildfires in neighbouring Indonesia, with Singapore now among the world’s most polluted cities.F1 looks amateurish and incompetent after farcical scenes in Sepang | Giles RichardsRead moreHaze is a recurring problem in Singapore during Indonesia’s dry season, but conditions have worsened this year as a “super” El Niño exacerbates fires across parts of Sumatra and Kalimantan.“Rainfall across the region has been about 80% below normal since June, fuelling the most intense fire season in over a decade,” said Wang Jingyu, an assistant professor at Singapore’s National Institute of Education at Nanyang Technological University.Air quality levels in Singapore were classified as “unhealthy” on Tuesday by the country’s National Environment Agency and F1’s travelling circus will be greeted by smoky skies when it arrives from Kuala Lumpur followingSunday’s eventful race at Sepang.The polluted conditions are not expected to cause any disruption to the racing schedule this weekend, but an FIA spokesperson said that “there is a contingency in place” if the haze worsens and there “may be some restrictions on outdoor activity”, although those are unlikely to apply to members of the paddock and would instead focus on “entertainment activities”.The organisers of the Singapore night race said they will ensure the availability of N95 masks on site if required and will “work closely with the relevant agencies” to make any decisions regarding the race weekend if the haze causes “visibility, public health or operational issues”.The polluted air will add another challenge for drivers racing around the Marina Bay Street Circuit, already regarded as one of the toughest events on the F1 calendar because of its high humidity and tight, twisting track.View image in fullscreenMembers of the all-women the Power of Mama volunteer firefighting team spray water on to smouldering peatland in Mensubuk Lama, West Kalimantan. Indonesia has been battling fires for weeks.Photograph: Heribertus/AFP/Getty ImagesChris Carlsten, a professor of medicine at the University of British Columbia and an expert in the effects of air pollution on physiology, said prolonged exposure to the haze during the race could affect drivers’ cognitive performance.In one study, participants spent two hours in conditions with high levels of air pollution before completing a series of cognitive tests, including assessments of their reaction times. “Our findings show that the pollution effect is similar to that of an alcoholic beverage,” Carlsten said.The haze could also affect the drivers’ pre-race preparations, said Chris Tyler, a reader in environmental physiology at the University of Roehampton who has worked with F1 drivers including Oscar Piastri and Carlos Sainz. Drivers often exercise outdoors to acclimatise to the Singapore heat in the run-up to the race, but Tyler warned that “these are the sorts of environments where prolonged exposure to the pollution over a number of days could be somewhat detrimental”.Lewis Hamilton received similar advice in 2019, when the Singapore Grand Prix was last held in hazy conditions. The seven-time world champion said he had been advised not to go running outside in the days leading up to the race. Carlsten said he would advise all drivers to wear masks if the air quality remains poor, allowing them to “keep their lungs clean” before the race.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |FortnightlySign up toThe HotspotA new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisisEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhile the murky air is currently shrouding Singapore’s striking skyline, it should not obscure the drivers’ view as they weave their way through the illuminated city streets this weekend. The FIA said it has “no concerns” about visibility. AFormula Onespokesperson said: “There is absolutely no risk to the event and the conditions where the event is taking place are not at any level of concern.”Quick GuideRussell set to start at back of gridShowGeorge Russell’s dwindling championship hopes have been dealt a further blow as he is set to start this week’s Singapore Grand Prix from the rear of the grid.Russell’s heartbreaking power-unit failure in the closing stages of Sunday’s Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia left him a whopping 84 points adrift of team-mate Kimi Antonelli with seven rounds left to run. It is now understood that the 28-year-old Russell will need to take a new power unit this weekend which means he will exceed the limit on several components and the penalties are likely to leave him starting from the rear of the grid around the streets of Singapore. Antonelli won the Italian Grand Prix last month having taken a similar penalty and Russell will need something similarly miraculous.Press AssociationPhotograph: David Davies/PAWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.There is also little indication that the teams are worried, with several saying they have made no changes to their plans. Audi, competing in their first Singapore Grand Prix, said their drivers are trained to cope with a range of conditions, including “varying levels of air quality”.For the hundreds of thousands of spectators expected to pack the circuit, however, the health implications are less straightforward. Unlike the drivers, who will spend only a relatively short period on track, fans could be exposed to the polluted air for several hours, particularly those attending the concerts and other events around the race.Wang said short-term exposure to haze will generally cause only mild irritation in healthy people, probably in the form of a dry or sore throat, coughing or sneezing, but vulnerable groups, including elderly people, pregnant women and children, face a higher risk, with haze potentially aggravating pre-existing conditions such as asthma or triggering acute bronchitis.Rain could offer some respite from the smoky conditions, with thundery showers forecast for Singapore on Friday and Saturday afternoon.Explore more on these topicsFormula One 2026Formula OneMotor sportEl Niño southern oscillationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Cristiano Ronaldo accuses Portugal coach Jorge Jesus of broken promises | Cristiano Ronaldo | The Guardian
description: Cristiano Ronaldo has accused the Portugal head coach, Jorge Jesus, of twice breaking his word, saying a failed agreement to publicly explain ⁠his omission against Norway
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Cristiano Ronaldo has accused the Portugal head coach, Jorge Jesus, of twice breaking his word, saying a failed agreement to publicly explain ⁠his omission against Norway
Content: Cristiano Ronaldo sits on the bench during the Nations League game between Norway and Portugal in Oslo.Photograph: Paulo Novais/EPAView image in fullscreenCristiano Ronaldo sits on the bench during the Nations League game between Norway and Portugal in Oslo.Photograph: Paulo Novais/EPACristiano RonaldoCristiano Ronaldo accuses Portugal coach Jorge Jesus of broken promisesForward says he will be available after punishmentRonaldo insists coach ‘had broken his word to me’ReutersTue 6 Oct 2026 15.48 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCristiano Ronaldo has accused the Portugal head coach, Jorge Jesus, of twice breaking his word, saying a failed agreement to publicly explain ⁠his omission against Norway drove him out of the camp but insisting he remained available after any punishment.In a lengthy statement, the 41-year-old gave his ⁠account of the dispute ⁠that promptedhis ​departure from Copenhagenbefore Portugal’s Nations League match against Denmark last week.Ronaldo’s break with Portugal is sad, fitting, and long overdue | Jonathan WilsonRead moreRonaldo said Jesus had agreed a plan under which the forward would ⁠miss the Norway and Denmark matches to manage his fitness. However, on the day of the Norway game, the coach told him he would play for 30 ⁠minutes.“Everyone knows the rest. I warmed up from half-time onwards, watched the minutes tick by and wasn’t called ​on,” Ronaldo said. “The manager had broken his ‌word to me.”Portugal’s captain and ‌all-time leading scorer said a subsequent meeting with Jesus, attended by his club side Al-Nassr’s sporting ‌director Simão Coutinho, produced an agreement for the coach to clarify events at his next press conference.According to Ronaldo, an eight-point document was prepared saying he had never demanded playing time, had respected Jesus’s decisions and that the coach asking him to warm up without bringing him on had been a mistake. Ronaldo said the agreed notes did not require Jesus to apologise to him ‌but said the coach’s public remarks bore no resemblance to their private discussion.“It was the second time he had broken his word to me,” Ronaldo said. “I decided ​to leave the training camp without waiting for any further broken promises.”The statement provided Ronaldo’s account but on Sunday, after Portugal’s win over Norway, Jesus denied he had made any agreement with the player but left the door open for his return.The Portuguese Football Federation (FPF) did not immediately respond to a request for ⁠comment about Ronaldo’s statement.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRonaldo apologised for failing to greet supporters after the Norway ​match and for leaving his ​teammates, accepting that his captaincy made ​his conduct more serious. “The consequences of my actions must be assessed and punished ​by the Portuguese Football ‌Federation,” he said.Despite ​the rupture, Ronaldo said ​he was not limiting his international ambitions to a farewell appearance. “If I’m physically fit, playing for my club – scoring goals, I hope – after serving whatever suspension is imposed on me, I’ll be available, as I’ve always been until now, to compete and win for our national team,” he added.Explore more on these topicsCristiano RonaldoPortugalNations LeaguenewsShareReuse this content

title: Fifa reportedly allowed DR Congo into World Cup despite ineligible player in qualifying | World Cup 2026 | The Guardian
description: Fifa allowed the Democratic Republic of the Congo to compete at this summer’s World Cup despite reports suggesting an internal investigation found that the country had fielded an ineligible player in qualifying
Author: Paul MacInnes
Headline: Fifa allowed the Democratic Republic of the Congo to compete at this summer’s World Cup despite reports suggesting an internal investigation found that the country had fielded an ineligible player in qualifying
Content: Lionel Mpasi played a key role for the Democratic Republic of the Congo at this summer’s World Cup.Photograph: Daniel Becerril/ReutersView image in fullscreenLionel Mpasi played a key role for the Democratic Republic of the Congo at this summer’s World Cup.Photograph: Daniel Becerril/ReutersWorld Cup 2026Fifa reportedly allowed DR Congo into World Cup despite ineligible player in qualifyingNigeria filed complaint over ineligible players in playoffFifa investigators aware of situation before tournamentPaul MacInnesTue 6 Oct 2026 14.12 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFifa allowed the Democratic Republic of the Congo to compete at this summer’sWorld Cupdespite reports suggesting an internal investigation found that the country had fielded an ineligible player in qualifying.The player in question, the goalkeeper Lionel Mpasi, starred for his nation at the tournament, including againstEngland in the last 32. Mpasi, who was born in France and played forLes Bleusat youth level, had never completed the process of switching nationalities, Fifa reportedly found. No punishment was levied against the Congolese federation, Fecofa.Lionel Messi has completed football and can bid Argentina farewell with prideRead moreThe news willagain raise questionsover the Fifa president, Gianni Infantino, with a series of governance scandals having brought heightened scrutiny on his position. Fifa’s investigative teams are independent and the president has no input into their proceedings. Fifa is understood to have denied that Infantino played a part in the decision-making process over Mpasi, but his name is likely to remain in focus owing to a former university associate, Véron Mosengo-Omba, being elected unopposed as president of Fecofa this May.The Nigerian Football Federation submitted a complaint over the DRC apparently fielding ineligible players during a World Cup playoff tie between the nations, which the DRC won on penalties, in November.According to reporting by the New York Times and Le Monde,Fifainvestigators were aware of Mpasi’s situation before the DRC defeated Jamaica in a final intercontinental playoff round in March. Faced with a series of possible responses, including banning the DRC from the playoffs, Fifa chose to reject the Nigeria complaint on the grounds it had not been submitted within the necessary timeframe.Nigeria appealed against the decision and government representatives have suggested they could seek financial compensation for their loss, with a member of the national sports commission , which regulates Nigerian sport, telling ESPN: “Nothing has been decided yet, but we will seriously consider seeking compensation from Fifa for all of the economic losses this has cost Nigeria.”Concacaf, the North and Central American and Caribbean confederation, which includes Jamaica among its members, said it “takes player eligibility matters very seriously and expects the applicable regulations and procedures to be applied consistently and fairly in all competitions”. In a statement it asked that any “concerns regarding player eligibility” be “thoroughly reviewed and addressed through Fifa’s appropriate governance and disciplinary bodies”.Fifa, Concacaf, Caf, the Nigeria Football Federation and Fecofa, were all approached for comment.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOn Tuesday the Norwegian football federation confirmed it had submitted a three-pronged complaint to Fifa over its governance, including the decision tooverturn a red cardawarded to the USA’s Folarin Balogun after a telephone intervention by Donald Trump. The other instances cited by the NFF are the Fifa peace prize and the abandoned plan to sell a share in the World Cup to investors, known as theFifa Forward Enterprise scheme.“Each of these cases must be assessed based on the facts of each individual case,” said the president of the NFF, Lise Klaveness. “At the same time, the cases point to a more fundamental question: has Fifa’s position, authority or influence been used in a way that was not appropriate, and if so, did the mechanisms that were supposed to prevent this function work as they should?”Explore more on these topicsWorld Cup 2026FifaDemocratic Republic of the Congo football teamGianni InfantinoWorld CupFootball politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Too nice: do Arsenal lack the grit and tenacity to end WSL title drought? | Arsenal Women | The Guardian
description: Renée Slegers’ team have the technical ability to succeed, but doubts remain over the nastiness needed to rival Manchester City and Chelsea
Author: Tom Garry
Headline: Renée Slegers’ team have the technical ability to succeed, but doubts remain over the nastiness needed to rival Manchester City and Chelsea
Content: Arsenal fell 10 points behind the WSL leaders Manchester City after a 4-2 defeat on Sunday.Photograph: Molly Darlington/WSL/WSL Football/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenArsenal fell 10 points behind the WSL leaders Manchester City after a 4-2 defeat on Sunday.Photograph: Molly Darlington/WSL/WSL Football/Getty ImagesArsenal WomenToo nice: do Arsenal lack the grit and tenacity to end WSL title drought?RenéeSlegers’ team have the technical ability, but doubts remain over the nastiness needed to rival Manchester City and ChelseaTom GarryTue 6 Oct 2026 12.55 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 14.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleArsenal, 10 points adrift of the Women’s Super League leaders, are poised to undertake a “big review” of their season during this international break to try to determine where things have gone so horribly wrong – again – in the early stages. After their4-2 loss at Manchester Cityon Sunday, it felt as if the agenda needs to include an unusual but potentially critical question: is this team nasty enough to win a WSL title?The technical ability throughout the world-class squad Arsenal have assembled could hardly be higher but the levels of grit, resilience and tenacity need examining in a group that appears unable to match Chelsea and Manchester City when it comes to the mental aspects of a title race. Arsenal last won the WSLin 2019.WSL talking points: heat cranks up on Arsenal but Putellas and Diani shineRead moreWhen speaking to sources close to the Arsenal players, it is common to hear of the squad being like a “family”, very supportive of each other and full of “great people”. Those admirable traits, and a general sense the club is full of nice characters, often come across when watching games or during player interviews. Arsenal have built a team of good eggs; polite, courteous and professional individuals who people would be glad to call friends. In the vast majority of scenarios in life this is, quite obviously, a good thing. But are they too nice to beat City?It is quite hard to imagine many of the Arsenal squad raising their voices in anger. It is equally hard to recall the last time anybody at the club engaged in so-called “housery”; perhaps not sinceKatie McCabe’s hair pullagainst Chelsea in last season’s Champions League quarter-final. The irony is that McCabe is one of the senior, influential players who left this summer – in her case to join Chelsea – and McCabe, regardless of what fans might think of her, is someone Arsenal could rely on to roll up her sleeves and get stuck in, to raise her game in a hostile atmosphere and be combative.Last term, no Arsenal players – not even McCabe – registered in Stats Perform’s list of the top 20 WSL players for percentage of duels won. Only one Arsenal player has been shown a red card in a WSL game since 2021-22. Admirable discipline, yes, but are they lacking that fire in the belly?This season, the team appear to be without a dogged, refuse-to-lose type of character in the mould of Lucy Bronze, whose never-say-die attitude has frequently come to England’s aid in crucial moments at major tournaments; or the gritty battling spirit of Erin Cuthbert, who has helped Chelsea lift seven league titles; or – to take an Arsenal example – a leader such as Gabriel Magalhães, a rock for others to lean on during tough games.It is possible to be successful without a Roy Keane in your squad and Arsenal do have Leah Williamson, who has led England to two European titles, so it would be wrong to imply there is no leadership in this group.
