Leaders can step up in different ways but recently RenéeSlegers, when praising her senior players’ reactions to theirdisappointing draw in Paris, mentioned there had been “lots of hugs” and praised how supportive everybody had been for each other. That sounds like the sort of unified workplace culture millions would envy, but to win titles sometimes you need to fall out, yell, be angry and demand higher standards.View image in fullscreenOnly one Arsenal player has been shown a red card in a WSL game since 2021-22.Photograph: Molly Darlington/WSL/WSL Football/Getty ImagesOn Friday I asked Slegers whether Arsenal had enough of a nasty edge to win the league, and she replied defiantly: “I think so, and nastiness or that grittiness, that can express itself in different ways, and I think we have certain ways in which we express that and [in] which we can do that. But of course, with our performances where we haven’t been at our best, you maybe don’t see those moments as much which we can bring, but we’re convinced that we can bring that to games as well, in our way, the Arsenal way, because it’s definitely there.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThat was not evident on Sunday in the little – but important – moments, such as shortly after Arsenal had twice taken a lead they would surrender. City seemed unfazed and carried the resolve of a team who had no doubt they would win.Part of the way that belief has been instilled into the defending champions was evidenced in a clip, released by Sky Sports, of Andrée Jeglertz’s pre-match team talk, which he concluded with the words: “The most important thing: we are Manchester City, we are playing at home and we are winning this game.” The matter-of-fact, defiant instruction was not easy to imagine hearing in this Arsenal dressing room with any real conviction right now, not from the players and not from Slegers, who has many excellent qualities as coach, and is, by all accounts, an intelligent, detail-oriented coach of whom the players are very fond.In decades to come, all the nice characteristics this Arsenal squad demonstrate will no doubt stand them in good stead in the real world, with their friendships, but the cliche “nice guys finish last” is starting to feel increasingly appropriate for this amiable side.Explore more on these topicsArsenal WomenWomen's Super LeagueWomen's footballfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: South Africa in running to stage Africa’s first Olympics as 2036 race hots up | Olympic Games | The Guardian
description: South Africa is in the hunt to stage Africa’s first Olympics after it was named as one of seven countries that will formally present its case to host the 2036 Games
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: South Africa is in the hunt to stage Africa’s first Olympics after it was named as one of seven countries that will formally present its case to host the 2036 Games
Content: Paris hosted a successful Olympics in 2024.Photograph: Michel Euler/APView image in fullscreenParis hosted a successful Olympics in 2024.Photograph: Michel Euler/APOlympic GamesSouth Africa in running to stage Africa’s first Olympics as 2036 race hots upQatar frontrunners of bidders, with India and HungaryTurkey, Germany and Korea to present to IOC next monthSean IngleTue 6 Oct 2026 10.05 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSouth Africa is in the hunt to stage Africa’s first Olympics after it was named as one of seven countries that will formally present its case to host the 2036 Games in November.However its bid, which would probably be spread across Cape Town, Johannesburg and Durban, is seen as a distinct outsider, with Qatar widely regarded as the frontrunner ahead of India and Hungary.Turkey, Germany and South Korea make up the remaining countries that have been asked to present to the International Olympic Committee’s future bid committee next month, marking the first stage of a process that will end with a vote in 2029.Warning over future of Olympic Games if Brisbane 2032 program is not modernisedRead moreQatar’s position at the top of the pecking order is partly down to the perceived strength of the bid and the fact that Asia will not have hosted a Games since Tokyo 2020. However a Doha Olympics would have to be moved from the Games’ traditional July-August slot due to the heat.India is seen as the closest challenger, although its bid to host in Ahmedabad is seen to have slipped back during the past 18 months.As the Guardian reported last year, the Indian bidwas given a wake-up callwhen it visited Lausanne in the summer of 2025, with concerns raised about mismanagement and governance issues at the Indian Olympic Association, the lack of detail in the bid and the country’s dismal performance in the Paris Games.If there is to be another strong challenger to Qatar, it could come from Hungary. Its bid, which is said to include not only Budapest but the Austrian capital, Vienna, and the Slovakian capital, Bratislava, is very well regarded. However it is unclear whether the new government in ­Hungary cares as much about hosting the Olympics as the previous prime minister, Viktor Orban.At this stage most of the other bids are being seen as placeholders for the 2040 Olympics. That includes Germany, given the ­potentially tricky optics surrounding a centenary Games.In a handbook published on Tuesday, the IOC said the bids would be based on a number of technical factors – including the venues and athlete experience, political and public support, and the ability to deliver a great Games and a long-term legacy – as well as their vision for the Olympics.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I was fortunate to compete at fiveOlympic Games, across four continents. Each had their own character,” said the IOC president, Kirsty Coventry. “Each host brought something unique through its people, its culture and the way it chose to stage the Games. But wherever the Games take place, one thing must never change: athletes have to be at the heart of everything we do.“As an athlete, you spend years working to make your Olympic dream come true. The experience you have when you finally reach the Olympic Games stays with you for the rest of your life. That is why, for every future host, delivering the best possible experience for the athletes must always be the starting point.”Other countries interested in bidding for 2036 have until the end of October to confirm their intention before nominations close. The IOC said it would conduct feasibility assessments by March 2027 and in December 2028 its executive board would open a “targeted dialogue with a select number of preferred hosts”. In the summer of 2029, a vote will then be taken to select who will stage the 2036 Games.Explore more on these topicsOlympic GamesInternational Olympic CommitteenewsShareReuse this content

title: Greek prime minister vows to ‘ramp up’ efforts to regain Parthenon marbles | Parthenon marbles | The Guardian
description: Kyriakos Mitsotakis says his UK counterpart, Andy Burnham, has been supportive of restitution efforts in the past
Author: Helena Smith
Headline: Kyriakos Mitsotakis says his UK counterpart, Andy Burnham, has been supportive of restitution efforts in the past
Content: Sculptures from the Parthenon have been housed in the British Museum for more than 200 years.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAView image in fullscreenSculptures from the Parthenon have been housed in the British Museum for more than 200 years.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAParthenon marblesGreek prime minister vows to ‘ramp up’ efforts to regain Parthenon marblesKyriakos Mitsotakis says his UK counterpart, Andy Burnham, has been supportive of restitution efforts in the pastHelena Smithin AthensTue 6 Oct 2026 12.50 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 14.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Greek prime minister has vowed to “ramp up” his country’s claims to get back theParthenon marblesfrom the British Museum, emphasising that his UK counterpart, Andy Burnham, was hugely supportive of restitution efforts before he moved into Downing Street.Kyriakos Mitsotakis said he would raise the issue in the strongest of terms when he met Burnham, who was culture secretary in a previous Labour government.Greece returns priceless relics – and suggests UK should follow suit with Parthenon marblesRead more“Unfortunately they have not progressed,” he told a conference in Athens when asked about talks with London over a muted “hybrid” deal to repatriate the fifth-century BC marbles in return for a treasure trove of other antiquities.“We will very clearly ramp up the intensity of our claims, not just with theBritish Museum, but also with the British government. I would also like to remind the audience that the new prime minister of the UK, unequivocally, was supportive of the return of the Parthenon sculptures before he became prime minister.”View image in fullscreenKyriakos Mitsotakis said there was room for a ‘win-win’ solution.Photograph: Stelios Misinas/ReutersIt was the first time Mitsotakis had conceded that negotiations with the British Museum, under the aegis of its chair, George Osborne, had failed to make headway.Upping the ante, he suggested the fate of the artworks was also connected toBurnham’s stated desire for the UK to have closer ties with the EU. Sculpted to adorn a monumental frieze that embellished the Parthenon, the carvings have been split between Athens and London since their controversial removal at the behest of Lord Elgin, Britain’s ambassador to the Ottoman empire, more than 200 years ago.“For those of us who were saddened to see the United Kingdom leave the European family, we took great interest in the comments made by the UK PM,” said the Greek leader, citing the possibility of “a stronger relationship between the UK and Europe”.“The Parthenon sculptures will be part of this debate, this is not just an issue forGreece. It’s an issue for Europe.”The combative remarks come amid thinly disguised disdain in Athens for Burnham’s seeming about-turn on the sculptures. In private, Greek officials have voiced dismay that within days of assuming office, he should so publicly reverse his position, stating in one of his first interviews that the dispute was “an issue for the British Museum” to resolve.Long seen as an advocate of repatriation, Burnham’s support for the antiquities to be returned to Athens dates back 25 years with Greek officials seeing his elevation as the best hope yet of finally ending the row.In 2023, as mayor of Greater Manchester, he appeared to go further than ever before, posting on social media: “Send them back, no strings. And let’s use culture to change how Britain is seen around the world.”“His change in stance caused great disappointment,” said one well-placed Greek heritage expert who has legally advised successive governments on the issue. “There was more than an element of perfidious Albion about it.”View image in fullscreenParthenon sculptures at the Acropolis Museum in Athens.Photograph: Louisa Gouliamaki/ReutersThe British Museum has been home to about 160 metres of the frieze since 1816, when a bankrupt Elgin was forced to sell the marbles in what, even then, was viewed as a controversial acquisition by the British government.Mitsotakis, whose centre-right administration has sought to refocus the campaign on the idea of reunifying the masterpieces within view of the Acropolis, said on Tuesday that changing attitudes in Britain could not be dismissed.There was, he said, still room for a “win-win” solution with the imminent closure and renovation of the National Archaeological Museum in Athens allowing gems that had never been seen outside Greece to be sent to the UK in exchange for the sculptures.“[The marbles] reunification in Athens would also set a precedent for a unique cultural partnership between Greece and the UK, and in particular between Greece and the British Museum,” he said. “I will certainly make the case very forcibly to the British PM when I meet him. I think the time has come. British public opinion supports reunification of the sculptures and I do believe that now is the time to push in this direction.”Explore more on these topicsParthenon marblesBritish MuseumGreeceHeritageAndy BurnhamSculptureArtnewsShareReuse this content

title: Ikea to pilot online buyback service for secondhand furniture | Ikea | The Guardian
description: Service to be tested in Spain and Portugal this year, with a UK rollout if successful, as pre-loved markets boom
Author: Sarah Butler
Headline: Service to be tested in Spain and Portugal this year, with a UK rollout if successful, as pre-loved markets boom
Content: Ikea, which already offers an in-store buyback service, predicts pre-owned goods will grab 16% of the UK homewares market by next year.Photograph: Phil Walter/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIkea, which already offers an in-store buyback service, predicts pre-owned goods will grab 16% of the UK homewares market by next year.Photograph: Phil Walter/Getty ImagesIkeaIkea to pilot online buyback service for secondhand furnitureService to be tested in Spain and Portugal this year, with a UK rollout if successful, as pre-loved markets boomSarah ButlerTue 6 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIkeais to test an online version of its buy-back service where the retailer offers vouchers for unwanted secondhand furniture.The service will be tested in Spain and Portugal before the end of December and will be launched in the UK if it proves successful.Ikeaalready offers buy-back in stores, including in the UK. The online version will extend it to a much wider audience, with Ikea predicting pre-owned goods are likely to grab 16% of the UK homewares market by next yearThe new plan emerged as the world’s largest furniture retailer takes on Vinted and eBay with itsown secondhand online marketplacewhich launches in the UK this week.The platform, which is already online in other countries including Spain and Portugal with bestsellers including the Kallax shelving system and Malm chest of drawers, will enable shoppers signed up to the Swedish company’s membership scheme to connect directly to one another to buy and sell pre-ownedIkeaitems locally.The UK service will be free initially, but a “buyer protection fee” of about 5% of an item’s price will be introduced in time. At launch, buyers and sellers will arrange collection or delivery directly with one another through the marketplace. Ikea said it is exploring ways to make delivery easier in future.“The secondhand market is growing and growing. It is now really significant,” said Greg Lucas, sustainability manager at Ikea’s UK & Irish division. “Secondhand browsing and shopping is now mainstream.“The way people furnish their homes has changed. Whether they are moving, redecorating or looking for a particular piece, more customers are considering pre-owned furniture alongside new and are actively searching for items that can help create a home that feels personal to them.”The secondhand home products market is now worth more than £4.5bn in the UK and is growing at about 6.5% annually. Ikea said its products accounted for about 9% of furniture sold on secondhand marketplaces in the UK.Ikea said it was making the sale of used versions of its products easier by providing pre-filled product descriptions and price suggestions. The company also offers sellers 15% extra on the price of the item sold if they agree to be paid in the form of an Ikea gift card.The change is part of a revolution in retail, where shoppers of all ages are now prepared to consider secondhand items.In 2025, 63% of UK consumers bought products through reselling platforms, up from 51% in 2024.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe trend has boosted sales at Vinted, which began as a clothing resale site but is nowexpanding into homewares and electronics, as well as at Facebook Marketplace, Gumtree and smaller, more upmarket sitessuch as Vinterior.The US secondhand site eBay recentlybought UK fashion seller Depop for $1.2bn(£900m). Preloved items now make up abouta 10th of global fashion sales.There is heavy competition for the secondhand market, with the electrical goods retailers Currys and AO, for example, both selling pre-owned items.AO expanded its secondhand position after acquiring MusicMagpie, which sells refurbished electronics and secondhand video games, in 2024. It recently also bought camera specialist Jessops, which controls the Camera Jungle secondhand site.Explore more on these topicsIkeaRetail industryRecyclingWasteEthical and green livingEuropeOnline shoppingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Reform MP raises concerns about second homes – then buys one for £800,000 | Reform UK | The Guardian
description: Sarah Pochin bought Anglesey property two days after writing to minister about impact of second homes on rural communities
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: Sarah Pochin bought Anglesey property two days after writing to minister about impact of second homes on rural communities
Content: Sarah Pochin became Reform UK’s first female MP after winning a byelection in May 2025.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSarah Pochin became Reform UK’s first female MP after winning a byelection in May 2025.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesReform UKReform MP raises concerns about second homes – then buys one for £800,000Sarah Pochin bought Anglesey property two days after writing to minister about impact of second home ownership on rural communitiesNadeem BadshahTue 6 Oct 2026 10.41 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAReform UKMP bought an £800,000 second home on a picturesque Welsh island two days after raising concerns in parliament about the impact of second homes on rural communities.Sarah Pochin completed the purchase of a Grade-II listed property on the southern coast of Anglesey (Ynys Môn).The MP for Runcorn and Helsby in Cheshire bought the property two days after she submitted a written question on 15 June to the housing minister Matthew Pennycook, according tothe Will Hayward newsletter.Pochin asked Pennycook “what assessment he has made of the potential impact of second home ownership on housing availability in coastal and rural communities”.Pennycook replied: “Excessive concentrations of short-term lets and second homes impact on the availability and affordability of homes for local residents to buy and rent, as well as local services.”According to the Land Registry, the purchase was made jointly with Pochin’s husband, Jonathan. The couple, who have submitted plans at Anglesey county council for changes to the property, retain ownership of another home in Cheshire.Anglesey, famous for its coastline and ancient Celtic and Roman history, has become a hotspot for second home ownership in recent years. The island had the largest increase in holiday home users among local authorities from 2011 to 2021, according to the Office for National Statistics.View image in fullscreenLlanddwyn island, Anglesey, Wales.Photograph: Stephen Williams/Getty ImagesAs of March 2026, Cyngor Sir Ynys Môn (Anglesey county council) recorded 2,635 furnished homes that were not an individual’s sole or main residence.The local authority introduced a council tax premium on second homes in 2016. Initially set at 25% on top of the standard rate, it has since risen incrementally to thecurrent 100% premium, to address local housing affordability.Critics have argued that second homes and short-term holiday rentals can adversely affect local communities by reducing housing supply, inflating property prices and putting a strain on infrastructure.Robin Wyn Williams, the deputy leader of Cyngor Sir Ynys Môn, said: “It has a longer-term impact on things like the provision of schools and other local services. That community spirit gets killed off. We’ve seen it in the likes of Rhosneigr, where it appears to have lost its identity because it is very much a village of second homes in the main these days.“It tends to be more middle-aged and older people, and that then can bring with it pressures on our adult services. Obviously then that has an impact on the situation whereby families are being displaced from certain parts of the island. And then you just end up in a situation where you have fewer children in the community and that has an impact on schools.”Pochin became Reform UK’s first female MP after winning the Runcorn and Helsby byelection in May 2025. She previously served as a Conservative mayor and a local councillor on Cheshire East council, latterly as an independent, before joining Nigel Farage’s party.Reform did not respond to a request for comment.Explore more on these topicsReform UKWalesSecond homesHousingnewsShareReuse this content

title: US man arrested as second suspect in Canada mass school shooting planned with ChatGPT | Canada | The Guardian
description: Justice department detained James Codey Bryant and allege he offered ‘technical advice’ to primary suspect
Author: Keely Aouga
Headline: Justice department detained James Codey Bryant and allege he offered ‘technical advice’ to primary suspect
Content: Officials announce the arrest of a 30-year-old Washington state man on a charge of conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country.Photograph: David Ryder/ReutersView image in fullscreenOfficials announce the arrest of a 30-year-old Washington state man on a charge of conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country.Photograph: David Ryder/ReutersCanadaUS man arrested as second suspect in Canada mass school shooting planned with ChatGPTJustice department detained James Codey Bryant and allege he offered ‘technical advice’ to primary suspectKeely AougaTue 6 Oct 2026 18.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA surprise suspected accomplice has been arrested in connection with a mass school shooting inCanadathat was made notorious after an 18-year-old allegedly killed six children after discussing it with the AI chatbot ChatGPT.The US Department of Justice said Tuesday it had detained James Codey Bryant, 30, a resident of western Washington state, on a charge of conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country.Bryant offered money and “technical advice” to the suspected shooter for six months leading up to the killings, the justice department alleged.Canadian police have identified the suspect in this year’s massacre of eight people – including her mother and half-brother, as well as the six children, making it the second-deadliest school shooting in the country’s history – as Jesse Van Rootselaar, who has a history of mental health problems.It had been known that Van Rootselaar had used ChatGPT to plan the attack, which took place in February. The safety team at OpenAI, the company that owns the chatbot, flagged Van Rootselaar internally after she conducted conversations with it about gun violence, but the company did not alert police. It did reportedly close Van Rootselaar’s account, but she started a second one that was not closed. Victims’ families and the province of British Columbiahave sued OpenAIand its CEO, Sam Altman, for failing to report her behaviour.It was not previously known publicly that Van Rootselaar was also talking to a human about her plans.In a joint press conference with the justice department and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) on Tuesday, authorities alleged that Bryant and Van Rootselaar met on the now-defunct messaging service Omegle about three years prior to the shooting and kept in contact.Neil Floyd, acting US attorney, and W Mike Herrington, the special agent in charge for the FBI’s Seattle bureau, said they believe Bryant sent Van Rootselaar about $100 to buy new shoes and aabout $15 for a lighter.Authorities said there is no indication so far that the two suspects ever met in person.According to an indictmentobtained by CBC, Bryant was “knowingly and wilfully” conspiring with Van Rootselaar beginning in or before August 2025.That August, Bryant told Van Rootselaar the pair should “find a way to delete” their messages, and in mid-December Bryant suggested getting a VPN to avoid detection for “posting a shooting video online”, according to the court document reviewed by CBC.Police said that on several occasions Bryant tried to talk Van Rootselaar out of committing the attack, but did not contact law enforcement.They added that after Van Rootselaar shot and killed her mother and brother in their family home, she was unable to start the car. Bryant advised her on how to turn on the engine, thereby allowing the shooter to reach the school and execute the attack, authorities said.Bryant also allegedly agreed to livestream the mass shooting, which Harrington said police were not sure Van Rootselaar would have committed had Bryant not done so.It was not clear whether the suspect was represented by a lawyer. Bryant will be prosecuted in the US as a US citizen under an investigation by the FBI, which said it will continue working closely with Canadian authorities.Explore more on these topicsCanadaGun crimeAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: New Zealand greenhouse gas levels hit record highs threatening catastrophic glacier melts | New Zealand | The Guardian
description: Government report finds the country could be hit with more frequent and intense heatwaves, as well as damaging storms and cyclones
Author: Eva Corlett
Headline: Government report finds the country could be hit with more frequent and intense heatwaves, as well as damaging storms and cyclones
Content: The view of Fox Glacier in winter in New Zealand. A government report has warned of rising temperatures and catastrophic glacial melt.Photograph: Gabor Kovacs/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe view of Fox Glacier in winter in New Zealand. A government report has warned of rising temperatures and catastrophic glacial melt.Photograph: Gabor Kovacs/AlamyNew ZealandNew Zealand greenhouse gas levels hit record highs threatening catastrophic glacier meltsGovernment report finds the country could be hit with more frequent and intense heatwaves, as well as damaging storms and cyclonesEva Corlettin WellingtonTue 6 Oct 2026 19.11 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 19.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNew Zealand could be hit with more frequent and intense heatwaves and catastrophic glacier melts in the near future, as greenhouse gas levels hit record highs, a new report about the nation’s climate has revealed.Released on Wednesday, the Our Atmosphere and Climate 2026 report shows New Zealand is experiencing mounting climate pressures, which will have wide-reaching implications for the environment, native species and communities.“The signal is just becoming clearer … there are multiple indicators that are showing increased warming and the likelihood of climate change,” Dr Alison Collins, chief science adviser for the ministry for cities, environment, regions and transport (Mcert) told the Guardian.World’s oceans absorbed record heat equal to 40 times annual global energy useRead moreNew Zealand’s annual average temperature has risen by 1.36C since records began in 1909, and seven of the 10 warmest years on record occurred in the last decade, the report said.“Whilst it sounds like a small amount … it is a significant baseline shift that’s having ramifications through nature, through our communities, and through businesses and industry,” Collins said.The report finds that as the climate heats,glaciers are shrinking. New Zealand has roughly 3000 glaciers, and they have shrunk in volume from 56 cubic kilometres in 1997 to 30 cubic kilometres in 2023, the report said.Modelling of glacier retreat shows a high risk of further decline on the horizon. Under the “low climate scenario” – which assumes low emissions – glaciers will very likely lose between 14 and 86% of their volume by 2100. Under the “high climate scenario”, that figure rises to between 69 and 100% of their volume.“We’re talking about substantial loss,” Collins said.View image in fullscreenFlooding caused by Cyclone Gabrielle in Awatoto, near the city of Napier.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesGreenhouse gases have increased to record levels in New Zealand’s atmosphere, the report shows. There was a 30% increase in carbon dioxide since monitoring began in New Zealand in 1972. Methane levels had also slightly increased in 2025 to their highest concentration ever.“That additional heat is showing up in rising temperatures, warming oceans, rising seas, shifting rainfall patterns and more intense extremes,” the report said.Among those extremes were heatwaves, which the report said were “very likely” to increase in frequency, length and intensity across the country. The number of days hitting more than 25C was also “very likely” to increase by 2050, which will expose people to heat-related health risks, including physical illness, disease and psychological distress.Marine heatwaves are also becoming more pronounced and affecting some native species, the report said. In 2025, the series revealed New Zealand’s oceans werewarming 34% faster than the global averagewhich has been linked tomass sea sponge bleaching, die-offs of southern bull kelp, large scalefish standingsandpenguin deaths.The three-yearly update from Mcert and Stats NZ collates statistics, data and research across five domains – air, atmosphere and climate, freshwater, land, and marine – to paint a picture of the state of New Zealand’s environment.The report outlined a myriad of issues that will stem from continued warming, including damaging storms and cyclones that pose a risk to life, droughts affecting species and agricultural industries, sea level rise eroding infrastructure and housing and Māori communities having reduced access to culturally significant places.Severe storms, includingCyclone Gabrielleand theAuckland floodsin 2023, have battered New Zealand in recent years, causing deaths, widespread devastation and billions of dollars in costs.New Zealand was built and developed around a relatively stable set of climate conditions and the report examines what happens when those conditions begin to change, Collins said.“Climate change is not just an environmental issue. It’s a human story. It’s an economic story.”Explore more on these topicsNew ZealandAsia PacificClimate crisisExtreme weathernewsShareReuse this content

title: Drax datacentre could create nearly twice the yearly emissions of all Gatwick flights | Datacentres - UK | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Campaign group’s analysis of North Yorkshire plans finds datacentre would have to burn 4.9m tonnes of wood a year
Author: Pippa Neill
Headline: Exclusive: Campaign group’s analysis of North Yorkshire plans finds datacentre would have to burn 4.9m tonnes of wood a year
Content: The Drax power station currently burns millions of tonnes of imported wood to create energy.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Drax power station currently burns millions of tonnes of imported wood to create energy.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesDatacentres - UKDrax datacentre could create nearly twice the yearly emissions of all Gatwick flightsExclusive: Campaign group’s analysis of North Yorkshire plans finds datacentre would have to burn 4.9m tonnes of wood a yearPippa NeillEnvironment reporterTue 6 Oct 2026 06.27 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 17.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDrax’s planned datacentre could produce nearly double the emissions of all flights out of Gatwick airport each year by burning 4.9m tonnes of wood annually, an analysis has shown.Campaigners say this would make it “one of the dirtiest datacentres out there”.Last year, the energy company Draxunveiled plansto convert part of its biomass power plant in North Yorkshire into a datacentre in response to the increase in demand for AI capability.AI datacentres use a massive amount of electricity to power servers and cooling equipment, and to run facility systems. There are 315 datacentres in the queue to connect to the UK’s electricity grid, representing 73GW of demand. This is almost double the peak winter energy demand for the entire UK.Two planned datacentres will have higher UK carbon emissions than ExxonMobil, analysis findsRead moreInpublic documents, Drax says it is developing options for a 1.2GW datacentre, with 100MW of this energy coming from the electricity grid and the rest from its own power station.The Drax power station currently burns millions of tonnes of imported wood to create energy. This has been touted as a clean way of producing energy that could even result in “negative emissions”, as replacement forests take up CO2from the air when they are grown.However, scientists and environmental experts strongly contest this accounting approach,with researchers findingsuch systems could take 150 years to be “carbon negative”.Based on information in Drax’s2025 annual report, the Natural Resources Defense Council (NRDC) estimated that if built, Drax’s datacentre will require 4.9m tonnes of wood each year.The campaign group calculated the total emissions from this to be 8.6m tonnes of CO2a year. This is based on an assumption that the datacentre would run at a constant rate for all hours of the year.This is nearly double the total CO2emissions of all flights fromGatwick airport, which measured 4.79m tonnes in 2024.Matt Williams, a senior advocate for NRDC, said this would make it “one of the dirtiest datacentres out there”.Oliver Hayes, head of policy at the campaign group Global Action Plan, said, “Burning millions of trees to power server farms is indefensible.”The datacentre has not yet entered the formal planning process but Drax said it could be fully operational from 2031 if secured the necessary consents.“The government must urgently set minimum standards for datacentres and rule out dirty energy generation like burning trees,” Williams said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThere is growing pressure for more transparency over how these energy intensive datacentres will align with the government’s legally binding net zero targets.Proposed London datacentre ‘incompatible’ with net zero with 1m-tonne carbon footprintRead moreIn response toprevious reportsthat just two planned datacentres in Buckinghamshire and Bedfordshire will have higher UK carbon emissions than ExxonMobil, Toby Perkins, a Labour MP and chair of the Commons environmental audit committee, said: “Without the right measures in place, datacentres could represent a serious threat to the environment and to our legally binding climate goals.”Hayes said the absence of coordinated government policy was a “dereliction of duty”.“The only sensible solution at this point is a moratorium on datacentres until very basic questions about how many we need, what for, where, and how pollution will be avoided are answered satisfactorily by the government,” he added.The government has previouslyruled outissuing a moratorium on datacentres, stating that doing so would send investment and good jobs abroad. In Scotland, MPsvoted in Septemberto pause all new datacentre planning applications for up to a year until a national strategy can be developed.A Drax spokesperson said: “The potential plans for datacentres at Drax Power Station can support UK economic growth as well as helping meet the government’s ambitions for industrial renewal, in places like NorthYorkshire, as well as AI sovereignty.“NRDC are a longstanding anti-biomass campaign group and have no positive vision for our Selby site. Their inaccurate assertions are not independently verified and are rooted in basic errors regarding the international standards for GHG accounting of biomass and bioenergy and on the potential datacentres’ power mix.”Explore more on these topicsDatacentres - UKDraxAI (artificial intelligence)Energy industryGreenhouse gas emissionsBiomass and bioenergyYorkshirenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘They take our water, our soil’: protesters fight ‘foreignisation’ as Javier Milei encourages land sales in Argentina | Indigenous peoples | The Guardian
description: The country’s far-right president is courting billionaire investors by removing a block on foreign ownership of land and natural resources
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The country’s far-right president is courting billionaire investors by removing a block on foreign ownership of land and natural resources
Content: Indigenous communities in Chubut province protest against the Argentine government’s plans to lift limits on the sale of land to foreigners.Photograph: Roxana SposaroView image in fullscreenIndigenous communities in Chubut province protest against the Argentine government’s plans to lift limits on the sale of land to foreigners.Photograph: Roxana SposaroSouthern frontlines: Latin America and the CaribbeanIndigenous peoples‘They take our water, our soil’: protesters fight ‘foreignisation’ as Javier Milei encourages land sales in ArgentinaThe country’s far-right president is courting billionaire investors by removing a block on foreign ownership of land and natural resourcesSupported byAbout this contentValentina Di Liscia. Photographs by Roxana SposaroTue 6 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn 19 September, Marta Sahores, an 84-year-old chemistry professor and activist who has mobilised against mega-mining projects for more than two decades, took to the streets inArgentina. Alongside workers, retirees, students, Indigenous groups and human rights organisations, Sahores was there to protest against the country’s far-right president, Javier Milei. During themarcha de la bronca– the “march of anger” – protesters held signs reading, among other rallying cries, “The land is not for sale”.Marching in Esquel, a town nestled in the foothills of the Andes in Chubut province, she also held up a sign defending the country’s water resources against what she called the government’s “handover” to investors.“When foreigners buy land, they buy land with rivers and lakes. They take our water, they take our soil,” says Sahores. “We stand for real democracy and environmental sovereignty.”View image in fullscreenMapuche-Tehuelche women lead a march on Interntional Women’s Day in Esquel, Chubut, on 8 March 2025.Photograph: Roxana SposaroSahores and fellow activists are rallying to overturnMilei’s broad deregulation decree, especially the measures against land protections. “Fortunately, we are many, and we are fighters,” Sahores says. “We’re in the streets when we need to be, and we’re in the courts when we need to be.”In Argentina, land rights have become a critical political issue. Foreigners own about13m hectares(32m acres) of the country’s land –approximately 5%, an area roughly the size of England. Since Milei took office on December 2023, his campaign to open resource-rich areas to foreign investment and roll back the protections of the2011 Land Law– which critics say is already undercut by its non-retroactive scope – has alarmed advocates who say it deepens extractivism, contributes to housing inequality and displaces Indigenous communities.View image in fullscreenEnvironmental activist Marta Sahores.Photograph: suppliedThe 2011 Land Law caps how much rural land foreigners can own: no more than 15% of any single department – the subdivision below a province – and no more than 30% in the hands of a single nationality. Yet departments such as Lácar, in the Patagonian province of Neuquén, exceed both limits, explains Tomás Costa, a researcher with theLand Observatoryat the University of Buenos Aires (UBA).In Lácar, part of a region known for its glacial lakes and native forests, about54% of landis foreign-owned. Of that, about 30% (144,313 hectares) is concentrated in asmall number of US entitiesthat own14 times as much land as the Curruhuinca, a Mapuche community that has spent yearsdemanding access to clean water.Last week, the supreme courtoverturned a previous rulingthat had blocked Milei’s attempts to repeal the Land Law, effectivelyclearing the pathfor the controversial reform to move forward just two months after a failed effort in Congress.Amid mass protests, Milei’s party, La Libertad Avanza passed astripped-down versionof its inviolability of private property bill in the Senate this August, withdrawing its two most contentious provisions: one that would have raised the foreign land cap from 15% to 25%, and another that would fast-track land developmentafter wildfires.The approved bill, still pending in the chamber of deputies, also included articles tofast-track evictionsandmake it harderto expropriate lands for public works, favouring private interests.The project is part of the libertarian president’s broader scheme to court foreign investors such as Peter Thiel, whorecently acquired a 1% stakein Vista, an oil producer in Argentina’s main fossil fuel reserves, Vaca Muerta.View image in fullscreenSince deregulation there have been a series of land evictions, such as this one at Cueva del Inca, a Kolla community in Tilcara, Jujuy province in April 2025.Photograph: Roxana SposaroIn 2024, Milei enacted his large investment incentive regime, orRigi, which relaxes limits on how much money investors can send back to their parent companies, lowers the corporate income tax rate and exempts imported machinery from tariffs, with 30 years of regulatory stability guaranteed.A proposed “super Rigi” expands on the regime for “frontier mega-projects” such as AI datacentres and semiconductor manufacturing, which require massive quantities of water and critical minerals including lithium, of whichArgentina has one of the largest reserves.Argentina’s future lies in the balance as vast oilfields poised for extractionRead moreThe impact of Milei’s agenda is being acutely felt by Indigenous communities threatened by eviction orders in land disputes that have dragged on for decades, says Pablo Volkind, professor at UBA’s School of Economic Sciences.“It’s not ‘what could happen’; it’s what’s already happening,” Volkind says, noting that Milei’s deregulation push has ushered in “a flood of evictions” in Jujuy, Neuquén, Chubut and Misiones, emboldening courts to move faster on property cases that might have been contested in a different political climate.Volkind heads the Land Observatory, which produced aninteractive mapof foreign land ownership in Argentina, letting users visualise how foreign holdings overlap with natural reserves, national parks, glaciers and Indigenous presence. Many of the lands exceeding the ownership cap sit along the Argentine cordillera, stretching from Salta and Jujuy in the north to Tierra del Fuego, rich in mining resources and freshwater reserves in glacial and periglacial zones.In April, Milei signed areform to the glacier lawthat authorises mining in previously protected regions.Another area of high foreign ownership is the Paraná River basin, along Misiones, Corrientes and Entre Ríos, a key export corridor. In Puerto Libertad, Misiones, near the Iguazu Falls, the Chilean forestry company Arauco controls so much land that the mayormust ask it for permissionbefore advancing public projects such as a10-hectare industrial park.View image in fullscreenThe Paraná River basin, a key export corridor where huge amounts of land are under foreign ownership.Photograph: Henri Martin/AlamyThe areas high in foreign landholdings are also among those with the largest Indigenous populations, for whom Milei’s advances are yet another chapter in what campaigners and experts consider a history of systemic racism and land dispossession.“This policy of ‘foreignisation’ has been happening since the very formation of the Argentine nation-state on Indigenous territories, the forcible occupation of ancestral lands,” saysMoira Ivana Millán, Mapucheweychafe(leader) in Lof Pillan Mahuiza, in the province of Chubut.Millán says the current administration represents an acceleration and official sanctioning of a practice once often carried out covertly. British billionaire Joe Lewis, for example, was accused of fraudulentlypurchasing 12,000 hectaresin a border security zone in Patagonia for his Lago Escondido estate in the 1990s. The property continues to block public access to a lakecampaigners sayshould not be private by law. Milei’s governmentdropped the state’s caseearlier this year.“What Milei is doing is legalising this. He’s giving the green light, without restrictions, to land purchases by foreigners,” says Millán.View image in fullscreenMapuche-Tehuelche people carry the flag of their people – theWenufoye– to reclaim ancestral lands in Chubut in 2024.Photograph: Roxana SposaroIn 2024,Milei’s government repealed a lawthat had suspended Indigenous evictions pending a national land survey and dissolved thenational registry of Indigenous communities, stripping another safeguard. Members of the Quintriqueo and Melo communities in Neuquén were forcefully threatened with removal from theirlofsin Augustin the latest escalation of a case brought forth by the Belgian Broers family.ThoughArgentinarecognised the community’s legal status in 2006 and its traditional land occupation in 2023, without a formal property title, they remain legally exposed to claims. “What this country has done is repeal what little Indigenous legislation we had, leaving us completely abandoned,” said Amancay Quintriqueo, thelonko(leader) of the community, at a press conference last week.Milei’s investment-friendly policies may also come at a price for everyday Argentines, some experts say. The Center for Argentine Political Economy (CEPA), for instance, estimates that the cost to the public coffers of Rigi-incorporated projects will bebetween $1.3bn and $2.3bn annually(£962m-£1.7bn).“What’s actually being proposed,” Volkind says, “is that individual private rights come to stand above any state authority meant to guarantee the common good – which is, supposedly, what states are meant to do.”Explore more on these topicsIndigenous peoplesSouthern frontlines: Latin America and the CaribbeanArgentinaJavier MileiAmericasLand rightsPeter ThielInternational land dealsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Former Obama official will review Cornell’s handling of sexual misconduct complaints | New York | The Guardian
description: School trustees appoint Sally Yates to review policies as university grapples with fallout from alleged frat gang rape
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: School trustees appoint Sally Yates to review policies as university grapples with fallout from alleged frat gang rape
Content: Sally Yates before testifying in front of the US Senate judiciary committee in Washington DC on 8 May 2017.Photograph: Jim Watson/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSally Yates before testifying in front of the US Senate judiciary committee in Washington DC on 8 May 2017.Photograph: Jim Watson/AFP/Getty ImagesNew YorkFormer Obama official will review Cornell’s handling of sexual misconduct complaintsSchool trustees appoint Sally Yates to review policies as university grapples with fallout from alleged frat gang rapeAssociated PressTue 6 Oct 2026 15.11 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 15.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA former high-ranking Department of Justice official will look at how Cornell handles sexual misconduct complaints, university trustees announced on Tuesday as they tried to address an outpouring of anger over allegations of a2024 gang rapeat a fraternity house.Sally Yates, who was a deputy attorney general in theObama administration, will spearhead the review, the trustees said. The assessment is to include how the Ivy League university investigates reports of sexual assault and sexual harassment, how the disciplinary process works, the adequacy of campus police responses, and more.“It is imperative that Cornell be willing to examine itself with the same rigor we expect of others,” the trustee chair, Anne Meinig Smalling, said in a statement.Before Cornell turmoil, successive US administrations seesawed in attitudes towards campus assaultsRead moreThe announcement comes after days of outrage and a large demonstration over Cornell’s response to a complaint from a woman known publicly only as Jane Doe. She told campus police in November 2024 that she had been sexually assaulted by multiple Chi Phi fraternity brothers the month before after being pressured into drinking and taking drugs.No criminal charges have been filed. The Chi Phi chapter at Cornell was shut down, and the Ivy League university has said it expelled some students and suspended others.Yates will look at how the woman’s complaint was handled and at the oversight of fraternities, sororities and other campus groups, Cornell said.The woman sued the university, seven former students, the fraternity and others last month.Lawyers for two of the former students denied they participated in a sexual assault. Attempts by the Associated Press to reach the other men or their representatives have been unsuccessful. Court records show that during an investigation that Cornell conducted under the federal Title IX law, some of the accused students contended that the sexual activity was consensual.The lawsuit put a new, nationwide spotlight on the allegations and how the campus police, university and local prosecutor had reacted.New York’s attorney general is now conducting a criminal investigation, and the state’s governor called for an independent review of Cornell’s handling of the matter – the review that Yates now will lead.Cornell students, professors and others thronged a campus plaza on Monday to protest the university’s response to the matter and demand more accountability, greater transparency, an overhaul of the disciplinary process and other changes.1:08Students protest Cornell University's response to gang-rape allegations – videoYates had a decades-long career at the justice department, serving for years as the top federal prosecutor in Atlanta and later as a deputy attorney general.She achieved particular prominence in January 2017, when, as acting attorney general in the early days of the Trump administration, she directed justice department attorneys not to defend the constitutionality of Donald Trump’s refugee and immigration ban. She was swiftly fired, with Trump accusing her of betrayal and insubordination.Yates also generated headlines when it emerged that, in a conversation days before her departure, she had expressed alarm to the Trump White House about contacts that Trump’s new national security adviser, Michael Flynn, had had with the Russian ambassador during the presidential transition period. Flynn later was fired.Yates has been in private practice since her departure from the justice department. Her practice at the King & Spalding law firm includes conducting independent investigations for outside organizations and companies.She led a high-profile inquiry into alleged abuse and misconduct, including claims of harassment and coercion, at the National Women’s Soccer League. The investigation concluded in 2022 with a finding of systemic abuse.Explore more on these topicsNew YorkRape and sexual assaultSexual consentUS universitiesSchoolsUS educationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Jailed Lego collector’s insurance scam highlights UK’s £1.3bn fraud problem | Insurance industry | The Guardian
description: Industry leaders say bogus claims rose 14% last year, pushing up premiums for all customers
Author: Julia Kollewe
Headline: Industry leaders say bogus claims rose 14% last year, pushing up premiums for all customers
Content: Matthew Johnson was jailed for 28 months for falsely claiming that MacBooks, televisions, gaming consoles, fishing equipment and collectible Lego sets had been stolen. Photograph: City of London policePhotograph: City of London PoliceView image in fullscreenMatthew Johnson was jailed for 28 months for falsely claiming that MacBooks, televisions, gaming consoles, fishing equipment and collectible Lego sets had been stolen. Photograph: City of London policePhotograph: City of London PoliceInsurance industryJailed Lego collector’s insurance scam highlights UK’s £1.3bn fraud problemIndustry leaders say bogus claims rose 14% last year, pushing up premiums for all customersJulia KolleweTue 6 Oct 2026 09.07 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 13.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn insurance fraudster who pocketed more than £14,000 for the supposed theft ofLegosets, fishing gear and gaming consoles was behind one of last year’s most high-profile bogus claims.Investigators uncovered £1.34bn of fraud in 2025, a 14% increase on the year before, according to the Association of British Insurers (ABI).The Lego fraudster, Matthew Johnson, was sentenced to 28 months in prison last December after aninvestigationby the City of London police’s insurance fraud enforcement department.Johnson, of Misterton in Nottinghamshire, submitted false claims to AxaInsurancebetween May 2021 and January 2022, relating to alleged burglaries at properties in Shetland and Goole, East Yorkshire.View image in fullscreenMatthew Johnson has been ordered to repay the money he pocketed for false insurance claims, including for collectible Lego sets.Photograph: City of London policeHe claimed that high-value items had been stolen, including MacBooks, televisions, gaming consoles, fishing equipment and large quantities of collectible Lego sets. Johnson received more than £14,000 in insurance payouts across four claims. He was ordered by Nottingham crown court to repay the money.Axa raised concerns after inconsistencies were identified in the documentation provided by Johnson, including repeated use of the same receipts across different claims and invoices that appeared to have been altered to match the policy address.The ABI and police warned that insurance fraud pushed up the cost of premiums for all customers.Mark Allen, head of fraud and financial crime at the association, said: “Anyone considering committing insurance fraud should be under no illusion – it’s a serious crime with serious consequences, including a criminal conviction and imprisonment.”While the number of detected fraudulent claims fell by 2.7% to 93,900 cases last year, the value of scams rose sharply. The ABI said this was a sign of its growing scale and sophistication.The average value of a fraudulent claim reached £14,300 last year – the second-highest figure on record, just below the peak of £14,600 in 2022.Motor insurance was again the area with the most fraud, accounting for 55% of all cases. With 51,900 fraudulent motor claims worth £625m uncovered last year, the figures point to fewer but more costly cases. The average value rose to £12,000, the second-highest figure since 2015.A fraudster who staged motor collisions using women he met online was sentenced for the “crash for cash” scheme designed to generate fraudulent insurance claims, the ABI said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAviva discovered bogus insurance claims worth £233mlast year, it said in June. Scammers tried new tricks including using artificial intelligence to fake car accident scenes and documents.Simon Klust, who heads the City of London police fraud team, said more than 250 bogus claims were detected each day but this was “likely to be just the tip of the iceberg”.The travel sector had the sharpest rise in the number of bogus claims. Investigators uncovered a £300,000 insurance scam that used multiple fake identities, fabricated medical documents and bogus websites to support false medical emergency claims.Exaggerated loss remains the most common type of fraud, with 26,900 cases identified. This is when someone deliberately increases the cost of a claim beyond its true value.Ursula Jallow of the Insurance Fraud Bureau, which is funded by insurers, said: “Insurance fraud is devastating. It costs honest consumers when times are already tough.”Explore more on these topicsInsurance industryInsuranceCrimeLegoScamsConsumer affairsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Alleged Iranian spies planned ‘serious violence’ against UK journalists, court hears | UK news | The Guardian
description: Mostafa Sepahvand, Farhad Javadi Manesh and Shapoor Qalehali Khani Noori did not dispute they surveilled their targets
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: Mostafa Sepahvand, Farhad Javadi Manesh and Shapoor Qalehali Khani Noori did not dispute they surveilled their targets
Content: Court artist sketch of (left to right) Shapoor Qalehali Khani Noori, Mostafa Sepahvand and Farhad Javadi Manesh appearing by videolink at the Old Bailey in March.Composite: PAView image in fullscreenCourt artist sketch of (left to right) Shapoor Qalehali Khani Noori, Mostafa Sepahvand and Farhad Javadi Manesh appearing by videolink at the Old Bailey in March.Composite: PAUK newsAlleged Iranian spies planned ‘serious violence’ against UK journalists, court hearsMostafa Sepahvand, Farhad Javadi Manesh and Shapoor Qalehali Khani Noori did not dispute they surveilled targetsNadeem BadshahTue 6 Oct 2026 13.34 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 17.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThree alleged Iranian spies carried out surveillance and reconnaissance to target journalists in the UK as part of a plan to commit “serious violence”, a court heard on Tuesday.Mostafa Sepahvand, 41, Farhad Javadi Manesh, 46, and Shapoor Qalehali Khani Noori, 57, are charged with offences under the National Security Act.Their “subjects” included Mojtaba Pourmohsen and Kambiz Hosseini, journalists for London-based Persian broadcaster Iran International, as well as a founder member of UK Lawyers for Israel, Jonathan Turner, the court was told.The prosecution alleges Sepahvand intended to physically carry out a “violent attack” against at least one of the targets, while Manesh and Noori assisted in planning.View image in fullscreenCourt artist sketch of Shapoor Qalehali Khani Noori appearing via videolink at the Old Bailey in London in March.Illustration: Elizabeth Cook/PASepahvand claims he was threatened into conducting surveillance against his will, but the prosecution described this as an “entirely bogus claim”, telling jurors he did it to get paid and have his theft conviction in Iran “fixed”.In a voice note read out to Woolwich crown court in London, Sepahvand told an associate he would “finish off” a target if he was paid £150,000.“They made me a promise and said: ‘We’ll sort out your matter/court case, and we’ll give you £150,000 as well. Finish the job. We’ll show you him/her (the target),’” he said.“This is an illegal job. It’s something that constitutes a criminal offence, and it carries a heavy prison sentence. At the absolute minimum, they should transfer £10,000 for now.“Wherever they tell me, I’ll go there and stand there. If the person (the target) is inside, they pay the £150,000, and I’ll finish him/her off.”The defendants were said to have visited addresses linked to their targets, taken photos and videos and used platforms such as ChatGPT to research them online between August 2024 and March last year.There was no dispute that the three defendants conducted the surveillance and reconnaissance, the jury was told.View image in fullscreenCourt artist sketch of Farhad Javadi Manesh appearing via videolink at the Old Bailey in London in March.Illustration: Elizabeth Cook/PASepahvand accepts he was doing so for the benefit of the Iranian regime but claims he was threatened or bullied into doing it, and that he “deliberately did a bad job of it”, the prosecution said.The crown added that Manesh and Noori claimed they did not know they were carrying out the surveillance to assist the Iranian intelligence service.The defendants are charged with engaging in conduct likely to assist a foreign intelligence service.Sepahvand, of St John’s Wood, north London, is also charged with engaging in surveillance, reconnaissance and open-source research with the intention to commit serious violence against a person in the UK.Manesh, of Brent, and Noori, of Ealing, are also charged with engaging in surveillance and reconnaissance, with the intention that serious violence against a person in the UK would be committed by others.The three men, who deny all the charges, were assisted by interpreters in the dock. The trial continues.Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: British man arrested over suspected RAF Fairford terrorism plot | UK news | The Guardian
description: Counter-terrorism police say 22-year-old detained in London on suspicion of terrorism offences
Author: Jamie Grierson
Headline: Counter-terrorism police say 22-year-old detained in London on suspicion of terrorism offences
Content: A police roadblock outside RAF Fairford base.Photograph: Ben Stansall/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA police roadblock outside RAF Fairford base.Photograph: Ben Stansall/AFP/Getty ImagesUK newsBritish man arrested over suspected RAF Fairford terrorism plotCounter-terrorism police say 22-year-old detained in London on suspicion of terrorism offencesJamie GriersonDan SabbaghandVikram DoddTue 6 Oct 2026 14.13 EDTFirst published on Tue 6 Oct 2026 08.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA seventh man has been arrested in London on suspicion of terrorism offences as part of the investigation related to threats to RAF Fairford, police have said.The 22-year-old British national was arrested in Westminster, central London, on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts under section 5 of the Terrorism Act 2006, counter-terrorism police said.Police are continuing to investigate a so far unexplained incident on 27 September, when five men from London driving three white vans were arrested in the small hours in a village outside the Gloucestershire airbase used by bombers from the US air force.A week later, on Sunday, the US decided to hastily withdraw all 12 of the B-1 Lancer bombers that had been based at Fairford back to the US. Some had only arrived at the base a week earlier, and refuelling aircraft had to be scrambled in order to complete the evacuation.There remains speculation that Iran wants to target the base, which was used for US bombing runs on the country earlier this year, but the US and UK appear to have divergent views about the security situation and level of threat.UK sources question whether Iran would have the capability to launch a Ukraine-style drone attack on military aircraft at the base, given the complexity of such an operation. On Monday, Downing Street said the base was safe.But some reports suggested the US feared a drone strike along the lines of Ukraine’s Operation Spiderweb attack on Russian airbases last year, and so did not want to leave its bombers stationed at Fairford.On Monday night Donald Trump, the US president, said the aircraft had been moved because “there were some threats, and rather than tempting the enemy – we’ll capture the enemy and beat the enemy, but why should we leave them there?”View image in fullscreenMunitions sit beside the runway as a Rockwell B-1 Lancer heavy bomber departs from RAF Fairford on Sunday.Photograph: Getty ImagesSo far there has been no breakthrough in the investigation by counter-terror police. The five men detained in Whelford on 27 September were released on police bail a day later, without charge.No explosive devices were found in their vans, though a barrel of petrol was recovered. One of the five had also called 999, and their intentions remain publicly unexplained.On Thursday, a 25-year-old dual UK-Iranian national was arrested in Westminster on suspicion of terrorism offences. He was also released on bail on Saturday.Speaking on Tuesday, the senior national coordinator for counter-terrorism policing, Vicki Evans, said: “This remains a live investigation and our specialist teams continue to pursue multiple lines of inquiry into the circumstances surrounding events near RAF Fairford.“Once again, I’d like to thank the public for their continued support and patience whilst we work through this highly complex investigation.“We’re acutely aware of the public interest in this investigation, and we are working around the clock, and at pace, to identify the motivation behind events in Gloucestershire. We remain committed to investigating all possible angles.”The 22-year-old is being held under rules that allow detectives to bail him, just like the other six men who have been arrested on a terrorism charge.People arrested for terrorism offences can be held under two legal schedules which dictate how long they can be detained without charge. Under the terrorism schedule a suspect can be held for up to 14 days, but cannot be bailed, meaning police have a fortnight to charge or release them.The 22-year-old arrested for alleged preparatory acts is being held under the Police and Criminal Evidence Act, a spokesperson for counter-terrorism police said on Tuesday. That means he could be released under investigation on bail, but detectives have much less time to hold him.The five men arrested close to RAF Fairford were held under the same act before being bailed the next day, to the surprise of some.Tensions have been high at RAF Fairford since Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said in July that the base was a legitimate target. Iran’s embassy in London has denied any involvement in the events of the past few days.Ministers have been briefed that Iran has various reasons for hiring proxies, who sometimes are unwitting, to carry out acts that aim to eat up resources and create chaos.The Iranian embassy in London has said it “categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations” of Iranian involvement.Senior US politicians, including the president, Donald Trump, have expressed surprise that the suspects were released on bail.Counter-terrorism police last week defended the move. “I understand why this development will have come as a surprise to many, but I’d like to reiterate that it was an investigative decision, and one which is grounded in experience and careful consideration of policing powers,” Britain’s head of counter-terrorism police said.Explore more on these topicsUK newsEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Google told to halt work on datacentres in Finland over environmental concerns | Google | The Guardian
description: Order on two construction sites comes after Google failed to carry out environmental impact assessments
Author: Miranda Bryant
Headline: Order on two construction sites comes after Google failed to carry out environmental impact assessments
Content: A view of the Muhos site on 29 September 2026.Photograph: Alessandro Rampazzo/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA view of the Muhos site on 29 September 2026.Photograph: Alessandro Rampazzo/AFP/Getty ImagesGoogleGoogle told to halt work on datacentres in Finland over environmental concernsOrder on two construction sites comes after Google failed to carry out environmental impact assessmentsMiranda BryantNordic correspondentTue 6 Oct 2026 14.02 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 14.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGoogle has been ordered to temporarily stop work on two datacentres inFinlandafter failing to do the necessary environmental impact assessments on its construction sites.The planned datacentres in Muhos and Kajanni are part of a €13bn (£11bn) project across multiple sites in northern Finland by the technology company amid huge demand for space to house online infrastructure.It comes after it emerged that Tuike Finland Oy, the company representingGoogle, had felled 330 hectares (815 acres) of forest in Muhos without completing an environmental impact assessment (EIA).In Kajaani, the company has reportedly been logging across just under 200 hectares (494 acres) of land.The Finnish Association for Nature Conservation said the sites had been reduced to “sand”, blaming the oversights on the “overheated” market for new datacentres.On Tuesday, the Finnish Licensing and Supervision Authority (LVV) said it had issued a notice to the company to “immediately suspend” – by 23 October at the latest – “preparatory measures that significantly change the environment” of the two sites until the environmental impact assessment had been completed. Google has until next Wednesday to submit a written explanation.The EIA is ongoing and expected to be completed later this year. But Google has gone ahead with “extensive preparatory measures”, including removing trees, stripping topsoil and constructing site roads, LVV said.Tommi Muilu, the head of the environmental department at LVV, said: “In our opinion, the measures in question will change the environment and cause impacts, the identification and assessment of which are among the key objectives of the EIA procedure.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIs the environmental impact of datacentres finally cutting through?Read moreIf Google does not comply, LVV said it would consider enforcement proceedings and a fine.In response, Google said in a statement “we understand the concerns” and that it had “fallen short of our own high standards”.The company added: “We will study the LVV’s findings and follow their guidance. We acted in good faith under the Forestry Act, and ran nature surveys and put in place measures to protect high-value areas. As we continue our long-term work in the region, we are advancing our landscaping and biodiversity plans, which include tree planting across 130 hectares (321 acres) at Muhos.”Tapani Veistola, the chief operating officer at the Finnish Association for Nature Conservation, said the malpractice across two sites appeared to be a “systemic problem”. The site at Muhos, he said, was “not a forest any more. It is a sand area.”One of the reasons behind it, he said, was the enormous demand to build datacentres in Finland, which is leading companies to work as fast as possible and overwhelming small municipalities.“The main reason behind everything is the overheated market situation that makes companies speed up processes so much. Also a lack of expertise in municipalities.”Explore more on these topicsGoogleFinlandDatacentres - UKEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: State parliament elects Germany’s first far-right speaker since second world war | Germany | The Guardian
description: Tobias Rausch secures role of president in Saxony-Anhalt after AfD’s election breakthrough
Author: Kate Connolly
Headline: Tobias Rausch secures role of president in Saxony-Anhalt after AfD’s election breakthrough
Content: Ulrich Siegmund, right, congratulates Tobias Rausch on becoming president of the federal state parliament of Saxony-Anhalt on Tuesday. Both represent Germany’s far-right AfD party.Photograph: Jan Woitas/Pool DPA/APView image in fullscreenUlrich Siegmund, right, congratulates Tobias Rausch on becoming president of the federal state parliament of Saxony-Anhalt on Tuesday. Both represent Germany’s far-right AfD party.Photograph: Jan Woitas/Pool DPA/APGermanyState parliament elects Germany’s first far-right speaker since second world warTobias Rausch secures role of president in Saxony-Anhalt after AfD’s election breakthroughEurope live – latest updatesKate Connollyin BerlinTue 6 Oct 2026 11.38 EDTFirst published on Tue 6 Oct 2026 11.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlternative für Deutschland has become Germany’s first far-right party to secure the position of speaker of a regional parliament since the second world war.Tobias Rausch, a former estate agent, was elected in the first round of voting on Tuesday in Saxony-Anhalt. He won 48 out of the 82 votes cast.Later in the day, Hans-Thomas Tillschneider, part of the AfD’s more extreme wing, was elected as Rausch’s deputy.The AfD, which is classed as “rightwing extremist” by the eastern state’s intelligence agency,won nearly 44% of votes in elections last month, dealing a hammer blow to Germany’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, and his centre-right Christian Democrats (CDU).Rausch’s election to the role of president of the parliament – and its speaker – took place at the inaugural gathering of members in the state capital, Magdeburg. Twenty-nine voted against Rausch and five abstained.View image in fullscreenProtesters console each other outside the state parliament in Magdeburg after the election of Tobias Rausch as speaker on Tuesday.Photograph: Maja Hitij/Getty ImagesThe AfD parliamentary group holds 39 seats, narrowly short of an absolute majority. Five politicians from the BSW, a small leftwing party that echoes the AfD’s stances on Russia and immigration, had already said they would vote for Rausch. Tuesday’s result means that four other MPs voted for the 35-year-old in the secret ballot.The willingness of politicians to break the “firewall” – a moral agreement among other parties to shun the AfD – gives the party a chance of being able to form a government in the state – a feat it had looked unlikely to pull off. This would be even more of a historical watershed in postwar Germany.The BSW’s support for Rausch came after the party’s founder, Sahra Wagenknecht, declared it was time to do away with “firewall idiocy”. The party’s deputy leader, Christian Leye, said the “firewall is not working” and the votes of nearly 44% of electors could not be ignored.“We need an intelligent way of dealing with the AfD and that means dealing with the content of their programme instead of a firewall,” Leye told German media.View image in fullscreenHans-Thomas Tillschneider in the state parliament after being elected deputy speaker on Tuesday. He is being lined up as Saxony-Anhalt’s culture and science minister.Photograph: Ronny Hartmann/ReutersIt was not immediately clear who was behind Tillschneider’s election because the BSW had said it would refuse to vote for him. He received 44 votes.As the architect of the AfD’s “radical” manifesto, he is lined up to become culture and science minister in the state. He has referred to the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, as “a real man with a sound set of values” and accused immigrants of “streaming in here in masses … wanting to squander our money”.Tillschneider is a scholar of Islamic studies who has described Islam as a “fungus” growing on the “German oak”. His family emigrated from Romania to Germany in the 1980s.In his acceptance speech, Rausch promised to represent all voices and “take different opinions seriously and to try to take decisions in a transparent way”. He was applauded by his own parliamentary group and the ranks of the BSW. The other MPs did not respond.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenDemonstrators read the German constitution during a protest outside Saxony-Anhalt’s state parliament on Tuesday.Photograph: Ronny Hartmann/AFP/Getty ImagesRausch was one of the key figures in a nepotism scandal over AfD MPs employing family members in parliament. He denied claims that several of his siblings and a brother-in-law were working in the state parliament but confirmed he was employing several players from the football club where he is a member.He is a close ally and confidant of Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD’s lead candidate, who is positioning himself to take over as leader of Saxony-Anhalt. He has yet to say which parties or politicians have agreed to cooperate with the AfD, only that “negotiations are going well”. The AfD claims to be courting members of the CDU to break the firewall, a claim CDU leaders deny.The BSW says it will support an AfD-led parliament only if a nonpartisan figure is appointed to lead it, a position the AfD rejects. Siegmund has until December to form a government.Opposition MPs raised alarm over the breaching of the firewall. “Whoever has invested a representative of extremist and anti-constitutional party with this office will bear responsibility for the consequences,” said Green MP Susan Sziborra-Seidlitz, to loud applause.The result of the Saxony-Anhalt poll, along with two other regional elections in September, has piled huge pressure on Merz, who pledged on taking office in 2025 that he would halve the AfD’s support by boosting the economy and reducing immigration. Instead, the CDU’s support has more or less halved and that of the AfD has surged to 30% in national polls.Before the vote, Eva von Angern of the leftwing Die Linke party and the longest-serving member of the Saxony-Anhalt parliament, drew parallels between Rausch’s election to the post of speaker, and Hermann Göring’s use of that role in the Reichstag in the 1930s to facilitate Adolf Hitler’s rise to power.She claimed that the negative consequences of the AfD’s win in the state were already being felt in lower tourist numbers and teachers withdrawing job applications.Explore more on these topicsGermanyThe far rightAlternative für Deutschland (AfD)EuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Asos warns customer data may be compromised after ‘unauthorised’ app access | Asos | The Guardian
description: Shares in fashion company fall nearly 10% after its app systems are accessed by ‘unidentified third party’
Author: Sarah Butler
Headline: Shares in fashion company fall nearly 10% after its app systems are accessed by ‘unidentified third party’
