Content: The retailer said basic personal information including name and contact details might have been accessed by an unidentified third party but it did not believe  payment card records or password s had been compromised.Photograph: Rafael Henrique/Sopa Images/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe retailer said basic personal information including name and contact details might have been accessed by an unidentified third party but it did not believe  payment card records or password s had been compromised.Photograph: Rafael Henrique/Sopa Images/ShutterstockAsosAsos warns customer data may be compromised after ‘unauthorised’ app accessShares in fashion company fall nearly 10% after its app systems are accessed by ‘unidentified third party’Sarah ButlerandDan MilmoTue 6 Oct 2026 13.44 EDTFirst published on Tue 6 Oct 2026 06.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAsos is investigating unauthorised access to its app system after shoppers received a notification claiming hackers had “fully compromised” its data.The online fashion retailer said basic personal information including name and contact details might have been accessed by an unidentified third party but it did not believe payment card records or passwords had been compromised.Money stolen by scammers hijacking UK social media accounts rises 400%Read moreIt said in a statement: “We are investigating unauthorised activity involving third-party platforms that we use to communicate with customers. We took immediate action to restrict access to the notification platforms and are working with our internal and external specialist advisers, as well as all relevant authorities.“Our website and app are operating as normal, with no current disruption to any aspects of our operations. Customer trust is incredibly important to us, and if the situation changes an update will be provided as appropriate.”It later apologised directly to customers, saying: “We’re sorry that you may have received an unauthorised push notification from us earlier today. Please disregard the notification and do not click or engage with the external third-party link it contained.”The value of Asos’s shares on the London Stock Exchange dived more than 14% after thousands of customers received a notification titled “Asos hacked” with a link that sent them to the Telegram messaging service.Shares closed down by 9.56% after Asos announced it had cybersecurity insurance with a large global provider, including business continuity insurance. However, the company added: “It is too early to quantify any potential impact on trading.”The message sent out to customers said: “Dear Asos DPO [data protection officer] and IT, we have fully compromised the Snowflake instance.”View image in fullscreenAn Asos app notification claiming the retailer has been hacked.Photograph: ScreengrabSnowflake is a cloud platform used to store, process and analyse data including transactions and demographic information such as clothing sizes and body measurements. It also enables push notifications to phones.The Telegram channel operated by the purported hackers, who have named themselves the Xuanye Group, carried a message assuring Asos customers that “payment information is not affected” and a further post stating “the app is safe to use”.Indicating that Asos had been set some form of deadline, the post added: “The incident involves customer information, it is safe on our server, and it will not be touched for a designated period.”The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), part of the government’s GCHQ intelligence agency, is offering assistance to Asos.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe NCSC chief executive, Dr Richard Horne, said: “The unauthorised notification sent out to Asos customers has brought into the light how cyber incidents do not simply affect big business but can have repercussions for individuals much more widely too.”Dray Agha, the senior manager of security operations at Huntress, an online security firm, said: “Sending a ransom demand directly to consumer devices is an aggressive extortion tactic designed to force the business into a quick negotiation. I strongly advise shoppers to watch out for targeted phishing attempts while we wait for official confirmation of a data breach.”The link directed Asos customers to a Telegram channel apparently operated by the Xuanye Group. Cyber experts said they had not heard of the group before and the push notification could be an attempt to grab wider attention.“It’s not unusual to see new groups emerge, and often they wait until they have what they see as a significant opportunity before they announce themselves so as to enter the ecosystem with ‘credibility’,” said Aiden Sinnott, the principal threat researcher at the cybersecurity firm Sophos.Xuanye had not been mentioned before on hacker forums or other Telegram channels, Sophos added.Marijus Briedis, the chief technology officer at the online service provider NordVPN, said: “High-profile cyber incidents create ideal conditions for phishing attacks. Criminals may exploit the publicity by sending emails and texts claiming to be from Asos, perhaps asking customers to reset a password, confirm payment details, check an order or claim a refund.”The potential hack comes after a string of British retailers, includingMarks & Spencer, theCo-opandHarrods, suffered cyber incidents last year. M&S and the Co-op experienced stock shortages and the former was forced to close its website for several weeks as it battled to ensure its systems were clean.Explore more on these topicsAsosRetail industryCybercrimeHackingInternetData and computer securityOnline shoppingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Paramount completes $111bn acquisition of Warner Bros to form new media empire Skydance | Business | The Guardian
description: David Ellison and ex-Mattel CEO Ynon Kreiz to oversee both film studios, HBO Max, CNN and CBS News as co-executives
Author: Gaya Gupta
Headline: David Ellison and ex-Mattel CEO Ynon Kreiz to oversee both film studios, HBO Max, CNN and CBS News as co-executives
Content: The Paramount water tower in Los Angeles, California.Photograph: Mario Tama/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Paramount water tower in Los Angeles, California.Photograph: Mario Tama/Getty ImagesBusinessParamount completes $111bn acquisition of Warner Bros to form new media empire SkydanceDavid Ellison and ex-Mattel CEO Ynon Kreiz to oversee both film studios, HBO Max, CNN and CBS News as co-executivesGaya GuptaTue 6 Oct 2026 10.14 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 17.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleParamountcompleted its $111bn acquisition ofWarner Bros Discoveryon Tuesday, consolidating some of the world’s most recognizable studios and news outlets after a bidding war with Netflix and months of legal turmoil.The new company, now called Skydance, will have David Ellison, the son of a billionaire tech mogul, at its helm, with the former CEO of Mattel, Ynon Kreiz, as co-executive. They will oversee Paramount and Warner Bros’ movie studios, HBO Max, CBS News and CNN.“Today is a historic day, not just for Skydance but for our entire industry,” Ellison said in a statement. “From the start, our ambition was to bring these two storied studios together and create a stronger competitor, with the talent, resources, and reach to tell great stories in every genre, on every platform, for audiences everywhere. Now that ambition is a reality.”The consolidation of Paramount and Warner Bros combines two of the last five legacy studios in Hollywood, which includes Disney, Universal Pictures and Sony Pictures.Mark Thompson will remain chief executive at CNN after Paramount saleRead moreThough the merger was approved in June, California, New York and 10 other statessuedParamount over concerns that the move would “extinguish” competition and lead to fewer movie theaters in theaters and at home.As part of thesettlement agreementreached last month, Skydance is required to release a minimum of 30 films each year and more than 180 television shows. CBS News and CNN will also berequiredto maintain independent editorial boards.A trustee will monitor Skydance’s compliance with the terms of the settlement. Rob Bonta, the California attorney general, said he would be prepared to go to court if the company ever fails to comply.“This settlement is not a vote of support for this merger; it’s not a blessing of the broader merger,” he said on 21 September, when the settlement was announced. “Broadly speaking, we believe further consolidation in markets that are essential to American economic life doesn’t serve the American economy, consumers or competition well.”The merger has also raisedconcernsabout Ellison’sinfluenceover CNN after his overhaul of CBS News. Ellison is the son of Larry Ellison, the co-founder of Oracle who was a Trump megadonor in the 2024 presidential election. The elder Ellison’s net worth is $193bn, according toBloomberg.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhen David Ellison’s Skydance CorporationacquiredParamount last year, he appointedBari Weiss, a former New York Times opinion writer who launched an “anti-woke” media outlet, as the head of CBS News, despite her lack of television experience. Since then, the television network has faced accusations of bias toward the Trump administration, though Ellison has defended his stewardship of both CBS and now, CNN.On Monday, CNN’s CEO, Mark Thompson,announcedthat he would remain in his role under its new parent company, saying that he had spoken with Ellison and Skydance leadership and that he has “real confidence that they both understand and will fully support the principle and practice of the kind of independent news that CNN has always stood for”.Explore more on these topicsBusinessMedia businessParamount+Warner BrosUS televisionUS television industryTelevision industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: Ofcom investigates Meta over Instagram Instants safety checks | Meta | The Guardian
description: Watchdog examining whether company carried out adequate risk assessment as required by Online Safety Act
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: Watchdog examining whether company carried out adequate risk assessment as required by Online Safety Act
Content: Instagram’s Instants feature allows users to send images that disappear after viewing.Photograph: Daniel Cole/ReutersView image in fullscreenInstagram’s Instants feature allows users to send images that disappear after viewing.Photograph: Daniel Cole/ReutersMetaOfcom investigates Meta over Instagram Instants safety checksWatchdog examining whether company carried out adequate risk assessment as required by Online Safety ActDan MilmoGlobal technology editorTue 6 Oct 2026 09.22 EDTFirst published on Tue 6 Oct 2026 06.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMark Zuckerberg’s Meta is under investigation for a potential breach of the UK’s digital safety laws after launching a Snapchat-style feature onInstagram.The communications watchdog,Ofcom, is investigating whether the $1.9tn (£1.4tn) company infringed the Online Safety Act (OSA) by failing to carry out adequate checks on whether its Instagram Instants product could show illegal content or be accessed by children.Social media companies are required to carry out risk assessments before making significant changes to their service’s design or operation. Breaching the OSA carries a range of potential actions, from a formal warning to a fine of up to 10% of global revenue.George Lusty, the director of enforcement at Ofcom, said risk assessments were a vital step in keeping tech platforms safe for users. “You wouldn’t launch a new car without testing it properly, and it’s the same for online services,” he said. “Safety by design must be built in, not bolted on, and today’s investigation shows we’ll take action where we have concerns that providers are failing to comply.”View image in fullscreenScreenshots of Instagram Instants.Photograph: Meta NewsroomInstagram’s Instants feature allows users to send images that disappear after viewing. The company said it had conducted a risk analysis of Instants and talked to Ofcom on a number of occasions before launching it. It said the feature carried protections such as blocking forwarding and included all the safeguards under itsteen account settings, the default mode for under-18s on Instagram, Facebook and Messenger.“We will of course cooperate with Ofcom during this investigation,” aMetaspokesperson said.The Molly Rose Foundation, a charity established by the family of Molly Russell, a teenager whotook her own lifeafter viewing harmful content on Instagram, said it was crucial that Meta was “held to account for their failures under the Online Safety Act”.Ofcom is already investigating whether Meta breached the law by failing to comply with a request for information related to its WhatsApp platform.Zuckerberg’s company is challenging Ofcom in court over the OSA. It is suing the regulator in the high court over how it charges tech firms fees to cover its operating costs and, in a further case, it is challenging Ofcom for placing WhatsApp and Instagram in a new category under the act thatsubjects it to additional duties.Meta has also joined TikTok and Elon Musk’s X in a court challenge over the amount of information Ofcom is demanding they provide under the online safety regime.Explore more on these topicsMetaInstagramOfcomSocial mediaInternet safetynewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Pull the plug’: protesters resort to direct action against AI firms | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Campaign groups report surge in membership after a spate of AI safety alerts and apocalyptic warnings
Author: Robert Booth
Headline: Campaign groups report surge in membership after a spate of AI safety alerts and apocalyptic warnings
Content: A protest against AI outside Downing Street in London last month. It was organised by PauseAI, a confederation of campaign groups in 17 countries.Photograph: Vuk Valcic/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenA protest against AI outside Downing Street in London last month. It was organised by PauseAI, a confederation of campaign groups in 17 countries.Photograph: Vuk Valcic/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockAI (artificial intelligence)‘Pull the plug’: protesters resort to direct action against AI firmsCampaign groups report surge in membership after a spate of AI safety alerts and apocalyptic warningsRobert BoothUK technology editorTue 6 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 06.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn a bar below Waterloo Bridge, a cell of a fast-growing anti-AI protest movement met last week to plot their latest move: disrupting a tech industry dinner being addressed by a senior executive from the chip maker Nvidia.Emma, a 28-year-old bartender, had never before taken direct action and was the most nervous of the four plotters from Pull The Plug, one of a growing number of AI-focused campaign groups around the world.Around the table were a former climate protester and a campaigner versed in the anti-nuclear movement. Emma signed up after a summer of feeling rising alarm at the catastrophic risks of AI, first when a swarm of OpenAI agents escaped their training “sandbox”, cheated, deceived and conspired tohackinto the Hugging Face website and then as Jacob Coxon, an Anthropic researcher, quit with anapocalyptic warningthat superintelligent AI “could kill us all by the end of the decade”.As darkness fell they crossed the Thames to the Claremont hotel where Emma filmed while two others unfurled a banner in a function room, shouting “Pull the plug on Nvidia” and “Pull the plug on Palantir”. Hundreds of protesters also staged a rally in front of Palantir’s London HQ last Thursday.“We did not consent to the kind of build-out that you are planning here,” the activists yelled as they were wrestled out of the door. They edited a video clip – “activist disrupts elite AI network dinner – Nvidia edition” – and uploaded it to Instagram. It was a small gesture, but they had made their stand.“I want to show other people that they don’t have to feel powerless among all of these articles coming out [about AI doom],” said Emma. “It’s easy to fall into a spiral that it’s too late. This shows people they can address the tech executives, disrupt their meetings, make them feel uncomfortable and get some answers.”View image in fullscreenA protest in London on 1 October against the AI firm Palantir, which has a series of UK government contracts.Photograph: Martin Pope/Getty ImagesPull The Plug was launched in January and has about 300 members – mostly aged from 20 to 40. It is backed by an anonymous funder who works in the technology industry, organisers said. Several campaigns resisting AI acceleration are funded bytech insiders.Pull The Plug advocates direct action – a tactic other AI campaigns have rejected. Last month, one of its members climbed on to a chair in a packed AI conference in London addressed by speakers from OpenAI and Amazon anddeliveredan impassioned speech.“Best case scenario: the men handling this technology are completely incompetent,” the female activist said in an outburst that garnered 153,000 Instagram likes and was picked up by the Washington Post. “Worst case scenario: we are all being led into a disaster.”Other AI protest movements are gaining momentum after a torrent of news about AI dangers. Anthropictold investorsthis week that advanced AI could pose “existential risks to humanity”. Pause AI, a confederation of campaign groups in 17 countries, saw a fourfold jump in sign-ups when worrying news about rogue AI agents was breaking in August and last month.“We have had a lot of volunteers who have suddenly decided to dedicate way more of their time to the cause,” said Maxime Fournes, a Cambridge-educated mathematician and deep learning engineer who is chief executive of PauseAI Global. Volunteer sign-ups doubled to about 100 a week after the Hugging Face incident and soared to 681 in the week of Coxon’s “kill us all” warning, when PauseAI organised protests in Paris, London and Berlin.Donald Trump may be one of the movement’s most important recruiting sergeants. Heannouncedlast week that he wanted AI companies to “self-police” despite widespread demands, including from the companies, for federal and international rules to limit AI-enabled cyber-attacks and bioweapons.The surge in worrying news has given campaigners like Fournes hope that “we could actually survive this situation”. He added: “Suddenly we have a large fraction of the world population that is waking up.”Joseph Miller, an AI safety researcher who has suspended his doctoral studies at Oxford University to run Pause AI’s UK branch, noticed the shift while campaigning outside Brixton tube station in London. He said: “It was the easiest flyering we’ve ever done, because people would just come and talk to me … one every few minutes.”People he spoke to were worried about cognitive decline in schools and AI resulting in sloppy work in the office. “I heard ‘killing everyone’ more from young people,” Miller added.Pausing or halting AI is a cause that cuts across political and generational boundaries, according to campaigners. University students sign up because they fear AI will wreck career paths, while older conservationists rally against datacentre construction.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn Scotland, where at least 21 datacentres are planned, Action to Protect Rural Scotland, a 100-year old charity better known for campaigning for green belt land, said its supporter list had swollen from 400 to 4,000.“I’ve never seen grassroots energy like this,” said Kat Jones, the charity’s director. She affectionately calls it “a campaign of nerds” with supporters probing the workings of AI datacentre cooling systems and the power grid and lodging freedom of information requests.AI’s need for vast physical infrastructure has provided a “very physical, concrete object of protest”, said Fournes, and, in some cases, a target for direct action. In the last year, far-left or anarchist groups protesting over the climate crisis and AI haveclaimedresponsibility for criminal attacks on infrastructure in France and Germany.In August, Wynd Kaufmyn, became the first anti-AI protester believed to have beenjailedfor taking direct action – in her case blocking the entrance to OpenAI’s HQ in San Francisco. In April, another protesterhurleda petrol bomb at the house of the company’s chief executive, Sam Altman. The same month, an attacker fired gunshots into the home of an Indianapolis politician in protest at datacentre plans.Mauro Lubrano, assistant professor of terrorism and political violence at the University of Leiden, said that if rising demands for accountability, transparency, and democracy in AI governance were not met, more people could get drawn to violence.“It’s quite likely that we will see anti-AI violence becoming more prominent as a driver to political violence,” he said, citing last month’s vandalism of a Canadian AI institute, Mila, and a nearby software company in Montreal. Windows were smashed and graffiti scrawled reading “burn the data centers”.Some Pull The Plug activists have diverted their energy from Just Stop Oil and Extinction Rebellion. One member of Emma’s cell glued herself to roads to protest against the climate crisis – tactics that have alienated the public.Such direct action is “extremely counterproductive”, said Fournes who predicted it would trigger “an immune response” from wider society and would provide “a golden opportunity for the AI labs … to say, they are criminals and it is easier to turn the broader public against the movement against the development of AI”.Whatever the tactics, a movement is stirring.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpenAIDonald TrumpComputingActivismnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Rip it open’: Big Girls Don’t Cry director explores wounds of early love in film festival hit | New Zealand | The Guardian
description: Director Paloma Schneideman explores issues of consent and queerness in coming-of-age film set in New Zealand
Author: Michelle Duff
Headline: Director Paloma Schneideman explores issues of consent and queerness in coming-of-age film set in New Zealand
Content: Paloma Schneideman, right, on the set of Big Girls Don't Cry.Photograph: Jen RaoultView image in fullscreenPaloma Schneideman, right, on the set of Big Girls Don't Cry.Photograph: Jen RaoultNew Zealand‘Rip it open’: Big Girls Don’t Cry director explores wounds of early love in film festival hitDirector Paloma Schneideman explores issues of consent and queerness in coming-of-age film set in New ZealandMichelle Duffin WellingtonTue 6 Oct 2026 19.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn Big Girls Don’t Cry, theNew Zealandcoming-of-age film quietly devastating film festivals, there is a scene on a moonlit beach. It features the main character, Sid, played by Ani Palmer, and one of the cool older city boys who has come to the small, golden-sand town of Ōmaha for the summer. It is a deeply relatable, deeply uncomfortable watch; reliving the teenage negotiation – or not – of consent feels unsettling and validating.“Yeah, an 18-year-old at the screening last night said, ‘I feel so seen and exposed,” director and writer Paloma Schneideman, 34, says. “I was like, whoa, that’s quite an astute way to think about it. One is cathartic and healing, and the other is quite confronting.”Schneideman says she wanted to tell a story about the place “between consent and non-consent, where it was just something we felt we had to do”.“It’s such a tricky space, and I don’t think we see it a lot. How do we make amends with the scars of that time?”View image in fullscreenAni Palmer plays the main character, Sid, who negotiates adolescence in the golden-sand town of Ōmaha.Photograph: Jen RaoultThe global response to Shneideman’s debut film, which also explores desire, queerness and finding your way – in this case, through small-town New Zealand in the early millennium – suggests the need to feel empathy for our teenage selves is universally felt.Since its debut at theSundance film festivalin February, the film has won the Nouvelle Vagues film festival’s Grand Prix – actorKristen Stewartsaid it “unpacks the early 2000s, and subliminal trespass, and pain and strength … with such an astounding touch” – and has been shown at major festivals from South by Southwest to London’s BFI Flare. Variety called it a “gentle, rigorous, queer coming of age story”, while the Hollywood Reporter said it “pulses with a powerful sense of place and terrifically charged scenes of chaotic intimacy”.The Quiet Earth: New Zealand post-apocalyptic classic preys on the fear of being totally aloneRead moreAhead of its general release in New Zealand and the US on 8 and 9 October, Shneideman is feeling grateful for the way it’s connected with audiences. “The most amazing part is seeing how many people take such ownership over the film, they think it’s for them. And it is.”‘Sleepless nights’The film’s protagonist, 14-year-old Sid, negotiates adolescence at a time of fledgling dial-up internet and brick phones, where options for connecting with like-minded people or exploring sexuality included booting up MSN messenger or flicking through satellite TV to covertly watch Red Shoe Diaries. It wasn’t a particularly safe moment to be queer, or a teenage girl in New Zealand.“I found the one queer person in [high school] and they very quickly became my best friend,” Shneideman says. “There was a boy in the First IV [rugby team] who people found out had two mums, and it was the point of gossip and bullying.”Shneideman developed Big Girls Don’t Cry while at Wave in the Ocean, the prestigious film school set up by Oscar-award winning directorJane Campion(The Piano, Power of the Dog) as part of its first 10-person intake in 2022. It’s the first feature film to be released by a graduate, and is supported by the New Zealand Film Commission.View image in fullscreenAni Palmer in Big Girls Don’t Cry, which explores desire, queerness, shame, and finding your way.Photograph: Jen Raoult“We were sort of these guinea pigs and we just had the best time, learning from the best practitioners in the country and if we weren’t doing that we were watching and shooting films and having mental breakdowns together,” Shneideman says. The script she began writing in 2019 kept evolving, even as it got into the hands of Palmer, Australian actor Noah Taylor, and American Rain Spencer in the 25 days it was shot between Ōmaha and Auckland early last year. “They’re all master improvisers, they meet me in this middle space between the script and the screen. Some of their best lines were theirs.”Campion, named as an executive producer on Big Girls Don’t Cry, encouraged creativity – including a daily movement practice – and listening to intuition, Schneideman says. “She was very much ‘the precedents you set for yourself in your first film will stay with you for the rest of your career,’ so lead how you want to lead.”As a result, Schneideman developed what she calls a “body gauge” during Big Girls Don’t Cry to help her discern if a shot, a performance, or a cut wasn’t right. ‘When the work’s not there, when the performance is not there, it actually just makes me feel quite sick. I can’t tell you how many sleepless nights I had, staring up at the wall being like – how do we blow that up and start it again and fix it?” she says. “My whole thing as a film-maker is to try and make you not notice any of the work, so as soon as something pulls you out, we’ve failed.”View image in fullscreenFrom left, Rain Spencer, Noah Taylor, Paloma Schneideman and Ani Palmer at the 2026 Sundance film festival.Photograph: Arturo Holmes/Getty ImagesShe’s got a whirlwind of international release dates ahead of her, but Shneideman is already looking ahead. On a taxi-ride recently to LAX, she found herself running through scenes for the next film she wants to make, which she describes as an “anti romance,” exploring the wounds of lost love.Will this be a hallmark of her career? “Yeah. Rip it open. Then when I finally feel healed, just rip it open again. We don’t want a film that’s just happy, and everything goes right. I think that would be deeply dissatisfying.”Explore more on these topicsNew ZealandJane CampionAsia PacificDrama filmsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I’m bringing together women who nourish me’: French film-maker Alice Diop on her debut installation | Installation | The Guardian
description: The Saint Omer director has gathered work by artists, writers, composers and poets for Geste de Consolation, set in the 60m-long central hall of the Palais d’Iena in Paris
Author: Caroline Roux
Headline: The Saint Omer director has gathered work by artists, writers, composers and poets for Geste de Consolation, set in the 60m-long central hall of the Palais d’Iena in Paris
Content: Sénégal en saison sèche (Senegal in the Dry Season), photograph, 1920 … part of Geste de Consolation, curated by Alice Diop.Photograph: Miu Miu, Art BaselView image in fullscreenSénégal en saison sèche (Senegal in the Dry Season), photograph, 1920 … part of Geste de Consolation, curated by Alice Diop.Photograph: Miu Miu, Art BaselInstallationInterview‘I’m bringing together women who nourish me’: French film-maker Alice Diop on her debut installationCaroline RouxThe Saint Omer director has gathered work by artists, writers, composers and poets for Geste de Consolation, set in the 60m-long central hall of the Palais d’Iena in ParisTue 6 Oct 2026 09.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlice Diop has just returned to France from California when we speak. It’s a Zoom meeting with a bad connection, and Diop leans close to the camera, always in frame, barely moving. It’s like watching the characters in her documentaries and films, where her camera lingers on its subject with a slow, cool intensity.Diop had been attending a two-week celebration of her work organised by the French department at University of California, Berkeley, in which academics pored over her documentaries (Nous(We),Vers La Tendresse(Towards Tenderness)) and her first feature film,Saint Omer, which received the Silver Lion in Venice in 2022. The courtroom drama was inspired by a real trial that Diop attended, of a Senegalese woman who had allowed her baby to drown in the sea. Over two hours, it explored the complexities of race, culture and motherhood in contemporary France. The film was the first by a black female director to be entered by France as its official entry in the 2023 Academy Awards.View image in fullscreen‘Maybe I make films because I’m a frustrated writer’ … Alice Diop.“To be studied like that, in such a temple of intellectual resistance, I was bowled over,” says Diop of UC Berkeley. “As a film-maker, it’s not up to me to analyse my work. But listening to them, it was good to feel understood.”As a film-maker, it’s also not her usual role to be putting on an exhibition. But today, we are here to discussGeste de Consolation(Gesture of Consolation), a multipart installation involving film, artworks, readings, music and dance, soon to open in Paris, coinciding with theArt Basel fair. Diop was invited by the Italian fashion house Miu Miu to create the five-day extravaganza, and is approaching it scene by scene, like a film director. “I’m not an artist, I’ve no desire to be an exhibition curator,” she says.Instead, it offered an opportunity to “bring together in one space, many of the women who work with me, who nourish me, who have helped me heal, and have together enabled this notion of consolation”. They includeMarie Ndiaye, with whom she writes her films, the American poetRobin Coste Lewis, Chicagoan composerAngel Bat Dawidand historical figures such as Virginia Woolf.View image in fullscreenA towering presence … Simone Leigh’s Mami Wata.Photograph: Alex Marks/Courtesy Prospect New OrleansThe exhibition will open with a poignant image from the South African artistZanele Muholi, of a woman looking at herself naked in the mirror. “Zanele gives dignity and a voice to those who are marginalised,” says Diop. It closes withSimone Leigh’s sculpture Mami Wata, representing diasporic west African spirituality. “You will be able to see her from all over the hall,” says Diop of Mami Wata’s towering presence. “Simone is a star in her native US, and has a huge retrospective coming to London in 2027. But she’s never had a show in France. This is an attempt to redress that.”This is the third year that Miu Miu has sponsored this exhibition, set to take place in thePalais d’Iéna, a modernist masterpiece from the early 1940s with an extraordinary 60m-long uninterrupted central hall. It’s where the house puts on its catwalk shows, and it applies the same no-expense-spared policy to the presentation of art. The first iteration in 2024, by the Polish artistGoshka Macuga, included a massive mechanical conveyor belt and a cast of about 100 actors. Diop’s will offer four principal scenarios, including a library of the texts that have most informed her work and life, where visitors are invited to read and relax. She says she reads more than she watches film, “But cinema is my language. It allows me a precision that I couldn’t achieve in literature … Or maybe I make films because I’m a frustrated writer.”In 2025, Diop contributed to Miu Miu’s Women’s Tales, a series of short films by female directors. In her 20-minute film, Fragments for Venus, art looms large as actor Kayije Kagame stares at paintings with black subjects in the dwarfingly large galleries of the Louvre, before the action shifts to a Brooklyn street where the gaze belongs instead to the phenomenal Séphora Pondi and the women around her, full of agency and vitality. Kagame and Pondi could be Diop herself – the still, silent observer.“From the moment I agreed to take on this project, I decided it had to be another opportunity to pursue all the questions that I ask in my films,” says Diop. Her own work in the exhibition is a split-screen video installation of archival imagery and film clips that she says have formed own cinematic image bank. “Some of them are quite troubling, violent,” she says. “In others I have found consolation.” In Diop’s world, it seems there is rarely one without the other.Alice Diop: Geste de Consolation is atPalais d’Iéna, Paris, 21-25 OctoberExplore more on these topicsInstallationDocumentary filmsSculptureArtMiu MiuExhibitionsinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Hamlet’s goodbye, the last of Leigh, Birmingham blues and a vampire in Vienna: 12 great films at the London film festival | London film festival | The Guardian
description: Our critic picks out some of the most outstanding cinema screening at the UK’s most prestigious film event in 2026
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Our critic picks out some of the most outstanding cinema screening at the UK’s most prestigious film event in 2026
Content: Final bows … Andrew Scott as Ian Charleson in Elsinore.Photograph: Anthony Dickenson/Focus FeaturesView image in fullscreenFinal bows … Andrew Scott as Ian Charleson in Elsinore.Photograph: Anthony Dickenson/Focus FeaturesLondon film festivalHamlet’s goodbye, the last of Leigh, Birmingham blues and a vampire in Vienna: 12 great films at the London film festivalOur critic picks out some of the most outstanding cinema screening at the UK’s most prestigious film event in 2026Peter BradshawTue 6 Oct 2026 07.29 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 07.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleElsinoreThis film puts Andrew Scott in line to becomethe first out gay man to win the best actor Oscar. He plays Ian Charleson, who became a star in Chariots of Fire and in 1989 took on the role of Hamlet at London’s National Theatre when Daniel Day-Lewis withdrew, despite being desperately ill with Aids, knowing that the strain would accelerate his illness. For Charleson, the play’s themes of life and death, truth and falsehood, justice and injustice, were all too real.7 Miles OutFans of Manchester, Manchesterism and indie British film-maker Carol Morley will relish the thought of her much anticipated new movie, adapted from her autobiographical novel of the same title. The lead character, Ann, based on Morley herself, experiences an emotional crisis as a teen and takes refuge in the thrilling new Manchester music scene, featuring bands including Joy Division, New Order and Magazine. Lucy Halliday is Ann and her mum and dad are played by Gemma Whelan and Aidan Gillen.FatherlandPolish film-makerPaweł Pawlikowskihas created a brilliantly poised, superbly performed historical vignette in black-and-white whose brevity and control can hardly contain its characters’ anguish. Hanns Zischler and Sandra Hüller play Thomas and Erika Mann – that is, the great Nobel-winning German author and his daughter. After the war and the destruction of the Nazis, whose tyranny he escaped by fleeing to the US, Mann returns to Germany with daughter in tow, to accept prizes in the fatherland’s capitalist West and communist East. But he is in denial about a terrible family crisis.View image in fullscreenSuperb …  Hanns Zischler and Sandra Hüller in Fatherland.Photograph: Agata GrzybowskaLa GradivaSurely the year’s best debut feature? French cinematographer turned director Marine Atlan tells a gripping story of a school trip to Pompeii: an emotionally troubled teacher has to keep an emotionally troubled bunch of kids in line. Perhaps the most difficult is a boy called Toni, who has always believed a story told him by his mum that he has aristocratic lineage from a Pompeii nobleman whose castle was reduced to rubble by southern Italy’s 1980 earthquake, an event he thinks is thrillingly analogous to the Pompeii disaster. He’s heading for his own emotional earthquake.I See Buildings Fall Like LightningBirmingham is the setting for this absorbing and moving social realist picture from film-makerClio Barnard, featuring terrific performances from its young cast. It’s a home town drama about a city to which the characters are fundamentally loyal while simultaneously longing to escape; as they approach the end of their 20s, they must come to terms with decisions and life choices. Joe Cole, Daryl McCormack, Lola Petticrew, Anthony Boyle and Jay Lycurgo are the cast-members bursting with energy, tenderness and vulnerability.View image in fullscreenStriking … I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning.Photograph: Chris HarrisA Long WinterAndrew Haigh’s mysterious and beautiful new film is adapted by him from a story by Colm Tóibín: a poignant, subversive study of grief and desire, and the terrible, infantilised loneliness of men without women. A family living a tough existence in remote 1950s Colorado are traumatised when the troubled mother of the household, played by Caitriona Balfe, disappears one winter and the menfolk, having decided that the search can only resume once the snows have melted, enter into a strange new period of bachelor freedom.The Blood CountessIt’s the part she was born to play.Isabelle Huppertis Countess Elizabeth Báthory, a 16th-century Hungarian noblewoman and serial killer, legendary for having the blood of hundreds of young girls on her hands, and indeed all over the rest of her body, in an attempt to attain eternal youth. Her Báthory is a vampire who has returned to present-day Vienna, the historical seat of the Austro-Hungarian empire, seen initially gliding through its sewers as if on a royal barge, making her way far more coolly than Harry Lime in The Third Man.I Love BoostersChicago rapper and film-makerBoots Riley, the comic bard of black anxiety and white privilege, returns with a hyperactive romp about a bandit group of fashion influencers who deal with the issue of price by simply “boosting” clothes from stores. This group of outlaws includes Naomi Ackie and Taylour Paige, and the resentful fashionista ice-queen whose wares are being sticky-fingered in this way is played by Demi Moore.View image in fullscreenColour clash … I Love Boosters.Photograph: NeonGentle MonsterHere is a coldly eloquent and disquieting drama starringLéa Seydouxabout women who find themselves imprisoned by a duty of care and loyalty to the men in their lives. Seydoux plays Lucy, an acclaimed musician with a TV director husband and three-year-old child; one day, the police show up at their door to take away the husband’s computers, tablets and smartphones. The husband replies unconvincingly to Lucy’s desperate questions as to what this is all about, and her ordeal is her need to believe him, to twist and contort what she sees so it will fit into the husband’s shapeshifting explanations.The DebutJesse Eisenberg follows up his excellent dramaA Real Painwith this much admired and widely enjoyed dramedy about community theatre, for which Julianne Moore may be once again in the Oscar conversation. She plays a neglected housewife, going mad with boredom and emotional neglect in her Stepford prison; she tries out for a local amateur troupe’s production of a musical (whose hokey songs Eisenberg has himself written). Needless to say, she transforms from a suburban doormat into a Bette Davis-level diva.View image in fullscreenA star is born … Julianne Moore in The Debut.Photograph: Matt Infante/A24/APMy Notes on MarsHungarian film-maker Lili Horvát has always had a taste for the inexplicable; now she makes her English-language debut with a film that fuses romance, science fiction and mystery. Mackenzie Davis is Margot, a scientist with emotional problems who vanishes while on a hiking trip with her husband Sam, played by Rupert Friend. Much later, at her memorial service, Margot sensationally reappears, with no memory of what happened, but a determination to destroy her notes on Mars. Is that where’s she’s … gulp … been?Tender Loving CareIs thisMike Leigh’s final film? Let’s hope not. It’s a tender, poignant drama that is also candid and forthright, muscular in its effects. It’s an intergenerational story about the friendship of two women from west London, Rosie and Amy, who share a flat and work in social care. The film gives a complex, interrelated pattern of scenes showing their personal and professional lives and the people close to them. It is a lovely film.TheLondon film festivalis on 7-18 OctoberExplore more on these topicsLondon film festivalFestivalsAndrew ScottPaweł PawlikowskiClio BarnardAndrew HaighIsabelle HuppertfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: House of Stassi: never before has reality TV been this self-aware – and truly brutal | Reality TV | The Guardian
description: After being cancelled, former Vanderpump Rules star Stassi Schroeder is fighting for redemption with her own show – never mind what her family and friends think
Author: Wendy Syfret
Headline: After being cancelled, former Vanderpump Rules star Stassi Schroeder is fighting for redemption with her own show – never mind what her family and friends think
Content: ‘From the moment she appeared on screen … it was clear that Stassi Schroeder was an early master of the reality genre.’Photograph: DisneyView image in fullscreen‘From the moment she appeared on screen … it was clear that Stassi Schroeder was an early master of the reality genre.’Photograph: DisneyStream teamReality TVHouse of Stassi: never before has reality TV been this self-aware – and truly brutalAfter being cancelled, former Vanderpump Rules star Stassi Schroeder is fighting for redemption with her own show – never mind what her family and friends thinkWendy SyfretTue 6 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 17.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAcross the 2010s, Stassi Schroeder was the star of Vanderpump Rules,the hit reality TV show that tracked the near-psychopathic interpersonal relationships between the staff at Lisa Vanderpump’s peak-millennial restaurant SUR. From the moment she appeared on screen – all statement necklaces and crispy flatironed hair – it was clear that Schroeder was an early master of the reality genre. While the cast were all villainous in their own ways, she stood apart for her singular mix of charisma and chaos.For eight years, Schroeder slapped her friends, belittled her bosses, bullied other women, insulted customers and was generally terrible at her job. But despite the frequent physical and psychological violence, she remained a firm audience favourite. In the years since, she has spoken about the impact this kind of adoration can have on a person: the worse she behaved, the more she was rewarded with attention from producers and the adoring – and admonishing – public. For a time, she was the people’s princess of darkness. That was until 2020, when she discovered there are limits to what even blond, leggy reality TV prodigies can do.Horny, horrifying and unhinged: why Vanderpump Rules is the best reality show of all timeRead moreDuring the 2020 Black Lives Matter reckoning, it emerged that Schroeder and castmate Kristen Doute had oncefalsely reported their Black cast mate Faith Stowersto police for a crime she didn’t commit. For the first time, her actions were seen not as the plotting of a wily mean girl, but as the calculated acts of a privileged woman wielding her power to harm a woman of colour. Schroeder was fired from the show she helped make famous. More specifically, she was cancelled.Schroeder has spoken at length about what the “cancellation” did to her life and ascendant TV career. At the time, she was newly engaged and preparing for her inevitable TV wedding and spin-off show with her surprisingly sweet partner Beau Clark. Instead, she spent the following years languishing in the purgatory of once-beloved, now problematic, celebrities: making a lot of money through podcasts, social media and brand endorsements. Then, this year, Disney and Hulu announced the prodigal daughter’s return via her own eight-episode series House of Stassi.You don’t need to be a reality TV producer to understand what this show wassupposedto be. All parties signed on for a self-aware redemption arc that allowed a former golden girl to reflect, grow and in turn permit an ocean of sheepish fans to click “follow” again.Watching Schroeder sit down for her first confessional interview, one wonders if anyone haseverlooked more at home in any situation. She jokes with off-screen producers, makes self-aware digs and notes that Disney money has improved the set design. Immediately, two things are clear: Schroeder is still a beautiful, charismatic, articulate narcissist who you can’t look away from. And, after fighting for years to secure another big break, she is not going to waste it.On one level, the following eight episodes are exactly what you’d expect. Schroeder fights, cries, screams and cracks decent jokes while making you wonder if you would also look good in a pair of brown silk pants. On another, it’s a study in how this kind of work rots your brain and life, while leaving you desperate for more. At one point she admits: “I’m scared of reality TV, but it’s all I know … I love it, but I’m also traumatised by it. I can’t stay away from it.”Schroeder came to LA to be an actor, but quickly realised her skill was acting as a version of herself. Watching House of Stassi, it’s clear she also considers herself to be a canny reality TV producer. Far from breaking the fourth wall, the show never constructs one. Producers’ voices are constantly heard off-screen as Schroeder chats about the process of not only pitching the show to Disney, but remaking her own existence to fit the pitch.View image in fullscreen‘Early episodes see her arrange friends and family members like dolls.’Photograph: DisneyOver the years between reality TV ventures, Schroeder has built a nice life for herself. But nice doesn’t make good TV. Understanding the need for drama, she gets to work pushing every emotional bruise in reach. Early episodes see her arrange friends and family members like dolls, sometimes openly coaching them about how to appear engaging on camera.Other times, her methods are more machiavellian. She arranges confrontations between former friends, triggers her younger sister’s insecurities and openly baits her mild-mannered husband Beau into fighting about their marriage on camera. All the time she justifies this chaos, to herself and the camera, by explaining that the whole show was pitched as a way to help her loved ones “level up their lives” and “all become rich and famous – like the Kardashians!” It never seems to bother her that many of them openly express that this isn’t the life they want, or that her actions are actively making their daily existence more miserable.The results of this manipulation are mixed. Often, the cast seem baffled about how pieces of their lives are being moved around them. Old friends are destabilised by the appearance of faded acquaintances, seemingly brought in because they’re not interesting enough to occupy the screen alone. As a result, even the more stilted early episodes have a postmodern quality as Schroeder manipulates “reality” to fit her preferred version of the show.View image in fullscreen‘It’s quickly made clear to everyone – except shockingly, Schroeder – that Beau is deeply unhappy.’Photograph: DisneySchroeder is at her most alive and natural in the show’s confessional segments. There, speaking to producers, she sparkles. In contrast, with her “real” friends and family she is often awkward and clumsily abrupt.Eventually, things pick up as Schroeder begins to lose her carefully produced control. It’s clear the intention of this show was to present a post-cancellation, girl-boss success story. One semi-interesting part of Stassi’s life is that she is the breadwinner and Beau is the “house husband”. This was supposed to be a tongue-in-cheek play on the nuclear family. Except it plays more Sylvia Plath than Lucille Ball.It’s quickly made clear to everyone – except shockingly, Schroeder – that Beau is deeply unhappy. Beau complains to everyone – except shockingly, Schroeder – about how lost he feels after years of being out of the workforce and how badly he wants to return to his former career as a casting director. But Schroeder blocks all his attempts to not only go back to work, but even speak meaningfully about it. What plays out is not a career-Barbie fantasy, but a simmering look at a marriage turning toxic.Being a self-aware reality TV show, of course this must all come to a head in a finale dinner on a haunted boat. Except, this isn’t one of the confrontational showdowns Schroeder has been building to all season between her friends/employees/cast members. Instead, she herself is blindsided as all her friends effectively stage an intervention about the state of her marriage.View image in fullscreenOne of Schroeder’s friends and collaborators Taylor Strecker.Photograph: DisneyWhether you think Schroeder is a Cassandra-style truth-teller or a garden-variety narcissist, it’s fair to say this would be anyone’s nightmare. And, true to form, Schroeder delivers an epic meltdown, more feral and unfiltered than she clearly ever planned to share. By the end of the final episode she’s cowering on the floor after admitting to being afraid of her own children, screaming at her loved ones and telling her husband she never wants to see him again.When TV turns sour: the shows we simply can’t stomach any moreRead moreFor the most part, House of Stassi is never as clever or innovative as it thinks it is. It aims for a self-aware reality TV critique, gets stuck along the way and largely just feels smug and overly produced. But in these final moments, Schroeder and friends accidentally deliver something truly “real”.While her SheEO-shtick feels plastic, this is a truly brutal look at the complexities of motherhood. It’s hard to think of another piece of media – scripted or not – that so bracingly shows a woman not only cycling through the guilt and shame of having to admit she cannot handle her own children, but doesn’t really want to.At the end of the season, Schroeder turns to the last individual left she can trust: the camera, admitting: “I feel stupid because I didn’t see this coming, and I should have.”Ultimately, House of Stassidoes say something interesting about the reality genre – just not what it was intending to. Because if Stassi Schroeder can’t bend this beast to her will and get out unscathed, no one can.House of Stassi is available on Disney+ in Australia and the UK, and on Hulu and Fubo in the US. title: V/H/S/Mixtape review – murderous puppets pull the strings in mixed bag of gory music-themed mini-movies | Movies | The Guardian
description: Metal band Gwar host this instalment of the horror series, which serves up darkly humorous movie morsels that would struggle to frighten a toddler
Author: Leslie Felperin
Headline: Metal band Gwar host this instalment of the horror series, which serves up darkly humorous movie morsels that would struggle to frighten a toddler
Content: They’re no muppets … puppets seek revenge on studio executives in Renee Zhan’s short film Dance, Dance, Dance, Dance, featured in V/H/S/MixtapeView image in fullscreenThey’re no muppets … puppets seek revenge on studio executives in Renee Zhan’s short film Dance, Dance, Dance, Dance, featured in V/H/S/MixtapeMoviesReviewV/H/S/Mixtape review – murderous puppets pull the strings in mixed bag of gory music-themed mini-moviesMetal band Gwar host this instalment of the horror series, which serves up darkly humorous movie morsels that would struggle to frighten a toddlerLeslie FelperinTue 6 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe latest in the long-running horror-feature series is, as per usual, a decidedly diverse ragbag of shorts, strung together with the thinnest of connective tissue. The theme this go-round seems to be music and sound, so it sort of makes sense that hosting duties for the interstitial bits fall to the goofy metal bandGwar, its assorted members met here cracking Halloween dad jokes in their trademark extravagant outfits.The five mini movies vary significantly in length as well as quality. Flying Lotus’s stop-motion exercise Another Cabin posits a young boy in a rural cabin living with a mean old grannie who tries to push him forward when a tentacled demon tears the roof of the house in search of a snack. The characters’ resemblance to the cast of early 2000s series The PJs is slightly jarring, given this is such a different register, but the brevity works in its favour. In contrast Renee Zhan’s Dance, Dance, Dance, Dance, the opener, drags on a bit, but has a reasonable gags-to-gore ratio in its tale of murderous puppets taking revenge on visiting studio execs who would dare to “reimagine” some ageing IP best left dormant. The funniest gag is the bright major-scale title song the puppets (designed by Jim Henson’s Creature Shop) sing about how all things must die.Venerable cinematographer turned director Ernest Dickerson (who filmed several key Spike Lee films including Do the Right Thing and Malcolm X) turns the unsurprisingly beautifully shot and designed but thinly written amuse-bouche The Music of Mr Sze. This features Jihad Brent as an aspiring film-maker who becomes bewitched by the violin melodies emanating from the bedsit of his upstairs neighbour (Alex Hsu), a story that escalates into a fantasia of trippy but borderline incomprehensible imagery.Far more straightforward narratively but repetitive, Death Tone (directed by RZA) stars Neela Jolene as the daughter of a famed music producer who follows her late father’s instructions – and dips into his narcotic supply – to make the perfect song, featuring the screams of agony from a range of random victims. RZA is clearly having a jolly chuckle to himself over gags that might crack them up in the sound booth, but they don’t travel as well as he seems to think. Somewhere in the middle of this package David Moreau’s Heartbeat is a snoozy riff on a theme from Edgar Allan Poe, about obnoxious YouTubers who get trapped in a Bulgarian military base.Throughout the practical effects are over the top, rubbery and absurd; so much so they would struggle to frighten a toddler, but with its unpleasantly warped humour it’s not really for kids anyway.V/H/S/Mixtape is on Shudder and AMC+ from 9 OctoberExplore more on these topicsFilmHorror filmsFlying LotusComedy filmsComedyreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Celibidache was a musical visionary, an uncompromising perfectionist – and my father  | Classical music | The Guardian
description: The legendary conductor was acclaimed for his dazzling music-making, and infamous for his hatred of recordings. His son, writer of a new film about him, remembers a loving yet intransigent and demanding father
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The legendary conductor was acclaimed for his dazzling music-making, and infamous for his hatred of recordings. His son, writer of a new film about him, remembers a loving yet intransigent and demanding father
Content: Convinced that music can only be experienced live… Sergiu Celibidache (1912-1996) conducting in the early 1980s.Photograph: INTERFOTO/AlamyView image in fullscreenConvinced that music can only be experienced live… Sergiu Celibidache (1912-1996) conducting in the early 1980s.Photograph: INTERFOTO/AlamyClassical musicCelibidache was a musical visionary, an uncompromising perfectionist – and my fatherThe legendary conductor was acclaimed for his dazzling music-making, and infamous for his hatred of recordings. His son, writer of a new film about him, remembers a loving yet intransigent and demanding fatherSerge CelibidacheTue 6 Oct 2026 04.27 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 04.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMy father, Sergiu Celibidache, loved children more than anything because they are free and true to themselves. And yet, he once made a young boy wet himself when he dared to ask for an autograph, shouting at the poor child as if he had committed a federal crime because he knew there was a black market selling his signature behind his back.I grew up a privileged child with presents from all around the world. I was spoiled – to the despair of my mother, who always tried to keep my feet on the ground. But the gifts were part of my father’s way of making up for his long absences – he was often away touring with his orchestras.View image in fullscreenI missed him terribly when he was away on tour… Serge with his father Sergiu Celibidache,  in the 1970s.Photograph: Serge CelibidacheAs a young boy I had very little understanding that my father was a world-renowned conductor. I always missed him terribly when he was away, and yet he was nonetheless always very present in my life, and we were close. He was generous and attentive. There were frequent speeches about the less privileged and our duty to do something for them, and he was always eager to share stories of his picturesque childhood in Iași,Romaniaand his many adventures after leaving home to pursue music, without any support from his family.Those tales – some of which would eventually become part of The Yellow Tie – were fascinating. And he was such a good storyteller that I could hardly wait for my bedtime stories whenever he was around.But as much as I had a generous and entertaining father I also had an intransigent and demanding one.Whatever the school activity, whatever the situation at home, he expected me to be the best version of myself. If I received a disappointing grade or disrespected my mother in any way, I would have to explain myself. I was not to begin a sentence unless I knew where it was leading. If the structure of your thought was not clear, silence was a much better choice, he said.My father could not accept doing anything half heartedly. You had to be completely immersed in whatever you were doing at that very moment, fully invested in the “now”. Looking back, I remember the joy he found in preparing food for the four St Bernards at our country house, or in feeding the wild ducks at the river with such patience and dedication. So much life invested in the simplest activities. And he expected me to treat life as he did: with that drive, that indestructible belief in God and in oneself, and that absolute dedication.double quotation markHe considered it his duty to pass knowledge on to the next generation, but he was a highly demanding teacher who spared no one’s feelings.This pursuit of perfection was present throughout our daily lives. Even if only on a subconscious level, the pressure was constant for all of us – family, friends, colleagues and students. Oh, the poor students! As much as he was a phenomenal musician, my father’s approach to teaching remains questionable to this day. “Teaching is the most noble activity to which one can dedicate oneself,” he said; he loved it and considered it his duty to pass knowledge on to the next generation, in the manner of Socrates.Yet he was a highly demanding teacher who spared no one’s feelings. I remember one masterclass in Paris, at the Schola Cantorum. I was filming the session in which experienced students were invited to conduct the student orchestra in front of a live audience. Almost none of the trainee conductors escaped his harsh criticism – for an unjustified and perhaps overly expansive gesture or – God forbid – a forgotten background musical phrase. Sometimes, he would even ridicule them, to the audience’s amusement and their evident humiliation. I hid behind my camera, thanking God I had decided not to pursue a musical career. But I also knew that he loved them as he loved me, and wanted them to become the best versions of themselves. His intentions were pure but did his methods work? It’s debatable.View image in fullscreenBen Schnetzer as Celibidache in The Yellow TiePhotograph: Adi MarineciHis uncompromising perfectionism mixed with a deep sense of integrity led him to develop, over time, a profound disdain for recordings, which were, in his view, a dangerously false representation of live music experienced in a concert hall. Refusing lucrative offers from the four corners of the globe, he remained faithful to his conviction that music can only be experienced live.With no recordings of my father available, my thirst for knowledge drove me to discover the classical repertoire through the recorded music of the conductor who, judging by the music store shelves lined with his name seemed, at the time, to be the most widely acclaimed – Karajan. In my quest to absorb the masterworks, I was turning to the ultimate commercial recording figure as a substitute for a conductor who rejected recordings entirely! Still, I eased my conscience, remembering my father saying that when they first met in Berlin, Karajan was a genuine talent. (What happened later is another story …)As a small act of provocation, I would occasionally play a piece louder than necessary to provoke a reaction from my father. I found it difficult to accept that he would not make “his music” available to everyone – that he would not leave behind something of his extraordinary musical vision. In fact it infuriated me. So much so that, upon my return from NYU, I did exactly what you see in the film: I played a bootleg recording of one of his performances and pretended to him it was by a new conductor I’d discovered ... Needless to say, that conversation didn’t end well.double quotation markI grew up in awe of my father, but I did not agree with all that he did. That distance helped me approach a biopic about himI believed that even if a recording was not authentic music in his sense of the word, it would still have been the memory of a musical moment – and that, in itself, had value. I was so convinced of this that I agreed to let some of the orchestras he conducted in his later years record his concert performances without his knowledge. It was never about money, but about the genuine value of the documents themselves. He knew nothing about it, and, of course, I could not tell him. But today, I feel blessed that these “memories” exist.I grew up in awe of my father, but I did not agree with all that he did. That distance helped me find the courage to approach a biopic about his life. The goal was never to put him on a pedestal. The opening scene – where Japanese record company executives offer him a lucrative recording deal alongside a concert tour – does more than just show his aversion to recorded music. It introduces him as an impetuous and unpredictable man who wasn’t afraid of confrontations.View image in fullscreenHis is a truly inspirational story… Serge with his father Sergiu Celibidache.Photograph: Serge CelibidacheI and my co-writer James Olivier tried to remain faithful to the man we knew. The Yellow Tie is not only a story about music, love and integrity. It is a story about sacrifice, survival and identity. Beyond my father’s devastating exile from his familial roots, his is a deeply inspirational true story about an immigrant trying to succeed in a country that is largely hostile.All I can hope is that my father’s story may inspire those who sometimes struggle to find and define their own path. If he could do it against all odds, perhaps we can too.Serge Ioan Celibidachi is the director and co-writer of The Yellow Tie, in UK cinemas from Friday 9 October.Read Peter Bradshaw’s reviewExplore more on these topicsClassical musicRomaniaEuropefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Partita By Barbara Kingsolver review – a midlife follow-up to Demon Copperhead | Barbara Kingsolver | The Guardian
description: The sex writing threatens to throw the novel off-kilter, but there are rich rewards in this tale of music and middle-aged compromises
Author: Lara Feigel
Headline: The sex writing threatens to throw the novel off-kilter, but there are rich rewards in this tale of music and middle-aged compromises
Content: ‘Fascinated by how to write about music’ … Barbara Kingsolver.Photograph: Ian Curcio/The ObserverView image in fullscreen‘Fascinated by how to write about music’ … Barbara Kingsolver.Photograph: Ian Curcio/The ObserverBook of the dayBarbara KingsolverReviewPartita By Barbara Kingsolver review – a midlife follow-up to Demon CopperheadThe sex writing threatens to throw the novel off-kilter, but there are rich rewards in this tale of music and middle-aged compromisesLara FeigelTue 6 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 08.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhat is the role of art in an artist’s life? Should you commit everything to honing your talent in the hope of becoming a great master? Or should you use your artistic gift to enrich your life and that of your community? In Partita, acclaimed American novelistBarbara Kingsolvergrapples with these questions seriously and passionately through the story of a piano prodigy turned music teacher.The novel opens in the present, where Livia is a school music teacher in the same part of rural Tennessee where she grew up, married to a farmer who once worked on her father’s farm. Contented middle age has been disturbed by a phone call from Sigurd, a man she had an all-consuming, destructive love affair with at college. This pulls her back into her past: both the period of her brother’s suicide when she was 11, and the years when she escaped on a music scholarship to Indiana, convinced she was leaving her parents’ world behind for good. We discover that her dreams of being a world-class pianist were shattered by an accident that damaged her hand, and that Sigurd played a part in this.The two timeframes present two visions of the role of music in a life, and two visions of love as well. Livia in the present seems content to be the inspirational local music teacher that she herself had to go much further to find, but it’s clear that the 20-year-old Livia would have considered such a life a failure, and that her faith in her own talent was justified. Livia now is happy with sex as comfort – “like putting a heating pad on an aching muscle”. Yet she still relies on memories of another kind of sex to reach orgasm – sex with Sigurd that she remembers as comprising the tension and release of music: “harmonic tension, dynamic tension, oh my dear lord, the rubato, his movements slowing, slowing, robbing me of the truth of the beat until I begged for justice … Sometimes we both shed tears.”double quotation markPartita is an impassioned testament to the need for art in ordinary communities, and the need for ordinariness in artIt’s unfair to quote sex writing out of context, and I feel bad doing it here, but this breathless, overwrought prose runs through the account of Livia’s affair with Sigurd, threatening to throw the whole novel off-kilter. We know from Kingsolver’s other novels how assured her writing usually is, so the gaucheness felt out of place. But Kingsolver commits to her protagonists’ language more fervently than most novelists and I ended up deciding that this must be what’s happening here. There’s no doubt inDemon Copperheadthat the brash vernacular is Demon’s own, because the voice is closer to speech than to writing. Here, Livia’s voice is more literary, and so harder to distinguish from Kingsolver’s. But sentences such as “this wasn’t proper by a long shot: fingers craving to know the sandpaper of his jaw” are surely Livia’s, and the florid prose is a sign that she’s carried away by memories of the erotic apex of her life.Indeed, it’s revealing that Livia’s voice is subtler when it comes to music, which has seen her through into middle age while lust’s flame has faded. Kingsolver – who herself went to college with a music scholarship to study classical piano – is clearly fascinated by music, and how to write about it, and her gifts seem to entwine with Livia’s in the descriptions of piano pieces. Injured and learning to play again, Livia tries Chopin’s B minor Prelude, slowly and tentatively, and finds her own sadness reflected and transformed. “The sadness is all in the melody line the left hand keeps bringing up from below, a slow arpeggio trying to climb up out of the dark, but after a few notes of rising, it falls back down … It’s the God’s honest truth of grief. It doesn’t resolve.”Livia’s discovery here is huge; she’s coming to understand that a piece of music can enrich the performer and her audience even when the performance might be judged second-rate. Kingsolver is a committed social novelist – she’s even set up a prize to honour the socially engaged novel – and, ultimately, Partita is an impassioned testament to the need for art in ordinary communities, and the need for ordinariness in art. This means, in turn, that these communities have to put aside their own suspicions about artistic elitism, honouring the talents of artists in their midst by sending them away to study if necessary.Livia says early on that when you have a gift, “it feels like there’s a rule that you have to keep doing it. Not just that you owe it to yourself, you owe it to the world. Maybe to God. As payback on the borrowed gift.” She manages to sustain this vision, even as what it means to “keep doing it” changes for her. Her sister-in-law – herself a gifted scholar of literature, now happy to teach English – helps her to see that “the point of art is to help you like your life better” and that this can mean being a local piano teacher rather than an international soloist. “This was all I needed, back then,” Livia thinks sadly, “Somebody to tell me this.”Partita doesn’t offer the immediate satisfactions of Demon Copperhead; it’s a quieter book, slower to get going and to make its world enticing. But it’s a rich novel and one that I’ve found has opened up a dialogue with me as a reader that’s continued long after I finished reading it. Kingsolver doesn’t make light of what Livia has lost, and so she’s all the more convincing in her insistence that there’s as much to be gained in the compromises of middle age, and that artists may be following their calling most fully when they find ways to make their art part of a vibrant, loving collective life within our communities.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. title: Holding Lightning by Emily Lordi review – an intimate portrait of Whitney Houston | Whitney Houston | The Guardian
description: An empathetic biography of the the singer recasts her tumultuous later career as a triumph of self-expression
Author: Priya Elan
Headline: An empathetic biography of the the singer recasts her tumultuous later career as a triumph of self-expression
Content: Whitney Houston in 1999.Photograph: Goedefroit Music/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWhitney Houston in 1999.Photograph: Goedefroit Music/Getty ImagesWhitney HoustonReviewHolding Lightning by Emily Lordi review – an intimate portrait of Whitney HoustonAn empathetic biography of the the singer recasts her tumultuous later career as a triumph of self-expressionPriya ElanTue 6 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSince Whitney Houston’s death in 2012, a flurry of books and documentaries have appeared, most of them presenting her life as a cautionary tale. In this new biography, Emily Lordi, a professor of English at Vanderbilt University, refuses to reduce Houston’s story to another “good girl gone bad” narrative. Instead she presents a pluralistic take on her life in which Houston’s queerness, drug use and eccentricities are not dismissed as aberrations (as they were in her lifetime) but rather seen in the wider context of her unique talent and the pressures placed on her to embody black excellence.Lordi describes the unsteady building blocks of Houston’s family (her mother Cissy’s band The Sweet Inspirations were in-demand session musicians who worked with Elvis, as well as on Van Morrison’s Brown Eyed Girl and Dusty Springfield’s Son of a Preacher Man). When Cissy was still a child, Houston’s grandmother had a debilitating stroke following a miscarriage, eventually succumbing to a cerebral haemorrhage during a later pregnancy. The response to this trauma was to bury it. As Lordi writes: “Here was a lesson in suppressing your feelings and getting on with it.” But in a book where the act of singing through the pain is invoked multiple times, it is striking that reports Houston was molested as a child (a pivotal part of Kevin Macdonald’s 2018 documentary, which drew a line between that and her addictions) are not discussed.After an annus horribilis which included the dissolution of her parents’ marriage, a teenage Houston found comfort in a relationship with a friend from summer camp. The connection began as a sexual one, but deepened as a result of a shared interest in the vocal gymnastics of other singers and eventually Houston’s own music. At one point Crawford is caught on camera lip-synching to every ad lib Houston performs in a song on tour. Lordi calls it a “breathtaking act of attention”. Crawford is mystified by Houston’s marriage to singer Bobby Brown (she says it was like watching a foreign film without subtitles), but Lordi sees them united by showmanship and traditional values.In a decision that may force some readers to adjust their definition of the term, Lordi brands Houston a musical genius. She was, after all, a non-songwriter in an era of writer/producer/performers such as Prince and Michael Jackson, but the author argues that the choices Houston made in phrasing, tone, inflection and gesture were unique acts of creation. Her melismatic vocal style had a ripple effect, becoming a musical ground zero for everyone from Ariana Grande to Taylor Swift. Lordi’s promise early on that her book would dissect Houston’s “profoundly under-analysed body of work” doesn’t bear fruit, however. There are some in-depth interpretations (she breaks down the unique phraseology of I Will Always Love You and Houston’s pro-black retooling of The Star-Spangled Banner) but too many deep cuts are passed over, an odd decision considering Houston’s relatively slim discography.The case for Houston’s genius is made most persuasively in the latter half of the book. Instead of seeing her post-Bodyguard work as a descent into a druggy hellscape, Lordi portrays it as the period when her “blackest, queerest, most feminist work” emerges, including Waiting to Exhale and It’s Not Right But It’s Okay. Houston began to nurture younger black talent, offering the kind of musical mentorship given to her when she was starting out. In Lordi’s telling, albums like My Love Is Your Love riff on Houston’s exploitation by the media, presaging albums like Beyoncé’s Lemonade. It’s during this time that she jettisons the “black Barbie” image of the 80s, allowing imperfection into her art in a way that makes it all the richer.In the end Holding Lightning is the kindest portrait of Houston since Crawford’s book A Song For You. While not quite definitive, it is a consistently insightful, refreshing, restorative portrait of the artist once known simply as “The Voice”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories.
