title: Silver Pines review – a stylish, neo-noir detective drama | Games | The Guardian
description: Abandoned shops, ruined apartment buildings and rotting sewer networks make up a dark landscape in which you play a private eye searching for a missing singer-songwriter
Author: Keith Stuart
Headline: Abandoned shops, ruined apartment buildings and rotting sewer networks make up a dark landscape in which you play a private eye searching for a missing singer-songwriter
Content: A game to sit back and wallow in … Silver Pines.Photograph: Wych Elm Games, Team 17View image in fullscreenA game to sit back and wallow in … Silver Pines.Photograph: Wych Elm Games, Team 17GamesReviewSilver Pines review – a stylish, neo-noir detective dramaPC, PS5, Switch 2; Wych Elm Games, Team 17Abandoned shops, ruined apartment buildings and rotting sewer networks make up a dark landscape in which you play a private eye searching for a missing singer-songwriterKeith StuartTue 6 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 09.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn a weird deserted town miles from anywhere, a troubled detective searches for a missing musician and the girl he may or may not have murdered. It could be a Silent Hill game or a lost David Lynch movie from the 1990s – in fact, it’s neither. And also both. If that whets your appetite, stick around, there’s plenty more to come.Developed by Scandinavian studio Wych ElmGames, Silver Pines is a dark Metroidvania-style adventure, where you play as shambling private eye, Red Walker, exploring a 2D universe of abandoned shops, ruined apartment buildings and rotting sewer networks. Officially, everyone has left because of an incoming storm, but very quickly you learn that something much darker is afoot. Someone has hired you to find singer-songwriter Eddie Velvet, but you don’t know why; your only contact with your client is via the payphones dotted around town, where you can also save your progress – as long as you have a dollar to pay for the call. Each location is filled with clues and puzzles – a weird newspaper story pinned to the wall, a strange statue that needs a missing piece – and through these artefacts you unlock new rooms and descend further into the mystery.View image in fullscreenVery quickly you learn that something much darker is afoot … Silver Pines.Photograph: Wych Elm Games, Team 17This format will be incredibly familiar to anyone who has played a point-and-click adventure in the last 30 years; it’s not doing anything wildly original with the formula. And when the monsters inevitably emerge, you find yourself fighting them off with knives that break easily, and pistols that have to be painstakingly re-loaded with limited ammo, reminding you that you’re in survival horror territory, too.But what makes this game much more than an amalgam of familiar adventure tropes is its brilliant sense of style, it’s considered pace and it’s wonderfully constructed mythology. Using rotoscoping to create the lead character’s animation, he looks like some film noir drunk sloping around in the darkness, fumbling with clues. Each location is loaded with detail, from strange paintings, to battered furniture and fizzing neon signs, while parallax scrolling is used to brilliant effect, allowing you to see forthcoming locations in the distance as you wander the streets. Each room is beautifully constructed, so that as you move, the light coming from filthy windows or an old reading lamp sends slivers of shadow creeping over the walls. This is a design team that really understands the aesthetics of film noir, a fact underscored by the soundtrack a sleazy jazz club combo of Angelo Badalamenti and Vangelis.Silver Pines trailerAs you progress, new areas of the town open up, and you meet a few weird inhabitants that stuck around despite the incoming weather emergency, among them a cynical police chief and a brooding femme fatale. The puzzles can be obtuse, but thorough exploration often yields the answers you need: could you squeeze through that air duct? Could you climb that apparently impassable wall? Sometimes the answer is yes. Combat is always tense and panicked, especially the boss battles, where you’ll be floundering about with different weapons and ammunition as some Lovecraftian monstrosity pummels you. But then, this is very true to the earliest survival horror titles, where the inability to actually move, shoot and/or avoid incoming blows was part of the drama – you were always a victim and never a super cop. Besides, you can turn the difficulty right down if it’s the story you want to experience.As I played, I discovered countless references to 80s and 90s neo-noir culture – from Blue Velvet to Twin Peaks (you drink coffee to increase your stamina), from the X-Files to Alan Parker’s hellish Angel Heart. It was a pleasure to explore every broken-down movie theatre, oily car garage and sweat-stinking interrogation room, collecting weird trinkets and working out how they’d all fit together – then exploring them again (and again) when the answers failed to show up. Silver Pines is a game to sit back and wallow in, like a private eye, kicking off his wingtip shoes and pulling that bottle of bourbon from the bottom drawer as rain trickles down the window and sodium street lights paint the walls a sickly shade of yellow.Silver Pines is out 8 OctoberExplore more on these topicsGamesPCNintendo Switch 2PlayStation 5reviewsShareReuse this content

title: The 90s: Art and Fashion review – this isn’t an exhibition, it’s a magazine spread | Art | The Guardian
description: The Young British Art of the 1990s was brash and macabre but also intelligent and emotional. This breathlessly superficial show reduces it to a stylish pose
Author: Jonathan Jones
Headline: The Young British Art of the 1990s was brash and macabre but also intelligent and emotional. This breathlessly superficial show reduces it to a stylish pose
Content: Great Deeds Against the Dead, 1994, by Jake and Dinos Chapman.Photograph: Jake and Dinos Chapman/Jake and Dinos Chapman. All Rights Reserved, DACS ImagesView image in fullscreenGreat Deeds Against the Dead, 1994, by Jake and Dinos Chapman.Photograph: Jake and Dinos Chapman/Jake and Dinos Chapman. All Rights Reserved, DACS ImagesArtReviewThe 90s: Art and Fashion review – this isn’t an exhibition, it’s a magazine spreadTate Britain, LondonThe Young British Art of the 1990s was brash and macabre but also intelligent and emotional. This breathlessly superficial show reduces it to a stylish poseJonathan JonesTue 6 Oct 2026 05.54 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 14.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJake and Dinos Chapman were dismissed by some even in the 1990s as overgrown adolescents selling shock for its own sake, and yet it is their work that brings this dismally shallow show closest to a moment of depth. Their sculpture Great Deeds Against the Dead, based on a print of Napoleonic war atrocities by Goya, is a display of dismembered, bleeding nude corpses hung on a tree. It asks questions about war and art, the representation of pain, whether art can have a moral purpose. The best British art of the 1990s was like that, coming on as brash, vulgar, macabre, yet also unexpectedly intelligent and emotional. Unfortunately this show is neither.You’d thinkTate Britainwould want to do justice to a decade in which these Millbank premises played a starring role, staging the Turner prize in the years when bisected cows, concrete houses and elephant dung got the nation arguing. At the start of the 1990s no one thought Britain was a leader in contemporary art. By the millennium, we were better known for new art than new novels.View image in fullscreenHarmless … Two Similar Swimming Forms in Endless Motion (Broken), 1993, by Damien Hirst.Photograph: Damien Hirst and Science Ltd/DACS ImagesA show that spectacularly revisited fin-de-siecle British art would be an interesting proposition. Instead former Vogue editor Edward Enninful has been invited to stage his personal fantasy version of that decade, mixing up art and fashion, with the emphasis very much on fashion. There’s more about Isabella Blow than Rachel Whiteread, who is represented by an early cast of the inside of a hot-water bottle. Damien Hirst has a couple of small, harmless-looking sharks balanced on a circular rail. There’s no chance of understanding from this how his early work seemed to confront the tiger shark’s maw of death. Perhaps his 1990s art can still move, or perhaps it has become silly with time, but there is not enough of it to even begin to decide.This is not a real exhibition. It’s a magazine spread. Not only are there style mags in the show, its design has the breathless superficiality of a glossy layout bigging up its glib theme, in this case “The 90s”, in a glamorous sweep of strikingly juxtaposed images. But setting fashion photography alongside works of conceptual art is a terrible idea. If you take the fashion images seriously you reduce the art to another stylish pose. If, like me, you care about the art, the fashion looks pretty vacant.Juergen Teller’s 1996 photograph Kristen McMenamy No 3 is hung next to Sarah Lucas’s 1997 work Chicken Knickers. Teller’s picture depicts its subject naked and smoking with a lipstick heart drawn on her containing the word “Versace”. What is it saying other than “Buy Versace”? Now look at Lucas’ photograph of a raw chicken stuck to someone’s knickers. It’s funny – a great deed against a dead chicken from an artist with a genius for estrangement, as a Lucas sculpture of a “Bunny” on a chair with thin stockinged legs reminds you.View image in fullscreenA genius for estrangement … Chicken Knickers, 1997, by Sarah Lucas.Photograph: Tate Photography/Courtesy the artist and Sadie Coles HQ, LondonTeller is exposed as just a clever stylist whose images lack poetry or meaning. His portrait of Kate Moss has none of the distance or mystery of Gary Hume’s painting of her with a shiny, metallic, mirroring face. Hume provides one of the few moments when fashion and art genuinely overlap – but as pop art, his Kate is more a baleful, Richard Hamilton-like comment on celebrity than a celebration of Cool Britannia.Not that the show has much to say about that wider pop cultural fizz. There’s an entire room full of party pics depicting the club scene, but surely another point of the 90s was that mainstream British pop was revived – I guess Enninful is too sophisticated to find space for Oasis or Blur, let alone Fat Les.Instead we get couture. You can obviously see Alexander McQueen as an artist. But honestly. The room dealing with “body horror” is dominated by his costumes that are just mannered and pretentious. If they express anything it might be a hatred of women whom he forced to go on catwalks in suits of wire and steel bouquets. In the same room pompous, awful images shot by Sean Ellis for The Face take up an entire wall. It’s next to these that Jake and Dinos look so profound.View image in fullscreenPompous, awful images … The Dark Knight Returns, by Sean Ellis for the Face, 1998.Photograph: © Sean EllisOther fine artists don’t fare so well. Helen Chadwick gets two tokenistic eerie photoworks while the death-obsessed art of Hamad Butt, shown beautifullyat the Whitechapelnot so long ago, is squeezed to the end of the gallery. Chris Ofili is namechecked with No Woman, No Cry; Tracey Emin gets one neon. Other artists are noticeable by their absence, from Jeremy Deller to Mat Collishaw to the late and missed Christine Borland.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toArt WeeklyYour weekly art world round-up, sketching out all the biggest stories, scandals and exhibitionsEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHard parties, cheap rents and horrible flats: how 90s art and fashion redefined British cultureRead moreOr am I wrong? Does Young BritishArtfully deserve the dismissive treatment that Tate, which did so well out of these artists, gives it? Perhaps it really was a load of codswallop. But even if you don’t share my belief that some of the art of that time is powerful and enduring, surely it deserves enough space to be seen and judged.After just seven rooms it suddenly ends. I hoped what I’d seen was a prologue to more art, bigger art, with enough space to appreciate it. But no. That’s it. You leave as dissatisfied as you might after flicking through a 30-year-old copy of The Face in a dentist’s waiting room.The 90s is atTate Britain, London, from 8 October 2026 until 14 February 2027Explore more on these topicsArtTate BritainExhibitionsMuseumsPhotographyreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Affluenza review – Stranger Things star Noah Schnapp can’t save this baffling disaster | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Andy Sandberg’s play gets off to an intriguing start before coming off the rails in spectacular, almost fascinating style. For all the wrong reasons, it’s hard to look away
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: Andy Sandberg’s play gets off to an intriguing start before coming off the rails in spectacular, almost fascinating style. For all the wrong reasons, it’s hard to look away
Content: Strange thing … Noah Schnapp as Dylan in Affluenza.Photograph: Danny KaanView image in fullscreenStrange thing … Noah Schnapp as Dylan in Affluenza.Photograph: Danny KaanTheatreReviewAffluenza review – Stranger Things star Noah Schnapp can’t save this baffling disasterRiverside Studios, LondonAndy Sandberg’s play gets off to an intriguing start before coming off the rails in spectacular, almost fascinating style. For all the wrong reasons, it’s hard to look awayArifa AkbarTue 6 Oct 2026 07.37 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 07.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt starts off with a car crash, and enters its own pile-up before your eyes. There is some initial coherence, at least: Dylan, the son in a filthy rich family, played by Netflix star Noah Schnapp, has killed two people while drink-driving and injured several more. His parents, at their Hamptons home, are hashing out Dylan’s defence with a hotshot lawyer. They deny he did anything wrong – “people died, he didn’t kill them” – and throw money at the problem in hope it goes away. All the while, 16-year-old Dylan plays Nintendo upstairs.An original legal defence is invoked, along the lines of the poor little rich boy, suffering from “affluenza”, a psychological malaise in which a crime becomes the fault of wealthy parents who have failed to teach their progeny right or wrong. It is an intriguing setup with some parallels tothe hit-and-run case involving teenager Harry Dunn and Anne Sacoolas. Its moral dilemma is promising, its echoes of victim culture resonant.So we are set to watch the court case play out in Andy Sandberg’s play but a minute later, it is reported to be over. Where to go from here? Under Sandberg’s direction, it screeches around a corner, on to the highway of the truly bizarre. The plot has moved on several decades after the interval. Dylan, now played by Rupert Young, who played the lawyer in the first half, is a middle-aged man and divorcee, while Schnapp now plays his 17-year-old son, Todd.View image in fullscreen‘On the highway of the truly bizarre’ … Rupert Young and Juliet Cowan in Affluenza.Photograph: Danny KaanDylan has repurposed his past for a reality TV show and what follows is a satire of the genre. A TV producer is choreographing the action, Todd doesn’t want any part of it, and a cameraman shooting the show has a breakout moment to lip-sync to Joan Osborne’s One of Us, apropos of nothing. Dry ice emanates from the wings. Is this smoke rising from the play’s mangled car engine?Schnapp, star of hit showStranger Things, faced some backlash for comments made soon after the 7 October Hamas attacks. The Israel-Palestine conflict is the least of his problems here. Both his characters are supporting parts, taking up so little oxygen on stage that you wonder why anyone would cast a big name and then tuck it away in two bit-parts?Speaking of bit-parts, former Strictly Come Dancing pro dancer Janette Manrara is acting rather than foxtrotting here, but again plays a host of tiny roles, from the family’s Mexican cleaning lady to the woman who holds the mic on the set of the reality TV show. Who put Manrara in a corner? And who didn’t see the irony in delivering a tirade against reality TV in the presence of such reality TV royalty?It is hard to decipher what we are watching here – comedy, drama or a theatrical car crash in slow motion. If it is the latter, it is the kind thatJG Ballard’s voyeurs watch in Crash,with a mix of biliousness and grimy fascination. How did this epic wreckage occur? Why does it keep getting bigger? You want to look away, for shame, but simply can’t stop gawping.Affluenza is at Riverside Studios, London, until 21 NovemberExplore more on these topicsTheatreStranger ThingsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I call them erotic landscapes’: fashion photographer Tim Walker on his powerful tapestry of queer Britain | Art and design | The Guardian
description: He has shot everyone from Madonna to Rihanna, Kate Moss and Frank Ocean. Now Walker has turned his lens on the activists, artists, writers, models and everyday heroes of gay life
Author: Jason Okundaye
Headline: He has shot everyone from Madonna to Rihanna, Kate Moss and Frank Ocean. Now Walker has turned his lens on the activists, artists, writers, models and everyday heroes of gay life
Content: Trademark white background … Chappell Roan in Walker’s show.Photograph: Courtesy Tim WalkerView image in fullscreenTrademark white background … Chappell Roan in Walker’s show.Photograph: Courtesy Tim WalkerArt and design‘I call them erotic landscapes’: fashion photographer Tim Walker on his powerful tapestry of queer BritainHe has shot everyone from Madonna to Rihanna, Kate Moss and Frank Ocean. Now Walker has turned his lens on the activists, artists, writers, models and everyday heroes of gay lifeJason OkundayeTue 6 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSix years ago, Tim Walker was walking in the Highbury Fields area of London when he came across a plaque on the side of a building. In 1970, at these now-converted public toilets,Louis Eakes, chairman of the Young Liberals, was arrested for importuning following a “pretty police” entrapment in which male officers posed as would-be sex partners.It was here, the plaque told the photographer, that the first ever gay rights demonstration in Britain had taken place, organised by the Gay Liberation Front, in protest at Eakes’s arrest. But Walker was jolted by the date: 27 November 1970. It was the day he was born. So he wondered: “Who were those people out marching that day? Where are they now?”This was the genesis of Walker’s new exhibition,Fairyland: Love and Legends, about to open at the National Portrait Gallery in London. Its rooms of photographic portraits represent a tapestry of queer community in Britain spanning decades and taking in activists, artists, writers, models and everyday heroes, from nurses to physicians and army veterans.The fairy concept was inspired by Walker’s childhood. “My brother and I used to share a bedroom, and over our beds was a scene of fairyland, with little pixies and elves. I was always making camps in the garden. And by the time I was sent to school, the word fairy was derogatory. So I think the fantasy and escapism got muddied by the bullying.” The exhibition, then, is a long-overdue self-affirmation.View image in fullscreen‘No ruffles or French hoods’ … activist Lady PhyllPhotograph: Courtesy Tim WalkerI meet Walker at his studio in Shoreditch. Gentle and attentive, he serves peppermint tea, ginger biscuits and gluten-free jaffa cakes on a tray of china and strolls around a scale model of the exhibition as he talks me through it. Of course, it starts with the gay men and women on the Highbury march: Ted Brown, Lisa Power and Andrew Lumsden. Power and Lumsden are shot to mimic the Northern Renaissance portrait style of Hans Holbein the Younger. “You’re in theNational Portrait Gallery,” Walker explains. “If you go to the top floor, you have all these Holbein paintings. I wanted to put the people at the march into that realm of Holbein-esque celebration.”Not everyone desired to be dressed up in ruffles and French hoods, so activists Peter Tatchell, Phyllis Opoku-Gyimah (Lady Phyll) and Sue Sanders are shot against Walker’s trademark white background, as are queer stars including Ian McKellen, Troye Sivan and Chappell Roan. Why this style? “That’s the cheapest way,” Walker says. His method is collaborative; he discussed with each person how they’d like to be shot and asked them to bring significant items. Russell T Davies is covered in pages from the script for his drama It’s a Sin, while photographer Sunil Gupta brings a camera.In the show’s most arresting moment, Graham McKerrow is depicted in a pork pie hat and suit, holding a November 1982 copy of Capital Gay, the newspaper he co-founded with the lateMichael Mason. The splash says: “US disease hits London.” This, says Walker, “really moved me, because he brought this newspaper from when the first news hit about Aids. That was the first time anyone was talking about it here.”That history of Aids runs through the exhibition. In one emotional image, nurse Jane Bruton, who has worked with HIV patients for 40 years, is depicted holding her former patient Tony Whitehead, one of the first people whose lives were saved by combination therapy in 1996. They are photographed with Jonathan Weber, a professor of medicine who was part of that scientific breakthrough. “It was such a beautiful reunion,” Walker says, “but what really touched me was their gestures: that care and pride was still alive.”View image in fullscreenStar power … Ian McKellen.Photograph: Courtesy Tim WalkerCapturing this was important to Walker because he remembered sitting in the living room as a teenager with his family watching the falling tombstone from the Don’t Die of Ignorance public health TV campaign launched in 1987 by health secretary Norman Fowler to warn the public about HIV and Aids. “I feel that set the whole gay liberation movement back, it was such a terrible thing.”After the white backgrounds, the fantasy portraits of fairies, floral teapots and Meissen candlestick holders, the most explicit photography comes at the exhibition’s close: erotic lesbian shots, a surrealist image of butt cheeks impressed on a goldfish bowl, a giant rat and octopuses strewn across submitting models and an S&M dalmatian pup suspended in the air. “There’s kinky play where people dress up as dogs,” Walker notes. “I think there’s worlds here, erotic sexual landscapes I call them.”The backgrounds to these images are baroque, Walker having been inspired byJean-Honoré Fragonard’s oil painting The Swingin London’s Wallace Collection. He originally conceived of these more risque images being scattered throughout the exhibition. But the National Portrait Gallery wouldn’t have it: “They wanted to push everything to the back so that could be an 18-plus room,” he says, scoffing.Walker was born in Guildford; his mother wrote cookbooks and his father worked in industry. He attended Charterhouse boarding school which he describes as “horrific, absolutely Victorian, so homophobic”. He met his first boyfriend when he attended ExeterArtCollege, but before that he’d had a sexual awakening watching Channel 4’s late-night progressive queer programming, Derek Jarman’s Latin-language film Sebastiane being one particularly vivid memory: “I wanked a lot watching it,” he says.View image in fullscreen‘I call them erotic landscapes’ … a fantasy fairy portrait.Photograph: Courtesy Tim WalkerHe didn’t really get involved in London’s gay scene until later into his 20s, living it vicariously through the queer pop soundtrack of the time; songs such as Bronski Beat’s Smalltown Boy, The Power of Love by Frankie Goes to Hollywood and Tainted Love by Soft Cell, whose singer Marc Almond is featured in the show. He eventually started going to Love Muscle at the Fridge in Brixton, “a big gay night of 1,000 people on a Saturday”.Walker found the studios of London’s East End to be “crummy” and, after graduating, moved to New York, which was experiencing a boom in fashion photography with the advent of supermodels and high-octane glamour rebelling against 90s minimalism. Here was the home of Irving Penn, Patrick Demarchelier and Richard Avedon, for whom Walker worked.What did he learn under Avedon’s tutelage? “Avedon was very good at communicating with the subject, and he was clear about connection. He would spend a lot of time with the subject before he photographed them.” He’d be playful with supermodels, not just telling them “beautiful, sexy!” but giving instructions such as: “OK, you’re a crow on a branch, and there’s a worm on the floor. I want you two birds to fight over the worm.”Walker has long worked at the very top of fashion and celebrity photography. He’s had a longstanding collaboration with Kate Moss and has shot the likes of Lady Gaga, Björk and Frank Ocean for fashion magazine W. He tells me about his most recent W subjects: Rihanna and her baby Rocki. “She’s mad!” he says. “She was in Paris looking at the couture shows and said, ‘I really want you to photograph me and my baby.’” The shoot was scheduled for 2pm; famously tardy, Rihanna turned up at 11pm. “I’ve never worked through the night with someone, but it was a vibe,” Walker says. “She’s someone you could photograph in seven frames and you’ve got a picture, because she’s so bodily aware.”View image in fullscreenThere’s Holbeins upstairs … Paul O’Grady and Julian Clary as the Glitter Queens.Photograph: Courtesy Tim WalkerNot all his shoots were so successful: he mentions a 2005 session with Madonna for American Vogue. At the time, Madonna was “obsessed with Cecil Beaton, in her English Lady of the Manor era”. They shot at Beaton’s old home in Ashcombe, which Madonna had recently bought: Walker photographed her dressed in tweed and cashmere, surrounded by chickens and holding a black lamb “because she’s the black sheep of the family”.Walker feels he fumbled the attempt to merge the worlds of Beaton and Madonna. “I look at all these pictures – she’s actually not big enough [in the frame],” he says. “But the awful thing is we had three days to do the shoot, and the first day was like a warm-up. The pictures weren’t great, but I thought we’ll get there. But at the end of day one she was like, ‘We’ve got the pictures, we’re done!’”double quotation markMadonna wanted a Guinness and food but was told the pub’s kitchen was shutMadonna later joined Walker and his team in the local pub. When she walked in with then husband Guy Ritchie, “the whole pub fell silent”. Madonna then asked Walker what was he was having for lunch. “And she said, ‘I’m going to have a pint of Guinness and I’m going to eat something.’ So she says ‘Excuse me’ to the waitress, ‘I’m going to get what he’s having.’ And the young waitress goes, ‘I’m sorry, the kitchen’s closed.’” Wow, no Madonna privilege? “Not in this pub!”Walker admits that he’s not particularly interested in fashion. His favourite pastimes are reading (Denton Welch’s In Youth Is Pleasure and Josh Silver’s Fruit Fly are recent favourites) and walking his dog, Jack: “That’s my absolute favourite thing to do!” He is far more interested in fantasy and fairytales, lighting up when he talks me through a book of old shoots which draw on Alice in Wonderland and the Wizard of Oz. “Fashion isn’t the reason I became a photographer, it was fantasy.”He regrets the fact that glossy magazines are in decline, and that his work perhaps belongs to an era that is dying. On his Instagram, he often reflects on past shoots, but he has a sense of inevitability about the digital world taking over. “We’re at the end of that time, which is sad. Looking at photographs in a magazine format is beautiful because of the scale. Just turning a page I lament that passing, but we are where we are.”Fairyland, then, is one way for him to continue working at an ambitious scale. I wonder if, in capturing everyday heroes, he’s also revealing an exasperation with celebrity. “I think as a photographer, or any creative, you’re always looking for something different,” he says. “That pendulum does often swing a long way from where you’ve been.”He leans over the scale model, closes his eyes, and muses on the six years it took to make: “I’ve been so nourished by these stories, and I’ve been moved to tears by these stories.” Fairyland may be new work, but for Walker it reframes the span of his career. “Doing this show, I now realise that everything I was doing as a fashion photographer was all camp and gay. It was my gayness escaping.”Tim Walker’s Fairyland: Love and Legends is at the National Portrait Gallery, London, from 9 October to 7 FebruaryExplore more on these topicsArt and designPhotographyFashion photographyNational Portrait GalleryArtLGBTQ+ rightsAids and HIVfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘My poetry won me asylum’: Cecilia Vicuña on exile life in ‘sad’ Britain after Pinochet’s coup | Art and design | The Guardian
description: Five decades after convincing judges she’d be killed if she returned to Chile, the artist is back with a politically charged retrospective in the country she grew to love
Author: Nadia Khomami
Headline: Five decades after convincing judges she’d be killed if she returned to Chile, the artist is back with a politically charged retrospective in the country she grew to love
Content: ‘My stories want to live again’ … Vicuña with Quipu Menstrual at her new Whitechapel exhibition.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘My stories want to live again’ … Vicuña with Quipu Menstrual at her new Whitechapel exhibition.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianArt and design‘My poetry won me asylum’: Cecilia Vicuña on exile life in ‘sad’ Britain after Pinochet’s coupFive decades after convincing judges she’d be killed if she returned to Chile, the artist is back with a politically charged retrospective in the country she grew to loveNadia KhomamiTue 6 Oct 2026 10.28 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 17.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCecilia Vicuña was 24 when she first arrived in London. She had come from Santiago on a British Council scholarship to study at the Slade School ofArt, and her stay was supposed to be so brief that she didn’t even unpack her suitcase.Then, in September 1973, General Augusto Pinochet’s military coup overthrew Chile’s democratically elected president, Salvador Allende. Vicuña was one of a handful of Chilean students in London immediately expelled from their universities and expected to leave Britain. At a Home Office hearing, her pro-bono lawyers argued that she would be killed if she returned to Chile, and showed the judges her recently published art and poetry book, Saborami, which documented the aftermath of the coup. The judges granted her asylum.“It’s really one of the main stories of my life,” Vicuña says now. “How my poetry came to protect my wellbeing.”We meet on Zoom, with Vicuña in her apartment in New York, where she has lived since 1980. Wearing a knitted hat, she speaks softly and sagely, like a shaman offering advice – small and fragile, but with big, existential ideas about life and art.More than half a century since her arrival in London, Vicuña, now 78 and one of Latin America’s most renowned artists, poets and feminist activists, is returning – specifically to Stepney Green, where she lived as a young artist – for her first major UK exhibition, at theWhitechapel Gallery. She has mixed feelings. “In a way, I’m going back to relieve my original experience,” she says.View image in fullscreenSpeaking to things lost … aprecariofrom 1967.Photograph: © 2026 Cecilia Vicuña/Artist Rights Society (ARS), New York Courtesy the artist and Lehmann MaupinThe London Vicuña encountered in the 1970s was very different from the image of “swinging London” exported around the world. “When you walked down the streets, people were extremely poor,” she says. “People had to put a penny to heat their little apartments. There was a feeling of sadness, of not being able to realise one’s full potential.”But she began meeting exiles from failed revolutions across Africa, the Middle East, Greece and Latin America, found a thriving art community, and published her first book in London after it had been censored in Chile. “I grew to love it,” she says. “But I also understood that true creative energy was on the other side of the continent.”The new exhibition, Living Threads, brings together six decades of Vicuña’s work across painting, textile, photography, installation and film. It also returns to her political life as a young artist speaking at trade union gatherings on the top floor of English pubs. A room is dedicated to Artists for Democracy, which Vicuña co-founded in 1974 with Guy Brett, David Medalla and John Dugger in solidarity with Chile and other liberation struggles worldwide, bringing together never-before-seen documents, photographs and printed materials.“There have been a few attempts to tell this story without my presence,” she says. “The story has been told as if I was a visitor to the organisation.”View image in fullscreenPerformance protest … Nudo de tres, 1969-1970.Photograph: © 2026 Cecilia Vicuña/Artist Rights Society (ARS), New York Courtesy the artist and Lehmann MaupinHer involvement began after artist Conrad Atkinson invited her to an ICA discussion about artists’ rights and sales. Shocked that people were discussing money while artists were being killed in Chile, Vicuña stood up to speak. Brett, Medalla and Dugger, sitting at the back, sent her a note afterwards. “I proposed that we should found an organisation for democracy,” she says.“England was the first country to acknowledge Pinochet as the new leader of Chile,” she adds. “This violent overthrow of democratic government was celebrated by Britain.” Yet the same country had granted her the legal protection to stay: “The place where the defence of the law was powerful enough to grant me that.”The exhibition also brings back a painful part of that period: the work Vicuña lost. During her exile, she left pieces with friends in London, Chile and Bogotá; one trunk contained 400 sculptures, eventually thrown away.“I was so devalued as a person, as an artist,” she says. “To be a dark little South American woman, even in Latin America, is to be in a position of pain, disrespect and inappreciation.” Some have since been recreated from memory and photographs – not reconstruction, she says, but something closer to reincarnation. “It’s the stories and images that want to live again.”View image in fullscreen‘Will greater visibility of women translate to women being valued as equals? We will see’ … Llaverito (Blue Lady) / Ladilla, Crab, 2019 after a lost original 1979 work.Photograph: © 2025 Cecilia Vicuña Courtesy of the artist and Lehmann MaupinThat idea of disappearance runs through the two forms Vicuña is best known for. She began making what she callsprecariosin the 1960s from sticks, feathers, leaves, stones, bones and debris – deliberately fragile, impermanent works, a response to standing as a 17-year-old on a Chilean beach, in the shadow of an oil refinery built over an ancestral burial ground, suddenly aware of the relationship between sea, wind and objects. The only survivingprecariofrom her London years is in the show.“To preserve and disappear are not opposite things,” she says. “Awareness of disappearance is what needs to be preserved. It’s the belief that life itself is poetry, and poetry is life. Disappearance is regeneration.”Herquipus, meanwhile, are made from knotted and unspun fibre, drawing on an ancient Andean system of recording and communication. Vicuña has spent decades reimagining the form, including in Quipu Menstrual, a towering installation in deep red that will be shown at Whitechapel.Her work has increasingly turned towards ecology. She has worked with water for more than 50 years, and she describes the current situation in Chile as both devastating and potentially transformative.“Latin America is the most destroyed of all continents: 95% of its biodiversity has been destroyed already, because people continue to vote for leaders who open the gates to this violent extraction. They call them resources, but it’s not resources. It’s life.” But she points to hope: “Reports show that young Chileans see their future as professional defenders of the land. That, to me, is the most beautiful sign that this shift is still possible.”double quotation markI think, in truth, democracy was never really practised in the westThe current shift to the right in Chile, she argues, doesn’t simply repeat 1973. Back then, she says, those seeking justice, democracy and freedom of expression were the majority and were “violently crushed by foreign intervention. Now, people are willingly choosing to be aligned with the forces that deny global warming and deny people’s rights, women’s rights, the rights of nature.”I ask her if democracy has become more fragile. “I think, in truth, democracy was never really practised in the west.” She points to Allende’s Chile as one example of participatory democracy, and argues that many indigenous societies offered earlier models that were destroyed by colonisation.The internet, she adds, was another squandered chance: a tool for universal access to knowledge that became a place of surveillance and misinformation. “Each chance that the people of this planet have had to open up to the potential of democracy a destructive force comes in to stop it.”View image in fullscreen‘My work was acknowledged for the first time as a work that had meaning and importance’ …Vicuña at her Whitechapel show.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianShe sees artificial intelligence through a similar lens. Her concern is that AI is controlled by private companies for profit, while governments have failed to regulate what she sees as an existential threat.“Now AI has been trained to train itself, and as soon as that happens, it started to behave in a destructive way. Powerful people are saying the existential threat to humanity is a hoax. I have the feeling most people in the world don’t feel it’s a hoax at all. So where is the democratic will of this planet? Is it crushed or prevented?”Vicuña spent decades operating relatively under the radar before a burst of institutional recognition began with her inclusion in Documenta in 2017, aged 69 – she was the youngest artist in a group that included women in their 80s and 90s. “It was the event that changed my life,” she says. “My work was acknowledged for the first time as a work that had meaning and importance.” The museum told her visitors came looking for “the red thing” – herquipu. Since then she has won the Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement at the Venice Biennale, received a Guggenheim survey, and completed a Tate Modern Turbine Hall commission.That 2022 work, Brain Forest Quipu, featured huge mobiles of fraying wool, knotted rope and debris mudlarked from the Thames, an elegy to lost language and wilful destruction;the Guardian’s five-star reviewcalled it the most moving Turbine Hall commission in years.She sees the greater visibility of women, and of Latin American, Asian and African artists, in major museums as a genuine shift – but remains cautious. “Will that translate to women being valued as equals? We will see.”For now, she is returning to the neighbourhood where the young artist she once was became an exile and activist. The Whitechapel exhibition brings together works that survived, works that disappeared, and works that have been remade. “I do hope it will be healing,” she says.Cecilia Vicuña: Living Threads is at theWhitechapel Gallery, London, from 7 October until 14 FebruaryExplore more on these topicsArt and designSculptureWhitechapel GalleryArtInstallationPaintingExhibitionsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A medieval manuscript has confounded scholars for centuries. Have they been reading it wrong all this time? | Culture | The Guardian
description: Researchers argue incorrect binding of Voynich manuscript radically changes ideas about its drawings and indecipherable text
Author: Philip Oltermann
Headline: Researchers argue incorrect binding of Voynich manuscript radically changes ideas about its drawings and indecipherable text
Content: Folded page from the Voynich manuscript.Photograph: Universal History Archive/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFolded page from the Voynich manuscript.Photograph: Universal History Archive/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesCultureA medieval manuscript has confounded scholars for centuries. Have they been reading it wrong all this time?Researchers argue incorrect binding of Voynich manuscript radically changes ideas about its drawings and indecipherable textPhilip OltermannEuropean culture editorTue 6 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt has been called the world’s most mysterious manuscript: a medieval set of pages filled with botanical drawings, astronomical diagrams, pictures of nude women and indecipherable text. Claimed at various times to be a book in a lost language, a musical score, an instruction manual or just an elaborate hoax, the so-called Voynich manuscript’s true meaning has defied cryptographers and codebreakers for centuries.Now, new research offers an explanation for why a scholarly consensus over this enduring puzzle has been so hard to come by: not only because its truth is so profoundly mysterious – but because everyone has been reading its pages in the wrong order.In an article published in peer-reviewed journal Digital Medievalist, Colin Layfield and Lisa Fagin Davis argue that the manuscript’s folded sheets may have originally been piled on top of each other as “singulions” – like a stack of Christmas cards – but were mis-bound in a more typical “nested” arrangement at some point in the mid to late 15th century.View image in fullscreenA page from The Voynich manuscript.Photograph: Photo 12/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesWhile their finding does not immediately de-code the script, written in what has commonly become known as “Voynichese”, the authors say their finding radically changes our idea of the manuscript’s function.“There are a lot of people who wanted the Voynich to have been created by one mad genius working in their attic in medieval London or wherever,” said Davis. “In fact, the evidence suggests we’re talking about a more communal object, perhaps a set of booklets through which information was passed down from one generation to the next – the ‘lone genius’ idea is kind of out of the door.”The manuscript’s unknown provenance has piqued scholarly interest ever since it surfaced in book collectors’ records in the 17th century. When it was bought in 1912 by Wilfrid Voynich, a Polish revolutionary and book dealer with a shop on London’s Soho Square, it was thought to be a scientific diary written by the 13th-century polymath Roger Bacon. Others have credited the codex to Leonardo da Vinci.Voynich manuscript misboundRecent chemical analyses of the manuscript, which is held at Yale University, have carbon-dated its parchment to between 1404 and 1438, ruling out these famous authorships.Some scholars have argued that the text of the Voynich Manuscript is nothing more than gibberish intended as a hoax or a forgery, thoughrecent linguistic analysishas found it more likely that it is written in a natural, if yet unidentified, language.In 2019, a biology research assistant at the University of Bristol,claimed that the manuscript was written in a “calligraphic proto-Romance” language, but the findings were later disputed, and the university subsequently removed a reference to the claims from its website.For their article “Singulion Structure and the Voynich Manuscript”, Layfield and Davis used a numerical analysis tool to compare blocks of text and found that many of the attached pages scored highly for coherence even when there were many intervening pages, suggesting the manuscript had been mis-bound.View image in fullscreenA page from the Voynich manuscript, an illustrated codex hand-written in an unknown writing system.Photograph: GL Archive/AlamyThere were also visual clues suggesting the pages were supposed to be read in a different order. In the current binding, some illustrations of streams or pipes run into the gutter – the blank space along the inner margins where pages are bound – but don’t fully match with the pictures on the opposite page. “Once you treat them as loose pages stacked together, all these artistic anomalies suddenly join up”, said Layfield, a senior lecturer in information systems at the University of Malta.“Our hypothesis fixes a lot of problems with the structure of the manuscripts in a really elegant way”, said Davis, an expert on medieval handwriting.She said the only other known medieval manuscripts she has found preserved in a singulion arrangement were Qurans from north Africa, which were likely meant to be handed out as small booklets for instruction purposes.“I think it’s likely we are looking similarly at an object that was made by a community that wanted to pass its knowledge forward,” said Davis, adding that her hypothesis was supported by paleographical analysis suggesting the manuscript was written by up to five different scribes.View image in fullscreenThe quality control operator of the Spanish publishing outfit Siloe Luis Miguel works on cloning the illustrated codex hand-written manuscript Voynich in Burgos in 2016.Photograph: César Manso/AFP/Getty ImagesSome of the drawings in the manuscript resemble the female reproductive system, while others hint at herbal lore and astrology. “When you put all of this together, it starts to feel like a book of women’s folk knowledge that’s being preserved,” she said. “But you cannot prove that yet.”As to the mystery of the manuscript’s language, Davis said it wasn’t out of the question that there would have been other manuscripts written in Voynichese.“The problem is that so few manuscripts have survived from the middle ages, because they weren’t bound. The irony is that whoever mis-bound this manuscript still did us a huge favour by ensuring its survival.”Explore more on these topicsCultureEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘We got that bad guy and took him down!’ Jaclyn Smith on the fun, friendship and frustration of Charlie’s Angels | Television | The Guardian
description: It’s 50 years since Smith joined TV’s bikini-clad crime fighters alongside Farrah Fawcett and Kate Jackson. She talks about the love she found on set, the harassment she endured off it and the drug-taking she did her best to ignore
Author: Emine Saner
Headline: It’s 50 years since Smith joined TV’s bikini-clad crime fighters alongside Farrah Fawcett and Kate Jackson. She talks about the love she found on set, the harassment she endured off it and the drug-taking she did her best to ignore
Content: ‘Pretty clothes, pretty locations, fast cars … come on, it was just having fun’ … Jaclyn Smith.Photograph: Randee St NicholasView image in fullscreen‘Pretty clothes, pretty locations, fast cars … come on, it was just having fun’ … Jaclyn Smith.Photograph: Randee St NicholasTelevisionInterview‘We got that bad guy and took him down!’ Jaclyn Smith on the fun, friendship and frustration of Charlie’s AngelsEmine SanerIt’s 50 years since Smith joined TV’s bikini-clad crime fighters alongside Farrah Fawcett and Kate Jackson. She talks about the love she found on set, the harassment she endured off it and the drug-taking she did her best to ignoreTue 6 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 07.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor a TV show that only ran for five years, Charlie’s Angels packs a punch like a bikini-wearing big-hair-flicking private investigator. “We never thought we’d be talking about it 50 years later,” says Jaclyn Smith, the only original Angel to make it to the end of the show’s run. Smith, 80, has now written a memoir, I Once Knew a Guy Called Charlie – she is not, you gather, the type of actor to want to distance herself from her defining project.As I read her book, and speak to her over Zoom, she comes across as sensible, hardworking and optimistic. Also lucky: loving and supportive parents, agents who seem to appear from nowhere and offer her work, an early hit show, a gift for making friends and getting over heartbreak. Even when she was diagnosed with breast cancer more than 20 years ago, terrifying as it was, it was caught early and successfully treated. Her positive outlook seems to extend to the excesses of US TV in the 1970s and 80s (drug use on set only gets a brief mention); her three ex-husbands get off fairly lightly; and any difficulties – her OCD, the men who stalked her at the height of her fame – are not dwelled on.View image in fullscreenThe original Angels …(from left)Jaclyn Smith, Kate Jackson and Farrah Fawcett in 1976.Photograph: THA/AlamySmith wanted to be a dancer. By the late 50s, she was attending a dance school in Houston, where she grew up, which was run by Patsy Swayze (mother of Patrick, who would go on to be a successful actor, but was then around seven and, Smith says, “an absolute doll”). She describes an idyllic childhood – happily married parents and a Methodist minister grandfather who was a steady and reassuring presence. Her dad was a dentist and “gave me my work ethic”; her mother was a “goddess of love – she just made you feel No 1”. Smith recalls: “Whatever I am happened in that secure family they provided for me – morals, ethics, values.” Downtime was spent at the family farm in Texas: “Two hundred acres with the San Marcos river running through it. It was life at its best.”But her childhood was also when her compulsive behaviour started. “It became sort of a form of prayer for me – it’s probably the way my brain works – but that all came about protecting loved ones,” she says. She would pray obsessively, thinking it would keep her grandfather safe; later, she would do the same when her two children were born, and she says it still flares up in times of stress.View image in fullscreen‘I didn’t walk on the wild side ever.’Photograph: Randee St NicholasAfter leaving school, Smith convinced her parents to allow her to go to New York to train as a dancer. Her father insisted she live at thewomen-only Barbizon hotel, one-time home to Sylvia Plath, Grace Kelly and Joan Didion among many other notable women. “There were such strict rules there,” she says. “You couldn’t wear slacks in the lobby. I was in hose and a dress and a pair of heels. And boys could not go above the mezzanine.”It must have been exciting to have been a young dancer in New York in the late 60s? “Very competitive,” says Smith. But also a lot more accessible than it is now. “There were open calls for Broadway shows, whereas today you have to have a social media following, an agent, a manager, everything. When I started, you’d read about auditions, and it would be a mass cast call, and maybe you’d make it, maybe you wouldn’t.”Offers for roles in shows started coming in, and Smith – beautiful, classy – was also in demand for lucrative advertising work. While her peers were protesting, taking drugs or embracing early 70s counterculture, Smith married the actor Roger Davis – famous, she writes, for his role in Dark Shadows, the “daytime vampire-themed soap opera”.“I just didn’t get into it,” she says of New York’s bohemian scene. “Did I go to a discotheque and dance? Yeah, I loved it, but no, I didn’t walk on the wild side ever. I was a hard worker.”Perhaps also a little square. When she turned up to audition for Hair, she wore a blue leotard, with pink tights and hair in a neat bun. Smith laughs at her naive Texas primness when trying to convince producers she could be in a taboo-breaking hippie musical: “I looked like I had come from another planet.”Sexual harassment was usual. “I experienced it. I think every actress does,” says Smith. “You can walk away. You can say, ‘Hey, I don’t need that movie. I don’t want it if this is what it requires.’” Were there ever expectations that certainthingswere expected? “Yeah, there was some of that, but you can say no. I think I was never, ever desperate about a career. Maybe that’s because where I came from with my parents, and I knew I could make my own way.” She says she would have been offered a bigger part in one early film if she’d done a nude scene (she refused), and was dropped from another after she got married. Because she was expected to be single, or available? “I guess. But I wanted to be cast not because I was single, but because I was right for the part.”Her first marriage didn’t last; neither did her second to another actor, Dennis Cole. But her career zipped along – small parts in successful series such as the police drama McCloud, and TV movies. She got her first regular job opposite Robert Wagner in the crimefighting caper Switch. It was Wagner who recommended her to producers Aaron Spelling and Leonard Goldberg, who were putting together a new show featuring three female detectives.View image in fullscreenSmith with her fourth husband, Brad Allen, at a Farrah Fawcett Foundation benefit gala in October 2022.Photograph: Rick Kern/Getty Images for Farrah Fawcett FoundationSmith was the last to be cast in Charlie’s Angels, as calm and empathetic Kelly Garrett, and was offered the lowest fee – $3,000 an episode, compared with her original co-stars Farrah Fawcett ($5,000) and Kate Jackson ($10,000). Jackson was a more established star, but Smith demanded to be paid at least the same as Fawcett, whom she reasoned had done a similar level of work to her. “My agent said, ‘Are you sure? We have a good feeling about this series.’ I stood my ground, and I got it.” She would have walked away, she says. “It wasn’t about money. It was the fact that we’d done the same thing, and I thought that was only fair.” (By the fifth season, Smith was earning $100,000 an episode.)The show was an instant hit when it was first broadcast in 1976. “I was excited because I knew it was different – three women instead of three men, chasing danger instead of being rescued from danger.” It was often ridiculous – the three private investigators, working for a mysterious Charlie who only appeared via speakerphone, would go undercover to catch criminals as, Smith writes, “stewardesses, beauty pageant contestants, singers, magicians’ assistants, Ice Capades skaters, football players, jewel thieves, Keystone Cops, toy makers, tennis champions and exotic dancers”. In one episode, Kris Munroe (played by Cheryl Ladd, replacing Fawcett, who left after the first season), wrestles an alligator.View image in fullscreenOn the cover of Time magazine in 1976.Photograph: Patti McConville/AlamyPeople questioned why they had to do all of this looking like supermodels, or criticised the show for objectifying women. “I thought it was silly,” Smith says. “We were not controlled by Charlie. We were working hard, courageous, we went about our job. Usually women on TV then were nurses, mothers, wives. We went into a territory that only men occupied. We got that bad guy and took him down. Also, it was fun and it was escapism. Pretty clothes, pretty locations, fast cars, thin girls taking down a 200lb man … come on. It was just having fun.”Did she ever think they shouldn’t be in bikinis so often? Smith laughs. “I think we did say to Aaron, ‘We don’t want to be in a bikini unless we’re near water.’” But it looks so innocent, she says, “compared to today. Our characters were loyal, chaste, involved in the friendship part of it … we never really had love affairs. It was always the sisterhood.”The original three Angels got on instantly, says Smith, even though inevitably the media tried to create rumours of rivalries and conflict. “Definitely no jealousies,” says Smith. “We loved one another. It was a fellowship, a sisterhood, a team.” They became lifelong friends (Jackson is godmother to Smith’s daughter). “We held each other up during breast cancer, during different things.” Although Fawcett only did one season, Smith says, “I adored Farrah. What you saw was what you got. She was beautiful, had fun, liked to laugh and had great humour.” Fawcett died in 2009, but “we were close until the end of her life”.Having two co-stars go through the strain of becoming famous overnight helped them all, she says. The show had to employ bodyguards for the three Angels, and Smith was a victim of stalking. “I had many restraining orders after Charlie’s,” she says, describing one man who climbed over a security fence during a shoot and claimed to be her husband. He later turned up at her house. “When you’re in someone’s living room every week, I guess they feel they know you.”View image in fullscreenSmith in the 1981 film Jacqueline Bouvier Kennedy.Photograph: Walt Disney Television Photo Archives/ABCBy the fifth and final season, Smith, the only original lead, wasn’t finding it as fun. It was the 1980s and the Angels had to be even more glamorous. Drugs, especially cocaine, were also on set, she writes, “with some people using it constantly”. It took her time to realise, she says. “I was innocent to drugs, but then you tune in to it because people slow down and can’t perform.” Was it common for big TV shows to have drug use? “I think it was,” she says, but she doesn’t approve of it. “It just takes out your spark.” She stayed distant from it all. “I just went about my business, then went to my trailer, and as long as we got our show, everything was fine.”Charlie’s Angels ended in 1981. Smith would later have cameos in the 2000 film reboot, starring Cameron Diaz, Lucy Liu and Drew Barrymore, and the2019 follow-up film. After the show ended, she believes she was typecast as glamorous, but frivolous.View image in fullscreen‘When you’re in every someone’s living room every week, they feel they know you.’Photograph: THA/AlamyBy 1981 she was in her mid-30s and had to fight to play the first lady in the TV biopic Jacqueline Bouvier Kennedy. “They didn’t want a Charlie’s Angel playing Jackie Kennedy,” she says. She is of the generation of actresses who struggled to find decent roles past 40, but by then Smith had two young children – with the cinematographer Tony Richmond, her third husband.As well as parenting, she had a lucrative fashion line and interiors brand, one of the earliest celebrity branding successes. Life, she says, has “been a pretty smooth ride. Yeah, there’s been things along the way, mainly marriages.” Smith has been with Brad Allen, a heart surgeon, since 1991. She spent decades trying to recreate her parents’ happy marriage. “Finally got it,” she says.Her memoir is already out in the US and, doing signings, Smith has loved meeting women who grew up with Charlie’s Angels. “Did the show give women a chance to break out of their mould, to be brave, to be independent? I like to think that.”I Once Knew a Guy Named Charlie by Jaclyn Smith (Simon & Schuster, £20). To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com.
