title: Axe used by Jack Nicholson in The Shining for sale as part of Stanley Kubrick auction | Stanley Kubrick | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Weapon is one of hundreds of items to be sold as part of the influential late director’s personal archive
Author: Matthew Weaver
Headline: Exclusive: Weapon is one of hundreds of items to be sold as part of the influential late director’s personal archive
Content: ‘Heeere’s Johnny!’ Jack Torrance played by Jack Nicholson in The Shining, directed by Stanley Kubrick.Photograph: BFA/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Heeere’s Johnny!’ Jack Torrance played by Jack Nicholson in The Shining, directed by Stanley Kubrick.Photograph: BFA/AlamyStanley KubrickAxe used by Jack Nicholson in The Shining for sale as part of Stanley Kubrick auctionExclusive: Weapon is one of hundreds of items to be sold as part of the influential late director’s personal archiveMatthew WeaverTue 6 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 13.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA special effects axe wielded byJack Nicholsonas he delivered his chillingly manic line “Here’s Johnny!” in the 1980 horror movie The Shining is to go on sale.View image in fullscreen‘That’ axe.Photograph: BonhamsNicholson’s character, Jack Torrance, uses an axe to hack out an opening in a locked door protecting his terrified wife Wendy, played byShelley Duvall. It is also the murder weapon in the killing of Scatman Crothers’ character, Dick Hallorann. One of cinema’s most famous axes could be yours for a list price of between £30,000 and £50,000.View image in fullscreenWendy reacts as Jack Torrance hacks through the bathroom door.Photograph: Maximum Film/AlamyIt is one of hundreds of items in the first auction of the personal archive of The Shining’s influential director,Stanley Kubrick, who died in 1999.The sale includes several other lots from the film, including two sky-blue dresses worn by the twin sisters Alexa and Alexie Grady. They appear in the frocks in a memorable scene when they invite Torrance’s son, Danny, to “come play with us” as he pedals on his tricycle through the corridors of the Overlook Hotel.View image in fullscreenThe dresses worn by the characters Alexa and Alexie Grady.Photograph: Nils Jorgensen/REX/ShutterstockThe boy’s trike is not part of the sale, but a clapperboard used in the film is one of four from Kubrick’s movies to go under the hammer. The others are are from2001: A Space Odyssey, the 1975 historical drama Barry Lyndon and Kubrick’s last film, Eyes Wide Shut.View image in fullscreenOne of four clapperboards up for sale.Photograph: BonhamsThe auction will take place at Bonhams in London on 3 February, after public exhibitions that start next week at Bonhams in New York, before going on to Los Angeles, Paris and then London on 18 January.The lot expected to fetch the highest price is the model of a cosmic foetus that appears in the final scene of 2001: A Space Odyssey. Also known as the “star child prop” it is predicted to fetch as much as £800,000.View image in fullscreenThe ‘star child prop’.Photograph: BonhamsJustifying the list price, Claire Tole-Moir, the head of popular culture at Bonhams, said: “It is the final, enigmatic image of one of cinema’s most influential science fiction films. It represents evolution, new beginnings, naivety and ambiguity. 2001: A Space Odyssey is not just one of Kubrick’s most finest films, it is a cinematic masterpiece, and so to be able to offer this iconic prop from the final scene of the film is incredibly exciting.”She said the auction gave “fans, collectors and historians the chance to own a piece of this remarkable collection” and that the exhibitions were “a landmark moment to get closer to some of the most iconic films ever made”.Tole-Moir’s favourite items in the auction are Kubrick film scripts, complete with his personal annotations, drawings and alternative scenes.She said: “His scripts are incredibly special … providing us with an exciting insight into Stanley’s creative journey whilst making some of his most famous films such asThe Shining, 2001: A Space Odyssey and Lolita among others.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThere is also Kubrick’s personal script from his 1960 film Spartacus.TheGuardian’s obituary of Kubrickdescribes him as enigmatic, obsessive and dictatorial, and his movies as deeply pessimistic. The auction includes his director’s chair, valued at up to £12,000.Tole-Moir said: “Few people had as much of an overwhelming impact on visual culture as Kubrick.” She pointed out that his work was so influential that it spawned the adjective Kubrickian, meaning marked by “meticulous attention to detail, technical mastery, precision and a distinctive visual or creative style”.View image in fullscreenA Stanley Kubrick self-portrait taken circa 1949.Photograph: BonhamsTole-Moir said the lot that best illustrated Kubrick’s personality was his chess set. “He valued chess for its combination of strategy, patience, discipline and intellectual precision - qualities that would become hallmarks of his film-making,” she said.“Later on, during breaks in filming, he would play games with members of the cast and crew, and has often been photographed alongside a chess board.“Other directors’ collections have appeared at auction over the years, but Stanley Kubrick’s archive is truly distinctive in its depth, quality and intellect. It encompasses not only the extraordinary objects themselves, but decades of scholarship, research, documentation and deliberate preservation.“It is hard to think of another collection of this calibre, nor a director who has inspired so many.”Explore more on these topicsStanley KubrickThe ShiningJack NicholsonShelley Duvall2001: A Space OdysseyLolitanewsShareReuse this content

title: Making scents: could AI help perfumers take pressure off endangered plants? | Science | The Guardian
description: Firms working on reproducing compounds without need for repeated harvesting but conservationists are sceptical
Author: Amelia Hill
Headline: Firms working on reproducing compounds without need for repeated harvesting but conservationists are sceptical
Content: Scientists say the fragrance industry will soon be able to reproduce scents and compounds from endangered plants without repeatedly harvesting them.Photograph: Pixel-shot/AlamyView image in fullscreenScientists say the fragrance industry will soon be able to reproduce scents and compounds from endangered plants without repeatedly harvesting them.Photograph: Pixel-shot/AlamyScienceMaking scents: could AI help perfumers take pressure off endangered plants?Firms working on reproducing compounds without need for repeated harvesting but conservationists are scepticalAmelia HillTue 6 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 13.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMany of the world’s most expensive perfumes begin with a wounded tree. When someAquilariatrees are damaged, they produce a dark, fragrant resin that becomes agarwood, or oudh – an ingredient so valuable that wild trees have been illegally felled in its pursuit.The result has devastated wildAquilariapopulations. But what if perfumers could create the smell without cutting down the tree?With the help of AI, scientists are learning to predict how molecules that have never been made will smell, reconstructing scent-producing genes from flowers believed to be extinct. Others have collected microbes from clouds and used them as a starting point for new perfumes.Now scientists and biotechnology companies say advances could soon allow the fragrance industry to reproduce scents and compounds from endangered plants without repeatedly harvesting them.“Being able to recreate the scent of an endangered plant would be a huge win for both the environment but also the brands,” said Alex Wiltschko, the founder of Osmo, a Google Brain spin-off that has raised $130m to develop artificial intelligence capable of predicting and recreating smells.Osmo has recreated the scent of a rare tree from a piece of bark “the size of a finger”, Wiltschko said. A spectrometer analysed the sample, its AI reconstructed the chemical formula and the scent was reproduced in its laboratory.View image in fullscreenAn illegally felledAquilaria sinensis, or incense tree, in Hong Kong.Photograph: Jérôme Favre/EPABioHarvest Sciences says it has created a stable cell culture from an endangered south-east Asian fragrance plant, allowing its valuable compounds to be produced without cultivating or harvesting the original plant.The plant has not been named for commercial reasons but BioHarvest has announced an agreement anticipating production of 20 tonnes of the fragrance composition, with limited production potentially beginning next year.“The challenge is that human demand can be effectively unlimited while biological supply is not,” said BioHarvest’s chief executive, Zaki Rakib. “We believe biotechnology can help close that gap, not by replacing nature but by allowing us to use what nature has given us without continually putting the source under pressure.”But conservationists and perfumers say such claims risk giving advances in fragrance technology an environmental gloss they have not yet earned.“Calling this conservation is greenwashing,” said Mandy Aftel, the pioneering natural perfumer, author and founder of the Aftel Archive of Curious Scents. “Making a synthetic version of an endangered plant’s smell doesn’t save the plant.” She said producing a substitute did not stop people buying the original – or address other causes of a species’ decline.Rhian Smith, of the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, agreed. She pointed to theAquilariatree. AI could help design an alternative to oudh, she said, but wild-sourced material remained highly prized. “It doesn’t completely take the pressure off wild plant species,” she said.There is also the question of motivation. Wiltschko admitted that conservation was not “an explicit priority” for Osmo’s work.View image in fullscreenOsmo says it has trained its AI on more than 5m human responses to smells.Photograph: ronstik/Getty Images/iStockphotoSynthetic perfume itself is nothing new: the industry has relied heavily on synthetic ingredients for more than a century, and machines have long been able to identify molecules in a scent.“What’s changed is what happens after the data comes off the machine,” Wiltschko said. “What’s new is prediction.” He claimed Osmo had trained its AI on more than 5m human responses to smells. “That means it can predict how combinations of molecules will be perceived,” he said.Elsewhere, AI is claimed to be changing the whole world in which perfumers work. Christina Agapakis is not a perfumer, but her work reconstructing genes from preserved flowers has produced fragrance compounds that perfumers can use to create new scents.Another perfumer, Future Society, has gone into the clouds, making two flights in a small plane to collect living microbes. Thirteen were identified, producing 57 scent molecules, which became the starting point for Cloud Reverie, a perfume launched this year.Even AI has its limits: a flower’s scent can contain hundreds of molecules and change according to which part of the plant they come from and the conditions in which it grows.It is still not enough for the purists. “The smell we got was this ghostly fragment of what had been lost,” Agapakis said of her project. She could not recreate the living organism, or the soil, climate, season and ecology that produced its scent, she said.“What we have to remember is, ultimately, however powerful AI is, a smell is not simply a formula or dataset.”Explore more on these topicsScienceFragranceBiologyBiotechnology industryAI (artificial intelligence)PlantsConservationnewsShareReuse this content

title: The butter boom – how the world fell back in love with the glorious golden spread | Food | The Guardian
description: It’s being sculpted for fashion parties, collected by tourists and hoarded in freezers. There are even entire shops devoted to it. What’s behind the revival of the much-maligned foodstuff?
Author: Morwenna Ferrier
Headline: It’s being sculpted for fashion parties, collected by tourists and hoarded in freezers. There are even entire shops devoted to it. What’s behind the revival of the much-maligned foodstuff?
Content: Morwenna Ferrier gets the goods from Erwan Leo at Le Butter in Paris.Photograph: Magali Delporte/The GuardianView image in fullscreenMorwenna Ferrier gets the goods from Erwan Leo at Le Butter in Paris.Photograph: Magali Delporte/The GuardianFoodThe butter boom – how the world fell back in love with the glorious golden spreadIt’s being sculpted for fashion parties, collected by tourists and hoarded in freezers. There are even entire shops devoted to it. What’s behind the revival of the much-maligned foodstuff?Morwenna FerrierTue 6 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 12.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTemperatures inPariswere nudging 41C when Erwan Leo opened Le Butter this summer. Wildfires had already been tearing through France and the city was quiet, particularly in the less touristy 8th arrondissement, a flex-your-wealth area near the Eiffel Tower known as the “golden triangle”. The last thing it needed, you would think, was a shop that sold loads of butter. “We were just so worried about the fridges,” says Leo, the 34-year-old owner. “We didn’t think anyone would even turn up.”I visit Le Butter, the first shop in Paris dedicated to selling the stuff, two months later in September. It’s a quaint, photogenic spot between a wine shop that was opened by Leo eight years ago and a cafe famous for being blown up in Christopher Nolan’s Inception. Inside there are candy-striped walls, little shopping baskets, a shelf of Instagrammable buttery merch (knives, hats, totes) and two double fridges containing 50 different types of butter. It’s a lot cooler today; the fridges purr away at an exacting 3C. And the past few months have been busy – so much so that Leo has had to erect a bench for those waiting outside, and a retractable barrier to manage the queues.Outside today, I find a gathering of butter fans comparing purchases. Among them is Clifford Yellen, a 66-year-old Italian-American chef and consultant who has bulk-bought “only pure stuff – salted”. He opens his paper bag to show me multiple packets, vacuum-packed for his flight home. “We chefs have a real thing about butter,” he says. He usually eats Italian, or the famously creamy Hokkaido from Japan.Inside the shop, tourists from Brazil and Korea are gathered around a glass display cabinet on the counter where staff dispense quenelles of wild garlic butter on to wooden tasting spoons. The tasters follow it with raspberry flavour, and chocolate. “I call Le Butter an ice-cream shop for butter!” Leo says with a laugh.View image in fullscreenDifferent varieties at Le Butter, Paris.Photograph: Magali Delporte/The GuardianAnd while British tourists have been banned from bringing French butter to the UK since 2025, to stop farm animal diseases spreading, as a nation we, too, revere butter. Earlier this year, the Pembroke Club in Belgravia, London, placed an advert for a butter sommelier in Country Life magazine, looking for someone able to confidently “curate our butter assortment and assist in training staff using our silver butter trolley”.For those who can take butter home with them, there are entire threads on Reddit discussing the best way to transport it via plane (frozen, vacuum-packed, ziplocked) and where to buy it. Guided by one, I head to La Grande Épicerie de Paris to lay eyes on its famous “wall of butter” where 150 types are sold. The two most popular varieties, according to the staff, are Le Beurre Bordier and Beillevaire. Like most good French butters, they have a fresh, rich flavour with tangy depths, which you could probably put down to their high butterfat content and the grass-fed cows from which they come.Even the high-end butter is relatively cheap, and right now, in this“little treat” economy, eking out €8 for a wheel of butter sprinkled with fleur de sel feels more manageable than buying a decent bottle of wine. The latest thing, Leo says, is people serving butter as they would cheese after dinner, on boards with crackers. “It’s also cheaper.”While I’m reporting from Paris fashion week, my Instagram becomes a cavalcade of ambrosial butters laid out on event tables with great loaves of bread, or pummelled into submission and piled up into small hills as table centrepieces. I watch influencers biting into whole sticks of butter, or being served plates of medjool dates stuffed with slivers of the stuff. It’s at once beautiful and grotesque.It has even become a material for food artists. Laila Gohar, the American-Egyptian artist, treats it like marble, and once carved it into a fragment of Michelangelo’s David. During a design festival, the food artist Imogen Kwok built a foot-high cone from whipped butter and foraged herbs.View image in fullscreenLaila Gohar’s fragments of Michelangelo’s David, carved from butter.Photograph: Laila GoharIt was the threat of shortage that turned South African journalist Safia Patel, 35, into a self-described “butter hoarder” who now collects and categorises it. At home in Istanbul she keeps cooking butter, eating butter and “ornamental” butter (too precious to eat), the last of which she stores in her freezer.Her love of butter comes from her grandmother, who ate it in thick, cold slices on bread. But it was during the pandemic that she realised how much it really meant to her. She’d buy Lurpak locally in Istanbul – but as the pandemic wore on, it became harder to find. “Once things returned to normal, I began coercing people into bringing me butter from around the world in case I ran out.” Most days she carries two or three portion-sized packs in her handbag, “just in case. Yes, it can get messy.”View image in fullscreenChocolate, pepper and date flavours sit among the salted and unsalted varieties at Le Butter.Photograph: Magali Delporte/The GuardianThe prettiness of Le Butter’s packaging has naturally made it a social media hit, which Leo describes as a double-edged sword. “Obviously, I’m grateful,” he says. “But it can also be overwhelming. The aim of the shop is to educate people beyond supermarket butter, and to serve the locals as well as the tourists. We can only do our best.”This fetishisation of butter is still quite divisive. “When it comes to food styling, some of what they do looks cool,” saysSeb Myersof the restaurant Planque in east London. “But when you see a mound of butter – all that extravagance for the sake of a photo? I’m quite squirrelly with food. Waste is my big thing.”In restaurants, I’ve lost count of the time I’ve been served butter shaped into little salted coins or whipped into something dippable. Bread and butter are still one of the most valued moments in a good meal. And as Anthony Bourdain wrote in Kitchen Confidential, “If you eat at any good restaurant, assume you’ve eaten a stick of butter.”View image in fullscreenButtery deliciousness at Planque, London.“That’s partly because it starts the meal,” says Myers, who takes his butter pretty seriously. “If someone serves you an ice-cold pat of butter, you know you’re not in for a good time”. His restaurant is a play on Parisian bistronomy, so “it’s in almost every dish”. They use Beillevaire butter demi-sel sprinkled with flakes, sliced and well tempered. He keeps it in “a cheese fridge for a week to slow-mature it”. For cooking, it’s Douceur de France (they get through 10kg a week in cooking alone).Pravin Nayar runsCastle Farmrestaurant in Somerset, and makes his own: “We like butter to be the hero product when we do supper clubs.” The key, he says, is how you serve it: room temperature, sprinkled with salt. “The way I see it, bread is just a spoon for butter.”Remember when butter was considered bad? After all those anti-saturated fat health campaigns, consumption hit a historic low by the late 1990s, with the average Brit consuming just 2kg a year. The perception around it seems to have shifted, although with 50% saturated fat – and I say this with love – butter is not exactly a superfood.“The heart-health advice hasn’t changed,” says Tracy Parker, a registered dietitian and an adviser for the British Heart Foundation. “If you’ve got high cholesterol, or your diet already leans heavily on saturated fat – think fatty meats, pastries, cakes, biscuits – then you should probably reconsider how much you’re eating and whether you could swap it for something like olive, avocado or nut oil.” Butter is fine in moderation, though. “A light scrape on your morning toast, and thinking about everything else you eat – you’re probably OK,” she says.So why the cultural rehabilitation of butter in a health-fad-mad 2026? Parker thinks it has become tangled up with the anti-ultraprocessed-food movement. “UPFs have been linked to poor health including obesity, type 2 diabetes and heart disease,” she says. Whereas butter is seen as a preindustrial, farm-adjacent product. “People view butter as a natural food and therefore better than, say, margarine,” she says.View image in fullscreenToo much, or not enough?Photograph: JoeGough/Getty Images/iStockphotoMy family of four eats a pack a week. Is that a lot? Not really. In the UK,we eat just over 3kg of butter per capita per year, which amounts to a modestly covered slice of toast each day. And that is nothing compared to the Belgians, who put away 8kg. Or the French and Danes, who consume almost 9kg per person per year.Many people I meet in Paris still believe in the French Paradox: the idea that they can eat butter and cheese without suffering the same rates of heart disease as other nations. One of the most popular flavours at Le Butter is chocolate, a nice riff on the traditional after-school snack (known as le goûter or le quatre-heures) of dark chocolate squares, salted butter and fresh bread. The fact that cardiovascular disease is the second leading cause of death in France probably won’t affect this too much. “It’s something we eat every day,” says Leo. “I don’t check my cholesterol – I don’t want to know.”I, on the other hand, have familial hypercholesterolemia, a fairly common genetic disorder that causes very high levels of low-density lipoprotein (LDL) or “bad” cholesterol from birth. When I tell Parker, she responds with a polite “ah”. I am not overweight but at some point I will need to go on statins; I also come from a long line of heart attacks. After we talk, I comfort myself with a slice of buttered rye toast, knowing I should probably also reconsider my life choices. But I, like so many people, love butter.For Patel, one pack of butter stands out from the rest of her collection: a half pack of Kerrygold from 2019, frozen ever since. “I have it partly as insurance, in case I run out. But also because it’s reassuring – it reminds me of a different time.” She loves her work but her dream job is to run a dairy farm. “Or at least go to Paris, to that shop, and eat all that butter.”Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Alice Zaslavsky’s shortcut beetroot baked risotto – recipe | Australian food and drink | The Guardian
description: An unconventional technique makes this vibrant rice – finished with dill fronds – a lower-touch dinner for weeknights
Author: Alice Zaslavsky
Headline: An unconventional technique makes this vibrant rice – finished with dill fronds – a lower-touch dinner for weeknights
Content: Magenta marvel: Alice Zaslavsky’s recipe for transforming rice into a shortcut beetroot risotto.Photograph: Rochelle EagleView image in fullscreenMagenta marvel: Alice Zaslavsky’s recipe for transforming rice into a shortcut beetroot risotto.Photograph: Rochelle EagleYou've got thisAustralian food and drinkAlice Zaslavsky’s shortcut beetroot baked risotto – recipeAn unconventional technique makes this vibrant rice – finished with dill fronds – a lower-touch dinner for weeknightsCheck out moreAlice Zaslavsky recipesAlice ZaslavskyTue 6 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 19.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis shortcut risotto will have purists shaking their fists, but I like to live dangerously. Unlike traditional risottos where you stir the whole time, this one gets bunged in the oven with all its liquid, then right at the end, use a whisk to release the starches for a creamy finish.Use a microplane to grate the parmesan over the risotto. This will yield a cloud-like consistency, but you could also just blitz the parmesan to a crumb in the food processor before grating the veg. I’d avoid buying pre‑grated parmesan, as it’s kept crumby with anti-caking agent, and the aroma is … not great.For extra flavour, use vegetable or chicken stock instead of water. And if you have herbs growing in the garden, some parsley, chives or even chervil won’t go astray.How to pick the best figs? Inspect their bottoms: Alice Zaslavsky’s figs on herby labneh with pomegranate dressing – recipeRead moreGrate, bake ‘n’ shake beet risotto – recipeServes4Chop and stir10 minutesSet and forget30 minutes1 brown onion, peeled and quartered1 beetroot, topped and tailed, scrubbed and quartered (about 200g)1 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil2 tbsp butter1–2 garlic cloves, peeled and minced250g uncookedcarnaroli or arborio rice(1 heaped cup)125ml white wine(½ cup)2 vegetable or chicken stock cubes2 bay leaves¼ bunch dill, stems finely chopped, half the fronds roughly chopped (reserve the remaining fronds for garnishing)60gfinely grated parmesan or pecorinoTo finish4 tbsp mascarpone or sour creamFinely grated parmesan or pecorinoDill fronds(reserved from above)35gslivered pistachios(¼ cup, optional)Freshly ground black pepperExtra-virgin olive oilOven goes onPreheat your oven to 240C/220C fanGrate the vegGrate the onion and beetroot using a box grater or the coarsest setting of your food processor. Chop up any chunkier bits.Start your baseGlug the olive oil and half the butter into a shallow flameproof casserole dish over medium heat. Dump in the grated veg and the garlic and stir about until you hear a sizzle. Whack the lid on and set the timer for six minutes, stirring halfway. Meanwhile, bring a kettle of water to the boil.When the onion and beetroot have softened and released a sweet aroma, stir in the rice and toss vigorously for a few minutes for the rice to get toasty and turn a provocative shade of pink.Splash in wine andstockSplash in the wine and crumble in the stock cubes. Let it all bubble for another minute to break up the stock cubes and cook out the booziness of the wine.Bay ’n’ bakeStir the bay leaves and dill stems through the rice, then pour in one litre (four cups) of the just-boiled kettle water, which will boil and bubble again in no time. Whack the lid back on, carefully transfer to the middle of the hot oven and set the timer for 12 minutes.Take a whiskPull the pan out of the oven. Remove the bay leaves, then whisk in the remaining tablespoon of butter, along with the parmesan.View image in fullscreenContinue whisking for a minute or two, whipping the lot into a frenzy. As you whip, the extra liquid in the pan will be absorbed and react with the starch in the rice and the fat in the cheese and butter, to encourage a silky, creamy texture.Put the lid back on and leave for another 12 minutes to let the risotto rest. Taste for seasoning, then give a final stir.Bring it homeSpoon the risotto on to plates with a lip. Top each with a spoonful of mascarpone, an extra grating of parmesan or pecorino, dill fronds and some pistachios if you have them. Finish with freshly ground black pepper and a drizzle of your best olive oil.This is an edited extract fromWeeknights with Aliceby Alice Zaslavsky, photography by Rochelle Eagle, available now through Murdoch Books (AU$49.99)Explore more on these topicsAustralian food and drinkYou've got thisRiceFoodVegetablesAustralian lifestylerecipesShareReuse this content

title: How to maximise the umami in mushrooms | Fungi | The Guardian
description: Whether you sizzle, sweat, wet-fry or oven-cook, enhancing the savoury flavour of your mushrooms will depend on the variety, says our panel of fun guys
Author: Anna Berrill
Headline: Whether you sizzle, sweat, wet-fry or oven-cook, enhancing the savoury flavour of your mushrooms will depend on the variety, says our panel of fun guys
Content: To bring out the flavour inFuchsia Dunlop's mushroom mapo tofu, cut it into 5mm cubes, then fry on a high heat for two to three minutes, until ‘tinged with gold’.Photograph: Patricia Niven/The Guardian. Food styling: Tamara Vos. Prop styling: Anna Willkins. Food styling assistant: Katie Smith.View image in fullscreenTo bring out the flavour inFuchsia Dunlop's mushroom mapo tofu, cut it into 5mm cubes, then fry on a high heat for two to three minutes, until ‘tinged with gold’.Photograph: Patricia Niven/The Guardian. Food styling: Tamara Vos. Prop styling: Anna Willkins. Food styling assistant: Katie Smith.Kitchen aideFungiHow to maximise the umami in mushroomsWhether you sizzle, sweat, wet-fry or oven-cook, enhancing the savoury flavour of your mushrooms will depend on the variety, says our panel of fun guysAnna BerrillTue 6 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHow do I cook mushroomsat homeso they have the umamiyou get in restaurant dishes?John, by emailFor Chantelle Nicholson, chef-patron ofApricityin London, boosting the savoury side of ’shrooms comes down to three main things. First, they hold a lot of water, so “you need to cook that out of them, so heat is super-important, as are fat and salt”. Tomás Gormley, chef-owner ofCardinalin Edinburgh, adds that he can “almost guarantee” that John isn’t using enough of the latter: “As a rule, I use 1.5% of the weight of whatever I’m seasoning. With mushrooms, especially, season early, before they hit the pan, to draw out their moisture. That resulting mushroomy water then cooks the mushrooms while it’s reducing and concentrating the flavour.”But there are so many varieties of mushrooms out there, and they all behave in different ways, so John needs to be using the right ones for the job. “If you’re making a soup, puree or paté, field, portobello or button mushrooms are fine,” Nicholson says. “But if you’re looking for a delicious sauteed mushroom, say, ideally you need something with less water content – chestnut, shiitake or blue/grey oyster mushrooms. Heat oil in a pan, then add the shredded or sliced mushrooms, and season with fine salt straight away.” Nicholson would be inclined to toss in a bay leaf and some thyme or sage, too, and maybe a smashed clove of garlic. “Cook over a high-ish heat until lightly golden, then add a bit of butter and keep cooking until golden. If you want to enhance the flavour even further, a splash of dry sherry works really well.”That said, Buttons Mira, author ofThe Mushroomery, throws her ’shrooms into a dry frying pan: “That’s right, no oil or fat! I put a lid on top and let them sweat out that rich, umami flavour.” Alice Zaslavsky, author ofWeeknights with Alice, deploys a similar tactic: “Cooking mushrooms the traditional way in fat can inhibit the intensification of umami and lock in too much moisture, which is why I’ve taken to wet-frying my mushrooms.” She first lets them bubble away in a little water “spliced with condiments: umami-rich soy sauce and/or Worcestershire sauce work well”, until all the liquid evaporates. “Only then do I add oil and/or butter to lift off the flavour in the base of the pan and encourage caramelisation for extra depth and sweetness.”Heading out of the frying pan and into the oven, a properly roasted mushroom can also be meaty and deeply flavoured: “That makes them super-nutty and delicious,” says Mira, who then uses them in pastas and risottos. The best way to do this is, again, with high heat, salt and oil, Nicholson says: “I’d also suggest using chestnut mushrooms over button mushrooms, and quartering them – hard herbs, such as thyme, bay or rosemary, will help as well.”Just like the rest of us, though, sometimes those mushrooms need a bit of a helping hand: “Up the umami potential by doubling down on the right kind of mushroom,” Zaslavsky says, which in her book includes sprinkling over dried shiitake or porcini in powdered form: “Both offer a deep, savoury aroma and flavour that helps enhance milder varieties.” Magic mushrooms, indeed.Got a culinary dilemma? title: Jose Pizarro’s recipe for poached pear and almond tart with PX caramel | Food | The Guardian
description: This tart uses the richness of red vermut to bring together the sweet and the nutty for a flavour explosion
Author: José Pizarro
Headline: This tart uses the richness of red vermut to bring together the sweet and the nutty for a flavour explosion
Content: Jose Pizarro’s poached pear and almond tart with PX caramel.Photograph: Ola O Smit/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Lilli Gavin.View image in fullscreenJose Pizarro’s poached pear and almond tart with PX caramel.Photograph: Ola O Smit/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Lilli Gavin.Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.FoodJose Pizarro’s recipe for poached pear and almond tart with PX caramelThis tart uses the richness of red vermut to bring together the sweet and the nutty for a flavour explosionJosé PizarroTue 6 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn Spain, vermut is traditionally enjoyed as an aperitif, while pedro ximénez is often poured at the end of a meal, alongside dessert or a piece of cheese, say. In this tart, however, they come together to tell the story of the Spanish table in the form of pudding. We have a wonderful tradition of fortified wines, and while lighter sherries often hog the limelight, vermut and pedro ximénez deserve just as much attention. They’re both made from wine, but each brings something completely different to a dish. Here, vermut, which is infused with herbs and spices, gently perfumes the pears, while PX, with its rich raisin, fig and caramel notes, introduces a flavour that’s impossible to resist.Poached pear and almond tart with PX caramelPrep15 minCook1 hr 50 minChill30 min+Serves10-12750ml bottle red vermut– I likeLustau Vermut Rojo, but any vermut rojo will do, or standard red vermouth3 tbsprunny honey1 vanilla pod, split and seeds scraped outPared zest of 1 orange4 just-ripe medium-sized dessert pears(williams or comice, say), peeledCream or creme fraiche, to serveFor the pastry225g plain flour,plus extra for dusting110g cold unsalted butter50g caster sugar2egg yolksFor the filling100mlpedro ximénez2 tbsp caramel sauce(Sainbury’s does a good one), or dulce de leche1 pinchflaky sea salt125g unsalted butter, softened125g caster sugar, plus 2 tbsp extra for the glaze2 mediumeggs125g ground almonds1 tbsp plain flourPut the vermut, honey, vanilla pod and seeds, orange zest and 300ml water in a pan just big enough to hold the pears snugly. Bring to a simmer, then add the pears and leave to poach gently for 20-25 minutes, until glassy-looking and just tender to the tip of a knife. Take off the heat and leave the pears to cool in the liquid.Meanwhile, in a food processor, pulse the flour, butter and sugar until they resemble breadcrumbs. Add the egg yolks and pulse again briefly to make a dough; if need be, add up to two teaspoons of water to help bring it together. Tip out on to a lightly floured surface, quickly shape into a ball, then press down into a flat disc. Wrap in baking paper and chill for at least 30 minutes.Roll out the pastry on a lightly floured surface, then use it to line a greased deep, fluted 23cm tart tin; the pastry will be very soft, so if it breaks, just press it back together with your fingertips. Return to the fridge to chill again.In a small pan, bring the PX to a simmer, then reduce until there’s only about two tablespoons of sticky liquid left. Tip into a bowl, blend with the caramel sauce and a pinch of salt, then spread the PX mix all over the base of the tart case, and chill again.Heat the oven and a baking sheet to 190C (170C fan)/375F/gas 5. Lift the cooled pears out of the poaching liquid, pat dry, then cut in half lengthways and scoop out the cores. Turn each pear half on to its flat side, then cut a few times across its width without slicing all the way through. Press down gently to fan out the slices, then pat dry again.Whisk the softened butter and caster sugar until light and fluffy, then work in the eggs, almonds and flour. Spread this evenly over the caramel layer in the tart case, then neatly top with the pear halves pointy ends in, and gently press them into the almond layer.Bake for 45 minutes on the heated tray, then cover with foil so the pastry doesn’t brown too much and bake for 15 minutes more, until set all the way through.Meanwhile, put 300ml of the pear poaching liquid in a pan, add two tablespoons of sugar, bring slowly to a boil, then reduce to a glossy, sticky glaze.Leave the tart to cool for 10 minutes, then remove from its tin and put on a rack. Once it’s just warm, brush the vermut glaze over the top and serve with cream or creme fraiche.Explore more on these topicsFoodDessertAutumn food and drinkFruitSpanish food and drinkBakingCakerecipesShareReuse this content

title: Cancer rates rising more quickly among younger people, international research finds | Cancer | The Guardian
description: Experts looking at UK, US and Dutch data found ‘significant increases’ in early onset cases of seven cancers, prompting warnings about lifestyle choices
Author: Anna Bawden
Headline: Experts looking at UK, US and Dutch data found ‘significant increases’ in early onset cases of seven cancers, prompting warnings about lifestyle choices
Content: A patient receiving a CT scan. Better detection of cancer is one of the factors behind the increase in diagnosis rates across age groups.Photograph: baranozdemir/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA patient receiving a CT scan. Better detection of cancer is one of the factors behind the increase in diagnosis rates across age groups.Photograph: baranozdemir/Getty ImagesCancerCancer rates rising more quickly among younger people, international research findsExperts looking at UK, US and Dutch data found ‘significant increases’ in early onset cases of seven cancers, prompting warnings about lifestyle choicesAnna BawdenHealth and social affairs correspondentTue 6 Oct 2026 00.01 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 03.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCases of seven types of cancer have risen sharply among younger people in England, major new research has found, prompting warnings that lifestyle choices are costing thousands of lives each year.The number of people under 50 diagnosed with prostate cancer in England has quadrupled since 2001, while early onset bowel, kidney and uterine cancer diagnoses more than doubled.Analysis ofEnglish,USand Dutch cancer data by World Cancer Research Fund identified “significant increases” in early onset cancers for seven cancer types in England, five types in the US and four in the Netherlands.Although cancer has been increasing across all age groups globally, the rate rise in early onset casesis greater than other ages.Experts said the figures reflected the growing global obesity epidemic, poor diets and insufficient exercise, as well as growing awareness of cancer and earlier diagnosis.Cancer among the under 50s is still uncommon, with the median age at diagnosis above 60, but the trend is worrying, the authors noted.Commenting on the findings, Mark Lawler, professor of digital health and the chair in translational cancer genomics at Queen’s University Belfast, called the problem “a ticking timebomb that we need to [defuse] as quickly as possible, otherwise the numbers will undoubtedly continue to grow”.He went on: “The overall trend is also particularly worrying as it comes on the backdrop of lifestyle factors contributing to thousands of deaths.”In England, of the 12 tumour types studied, incidence rates of prostate cancer among men under 50 jumped from one in every 100,000 people in 2001 to 3.6 in every 100,000 in 2023. Over the same period, rates of bowel cancer among the under 50s leapt from 3.9 in 100,000 people in 2001 to 8.4 in 100,000 in 2023, while early onset uterine and kidney cancers also doubled to 3.9 and 3 per 100,000 people respectively.The rate of breast cancer among the under 50s increased, albeit less sharply, from 42 to 47.5 per 100,000 in 2023, while there were also increases in the incidence of early onset pancreatic and liver cancers.In the US, analysis of official data since 2000 found that among patients under 50, incidence rates of kidney cancer more than doubled from 2.5 in 100,000 people in 2000 to 5.3 in 2023, while bowel, uterine and pancreatic cancers all increased by more than 50% and breast cancer by about 20%.New research finds 485 chemicals in US pesticide products linked to breast cancerRead moreFor the Netherlands, the researchers found significant increases in early onset bowel, kidney, liver and cervical cancers.In contrast, rates of lung cancer among the under 50s declined in all three countries, reflecting continuing declines in smoking in those countries.Dr Giota Mitrou, the executive director of research and policy at the World Cancer Research Fund (WCRF), called the trajectory “concerning”, and added: “Behind every figure is a person facing cancer earlier than they, their family and often their doctor would expect. While cancer is still much more common in older adults, these changing patterns among younger generations need to be treated as a serious research and cancer prevention priority.”WCRF said risk factors such as growing obesity levels, poor diet, insufficient exercise,alcohol consumption, smoking and environmental exposures (such as pollutants, chemicals, plastics, water and air pollution) could be contributing to the trend. About 40% of cancers are linked to these kinds of modifiable risks. However, greater awareness of cancer symptoms also means that people are more likely to be diagnosed earlier.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“While we don’t completely understand why more cancers are occurring in people under 50 years of age, it is likely that risk factors related to cancer – for example, overweight and obesity, diet, alcohol, consumption and smoking – play a role,” said Dr Vanessa Gordon-Dseagu, research translation manager at WCRF.“At the same time, the public are increasingly aware of the risk factors relating to cancer and the signs and symptoms of the disease to look out for, so are more likely to seek out healthcare when they experience them.”While more cancers are being diagnosed at an earlier stage, “increased diagnosis does not explain the whole story and more research is needed to understand early-onset cancers” she added.King’s College London has announceda new trial of 250,000 people, funded by Cancer Research UK, to investigate the increase in bowel cancer cases among younger adults.The study will seek a clearer understanding of the balance between worsening risk factors and better detection in the rise.A Department ofHealthand Social Care spokesperson said: “These findings underline why early diagnosis is at the heart of our national cancer plan. To help catch cancer sooner, we’re investing in new technologies to speed up diagnosis, expanding genetic testing, and supporting research to better understand the causes of cancer and who may be most at risk.We’re also prioritising research into less-survivable and rarer cancers, and our ambition is for three-quarters of people diagnosed by 2035 to be cancer-free or living well with cancer, saving 320,000 lives.“Our newly announced national cancer board has a specific representative for children and young people, as we’re aware of the devastating impact of getting cancer at an earlier stage of life.”Explore more on these topicsCancerMedical researchHealthProstate cancerBowel cancerBreast cancernewsShareReuse this content

title: Kenya confirms first Ebola case as virus ‘surges’ in DR Congo province | Ebola | The Guardian
description: Health minister says 28 contacts identified after death of citizen who arrived from DRC on Saturday
Author: Rachel Savage
Headline: Health minister says 28 contacts identified after death of citizen who arrived from DRC on Saturday
Content: Volunteer health workers at an Ebola emergency response training session conducted by Médecins Sans Frontières in Ongata Rongai, Kenya, in August.Photograph: Daniel Irungu/EPAView image in fullscreenVolunteer health workers at an Ebola emergency response training session conducted by Médecins Sans Frontières in Ongata Rongai, Kenya, in August.Photograph: Daniel Irungu/EPAEbolaKenya confirms first Ebola case as virus ‘surges’ in DR Congo provinceHealth minister says 28 contacts identified after death of citizen who arrived from DRC on SaturdayRachel Savageand agenciesTue 6 Oct 2026 08.46 EDTFirst published on Tue 6 Oct 2026 04.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKenya has reported its first-ever Ebola death, the health minister announced on Tuesday, as the disease continues to spread rapidly through the north-east of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), where the outbreak was announced in May.This is the 17th outbreak of the highly infectious, often deadly disease in the DRC. As of 2 October, 4,082 people had died out of 8,463 confirmed cases in the countrysince the emergenceof the Bundibugyo strain of the Ebola virus, for which there is still no vaccine nor specific treatment.A Kenyan man who had been living in the DRC for seven years died after returning to Kenya, the Kenyan health minister Aden Duale told reporters.The man, who has not been named, had been treated in the DRC after falling ill about a month ago. He then travelled overland to the Ugandan capital, Kampala, before flying to Nairobi on 3 October.Kenya has previously never reported a case of Ebola, but neighbouring Ugandarecorded 20– almost all people who had travelled from the DRC – and two deaths, before being declared Ebola-free in August.Duale said the man was taken by a relative and a friend from Nairobi’s international airport to Nairobi hospital, where he was immediately isolated, suffering from “fever, chills, intense fatigue, weakness, muscle pain, painful swallowing, sore throat and bleeding under the skin at the injection sites”.He said the man was subsequently screened and confirmed positive for the virus, but “regrettably passed on last night at around 1130” in the evening (2030 GMT).Duale said officials had listed 28 contacts of the deceased, including family members and healthcare workers, but that so far “only one test has turned positive and is the one that we have just discussed”.He added that authorities were looking for another 23 passengers and four crew members who were on the same flight with the man and that “arrangements” for quarantine for those at risk had been prepared. “I wish to assure the public not to panic, as all systems are in place to mitigate the spread of the disease,” he said.Duale said a “safe and dignified burial” of the man had been planned for later in the day, in line with public health standards, but did not give further details.Kenyansreacted furiouslyto government plans earlier this year to allow the US to set up an Ebola facility at Laikipia airbase, about 125 miles from Nairobi.After starting in the DRC’s north-eastern Ituri province, the current outbreak has spread to seven provinces in the country’s north and east.DRC politician beaten to death after radio appearance about Ebola outbreakRead moreThe response to the virus in the vast central African country has been hindered by instability, including clashes between armed groups, mistrust of authorities – which has led to violence against health workers and other officials – and a lack of resources amid huge cuts in international aid.The medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières warned on Monday of an “alarming surge” in cases in eastern North Kivu province, which borders Uganda. The province now accounts for 40% of all newEbolacases, compared with 24% at the end of August, the NGO said.“It is like fighting a megafire,” said Stephanie Hoffmann, coordinator at MSF’s Ebola treatment centre in the city of Butembo. “Multiple outbreaks are developing at the same time, with varying intensity and in different locations.”The wider Butembo health zone is home to around 2 million people and only has four Ebola treatment centres, two of which only opened recently, MSF said.Hoffman said: “Because there are not enough beds available, we are sometimes forced to refer confirmed Ebola patients elsewhere, despite the significant risk this poses to the wider community. In addition, standards of care in some peripheral facilities do not always meet the requirements for Ebola treatment.”North Kivu is particularly affected by conflict, with 134 violent incidents there in the past month, according to tracking group Armed Conflict Location and Event Data, more than any other province.Agence France-Presse contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsEbolaKenyaDemocratic Republic of the CongoAfricaInfectious diseasesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Chanel is all about joy as Blazy celebrates year at helm of world’s hottest brand | Chanel | The Guardian
description: Artistic director is all smiles as he swaps quiet luxury for bold colours and patterns at Paris show
Author: Jess Cartner-Morley
Headline: Artistic director is all smiles as he swaps quiet luxury for bold colours and patterns at Paris show
Content: ‘The new Chanel shouts with cereal-aisle colours.’Photograph: Ed Alcock/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘The new Chanel shouts with cereal-aisle colours.’Photograph: Ed Alcock/The GuardianChanelChanel is all about joy as Blazy celebrates year at helm of world’s hottest brandArtistic director is all smiles as he swaps quiet luxury for bold colours and patterns at Paris showJess Cartner-Morleyin ParisTue 6 Oct 2026 05.35 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 13.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“It’s a good start,” Matthieu Blazy said after a Paris show that marked a year of his tenure as artistic director atChanel. “I am happy with where we are at.”Chanel now holds the top spot in the Lyst index of the world’s hottest brands, which tracks demand and engagement across search and social media. The privately held company announces official financial results only once a year, but figures reported by Bloomberg showed 16% growth in the first half of 2026. InVanity Fair’s listof the world’s 50 most powerful people, published this month, Blazy is the only fashion designer to make the cut. People who don’t much care about fashion have noticed him; people who do care about fashion talk about him non-stop.View image in fullscreenModels on the runway for the show.Photograph: Ed Alcock/The GuardianBlazy’s Chanel is about joy. Smiley and chatty in person, he enthuses about his team and the women he dresses, presenting a friendly face of Chanel that contrasts with Karl Lagerfeld’s legendary acid tongue and Coco’s controlled brutalist chic. He talks about his job like a child in a candy store, not a tortured artist: he got the idea for this stage set, a flock of 95 giant white birds suspended from the domed steel and glass ceiling of the Grand Palais in Paris, while on holiday in southern Italy with his partner, watching migrating birds fly above the Crati River.View image in fullscreenMatthieu Blazy on the runway after the presentation.Photograph: Mohammed Badra/EPAOne of Chanel’s most famous adverts of the 1990s featuredVanessa Paradis in a birdcage; now, Chanel’s birds fly free. For the soundtrack of the show Blazy had asked Nicole Kidman to read a passage “about time, about freedom” from Virginia Woolf’s To The Lighthouse, which he had read on that Italian holiday. Fashion was “women’s homemade remedy for the dark times”, he said.View image in fullscreenAlexa Demie, Nicole Kidman, Dua Lipa and Pedro Pascal on the front row at the show. Kidman read a passage from To The Lighthouse in the soundtrack.Photograph: Swan Gallet/WWD/Getty ImagesAfter several years when the decaffeinated aesthetic of quiet luxury dominated fashion, the new Chanel shouts with cereal-aisle colours. A red and white embroidered jacket with a jade and turquoise skirt, plus bag and boots in navy and gold. The iconic two-tone pumps, but in zebra stripes and yellow polka dots instead of the traditional camel and black.View image in fullscreenChanel show with the 2.55 classic bag, a yellow twin set, a red and white embroidered jacket with a jade and turquoise skirt, and the same model closing the show with the 2.55 bag.Composite: Shutterstock/Stéphane Cardinale/Corbis/Getty ImagesThe same model opened and closed the show carrying Gabrielle Chanel’s very own 2.55 handbag. “Gabrielle actually had very few bags in her own life, which is something I find quite beautiful. So this bag is not broken, but it has a wonderful patina,” Blazy said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFashion StatementStyle, with substance: what's really trending this week, a roundup of the best fashion journalism and your wardrobe dilemmas solvedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenModels on the runway for the show.Photograph: Ed Alcock/The GuardianOn his moodboard were photographs of the founder he had found in the archive: Gabrielle as a child; with Gigot, her beloved great dane; on a boat; riding a horse; in a Harlequin fancy dress costume; smiling in a bold leopard-print coat and matching hat. “It is a side of Chanel that is not known: her funny side, her joyful side. I see women as a juxtaposition of so many selves, and Chanel had this incredible layering within herself.”View image in fullscreenA Chanel classic suit.Photograph: Ed Alcock/MYOP/The GuardianThe famous soft-shouldered Chanel suit came worn with nothing beneath, “like perfume” (Blazy, a student of Cocology, will not have missed the allusion to what Marilyn Monroe famously said she wore in bed: Chanel No 5). “I like the idea that when you wear it directly on the skin, it makes a fetish of the suit. A little punk Chanel,” he said. A year of fabric innovation was behind the newest versions of the suit, a smocked silk on an elasticated membrane, which “is my answer to what sporty could mean at Chanel”, Blazy said.Explore more on these topicsChanelParis fashion weekFashion weeksfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Fine scenery, historic towns and great pubs: a weekend walk on the Shropshire Way | Walking holidays | The Guardian
description: A new series of rambles cuts the 185-mile trail into bitesize portions reachable by train, with urban beavers the Devil’s Chair tor and some delicious food along the way
Author: Jane Dunford
Headline: A new series of rambles cuts the 185-mile trail into bitesize portions reachable by train, with urban beavers the Devil’s Chair tor and some delicious food along the way
Content: Linley Beeches on Linley Hill in Shropshire.Photograph: Simon Whaley Landscapes/AlamyView image in fullscreenLinley Beeches on Linley Hill in Shropshire.Photograph: Simon Whaley Landscapes/AlamyWalking holidaysFine scenery, historic towns and great pubs: a weekend walk on the Shropshire WayA new series of rambles cuts the 185-mile trail into bitesize portions reachable by train, with urban beavers, the Devil’s Chair tor and some delicious food along the wayJane DunfordTue 6 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 05.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFew pubs boast a more idyllic setting. As I emerge from the woods after a 15-mile hike,The Bridges, on the banks of the Onny River, in the rolling south Shropshire hills, glistens in the late afternoon sun. Inside it’s all wooden beams, with light streaming through stained glass and huge bunches of homegrown flowers adding splashes of colour. There’s time for a pint before general manager Sam Thompson shows me to my room in the recently converted stables.I’m here exploring part of the 185-mile (297km) Shropshire Way, on a two-day Heart of the Hills hike – one of the county tourist board’s newRail-Ready Short Breaks. Designed for people who don’t have time to tackle the whole route, the itineraries focus on loops that are easy to access by train, with illustrated PDF downloads, GPX files, accommodation suggestions and highlights of what to do along the way. My route will take me from Shrewsbury to Bishop’s Castle via Ratlinghope – about 27 miles, perfect for a weekend.View image in fullscreenThe Bridges pub in Ratlinghope.Shrewsbury itself is worth lingering in – the historic market town is crammed with independent shops and restaurants (I lovedCsonsfor its creative small plates) and impressive Tudor architecture. But I’m most intrigued to learn that beavers have been reintroduced here by the council and theShropshire Wildlife Trust. The first kit in the county in 400 years was born late last year and the Trust’s Tom Freeland shows me around the site, the Old River Bed nature reserve, just two miles north of the town centre. A boardwalk crossing wetlands allows an up-close view of the rewilding project. Although we don’t spy the elusive creatures (we see heron and plenty of moorhen), there’s still lots to learn. “It’s been a great success in inspiring the community to find out more about our local wildlife,” says Tom. Nature talks and guided tours of the beaver enclosure are in the pipeline, too.View image in fullscreenShrewsbury Square, Shropshire.Photograph: Nik Reates/AlamyBack at my base, the 16th-centuryLion + Pheasant townhouse hotel, I dine on pan-roasted trout in the beamed restaurant (there’s a popular wine and tapas bar on site too) and the next morning set off to walk the first leg to Ratlinghope. Crossing the River Severn, the city soon peters out and quiet country lanes lead to Lyth Hill Country Park where expansive views open up across Shropshire.It’s a steady climb to Wilderley Hill, past fields of rape, bright patches of yellow in a sea of green, and I stop under an oak tree to picnic. There’s no one around, just the songs of wren and chaffinch filling the air. The landscape changes on the approach to Ratlinghope as the route traces a brook, crosses wooden bridges and winds through pretty woodland. Just off the path lies the 12th-century St Margaret’s Church, the burial place of 19th-century farmer Richard Munslow, the last known “sin-eater”, whose job it was to eat bread and drink ale over corpses to absorb their sins.double quotation markThe Bridges is such a lively, friendly place I’m tempted to move nearby for the pub aloneI enjoy a drink instead in the pretty beer garden at The Bridges. The seven immaculate, minimalist rooms are round an adjacent courtyard – and guests have access to a lounge above the pub, too. The food in the bar includes Guinness rarebit and duck terrine, while the light-filled restaurant focuses on organic fare from the owners’ regenerative farm on the Linley Estate and the Welsh Marches. I feast on huge radishes with anchoïade, and hake with fennel, capers and crispy polenta. Breakfast the next morning – homemade granola and poached rhubarb – is equally delicious. It’s such a lively, friendly place I’m tempted to move nearby for the pub alone. They’ll even drive locals home if they’ve had one too many, Sam tells me.Blue skies and gentle sunshine greet me for day two of the hike, a 12-mile yomp across rugged moorland and pastures to Bishop’s Castle. The pub lies on the edge of the Long Mynd, a heath and moorland plateau, but I’m heading north to the Stiperstones, a national nature reserve with a wild, dramatic ridge of quartzite rock formations that pierce the ground. I climb higher, passing Devil’s Chair tor, watching skylarks and buzzards soar overhead.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThe Devil’s Chair on the Stiperstones Ridge, Shropshire.Photograph: Vincent Lowe/AlamyIt’s a beautiful walk. After several hours, a magnificent avenue of Linley Beeches line the descent into Bishop’s Castle, a charming town of half-timbered houses.Bank House B&B, a Georgian renovation with an oak-panelled drawing room and five antique-filled rooms, is my home for the night. I pop into thePoetry Pharmacywhere prescriptions are poems chosen to spark specific emotions, to be “taken” when required (I leave with a bottle of Joy). Although little remains of the medieval castle that once stood here and gives the town its name, the grandCastle Hotel, with its pretty gardens and welcoming restaurant, is worth a visit.With more time, I could, of course, carry on and add another loop of the trail. But the train back home beckons – Craven Arms station is a short bus or taxi ride away – and I leave feeling pleased to have dipped my toe into a small segment of theShropshireWay. As far as rambling weekends go, it’s ticked all the right boxes, and whetted my appetite to discover more.The trip was provided byVisit Shropshireand train travel from London to Shropshire was byVisit England.The Bridgeshas rooms from£120a night. title: The pest I’ll never forget: the cockroaches I still dream about | Insects | The Guardian
description: My student house in Manchester had several thousand other occupants. Despite pest controllers regularly dousing the property, the glossy, greasy, relentless insects marched onwards, endlessly reproducing
Author: Anna Moore
Headline: My student house in Manchester had several thousand other occupants. Despite pest controllers regularly dousing the property, the glossy, greasy, relentless insects marched onwards, endlessly reproducing
Content: ‘They are indestructible.’Composite: Guardian design; Alexey Protasov;vichie81/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘They are indestructible.’Composite: Guardian design; Alexey Protasov;vichie81/Getty ImagesThe pest I’ll never forgetInsectsThe pest I’ll never forget: the cockroaches I still dream aboutMy student house in Manchester had several thousand other occupants. Despite pest controllers regularly dousing the property, the glossy, greasy, relentless insects marched onwards, endlessly reproducingAnna MooreTue 6 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 12.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘You do know about the cockroaches?” I’ve forgotten most things people said to me in the 80s, but never that. It was said by one of the occupants of the student house in Longsight, Manchester, that I had signed up to live in the following year. When the landlord had shown me and my future housemates the property, the tenants had been out. He told us they were third years doing their finals and must not be disturbed under any circumstances. (What can I say? We were gullible back then.) Days before summer term ended though, I’d knocked on the door to show a friend where I’d be living. Instead, I learned that the house was infested.The weird thing is, we moved in anyway. In truth, although I understood this was very bad news, I didn’t quite realise what a cockroach was. There was no internet, so I would have had to go to a library to know what I know now: their march, their canter, their crunch if you step on one. Their soft, sweet, sour smell (uric acid which they store in their fat, apparently). Sometimes, in the back of a shop, or a restaurant loo, I catch that scent and I know what it is.I also know that they are indestructible. Just two German cockroaches left in one cosy crevice behind the fridge can be two million cockroaches in a couple of years. They are reproductive machines, and eat anything – rubbish, rot, dead skin, sleeping humans, each other. They can survive for days without heads! You’ll never win. A pest controller in a hazmat suit came regularly to spray white powder everywhere. The only benefit was that the chemicals on the carpet eradicated my housemate’s verruca, which she had been trying to get rid of for three years.The ‘Cockroach Lord’ who names new species after Tolkien and Pokémon charactersRead moreMy first sighting has always stayed with me. We had just moved in. One of my housemates was sitting in a big armchair, telling us about her summer, when a cockroach appeared behind her shoulder like a pantomime villain. We pointed and screamed while it lumbered over the back of the chair towards us – enormous, glossy, greasy, antenna waving, taking its time. (They’re excellent climbers, by the way.) This happened in broad daylight, even though this is meant to suppress their movement. Cockroaches prefer to wait quietly for darkness before coming out to party – a daytime sighting indicates a serious overcrowding issue where all their normal spaces are full. And so it turned out to be.To this day, we wonder why we didn’t move out – or even explore the possibility of leaving. By the end of that year though, we had all stood each leg of our beds in saucepans of water so that any cockroach attempting to join us while we slept would surely drown. Although I now know they can close off their breathing valves and survive submerged for 30 minutes.I still dream about them sometimes. I have a lifelong cockroach phobia – or katsaridaphobia – which seems entirely sensible to me. But it’s also made me tougher. Mice? Head lice? Threadworms? Scabies? I’ve raised a family since then and have known all of those closeup, but the bottom line is always: “At least it’s not cockroaches.” If it isn’t waxy and crunchy, if there’s no antenna, no oily shine and sickly scent, if it doesn’t march and scuttle and canter and climb on to my pillow at night … I’ll cope.Explore more on these topicsInsectsThe pest I’ll never forgetStudent experienceAnimalsWildlifefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Crossword editor’s desk: why the Independent’s puzzle should live on | Crosswords | The Guardian
description: An easy win for the newspaper, plus a puzzle with a hidden mathematical theme
Author: Alan Connor
Headline: An easy win for the newspaper, plus a puzzle with a hidden mathematical theme
Content: In Turnstone’s Genius puzzle for September, solvers remove Fibonacci-related words such as ‘artichoke’.Photograph: Kathrin Ziegler/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIn Turnstone’s Genius puzzle for September, solvers remove Fibonacci-related words such as ‘artichoke’.Photograph: Kathrin Ziegler/Getty ImagesCrossword editor's updateCrosswordsCrossword editor’s desk: why the Independent’s puzzle should live onAn easy win for the newspaper, plus a puzzle with a hidden mathematical themeAlan ConnorTue 6 Oct 2026 09.01 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 12.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Independent has an excellent puzzle made by excellent setters. Since 2016, it has, of course, been online-only. We used to link to gems from its cryptics on a weekly basis. Then something changed: the interface. The puzzle player had no links and trying to complete its puzzles was like trying to write on mashed potatoes with a hammer. It felt like it had been removed from the crossword ecosystem.Many of us have persevered, but the effort it takes to print a PDF is quite the challenge of a solver’s commitment. The Indy is planning to discontinue the crossword, which is baffling since a) the online puzzles could have a busy, happy home with little effort and expenditure and b) puzzles have never been bigger.On which topic, I am excited to share that the Guardian’s Cluesletter launches on 13 October. You don’t need to be a cryptic devotee to deduce that this will be a wonderful newsletter on all things puzzle-related.Sign up now!Meanwhile, the winner ofSeptember’s Geniusis Jude Barker from Nottingham. In Turnstone’s puzzle, solvers remove Fibonacci-related words such as “artichoke” from Fibonacci-numbered clues and indicate their grasp of the theme by placing ZERO at the unclued entry.October’s Genius now awaits your attention.View image in fullscreenGenius puzzle 279.Finally, thanks foryour clues for THEME. The audacity award must go to 10FootClaudicant for the preposterous “eg fish, that we may find in ship I ran haphazardly; picked out of rut in rowboat; or in the appropriate channel at last!”The runners-up are Peshwari’s casually plausible “Those people with energy, that’s what I’m talking about” and Newlaplandes purposeful “Meet up to tackle hot topic”; the winner is the timely “We ultimately must conclude other people matter”.Kludos to Falconbridge; to welcome the Cluesletter, please leave clues for NEWSLETTER below, along with any favourite clues or puzzles you have spotted.Alan Connor is the Guardian’s crossword editor. His book What Would Reacher Do? The Official Jack Reacher Puzzle Book is out now (Transworld, £16.99). To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. title: Houseplant hacks: Are windowsills too cold for plants in winter? | Houseplants | The Guardian
description: It may be flooded with light, but that window ledge is only a pane of glass away from the elements. What’s the best way to protect your plants?
Author: Gynelle Leon
Headline: It may be flooded with light, but that window ledge is only a pane of glass away from the elements. What’s the best way to protect your plants?
Content: Tropical plants such as anthuriums should be moved away from the glass overnight.Photograph: Photology1971/AlamyView image in fullscreenTropical plants such as anthuriums should be moved away from the glass overnight.Photograph: Photology1971/AlamyHouseplant hacksHouseplantsHouseplant hacks: Are windowsills too cold for plants in winter?It may be flooded with light, but that window ledge is only a pane of glass away from the elements. What’s the best way to protect your plants?Gynelle LeonTue 6 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 05.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe problemThat bright window spot you chose for your houseplants to receive maximum sunlight can become one of the coldest places in the house in winter. The glass itself can get cold, and with heavy curtains drawn, it creates a cooler box area around your window. For tropical plants like anthuriums and philodendrons, which are used to less temperature fluctuation, the cold can be fatal.The hackMove sensitive plants back from the glass overnight, then return them to their brighter position in the morning.The methodStart by using a thermometer to check how cold the windowsill actually gets. If you don’t have heavy curtains, keep leaves from touching the glass; if you do, move the plants from the windowsill into the room overnight.Houseplant hacks: can pothos help new cuttings to root?Read moreThe testDuring winter, I left some plants on a south-facing windowsill and moved others into the room. (For context, I live in a centrally heated home with double-glazed windows.) In rooms where I don’t use the heating, the windowsill temperature dropped to around 15C overnight. My more delicate tropicals were happier away from the cold windowsill, while hardier cacti were happy to stay put. I also saw less leaf damage by not letting foliage touch the cold glass.The verdictIf you have draughty glazing and tropical plants, it is worth the shuffle. Sometimes good winter care really is as simple as moving a pot.Explore more on these topicsHouseplantsHouseplant hacksGardening adviceGardensfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Country diary: On the bluest of days, the plaintive call of a pipit | Birds | The Guardian
description: Combs Moss, Derbyshire: There is plenty to be gloomy about, but today was not the day for it up on the moor
Author: Mark Cocker
Headline: Combs Moss, Derbyshire: There is plenty to be gloomy about, but today was not the day for it up on the moor
Content: A meadow pipit on Combs Moss. ‘They were once a default species on every moor.’Photograph: Mark CockerView image in fullscreenA meadow pipit on Combs Moss. ‘They were once a default species on every moor.’Photograph: Mark CockerCountry diaryBirdsCountry diary: On the bluest of days, the plaintive call of a pipitCombs Moss, Derbyshire:There is plenty to be gloomy about, but today was not the day for it up on the moorMark CockerTue 6 Oct 2026 00.30 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 04.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe morning was sunlit and the sky the sort of deepest blue dome that makes your heart sing – and all the louder for being at the time of least natural sound.Autumn is the most silent season for birds, but at least I could hear the passing meadow pipits more clearly as they came out of the blue in small numbers and crossed overhead on migration. There is something inherently melancholic about theirplaintive piping calls, which seem at one with the mood of upland treeless places.Meadow pipits also nest here, and I can recall post-breeding flocks of the past that involved clouds of birds. They were once a default species on every moor, but they have dwindled in line with a 19% national decline, which in turn accords with their global status as a near-threatened species. At least today’s passage – as the pipits abandon upland areas across England and Scotland, and head south-west on a light southerly – puts me in mind of their glory days.While I logged this specific draining away of pipits, I recalled recent media coverage ofthe proposed legislationconcerning ecocide. Building on the fabulous work of the latePolly Higgins, it is a bill intended to make the destruction of nature illegal.One can see it perhaps covering cases of massive or deliberate desecration, but isn’t the loss of meadow pipits also a kind of ecocide? As indeed is the slow haemorrhage of 3.6 billion breeding birds from the northern hemisphere. How could you intervene with legislation in what is essentially a process unfolding everywhere, every single day?At the heart of the dilemma is surely the deeper challenge that life is an endless unfolding, while anything expressed through language is necessarily fixed and categorical – in short, laws apply to events, while ecocide derives from the state of mind of an entire society.It was too blue today to be down. Along with the meadow pipits of Combs Moss, I saw ravens, peregrines, red kites, marsh harriers and buzzards, all of which species have increased in numbers in Britain this century.Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now atguardianbookshop.comExplore more on these topicsBirdsCountry diaryRural affairsAnimalsWildlifefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: NGOs say Israel bombed a journalist and appeared to attack ambulances trying to aid her – explainer | Lebanon | The Guardian
description: Beirut-based Guardian correspondent Will Christou explains how NGO investigations show Israel killed the journalist after a sustained attack by Israeli forces
Author: Boglarka Kosztolanyi
Headline: Beirut-based Guardian correspondent Will Christou explains how NGO investigations show Israel killed the journalist after a sustained attack by Israeli forces
Content: 3:33Under fireLebanonNGOs say Israel bombed a journalist and appeared to attack ambulances trying to aid her – explainerJournalistAmal Khalilwas killed in April in what colleagues described as a sustained attack by Israeli forces. Rescuers attempted to dig her out of the rubble of a building that had been targeted by Israeli forces, who had also prevented them from providing life-saving assistance.Beirut-based Guardian correspondent Will Christou explains how investigations by Human Rights Watch (HRW), Amnesty International and Legal Agenda show that Israel deliberately and directly attacked Khalil and her colleague Zeinab Faraj, with apparent knowledge that they were journalists. The organisations called for the attacks to be investigated as war crimes, while HRW called for states to halt arms sales to Israel and put targeted sanctions on Israeli officials responsible for ongoing crimes.Deliberately attacking journalists is a war crime. Israel has killed at least 15 journalists in Lebanon and 210 in Gaza since 2023, according to theUN human rights office.Israel said it 'regrets any harm caused to journalists', and that they were killed 'as part of a series of events' during which two Hezbollah military operatives were killedIsraeli strike that killed journalist in Lebanon was war crime, say rights groupsSupported byAbout this contentElena Morresi,William Christou,Kaamil Ahmed,Tom Levitt,Karif WatandBoglarka KosztolanyiTue 6 Oct 2026 10.13 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 10.22 EDTShareExplore more on these topicsLebanonUnder fireMiddle East and north AfricaIsrael

title: Kenya confirms first Ebola case as virus ‘surges’ in DR Congo province | Ebola | The Guardian
description: Health minister says 28 contacts identified after death of citizen who arrived from DRC on Saturday
Author: Rachel Savage
Headline: Health minister says 28 contacts identified after death of citizen who arrived from DRC on Saturday
Content: Volunteer health workers at an Ebola emergency response training session conducted by Médecins Sans Frontières in Ongata Rongai, Kenya, in August.Photograph: Daniel Irungu/EPAView image in fullscreenVolunteer health workers at an Ebola emergency response training session conducted by Médecins Sans Frontières in Ongata Rongai, Kenya, in August.Photograph: Daniel Irungu/EPAEbolaKenya confirms first Ebola case as virus ‘surges’ in DR Congo provinceHealth minister says 28 contacts identified after death of citizen who arrived from DRC on SaturdayRachel Savageand agenciesTue 6 Oct 2026 08.46 EDTFirst published on Tue 6 Oct 2026 04.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKenya has reported its first-ever Ebola death, the health minister announced on Tuesday, as the disease continues to spread rapidly through the north-east of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), where the outbreak was announced in May.This is the 17th outbreak of the highly infectious, often deadly disease in the DRC. As of 2 October, 4,082 people had died out of 8,463 confirmed cases in the countrysince the emergenceof the Bundibugyo strain of the Ebola virus, for which there is still no vaccine nor specific treatment.A Kenyan man who had been living in the DRC for seven years died after returning to Kenya, the Kenyan health minister Aden Duale told reporters.The man, who has not been named, had been treated in the DRC after falling ill about a month ago. He then travelled overland to the Ugandan capital, Kampala, before flying to Nairobi on 3 October.Kenya has previously never reported a case of Ebola, but neighbouring Ugandarecorded 20– almost all people who had travelled from the DRC – and two deaths, before being declared Ebola-free in August.Duale said the man was taken by a relative and a friend from Nairobi’s international airport to
