Nairobi hospital, where he was immediately isolated, suffering from “fever, chills, intense fatigue, weakness, muscle pain, painful swallowing, sore throat and bleeding under the skin at the injection sites”.He said the man was subsequently screened and confirmed positive for the virus, but “regrettably passed on last night at around 1130” in the evening (2030 GMT).Duale said officials had listed 28 contacts of the deceased, including family members and healthcare workers, but that so far “only one test has turned positive and is the one that we have just discussed”.He added that authorities were looking for another 23 passengers and four crew members who were on the same flight with the man and that “arrangements” for quarantine for those at risk had been prepared. “I wish to assure the public not to panic, as all systems are in place to mitigate the spread of the disease,” he said.Duale said a “safe and dignified burial” of the man had been planned for later in the day, in line with public health standards, but did not give further details.Kenyansreacted furiouslyto government plans earlier this year to allow the US to set up an Ebola facility at Laikipia airbase, about 125 miles from Nairobi.After starting in the DRC’s north-eastern Ituri province, the current outbreak has spread to seven provinces in the country’s north and east.DRC politician beaten to death after radio appearance about Ebola outbreakRead moreThe response to the virus in the vast central African country has been hindered by instability, including clashes between armed groups, mistrust of authorities – which has led to violence against health workers and other officials – and a lack of resources amid huge cuts in international aid.The medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières warned on Monday of an “alarming surge” in cases in eastern North Kivu province, which borders Uganda. The province now accounts for 40% of all newEbolacases, compared with 24% at the end of August, the NGO said.“It is like fighting a megafire,” said Stephanie Hoffmann, coordinator at MSF’s Ebola treatment centre in the city of Butembo. “Multiple outbreaks are developing at the same time, with varying intensity and in different locations.”The wider Butembo health zone is home to around 2 million people and only has four Ebola treatment centres, two of which only opened recently, MSF said.Hoffman said: “Because there are not enough beds available, we are sometimes forced to refer confirmed Ebola patients elsewhere, despite the significant risk this poses to the wider community. In addition, standards of care in some peripheral facilities do not always meet the requirements for Ebola treatment.”North Kivu is particularly affected by conflict, with 134 violent incidents there in the past month, according to tracking group Armed Conflict Location and Event Data, more than any other province.Agence France-Presse contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsEbolaKenyaDemocratic Republic of the CongoAfricaInfectious diseasesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Tigray rebel groups ‘forcibly recruiting boys as young as 15’ as fighting spreads | Global development | The Guardian
description: Civilians try to flee as men and boys rounded up on streets by new alliance as Ethiopia conflict erupts again
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Civilians try to flee as men and boys rounded up on streets by new alliance as Ethiopia conflict erupts again
Content: A Tigray People's Liberation Front fighter poses in Mekele, Tigray’s capital, in the 2020-22 war. The TPLF is now allied to Eritrean forces and Amhara militias it fought then.Photograph: AFPView image in fullscreenA Tigray People's Liberation Front fighter poses in Mekele, Tigray’s capital, in the 2020-22 war. The TPLF is now allied to Eritrean forces and Amhara militias it fought then.Photograph: AFPGlobal developmentTigray rebel groups ‘forcibly recruiting boys as young as 15’ as fighting spreadsCivilians try to flee as men and boys rounded up on streets by new alliance as Ethiopia conflict erupts againSupported byAbout this contentLucy KassaTue 6 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 01.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs renewed fighting has threatened a fresh humanitarian crisis in the northern region ofEthiopia, reports are emerging that a new alliance of armed groups in Tigray has been forcibly recruiting men and boys to its ranks.Renewed conflict erupted on 23 September between Ethiopia’s federal government and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), which rules the region, shattering the fragilePretoria peace agreementsigned between the two sides in November 2022.The latest fighting started after months of escalating tensions when the TPLF launched an attack in what it claims was a response to drone strikes by the federal government.Witnesses who spoke to the Guardian described a broad campaign of forced recruitment in Tigray, targeting men and boys between the ages of 15 and 65.The Eritrean Defence Forces and Amhara militias, which committed war crimes and crimes against humanity during the 2020-22 conflict, have switched allegiance and are now fighting in support of the TPLF.Along with this new alliance, testimonies of forced recruitment, child soldiers and fresh humanitarian crises are emerging out of the already battered region.Gezu*, 34, who fought with the Tigrayan forces in the 2020-22 war, lost many of his friends on the battlefield and was grateful to survive the deadly conflict. He was planning to start a family when he received a call from the TPLF authorities to join their armed group after the latest outbreak of hostilities.“I refused to join the war,” he said. “I responded to them to kill me rather than ever force me back to the horrors of the battlefield.“When they saw no one would join their army willingly, and people fleeing to the capital city, they started rounding up people from the streets. I didn’t want to leave my home town until things started getting worse.”In the past few months, Tigrayans with the means to leave have been heading for the capital, Addis Ababa, fearing that war was coming. But on 23 September, Ethiopian Airlines suspended flights to and from the Tigray region, stranding many people, after Tigrayan forces seized the airport in Mekelle, the capital of Tigray region.Solomon*, a 52-year-old man who was able to flee to Addis Ababa, said: “The main targets are those between the ages of 15 and 40. I have seen the armed group of the TPLF rounding up people as young as 15 and 16 at gunpoint from the streets and public transportation areas.“I know parents who tried to save their children by showing medical certificates. The officers don’t care whatever internal disease you have; they forcefully recruit anyone whose hands, eyes and feet work.”Ephrem, 40, is a father of three who, fearing conscription, was planning to leave the region weeks before the fresh fighting erupted. “Every time I go outside the house, my wife and the kids are anxious. The kids cry fearing that I will be rounded up from the street.“People who have money protect themselves and their children from the forced recruitment by bribing the officers. It is devastating; no one wants to join the war,” he said.View image in fullscreenMembers of the Tigray People’s Liberation Front in the regional capital, Mekelle, last month after TPLF rebels seized the city’s airport. Ethiopian forces later retook it.Photograph: AFP/GettyThe Tigray region has been under siege for the past week, when citizens’ bank accounts were abruptly frozen by the federal government, leaving people unable to withdraw their money. The banks have since reopened with a daily withdrawal limit of 2,000 birr (£9) and with long queues forming outside.Negus*, an elderly man in Mekelle,said:“We don’t know for how long the siege and the war are going to stay. A daily withdrawal limit of 2,000 birr can hardly afford to buy the skyrocketing food prices. It is impossible to leave this embattled region. There is no way for relatives outside to send medicine or cash. I am just hoping it all ends soon.”Internet and phone communications were also cut off on the orders of the TPLF until this week, leaving families desperate for news of relatives in the region.Meanwhile, the Ethiopian government has been accused of carrying out indiscriminate drone airstrikes and there have been reports of attacks by the opposition forces coming close to Addis Ababa.An estimated300,000 to 800,000 civilians diedduring the Tigray conflict, according to the British government. The Ethiopian army, Eritrean forces andAmhara nationalist “fano” militias, have previously committed grave atrocities against the Tigrayan population that amount to war crimes and crimes against humanity, according to theUN International Commission of Human Rights Experts on Ethiopia. Tigrayan forces were also accused in an Amnesty report of committingatrocities during the war.* Names have been changed to protect their identitiesExplore more on these topicsGlobal developmentEthiopiaAfricaChild soldiersInternally displaced peopleWar crimesConflict and armsnewsShareReuse this content

title: US man arrested as second suspect in Canada mass school shooting planned with ChatGPT | Canada | The Guardian
description: Justice department detained James Codey Bryant and allege he offered ‘technical advice’ to primary suspect
Author: Keely Aouga
Headline: Justice department detained James Codey Bryant and allege he offered ‘technical advice’ to primary suspect
Content: Officials announce the arrest of a 30-year-old Washington state man on a charge of conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country.Photograph: David Ryder/ReutersView image in fullscreenOfficials announce the arrest of a 30-year-old Washington state man on a charge of conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country.Photograph: David Ryder/ReutersCanadaUS man arrested as second suspect in Canada mass school shooting planned with ChatGPTJustice department detained James Codey Bryant and allege he offered ‘technical advice’ to primary suspectKeely AougaTue 6 Oct 2026 18.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA surprise suspected accomplice has been arrested in connection with a mass school shooting inCanadathat was made notorious after an 18-year-old allegedly killed six children after discussing it with the AI chatbot ChatGPT.The US Department of Justice said Tuesday it had detained James Codey Bryant, 30, a resident of western Washington state, on a charge of conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country.Bryant offered money and “technical advice” to the suspected shooter for six months leading up to the killings, the justice department alleged.Canadian police have identified the suspect in this year’s massacre of eight people – including her mother and half-brother, as well as the six children, making it the second-deadliest school shooting in the country’s history – as Jesse Van Rootselaar, who has a history of mental health problems.It had been known that Van Rootselaar had used ChatGPT to plan the attack, which took place in February. The safety team at OpenAI, the company that owns the chatbot, flagged Van Rootselaar internally after she conducted conversations with it about gun violence, but the company did not alert police. It did reportedly close Van Rootselaar’s account, but she started a second one that was not closed. Victims’ families and the province of British Columbiahave sued OpenAIand its CEO, Sam Altman, for failing to report her behaviour.It was not previously known publicly that Van Rootselaar was also talking to a human about her plans.In a joint press conference with the justice department and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) on Tuesday, authorities alleged that Bryant and Van Rootselaar met on the now-defunct messaging service Omegle about three years prior to the shooting and kept in contact.Neil Floyd, acting US attorney, and W Mike Herrington, the special agent in charge for the FBI’s Seattle bureau, said they believe Bryant sent Van Rootselaar about $100 to buy new shoes and aabout $15 for a lighter.Authorities said there is no indication so far that the two suspects ever met in person.According to an indictmentobtained by CBC, Bryant was “knowingly and wilfully” conspiring with Van Rootselaar beginning in or before August 2025.That August, Bryant told Van Rootselaar the pair should “find a way to delete” their messages, and in mid-December Bryant suggested getting a VPN to avoid detection for “posting a shooting video online”, according to the court document reviewed by CBC.Police said that on several occasions Bryant tried to talk Van Rootselaar out of committing the attack, but did not contact law enforcement.They added that after Van Rootselaar shot and killed her mother and brother in their family home, she was unable to start the car. Bryant advised her on how to turn on the engine, thereby allowing the shooter to reach the school and execute the attack, authorities said.Bryant also allegedly agreed to livestream the mass shooting, which Harrington said police were not sure Van Rootselaar would have committed had Bryant not done so.It was not clear whether the suspect was represented by a lawyer. Bryant will be prosecuted in the US as a US citizen under an investigation by the FBI, which said it will continue working closely with Canadian authorities.Explore more on these topicsCanadaGun crimeAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Outcry in Trinidad and Tobago after passing of police bill that could threaten press freedom | Trinidad and Tobago | The Guardian
description: Journalists call for urgent amendment to special operations bill, which increases police search and seizure powers
Author: Natricia Duncan
Headline: Journalists call for urgent amendment to special operations bill, which increases police search and seizure powers
Content: Officers in Port of Spain, the capital of Trinidad and Tobago.Photograph: Miami Herald/Tribune News Service/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenOfficers in Port of Spain, the capital of Trinidad and Tobago.Photograph: Miami Herald/Tribune News Service/Getty ImagesTrinidad and TobagoOutcry in Trinidad and Tobago after passing of police bill that could threaten press freedomJournalists call for urgent amendment to special operations bill, which increases police search and seizure powersNatricia DuncanCaribbean correspondentTue 6 Oct 2026 12.53 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 14.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJournalists inTrinidad and Tobagohave called for an urgent amendment to a sweeping new bill that increases police powers of search and seizure, which they argue threatens the country’s much-vaunted freedom of the press.The government says thespecial operations bill 2026, passed on 24 September, is designed to tackle alarmingly high crime and murder rates in the Caribbean nation.The country has spent more than a year in an almost perpetual state of emergency, with police empowered to bypass normal constitutional rights around arrest, detention, and search and seizure.But journalists in Trinidad and Tobago have called for explicit exemptions in the new legislation to prevent police from searching and seizing their notebooks, phones and laptops.In the past, journalists have been forced to challenge warrants empowering police to raid their homes and offices.Although the country prides itself in honouring freedom of speech, ranking 19 out of 180 countries in the 2025 Reporters Without Borders press freedom index, this year it fell13 placesto 32, and journalists say they are deeply concerned about whether they can protect whistleblowers and vulnerable sources who share information on the understanding that they will be protected.The president of theMedia Association of Trinidad and Tobago (MATT), Prior Beharry, said the organisation had called for clause 15 of the bill to be urgently amended “to explicitly shield our devices and materials … and confidential source information from standard police seizure”.Clause 15 prevents police from seizing “a tool of a lawful trade or business” or material protected by legal professional privilege. But MATT says journalism is not explicitly recognised as a protected trade, nor does the bill establish a procedure for handling confidential journalistic material discovered during searches. It wants the clause changed to “expressly name journalism as a protected lawful trade and safeguard journalists’ devices, materials and confidential sources”.Beharry said the bill’s search‑and‑seizure powers were particularly worrying in a digital era where “the tools of a journalist is … usually [a] cell phone”. Though he said journalists had not been directly threatened under recent states of emergency, he warned that other restrictions were worsening.“One of the issues we are having is the access to the government, the executive, including the prime minister, who has not had an official press conference for more than a year,” he said. “Ministries use state resources and we are not invited, but state media is invited.”The independent journalist Pearce Robinson said the combination of surveillance capability, expanded search powers – without explicit protection for journalistic practice – and declining access to government ministers created a “concrete” threat to press freedom, with a particularly significant impact on investigative reporting.“If your phone, your laptop and your notes can be searched or seized without explicit protection for journalistic material, that raises serious constitutional concerns,” he said. “Investigative journalism depends on people being able to speak confidentially.”He also raised concerns about phone tapping and surveillance, pointing to aninvestigation by the Trinidad and Tobago Guardianwhich said that “judges approved 314 warrants to intercept communications in Trinidad and Tobago between 2020 and May 2026”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe Long WaveNesrine Malik, Micha Frazer-Carroll and the team guide you through the biggest Black stories from around the worldEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“My concern is not that press freedom has disappeared,” he said. “It is that several of these pressures … are accumulating at the same time.”Pedro Cárdenas, of the press freedom and human rights organisationArticle 19, expressed concern about the clause in the new bill. “It empowers law enforcement officers to seize any vehicle, article or document deemed likely to be of substantial value. We find this clause particularly problematic because it is vague and opens up to discussion what is substantial value or not,” he said.He added that it “might directly counter” existing international human rights laws.The office of the prime minister did not respond to a request for comment.Stuart Young, Trinidad and Tobago’s former prime minister, labelled the bill “unconstitutional and very dangerous”, adding that it “breaches fundamental and entrenched constitutional rights” and was passed “without a required constitutional majority in highly questionable circumstances”.He said the government’s past use of emergency powers – including detaining citizens without charge – showed “the real likelihood of abuse” under the new legislation.Explore more on these topicsTrinidad and TobagoPress freedomNewspapers & magazinesJournalist safetyCaribbeanAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Argentina will stop Falklands exploiting offshore oilfields, foreign minister says | Falkland Islands | The Guardian
description: Pablo Quirno says move is part of Argentinian government’s strategy to peacefully assert sovereignty over the islands
Author: Daniel Boffey
Headline: Pablo Quirno says move is part of Argentinian government’s strategy to peacefully assert sovereignty over the islands
Content: Quirno condemned the British government for facilitating a significant offshore oil project in its waters.Photograph: PA Images/AlamyView image in fullscreenQuirno condemned the British government for facilitating a significant offshore oil project in its waters.Photograph: PA Images/AlamyFalkland IslandsArgentina will stop Falklands exploiting offshore oilfields, foreign minister saysPablo Quirno says move is part of Argentinian government’s strategy to peacefully assert sovereignty over the islandsDaniel BoffeyChief reporterTue 6 Oct 2026 07.40 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 11.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleArgentina’s foreign minister has told an audience that included the British ambassador that his government would stop theFalkland Islandsfrom exploiting its offshore oilfields as part of a strategy to take sovereignty.During a speech at a thinktank event in the Argentinian capital, Pablo Quirno condemned the British government for failing to open negotiations over the islands and facilitating a significant offshore oil project in its waters.Among those in the audience was David Cairns, the UK’s ambassador toArgentina. Cairns, who was photographed listening to Quirno, left the event shortly after the foreign minister returned to his seat.Quirno told the audience at the event organised by the Argentine Council for International Relations that his country’s president, Javier Milei, had a strategy for the “peaceful” assertion of Argentinian sovereignty.He said: “The British government not only refuses to enter into negotiations to resolve the sovereignty dispute, but is also taking unilateral measures regarding the exploitation of natural resources in the maritime areas that are part of the controversy.“Preventing the exploitation of our resources from consolidating the British occupation is part of a strategy to recover, through peaceful means, the full exercise of our sovereignty.”View image in fullscreenAt the UN general assembly last month, Javier Milei condemned the oil development in the North Falkland Basin as an ‘unlawful act’.Photograph: Heather Khalifa/APLast month, Milei told the UN general assembly in New York that the international organisation had failed his country as he condemned the Sea Lion project, an oil development in the North Falkland Basin, as an “unlawful act”.Argentina has accused the UK of flouting a 1976 UN resolution ordering both parties to desist from unilateral action on the islands.On 28 September, Milei gave the UK a two-week deadline stop the oil project or face arbitration and a binding decision under annex VII of the UN convention on the law of the sea (UNCLOS) at the international tribunal for the law of the sea.The UN does not officially recognise British or Argentinian sovereignty and maintains that the archipelago’s status remains a disputed matter that must be resolved through bilateral negotiations. It has repeatedly invited both governments to find a peaceful solution to the dispute that erupted into conflict in 1982 after an invasion by Argentinian forces.View image in fullscreenJavier Milei and Pablo Quirno at the UN last month. On Monday, Quirno warned third parties not to assist Falkland islanders in the exploitation of natural resources.Photograph: Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty ImagesThe 74-day war ended with the surrender of the Argentinian forces. It cost the lives of 649 Argentinian military personnel, 255 British military personnel and three Falkland islanders.The UK government has said that the islands, known as Las Malvinas in Argentina and which are home to approximately 3,600 people, will remain a British overseas territory for as long as it is the wish of those who live there. In a referendum in 2013, on a turnout of 92%, 99.8% voted to remain a British territory, withonly three votes against.In a statement issued last week, the Argentinian government rejected “the manipulation of the principle of self-determination of peoples that the United Kingdom seeks to impose upon it”.In his speech on Monday night, Quirno also warned third parties that they should not assist Falkland islanders in the exploitation of the natural resources.A new shipping link is due to be opened between Chile and the Falkland Islands by the end of the year.Quirno said: “Whoever contributes, directly or indirectly, to the illegitimate exploration or exploitation of resources that belong to all Argentinians will hardly be able to aspire to share in the benefits of our country’s growth.”Explore more on these topicsFalkland IslandsArgentinaAmericasForeign policyOilCommoditiesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Flávio’s surprise first-round election win highlights rapid rise of Brazil’s House of Bolsonaro  | Brazil | The Guardian
description: Four members of disgraced ex-president Jair Bolsonaro’s family have been elected to office, most notably his wife and son Flávio, who won the first round of voting to be Brazil’s new president
Author: Tiago Rogero
Headline: Four members of disgraced ex-president Jair Bolsonaro’s family have been elected to office, most notably his wife and son Flávio, who won the first round of voting to be Brazil’s new president
Content: Flávio Bolsonaro holds a photo of his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, as he rides a boat during a campaign rally in Angra dos Reis, Rio de Janeiro state, on 29 August.Photograph: Bruna Prado/APView image in fullscreenFlávio Bolsonaro holds a photo of his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, as he rides a boat during a campaign rally in Angra dos Reis, Rio de Janeiro state, on 29 August.Photograph: Bruna Prado/APBrazilFlávio’s surprise first-round election win highlights rapid rise of Brazil’s House of BolsonaroFour members of disgraced ex-president Jair Bolsonaro’s family have been elected to office, most notably his wife and son Flávio, who won the first round of voting to be Brazil’s new presidentTiago Rogeroin Rio de JaneiroTue 6 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 10.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe weekend’s elections in Brazil not only put Jair Bolsonaro’s eldest son, Flávio Bolsonaro, in the lead in thepresidential race, but also underscored how far the former president has come in building a political dynasty.As his far-right senator son heads into a runoff against the leftist incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, asweeping far-right victoryin congressional races also secured seats for Jair Bolsonaro’s wife, two of his sons and one of his brothers.Few in the family have spent much time working outside politics since the patriarch led the way four decades ago, but the offices they now hold have had a significant upgrade.Former first lady Michelle Bolsonaro, 44, who divided her campaign with caring for her husband as he serves a sentence under house arrest forattempting a coup, ran for public office for the first time and was elected senator.View image in fullscreenFormer first lady and senate candidate for the Liberal Party (PL), Michelle Bolsonaro, campaigning in Brasília.Photograph: Sérgio Lima/AFP/Getty ImagesBolsonaro’s second son, Carlos Bolsonaro, 43, regarded as the most radical of the siblings – he ran his father’s social media accounts and was indicted by federal police for leading a so-calledhate cabinetthat spread fake news and attacks on opponents – was also elected senator for the first time.His previous political career amounted to 25 years as a city councillor in Rio de Janeiro – starting at the age of 17, when his father put him up for a seatagainst his own mother, Rogéria Bolsonaro, who had divorced Jair. Carlos won. (Rogéria also ran last Sunday for a seat in the state legislature, still using the Bolsonaro surname, but lost.)View image in fullscreenFrom left, Jair, Michelle and Carlos Bolsonaro riding in an open car after Jair Bolsonaro’s swearing-in ceremony in 2019.Photograph: André Penner/APThe patriarch’s fourth son, Jair Renan Valle Bolsonaro, 28, who dropped his two middle names on the ballot to run simply asJair Bolsonaro, jumped from city councillor to federal congressman.Of Bolsonaro’s five children, only his 15-year-old daughter has never held political office.Even the former president’s younger brother, Renato Bolsonaro, 62, nicknamed the “brother who can’t win” after losing seven consecutive elections for lower-level offices, was elected. He went from fewer than 10,000 votes in a mayoral race two years ago to 380,000 votes for congress.During the campaign, Renato caused some friction within the family by saying that “Flávio is not Jair. He doesn’t draw crowds”. At the polls, however, Flávio ended up winning more votes than his father did in 2018 and 2022, although the result is seen by some as more of an anti-Lula vote than a strong preference for the senator.The number of Bolsonaros in office could have been even higher had “son 03”, Eduardo Bolsonaro, 42, not abandoned his seat in congress and gone into self-imposed exile in the US, where for more than a yearhe has lobbiedfor what Lula and many others see as Donald Trump’sattempts to interferein Brazil’s elections.Although Michelle is the most recent member of the family to enter politics, it is she who is often considered to be the leading figure among the Bolsonaros. In a July poll, she was named the most powerful woman in Brazilian politics, well ahead of the current first lady, Janja Lula da Silva, in addition to a supreme court justice and many members of congress.“She is a phenomenon,” said Camila Rocha, a researcher at the Brazilian Center for Analysis and Planning, who has interviewed voters and studied the Brazilian right for a decade. “Even Bolsonaro voters don’t like his sons very much, but many of them like Michelle, who is very charismatic.”View image in fullscreenEduardo and Jair Bolsonaro at press conference in Brasilia in November 2018.Photograph: Joédson Alves/EPAThe daughter of a housewife and a retired bus driver from the metropolitan region around Brasília, Michelle was working as a parliamentary secretary for another politician when, at 25, she met Bolsonaro, then a 52-year-old congressman. She is his third wife.When he took office as president in 2019, Michelle made history by becoming the first and only Brazilian first lady to deliver a speech at an inauguration. She did so in Brazilian Sign Language, which she had mastered while working as an interpreter at evangelical church services – her religiosity is seen as one of the main assets behind Bolsonaro’s close relationship with evangelical voters.Despite playing by Bolsonaro’s party’s rules, Michelle was at the centre of one of the most contentious moments of Flávio Bolsonaro’s campaign, when she said that she had been “humiliated”, “disrespected” and “mistreated” by the senator. Reports of friction between her and her stepsons are frequent. Given her popularity, Flávio had to apologise publicly – although Michelle accepted it, the two did not campaign together.Far right on the march and Lula’s failures: key drivers of Flávio Bolsonaro’s Brazil surgeRead morePolls suggested Bolsonaro supporters would have preferred the former first lady as the presidential candidate, but the patriarch opted for his eldest son, and gave her the senate mission instead. “That was the mission my husband entrusted to me, and I will represent him, God willing,” she said in August.Michelle and Bolsonaro’s sons were also widely seen as helping secure victories for other far-right candidates from Bolsonaro’s party, which will have by far the largest bloc in the next congress.“Although the family has been in politics for a long time, many voters still see the Bolsonaros as representing ‘renewal’ and an anti-system vote,” said Rocha.“So, to change everything, these voters want to throw a ‘bomb’ that blows up congress and Lula. And that bomb is the Bolsonaro family,” she added.Explore more on these topicsBrazilJair BolsonaroFlávio BolsonaroAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: New Zealand greenhouse gas levels hit record highs threatening catastrophic glacier melts | New Zealand | The Guardian
description: Government report finds the country could be hit with more frequent and intense heatwaves, as well as damaging storms and cyclones
Author: Eva Corlett
Headline: Government report finds the country could be hit with more frequent and intense heatwaves, as well as damaging storms and cyclones
Content: The view of Fox Glacier in winter in New Zealand. A government report has warned of rising temperatures and catastrophic glacial melt.Photograph: Gabor Kovacs/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe view of Fox Glacier in winter in New Zealand. A government report has warned of rising temperatures and catastrophic glacial melt.Photograph: Gabor Kovacs/AlamyNew ZealandNew Zealand greenhouse gas levels hit record highs threatening catastrophic glacier meltsGovernment report finds the country could be hit with more frequent and intense heatwaves, as well as damaging storms and cyclonesEva Corlettin WellingtonTue 6 Oct 2026 19.11 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 19.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNew Zealand could be hit with more frequent and intense heatwaves and catastrophic glacier melts in the near future, as greenhouse gas levels hit record highs, a new report about the nation’s climate has revealed.Released on Wednesday, the Our Atmosphere and Climate 2026 report shows New Zealand is experiencing mounting climate pressures, which will have wide-reaching implications for the environment, native species and communities.“The signal is just becoming clearer … there are multiple indicators that are showing increased warming and the likelihood of climate change,” Dr Alison Collins, chief science adviser for the ministry for cities, environment, regions and transport (Mcert) told the Guardian.World’s oceans absorbed record heat equal to 40 times annual global energy useRead moreNew Zealand’s annual average temperature has risen by 1.36C since records began in 1909, and seven of the 10 warmest years on record occurred in the last decade, the report said.“Whilst it sounds like a small amount … it is a significant baseline shift that’s having ramifications through nature, through our communities, and through businesses and industry,” Collins said.The report finds that as the climate heats,glaciers are shrinking. New Zealand has roughly 3000 glaciers, and they have shrunk in volume from 56 cubic kilometres in 1997 to 30 cubic kilometres in 2023, the report said.Modelling of glacier retreat shows a high risk of further decline on the horizon. Under the “low climate scenario” – which assumes low emissions – glaciers will very likely lose between 14 and 86% of their volume by 2100. Under the “high climate scenario”, that figure rises to between 69 and 100% of their volume.“We’re talking about substantial loss,” Collins said.View image in fullscreenFlooding caused by Cyclone Gabrielle in Awatoto, near the city of Napier.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesGreenhouse gases have increased to record levels in New Zealand’s atmosphere, the report shows. There was a 30% increase in carbon dioxide since monitoring began in New Zealand in 1972. Methane levels had also slightly increased in 2025 to their highest concentration ever.“That additional heat is showing up in rising temperatures, warming oceans, rising seas, shifting rainfall patterns and more intense extremes,” the report said.Among those extremes were heatwaves, which the report said were “very likely” to increase in frequency, length and intensity across the country. The number of days hitting more than 25C was also “very likely” to increase by 2050, which will expose people to heat-related health risks, including physical illness, disease and psychological distress.Marine heatwaves are also becoming more pronounced and affecting some native species, the report said. In 2025, the series revealed New Zealand’s oceans werewarming 34% faster than the global averagewhich has been linked tomass sea sponge bleaching, die-offs of southern bull kelp, large scalefish standingsandpenguin deaths.The three-yearly update from Mcert and Stats NZ collates statistics, data and research across five domains – air, atmosphere and climate, freshwater, land, and marine – to paint a picture of the state of New Zealand’s environment.The report outlined a myriad of issues that will stem from continued warming, including damaging storms and cyclones that pose a risk to life, droughts affecting species and agricultural industries, sea level rise eroding infrastructure and housing and Māori communities having reduced access to culturally significant places.Severe storms, includingCyclone Gabrielleand theAuckland floodsin 2023, have battered New Zealand in recent years, causing deaths, widespread devastation and billions of dollars in costs.New Zealand was built and developed around a relatively stable set of climate conditions and the report examines what happens when those conditions begin to change, Collins said.“Climate change is not just an environmental issue. It’s a human story. It’s an economic story.”Explore more on these topicsNew ZealandAsia PacificClimate crisisExtreme weathernewsShareReuse this content

title: From competing for food to a gold medal: the stories behind India’s Asian Games winners | World news | The Guardian
description: The country’s 85-medal haul included athletes who trained with limited money and borrowed equipment. Plus, the Mumbai performer turning everyday absurdities into comedy
Author: Niha Masih
Headline: The country’s 85-medal haul included athletes who trained with limited money and borrowed equipment. Plus, the Mumbai performer turning everyday absurdities into comedy
Content: Clockwise from top left, Sahil Jadhav, Neeru Dhanda, Aslam Inamdar (foreground), and Vithya Ramraj.Composite: Reuters/AP/Reuters/GettyView image in fullscreenClockwise from top left, Sahil Jadhav, Neeru Dhanda, Aslam Inamdar (foreground), and Vithya Ramraj.Composite: Reuters/AP/Reuters/GettyThis Is IndiaWorld newsFrom competing for food to a gold medal: the stories behind India’s Asian Games winnersThe country’s 85-medal haul included athletes who trained with limited money and borrowed equipment. Plus, the Mumbai performer turning everyday absurdities into comedyNiha MasihTue 6 Oct 2026 02.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn a country where cricket eclipses every other sport, the recently concluded Asian Games offered a much-needed reminder of India’s breadth of sporting talent. In this edition of the games, in Japan,India won 85 medals: 21 golds, 27 silver and 37 bronze medals. I admit I did not know many of the players competing, or even some of the sports they play before putting this piece together. Learning about the stories, I wonder why not.There were individual breakthroughs, records broken and history made. There were also hard-fought team victories, including theIndian women’s hockey teamgold medal after a 44-year wait.Sports broadcaster Siddharth Pandey cited an old saying in the world of sport: “You cannot be what you cannot see.” For Pandey, one of the most heartening sights was families and communities rallying around the four female players fromthe north-eastern states. (The region has endured decades of conflict and is often overlooked in the national conversation.) “We simply cannot underestimate the impact these games and medals have on future generations taking up non-cricketing sport and wanting to excel in it,” he told me.Recognition is also important. Vidya Pillai, the first Indian woman to win a snooker world championshiphas spoken abouther sport not getting the attention or respect it deserves. She felt unacknowledged following her 2023feat, despite the fact that it came aftersix unsuccessful world finalsand she beat two former world champions along the way.Behind India’s medal glory are dozens of athletes and families who have struggled financially, trained with limited facilities, and often without much institutional support.View image in fullscreenIndian athletes at the closing ceremony of the 2026 Asian Games, in Japan.Photograph: Chalinee Thirasupa/ReutersSo this week, I am sharing a sample of the many extraordinary stories from different parts of the country. These are only a fraction of the champions to emerge from the games, yet they provide a glimpse of the possibilities that can open up when a country sees and celebrates sporting talent across the spectrum.Neeru Dhanda(gold in trap shooting): Dhanda’s family in Haryana’s Jind relies on the government’s food subsidy programme and she began her sporting journey using a borrowed shotgun withtin cans as targets. Right before the games began, the 26-year-old spent a few days in a hospital recovering from an illness instead of training. But last week, asrain lashedthe shooting range in Urenocho, she became thefirst Indian womanto win an individual gold in trap shooting at Asian games. She won a second gold in mixed team trap event as well as a silver in the women’s team trap event.Vithya Ramraj(gold in 4x400m): Ramraj was one of the breakout stars of the event with a three-medal haul.NDTV reportedthat her father had to borrow money to support Ramraj and her twin sister’s athletic careers. Alongside the team gold in 4x400m, she won a silver in the mixed 4x400m relay. She also broke Indian legend PT Usha’s long-held national record in 400m hurdles which won her a bronze medal.Sahil Jadhav(gold in compound mixed archery team and men’s compound team): Not long ago, Jadhav contemplated quitting archery, frustrated by not making the progress he had hoped for. He had been forced to compete with borrowed arrows for selection trials,the New Indian Express reported, adding that his mother sold her jewellery to buy him professional compound bows. Now, the 25-year-old has two gold medals and an automatic entry to the 2028 LA Olympics.Lalremsiami Hmarzote(member of the gold-winning women’s hockey team): The women’s hockey team forward once had to travel about 100 miles from her home to reach theonly hockey academy in Mizoram. When she was growing up, her parents had no idea about what hockey and she played barefoot on dirt pitches. This month, playing her 200th international appearance, the 26-year-old struck gold. She scored the lone goal of the final against China, which Hockey India described as a “stunning reverse-stick strike”.Ancy Sojan(silver in long jump): With colourful beads glistening in her hair, Sojan flung herself 6.53 metres in long jump, to win the silver medal. Earlier this year, the 25-year-old broke thenational recordset in 2004. Her journey, from a village in Kerala’s Thrissur district to the international stage, has not been straightforward. Last year, she was diagnosed withpolycystic ovariansyndrome, forcing her to drastically change her diet and manage the medication-related weight gain she had before the tournament.Aslam Inamdar(a member of the gold-winning men’s kabaddi team): Inamdar came tokabaddi, a south Asian contact sport combining elements of tag and wrestling, from humble beginnings – he was partly drawn to it because it was affordable and didn’t require expensive equipment. Coming from a village in Maharashtra’s Ahilyanagar, he worked odd jobs – from cleaning washrooms to working in the fields – so he could spend evenings training. “It still feels like a dream to me,”Inamdar told the Indian Express. “I often think about how someone who didn’t even have food at home now holds two international medals.” The 26-year-old was instrumental in helping India win their gold-medal match against Iran.I would love to hear from you: which sportsperson from the Asian Games did you find most inspiring and why?What else we’re reading aboutView image in fullscreenA tribute to pilot Smit Machchhar, whose swift actions helped save the lives of 174 passengers on a flydubai flight to Israel.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesFlydubai incident| Indian pilot Smit Machchar is beinghailed as a herofor helping to save 174 passengers on the flydubai flight to Israel last week, after his co-pilot made an apparent effort to crash the plane. After being stabbed, Machchar opened the cockpit door, allowing passengers and crew to enter and overpower the attacker. He is recovering in a hospital in Saudi Arabia, where the plane eventually landed.Datacentres| Protests against water-guzzling datacentres erupting from the US to Australia are gathering momentum in India. South Asia correspondent Hannah Ellis-Petersen travelled to the small village of Tarluvada, in Andhra Pradesh, where the state government has been accused of fast-tracking plans for a$15bn AI datacentre for Google, allegedly to avoid stringent environmental scrutiny.Art and design|Designer Vikram Goyal, celebrated for his signature repoussé brass work, brings his installation Wings and Tales to a Georgian townhouse in London’s Mayfair from 12 to 16 October. The exhibition includes furniture designs inspired by landscapes from the Indian epic Ramayana.Guest shelfA recommendation from someone with great tasteskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is IndiaNiha Masih takes a look at the stories, ideas and news makers of modern IndiaEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenA detail of Al-Qawi Nanavati’s work.Shireen Gandhy, director of Mumbai’s pioneeringChemould Prescott Road Gallery, founded in 1963, recommends the work of artistAl-Qawi Nanavati. “[She] is a young artist from Bombay whose practice is rooted in printmaking and making her own paper. Her mother’s passing left her with a void,” says Gandhy. Nanavati created Letters to My Mother, an epistolary artwork crafted in, as Gandhy puts it, “a deeply personal language that is not known to anybody but her. Using fabrics and saris that belonged to her mother, she creates this tactile imagery for these letters. I find it very moving and like alchemy.”Count itA number worth knowingView image in fullscreenStudents at a cram school in Kota, where every year hundreds of thousands of students take the Indian Institutes of Technology exam.Photograph: Saurabh Das/AP13,626This is the number of students from disadvantaged communities who dropped out of some of India’s most prestigious institutions: central universities, Indian Institutes of Technology and Indian Institutes of Management between 2018 and 2023,according to Anubhuti Vishnoiof the Economic Times. The figure comes from an interim report by a committee set up by the supreme court last year to examine mental health and suicide prevention in higher education.Vibe checkView image in fullscreenNitesh Shetty plays know-it-all for laughs.Photograph: Instagram/@ nitesh_shetty99Nitesh Shetty’s sketchesfind absurdity in everyday life, turning familiar characters and social interactions into unexpected punchlines. This is what makes his work powerful: you’re laughing one moment and moved the next. There is a reel for every character imaginable: the person perpetually trapped in the limbo ofland disputes, the man who is strangelyknowledgeable about funerals, or the friend who hasa unique dressing sense.The 35-year-old from Mumbai didn’t plan on a career in comedy. “When you don’t know what to do, you try anything,” he told me. Now, Shetty rejects more conventional formats such as television in favour of challenging himself creatively. His advice for those who look up to him? “It’s a great time to build something. The [online] audience is ready-made for you. Be original and don’t follow trends.”Get in touchDo you have any thoughts or responses to this week’s newsletter? Is there anything you’d like us to cover in the future? Share your feedback by replying to this, or emailing us atthisisindia@theguardian.comand we may include your response in a future issue.Explore more on these topicsWorld newsThis Is IndiaIndiaSouth and central AsiaArcheryJapanAsia PacificnewslettersShareReuse this content

title: Plague epidemic risk in Russia low after death of lab technician, WHO says | Russia | The Guardian
description: World Health Organization detects no sign of further outbreak since Darya Shipilova died last week
Author: Luke Harding
Headline: World Health Organization detects no sign of further outbreak since Darya Shipilova died last week
Content: Darya Shipilova, 28, worked at a research institute in Siberia that studies dangerous pathogens including the plague.Photograph: Social MediaView image in fullscreenDarya Shipilova, 28, worked at a research institute in Siberia that studies dangerous pathogens including the plague.Photograph: Social MediaRussiaPlague epidemic risk in Russia low after death of lab technician, WHO saysWorld Health Organization detects no sign of further outbreak since Darya Shipilova died last weekLuke Hardingand agenciesTue 6 Oct 2026 19.14 EDTFirst published on Tue 6 Oct 2026 08.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe World Health Organization has said the risk of an epidemic in Russia is low after thesudden death of a lab technicianwho worked at a plague research institute in Siberia.Darya Shipilova, who was 28, died last week, two days after falling ill. Russian media reports suggested shemay have become infected after an accident at her workplace, where dangerous pathogens are kept and studied.Russian authorities have downplayed the incident andsay Shipilova died of “pneumonia of an unknown aetiology”. Strict quarantine measures have been imposed at the research centre in the city of Irkutsk and in several neighbouring hospitals.Christian Lindmeier, a WHO spokesperson, said on Tuesday that there was no sign of a wider outbreak. “All ‌of the patients’ contacts have reportedly been identified and are being monitored for ‌illness, and none to date have shown ​symptoms of illness,” he said.Russian ⁠officials were still ​investigating whether viral pneumonic plague caused Shipilova’s death but the WHO had assessed the health risk as “moderate to low” for Irkutsk, “low” for the rest of Russia and “very low” forEurope, he said.WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus urgedRussiaon Tuesday to be transparent about Shipilova’s death.“Timely, complete and transparent information sharing under the InternationalHealthRegulations is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public health risks,” he wrote on X.11:36Plague outbreak? Russian lab worker dies in Siberia - The LatestAccording to Russian media, 60 of Shipilova’s colleagues have been locked in the institute where she worked since Friday,sleeping on the floors and chairswhile tests are carried out. Similar measures have been imposed in five hospitals, with relatives forbidden to see patients.The Kremlin’s spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, urged people on Tuesday not to listen to rumours but to rely on statements from Russia’s health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor. Itsaid the situation in Irkutsk was stable, with no new infectious disease cases reported among institute employees.Washington has beenwatching developments closely. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, called on Moscow on Tuesday to release more details about the case. “I think it’s incumbent upon ⁠Russia to obviously share more information with ​the world,” he said. “We’re watching it very closely, hour ‌by hour.”The Wall Street Journal reported that the US state department had sent Russia a confidential diplomatic communication known as a demarche warning Moscow that failure to disclose details runs counter to its international health obligations.Trump said on Tuesday that he was due to speak shortly with Russian president Vladimir Putin about the technician’s death.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I have a call scheduled, yes,” Trump told reporters at the White House when asked if he had spoken to Putin on the issue yet, adding that it would happen “very soon”.Trump had said earlier that his administration was willing to offer assistance. “I hate to see them having it. We’ll help. Everybody who has that kind of a problem, we’ll always help,” he told reporters.In an apparent mirror response, Rospotrebnadzor announced that Russia was prepared to assist the US in combating its own outbreaks of infectious diseases.“The situation regarding dangerous infectious diseases remains unstable,” it said, highlighting a “significantly worsened” measles situation in three US states and a “fatal case of plague” recorded in New Mexico in June.*With Agence France-PresseExplore more on these topicsRussiaEuropeBubonic plagueWorld Health OrganizationHealthnewsShareReuse this content

title: Ikea to pilot online buyback service for secondhand furniture | Ikea | The Guardian
description: Service to be tested in Spain and Portugal this year, with a UK rollout if successful, as pre-loved markets boom
Author: Sarah Butler
Headline: Service to be tested in Spain and Portugal this year, with a UK rollout if successful, as pre-loved markets boom
Content: Ikea, which already offers an in-store buyback service, predicts pre-owned goods will grab 16% of the UK homewares market by next year.Photograph: Phil Walter/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIkea, which already offers an in-store buyback service, predicts pre-owned goods will grab 16% of the UK homewares market by next year.Photograph: Phil Walter/Getty ImagesIkeaIkea to pilot online buyback service for secondhand furnitureService to be tested in Spain and Portugal this year, with a UK rollout if successful, as pre-loved markets boomSarah ButlerTue 6 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIkeais to test an online version of its buy-back service where the retailer offers vouchers for unwanted secondhand furniture.The service will be tested in Spain and Portugal before the end of December and will be launched in the UK if it proves successful.Ikeaalready offers buy-back in stores, including in the UK. The online version will extend it to a much wider audience, with Ikea predicting pre-owned goods are likely to grab 16% of the UK homewares market by next yearThe new plan emerged as the world’s largest furniture retailer takes on Vinted and eBay with itsown secondhand online marketplacewhich launches in the UK this week.The platform, which is already online in other countries including Spain and Portugal with bestsellers including the Kallax shelving system and Malm chest of drawers, will enable shoppers signed up to the Swedish company’s membership scheme to connect directly to one another to buy and sell pre-ownedIkeaitems locally.The UK service will be free initially, but a “buyer protection fee” of about 5% of an item’s price will be introduced in time. At launch, buyers and sellers will arrange collection or delivery directly with one another through the marketplace. Ikea said it is exploring ways to make delivery easier in future.“The secondhand market is growing and growing. It is now really significant,” said Greg Lucas, sustainability manager at Ikea’s UK & Irish division. “Secondhand browsing and shopping is now mainstream.“The way people furnish their homes has changed. Whether they are moving, redecorating or looking for a particular piece, more customers are considering pre-owned furniture alongside new and are actively searching for items that can help create a home that feels personal to them.”The secondhand home products market is now worth more than £4.5bn in the UK and is growing at about 6.5% annually. Ikea said its products accounted for about 9% of furniture sold on secondhand marketplaces in the UK.Ikea said it was making the sale of used versions of its products easier by providing pre-filled product descriptions and price suggestions. The company also offers sellers 15% extra on the price of the item sold if they agree to be paid in the form of an Ikea gift card.The change is part of a revolution in retail, where shoppers of all ages are now prepared to consider secondhand items.In 2025, 63% of UK consumers bought products through reselling platforms, up from 51% in 2024.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe trend has boosted sales at Vinted, which began as a clothing resale site but is nowexpanding into homewares and electronics, as well as at Facebook Marketplace, Gumtree and smaller, more upmarket sitessuch as Vinterior.The US secondhand site eBay recentlybought UK fashion seller Depop for $1.2bn(£900m). Preloved items now make up abouta 10th of global fashion sales.There is heavy competition for the secondhand market, with the electrical goods retailers Currys and AO, for example, both selling pre-owned items.AO expanded its secondhand position after acquiring MusicMagpie, which sells refurbished electronics and secondhand video games, in 2024. It recently also bought camera specialist Jessops, which controls the Camera Jungle secondhand site.Explore more on these topicsIkeaRetail industryRecyclingWasteEthical and green livingEuropeOnline shoppingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Google told to halt work on datacentres in Finland over environmental concerns | Google | The Guardian
description: Order on two construction sites comes after Google failed to carry out environmental impact assessments
Author: Miranda Bryant
Headline: Order on two construction sites comes after Google failed to carry out environmental impact assessments
Content: A view of the Muhos site on 29 September 2026.Photograph: Alessandro Rampazzo/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA view of the Muhos site on 29 September 2026.Photograph: Alessandro Rampazzo/AFP/Getty ImagesGoogleGoogle told to halt work on datacentres in Finland over environmental concernsOrder on two construction sites comes after Google failed to carry out environmental impact assessmentsMiranda BryantNordic correspondentTue 6 Oct 2026 14.02 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 14.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGoogle has been ordered to temporarily stop work on two datacentres inFinlandafter failing to do the necessary environmental impact assessments on its construction sites.The planned datacentres in Muhos and Kajanni are part of a €13bn (£11bn) project across multiple sites in northern Finland by the technology company amid huge demand for space to house online infrastructure.It comes after it emerged that Tuike Finland Oy, the company representingGoogle, had felled 330 hectares (815 acres) of forest in Muhos without completing an environmental impact assessment (EIA).In Kajaani, the company has reportedly been logging across just under 200 hectares (494 acres) of land.The Finnish Association for Nature Conservation said the sites had been reduced to “sand”, blaming the oversights on the “overheated” market for new datacentres.On Tuesday, the Finnish Licensing and Supervision Authority (LVV) said it had issued a notice to the company to “immediately suspend” – by 23 October at the latest – “preparatory measures that significantly change the environment” of the two sites until the environmental impact assessment had been completed. Google has until next Wednesday to submit a written explanation.The EIA is ongoing and expected to be completed later this year. But Google has gone ahead with “extensive preparatory measures”, including removing trees, stripping topsoil and constructing site roads, LVV said.Tommi Muilu, the head of the environmental department at LVV, said: “In our opinion, the measures in question will change the environment and cause impacts, the identification and assessment of which are among the key objectives of the EIA procedure.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIs the environmental impact of datacentres finally cutting through?Read moreIf Google does not comply, LVV said it would consider enforcement proceedings and a fine.In response, Google said in a statement “we understand the concerns” and that it had “fallen short of our own high standards”.The company added: “We will study the LVV’s findings and follow their guidance. We acted in good faith under the Forestry Act, and ran nature surveys and put in place measures to protect high-value areas. As we continue our long-term work in the region, we are advancing our landscaping and biodiversity plans, which include tree planting across 130 hectares (321 acres) at Muhos.”Tapani Veistola, the chief operating officer at the Finnish Association for Nature Conservation, said the malpractice across two sites appeared to be a “systemic problem”. The site at Muhos, he said, was “not a forest any more. It is a sand area.”One of the reasons behind it, he said, was the enormous demand to build datacentres in Finland, which is leading companies to work as fast as possible and overwhelming small municipalities.“The main reason behind everything is the overheated market situation that makes companies speed up processes so much. Also a lack of expertise in municipalities.”Explore more on these topicsGoogleFinlandDatacentres - UKEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Greek prime minister vows to ‘ramp up’ efforts to regain Parthenon marbles | Parthenon marbles | The Guardian
description: Kyriakos Mitsotakis says his UK counterpart, Andy Burnham, has been supportive of restitution efforts in the past
Author: Helena Smith
Headline: Kyriakos Mitsotakis says his UK counterpart, Andy Burnham, has been supportive of restitution efforts in the past
Content: Sculptures from the Parthenon have been housed in the British Museum for more than 200 years.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAView image in fullscreenSculptures from the Parthenon have been housed in the British Museum for more than 200 years.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAParthenon marblesGreek prime minister vows to ‘ramp up’ efforts to regain Parthenon marblesKyriakos Mitsotakis says his UK counterpart, Andy Burnham, has been supportive of restitution efforts in the pastHelena Smithin AthensTue 6 Oct 2026 12.50 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 14.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Greek prime minister has vowed to “ramp up” his country’s claims to get back theParthenon marblesfrom the British Museum, emphasising that his UK counterpart, Andy Burnham, was hugely supportive of restitution efforts before he moved into Downing Street.Kyriakos Mitsotakis said he would raise the issue in the strongest of terms when he met Burnham, who was culture secretary in a previous Labour government.Greece returns priceless relics – and suggests UK should follow suit with Parthenon marblesRead more“Unfortunately they have not progressed,” he told a conference in Athens when asked about talks with London over a muted “hybrid” deal to repatriate the fifth-century BC marbles in return for a treasure trove of other antiquities.“We will very clearly ramp up the intensity of our claims, not just with theBritish Museum, but also with the British government. I would also like to remind the audience that the new prime minister of the UK, unequivocally, was supportive of the return of the Parthenon sculptures before he became prime minister.”View image in fullscreenKyriakos Mitsotakis said there was room for a ‘win-win’ solution.Photograph: Stelios Misinas/ReutersIt was the first time Mitsotakis had conceded that negotiations with the British Museum, under the aegis of its chair, George Osborne, had failed to make headway.Upping the ante, he suggested the fate of the artworks was also connected toBurnham’s stated desire for the UK to have closer ties with the EU. Sculpted to adorn a monumental frieze that embellished the Parthenon, the carvings have been split between Athens and London since their controversial removal at the behest of Lord Elgin, Britain’s ambassador to the Ottoman empire, more than 200 years ago.“For those of us who were saddened to see the United Kingdom leave the European family, we took great interest in the comments made by the UK PM,” said the Greek leader, citing the possibility of “a stronger relationship between the UK and Europe”.“The Parthenon sculptures will be part of this debate, this is not just an issue forGreece. It’s an issue for Europe.”The combative remarks come amid thinly disguised disdain in Athens for Burnham’s seeming about-turn on the sculptures. In private, Greek officials have voiced dismay that within days of assuming office, he should so publicly reverse his position, stating in one of his first interviews that the dispute was “an issue for the British Museum” to resolve.Long seen as an advocate of repatriation, Burnham’s support for the antiquities to be returned to Athens dates back 25 years with Greek officials seeing his elevation as the best hope yet of finally ending the row.In 2023, as mayor of Greater Manchester, he appeared to go further than ever before, posting on social media: “Send them back, no strings. And let’s use culture to change how Britain is seen around the world.”“His change in stance caused great disappointment,” said one well-placed Greek heritage expert who has legally advised successive governments on the issue. “There was more than an element of perfidious Albion about it.”View image in fullscreenParthenon sculptures at the Acropolis Museum in Athens.Photograph: Louisa Gouliamaki/ReutersThe British Museum has been home to about 160 metres of the frieze since 1816, when a bankrupt Elgin was forced to sell the marbles in what, even then, was viewed as a controversial acquisition by the British government.Mitsotakis, whose centre-right administration has sought to refocus the campaign on the idea of reunifying the masterpieces within view of the Acropolis, said on Tuesday that changing attitudes in Britain could not be dismissed.There was, he said, still room for a “win-win” solution with the imminent closure and renovation of the National Archaeological Museum in Athens allowing gems that had never been seen outside Greece to be sent to the UK in exchange for the sculptures.“[The marbles] reunification in Athens would also set a precedent for a unique cultural partnership between Greece and the UK, and in particular between Greece and the British Museum,” he said. “I will certainly make the case very forcibly to the British PM when I meet him. I think the time has come. British public opinion supports reunification of the sculptures and I do believe that now is the time to push in this direction.”Explore more on these topicsParthenon marblesBritish MuseumGreeceHeritageAndy BurnhamSculptureArtnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘This is state violence’: Paris students rage at politicians and heavy-handed policing | France | The Guardian
description: Unprecedented protests that began in low-income suburb are turning ugly, with investigations under way into police brutality
Author: Angelique Chrisafis
Headline: Unprecedented protests that began in low-income suburb are turning ugly, with investigations under way into police brutality
Content: Protests in Lyon on Tuesday.Photograph: Olivier Chassignole/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenProtests in Lyon on Tuesday.Photograph: Olivier Chassignole/AFP/Getty ImagesFrance‘This is state violence’: Paris students rage at politicians and heavy-handed policingUnprecedented protests that began in low-income suburb are turning ugly, with investigations under way into police brutalityEurope live: latest updates from protests in FranceAngelique Chrisafisin ParisTue 6 Oct 2026 12.23 EDTFirst published on Tue 6 Oct 2026 07.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBefore dawn on Tuesday outside the Lycée Sophie-Germain in centralParis, hundreds of teenagers dragged wheelie bins, metal barriers and shopping trolleys to build a barricade outside the front door of their secondary school.Climbing to the top of the piles of bins, pupils held banners calling for more funding and greater equality in French schools.But they were also protesting against French riot police, who have been accused by human rights groups of using disproportionate force against children in what is fast becoming thebiggest youth protest movement in decades.“Everyone hates the police,” chanted a group of 15- and 16-year-olds. At least 215 teenagers, 715 police officers and 85 teaching staff have been injured in clashes in recent days, according to the government.“We’re teenagers with wheelie bins, and the police have heavy weapons, it’s totally mismatched,” said Livia, 17, who was studying theatre at a lycée in northern Paris and did not want her real name published.“The police are extremely violent inFrance. This is state violence and it’s horrible seeing police allowed to target children. It’s important to remember this is institutionalised violence, it’s planned and deliberate.”View image in fullscreenA large student protest in Nantes on Tuesday.Photograph: Stéphane Mahé/ReutersTen investigations into possible police brutality are under way after injuries allegedly involving the use of police weapons, including one 15-year-old wholost his hand, another who lost his eye and a boy whose jaw and teeth were shattered, leaving him, as his mother said, barely able to eat with a straw in hospital.“The policing is catastrophic, people have been mutilated by weapons – one boy has lost an eye – it’s horrible,” said Lily, 17 (not her real name), who was studying social sciences in her final year of school and demonstrating for more funding in what she called a discriminatory education system that left poorer children behind.“My parents support me being on the barricades and at the protests. They’re worried about the policing, but they said they’d come and get me from the police station if I was arrested.”View image in fullscreenFrench riot police in Lyon on Tuesday.Photograph: Denis Balibouse/ReutersTeenagers nearby held up cardboard signs protesting against the use of teargas and the deployment of riot police.“A state that gasses high school students is a weak state,” read one banner. “Gas rapists, not children,” said another sign in reference to calls for tougher laws against sexual violence. Another banner read: “Not here to riot.”The unprecedented protest movement that began outside one school in a low-income Paris suburb has spread across the country, taking the government by surprise.Students take part in protests across FranceHundreds of high schools have been barricaded and forced to close as pupils protest against teacher shortages, crumbling buildings and overcrowded classes.The justice ministry said 5,060 people had been arrested ⁠since the protests began, 87% of them minors. More than 1,800 people had been prosecuted, ​including 1,483 minors, the ministry said, without specifying ​the crimes. It said 790 cases had been ​dismissed. The government said 24 schools had been burned or ransacked.“In more than 20 years of teaching, I’ve never seen protests this big,” said one teacher at Sophie-Germain high school who planned to join the Paris demonstration on Tuesday afternoon.“The students in central Paris have shown a great sense of solidarity with those in the Paris suburbs who face much worse conditions in their schools. There’s a feeling of solidarity and generosity between teenagers that flies in the face of the notion that we live in an era of selfishness. No one knows how long this will go on for.”View image in fullscreenA protester in Montpellier on Friday.Photograph: Horcajuelo Guillaume/EPATens of thousands of students, trade unionists and parents were expected to march in support of the protests across France on Tuesday afternoon, including in Paris, Toulouse, Nice and Bordeaux, with riot police on alert.Isabella, 16, said she had the backing of her parents, who work in film and music.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Young people have been teargassed for doing nothing but trying to express their opinion,” she said.“Everybody told us that school was the great leveller, but today that is not the case at all. A teenager in thebanlieue[suburbs] of Paris is never going to have the same opportunities as a student from the city centre. That’s why we’re here today.”Lionel, 17, who was in his final year at school and hoped to study English at university, said: “The aim isn’t to riot or smash things up, we just want to protest peacefully.”View image in fullscreenDemonstrations in Paris on Tuesday.Photograph: Tom Nicholson/ReutersTeenagers also chanted songs againstMarine Le Pen, the far-right, anti-immigration candidate in the 2027 presidential election, who is high in the polls as Emmanuel Macron steps down after a decade in office.Many teenagers were worried about the election. “We’re also protesting against the growth of the far right,” said Aislinn.Justine, 17, who had been at the barricade since before dawn, said she hoped the protest would continue and grow into a “massive” movement.“For years, there has been a mental health crisis among young people in France and anger at rundown schools and the stresses of the education system. We need the government to listen to us and make radical change.”Maya, an 18-year-old sports science student, had spent two days on a barricade at her university building in Bobigny in solidarity with school students, and joined the Paris protest march on Tuesday.She had attended high school in Drancy in Seine-Saint-Denis outside Paris, in a school she said had mould on the walls, not enough chairs for class and absent teachers who often were not replaced.“It’s only when we spoke to other students at university who came from different types of schools in the countryside or city centres that we realised our experience was so different and that there was a real injustice to the conditions we had to learn in,” she said.View image in fullscreenProtests in Lyon on Tuesday.Photograph: Denis Balibouse/ReutersJulie, 46, a self-employed parent of two high schoolchildren from Levallois, in the west of Paris, had joined her husband to accompany her sons to the Paris march.She said: “We’re here to support our children but also to protect them from what is going on with the police and the violence we’ve seen with the police these last few days. We’ve seen our own child teargassed many times in front of his school … it’s unbelievable.”Students’ names have been changed.Explore more on these topicsFranceProtestYoung peopleParisEuropefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Israeli settlers beat press photographer as soldiers watch in West Bank | West Bank | The Guardian
description: Jaafar Ashtiyeh was covering violence against olive farmers when settlers set upon him with the butts of their rifles
Author: William Christou
Headline: Jaafar Ashtiyeh was covering violence against olive farmers when settlers set upon him with the butts of their rifles
Content: Agence France-Presse photographer Jaafar Ashtiyeh being carried by Palestinian first responders to get medical attention after being beaten.Photograph: John Wessels/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAgence France-Presse photographer Jaafar Ashtiyeh being carried by Palestinian first responders to get medical attention after being beaten.Photograph: John Wessels/AFP/Getty ImagesWest BankIsraeli settlers beat press photographer as soldiers watch in West BankJaafar Ashtiyeh was covering violence against olive farmers when settlers set upon him with the butts of their riflesWilliam Christouin Jerusalem and agenciesTue 6 Oct 2026 17.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 17.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleArmed Israeli settlers beat a photographer in the presence of Israeli soldiers, hospitalising him, as he covered worsening settler violence against olive farmers in the occupiedWest Bank.Jaafar Ashtiyeh, a 58-year-old veteran photographer for Agence France-Presse inPalestine, was assaulted by a group of settlers, who beat him with the butts of their rifles, despite him being marked as press. He was assaulted in view of about a dozen armed Israeli soldiers.Ashtiyeh suffered bruises to his head and torso and was taken to hospital, according to witnesses, his family and fellow journalists.Israeli forces overwhelmed by violent settlers in ‘terrorist attack’ on Palestinian familyRead moreHis assault came amid a worsening wave of Israeli settler violence in the West Bank. Every year, settlers attack Palestinian farmers trying to harvest their olives – an economic lifeline for the beleaguered Palestinian economy – with few legal consequences.This harvest season has been particularly violent as the Israeli elections approach at the end of the month.Ashtiyeh and another AFP photographer, John Wessels, were near the northern village of Aqraba when they noticed an Israeli soldier detaining a man as local Palestinians picked olives.A quad bike suddenly raced towards the AFP journalists on top of a hill and a man on it opened live fire, with one Palestinian dropping to the ground. He was also hospitalised, with a gunshot to the foot, according to the Palestine Red Crescent Society.At least six other people then rushed towards the AFP journalists firing guns. As Ashtiyeh attempted to enter a car, which was clearly marked “Press”, two men jumped on him and beat him repeatedly with the butts of their rifles.A group of at least a dozen Israeli soldiers were about 500 metres away at the time of the attack, according to Wessels.“I could hear his screams,” said Wessels, who was also threatened at gunpoint. The assailants also took Ashtiyeh’s camera equipment.Ashtiyeh, who is Palestinian, was conscious in a hospital in Nablus. He underwent X-rays which did not detect broken bones but he will remain in hospital for round-the-clock observation, his son, Zain Jaafar, said.The man who initially fired the gun was wearing a long white shirt as well as military fatigue trousers and boots, which are commonly worn by soldiers, Wessels said.UN adds 61 firms to settlements blacklist over alleged human rights violations against PalestiniansRead moreAFP has asked the Israeli military for comment. Settlers are rarely arrested or charged for their attacks against Palestinians.“We strongly condemn yet another serious attack on journalists trying to report on events in the West Bank and demand a full investigation. It is unacceptable that journalists can be beaten and robbed by armed settlers in front of Israeli security forces who made no attempt to intervene,” said Phil Chetwynd, AFP’s global news director.The Foreign Press Association, which represents international media in Israel and the Palestinian territories, said it was “deeply alarmed”.“Israeli authorities must investigate why soldiers present in the area did not intervene in this attack against clearly identified journalists,” it said.“This attack is a blatant attempt to intimidate the press and obstruct accurate reporting from the West Bank.
