International media have a responsibility to tell all sides of the story and will not be deterred by physical assaults or threats.”Israel was the world’s leading killer of journalists in 2025, and has killed at least 225 journalists in Lebanon and Gaza, according to the UN Human Rights Office.Violence has flared in recent months in the West Bank with near-daily attacks, thefts or vandalism by Israeli settlers against Palestinians.There have also been attacks against Israelis, with a Palestinian shooting dead a settler last month.Extremist Israeli settlers have been seizing olive groves owned by Palestinians, who consider the trees a cultural symbol.About 500,000 Israeli settlers live in the West Bank – which Israel captured in 1967 – among 3 million Palestinians. Settlements in occupied territory are illegal under international law.Media rights groups say Israeli settlers have increasingly targeted journalists and that authorities have imposed growing impediments to coverage.Israeli authorities have detained 19 journalists in the West Bank, including one AFP contributor, in the three years since the 7 October, 2023 Hamas-led attack on Israel, according to Paris-based Reporters Without Borders.Agence France-Presse contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsWest BankMiddle East and north AfricaJournalist safetyPress freedomNews photographyIsraelPalestinenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘All I want to do is cry’: trauma of 7 October survivors three years after the attacks | Israel | The Guardian
description: Israeli communities shattered by Hamas massacres are torn between rebuilding their lives and remembering lost friends and relatives
Author: Emma Graham-Harrison
Headline: Israeli communities shattered by Hamas massacres are torn between rebuilding their lives and remembering lost friends and relatives
Content: Pictures on a blackened wall in Nir Oz commemorate victims of the 7 October attacks. The sign says Benjamin Netanyahu has blood on his hands.Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPictures on a blackened wall in Nir Oz commemorate victims of the 7 October attacks. The sign says Benjamin Netanyahu has blood on his hands.Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The GuardianIsrael‘All I want to do is cry’: trauma of 7 October survivors three years after the attacksIsraeli communities shattered by Hamas massacres are torn between rebuilding their lives and remembering lost friends and relativesEmma Graham-HarrisonandQuique Kierszenbaumin Nir OzTue 6 Oct 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKeith Siegel spent many of his long hours in Hamas captivity inGazaetching everything that happened after 7 October 2023 into his memory. For 484 days, he recited to himself every place he was held, the dates he was moved and every attack or humiliation he endured or witnessed.He aimed to store intelligence that could help Israeli forces free other hostages if he was released, to keep track of time as the days slid by and be able to tell his family what happened to him. Now his body is free, but he cannot loosen those memories.“I’m living a kind of dual life,” he said in an interview in Tel Aviv. “I’m here for some of the time, and I’m in Gaza some of time. It’s very challenging to convey in words what it was like.”View image in fullscreenAviva and Keith Siegel were abducted from their home in Kfar Aza in southern Israel by Hamas on 7 October 2023.Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The GuardianSiegel and his wife, Aviva, were among 251 people taken captive to Gaza on the deadliest day in Israel’s history, when Hamas militants broke across the border to launch a wave of attacks on kibbutzim, border towns, military bases and music festivals.Israel’s security forces were caught by surprise, and by the time they regained control of the area, 1,209 people had been killed, the majority of them civilians,including36 children, according torecordskept by the IsraelinewspaperHaaretz.The cemetery at Nir Oz contains two lines of fresh headstones, marking lives that all ended on that same date. A shared plot for a family of five – a mother, father and their three young children – has been made into a garden with space left for their still-living grandparents.Caretaker Shlomo Margalit, who will soon turn 89, points to the graves of three of his oldest friends, founding members of the kibbutz who came to Nir Oz from Haifa with him in the 1950s.“This is my life project, as well as my home,” Margalit said, explaining why he has come back to a place of such loss. He is waiting for a new house but, for now, staying in the former home of Gadi Moses, 82, who survived 482 days as a hostage.View image in fullscreenShlomo Margalit, a founder of Kibbutz Nir Oz, survived the Hamas attack in his safe room together with his wife, Hanna.Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The GuardianThe graves he tends are a silent testament to the brutality of the attacks and the scale of the state’s failure, which in Nir Oz was staggering, even on a day of terrible failures.A five-person volunteer defence force held Hamas at bay for at least two hours, Margalit said. When they had all been shot, the kibbutz was taken over and sacked, homes burned, families slaughtered and kidnapped.Then, before the first Israeli soldier arrived, the Hamas forces, other Palestinian gunmen and civilian looters all left. Nir Oz had beenforgotten by the armyand ripped apart without the military firing a single shot to defend it.In total, 47 people were killed and 76 taken to Gaza, includingShiri Bibas, her 10-month-old baby Kfir and four-year-old Ariel, who were killed in Gaza. The dead and hostages represented more than a quarter of the small community.View image in fullscreenShlomo Margalit tends to the graves in the Nir Oz cemetery, a silent testimony to the 7 October attacks.Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The GuardianRevisiting that terrible day, and the trauma that followed, is painful and exhausting for Margalit, but he still accepts interviews for a simple reason. “I want people to know what really happened here,” the 89-year-old said.The third anniversary of the 7 October attacks falls a few weeks before national elections, and much of the country is caught up in a furious debate about responsibility for the deadliest day in Israel’s history and the conduct of the war that followed.Survivors and bereaved relatives are avoiding the political fray, still grappling with the trauma and the struggle to rebuild something like normality.In Nir Oz, there is a terrible, almost irreconcilable struggle between re-establishing the kibbutz as a living community, and preserving physical testimony of the attack.Freed Israeli hostage Aviva Siegel on Netanyahu’s unbearable strategy and waiting for her husband to come homeRead moreThe cemetery echoes with the sound of construction and families have already moved into several rows of new houses near the kibbutz entrance.But on the other side of the compound, paths still lead between blackened ruins and memorials to the dead. Some bereaved survivors want the homes of loved ones preserved this way as permanent monuments to mark their loss.“There are families that can’t [bear to] live here, but want a memorial place to come to visit,” Margalit said. “On the other hand, can you build a new kibbutz where children grow up running around between burnt houses?”He is on the remembrance committee and, two years on, they are struggling to reach a decision on this impossible choice. “Is there right or wrong here? No,” he said. “We are dealing with that, trying to find an answer.”One compromise might be a memorial garden on the border of the kibbutz. For now, there are plaques with the stories of families attacked on that day and a memorial house to remember the dead and kidnapped.When the kibbutz took a collective decision to return and rebuild, Margalit and his wife, Hanna, knew they wanted to join. His only concession to the trauma was asking for a new home that did not face Gaza.View image in fullscreenAbout 60% of the houses in Nir Oz were destroyed on 7 October and some families have decided not to return.Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The Guardian“I’ve found myself building this place for the second time,” he said. “I know when I’m gone, I will have done something with my life. I took part in putting this spot on the map.”The Siegels, who lived in the nearby kibbutz of Kfar Aza, also among the worst hit, have decided not to return as they focus on mental and physical recovery. Aviva was 62 when she was kidnapped. Keith was 64.“What happened to me in Gaza, what happened with Keith in Gaza, it’s there all the time,” said Aviva.“I understand that it’s going to be a process of healing. There’s always things that remind me, and if I don’t remember, then he reminds me. If I’m cooking lunch or making a cup of tea and I turn around and see Keith with tears in his eyes, because he just read something or let himself feel.”The days approaching the anniversary have been particularly difficult, she said. Last year, at this time, she was still campaigning for the release of other hostages, her own emotions held at bay by the urgency of that campaign.For a time, she tried to deal with the trauma by telling herself, over and over again “I must feel lucky,” simply because she had made it back alive.Now she has allowed herself to feel again, and as 7 October approached, she has realised how raw the wounds still are. “Getting ready [for the anniversary] has been very very painful,” she said. “The last couple of weeks all I want to do is cry. Now I’m feeling things I didn’t feel before.”View image in fullscreenAviva Siegel has written a book about her ordeal, saying it was therapy and an act of celebration.Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The Guardian“When I hear my grandson say he is afraid of being kidnapped in the middle of the night, it breaks my heart.”She has written a book,Survived to Tell, about the ordeal, which she describes as therapy and an act of celebration. She wrote so her grandchildren could read about what she and Keith endured, for other hostages who couldn’t tell their own stories and to inspire a broader audience in Israel and beyond.After the exhausting campaign to get Keith and other hostages home, she said she had struggled to concentrate on the election. Keith’s political focus is an independent inquiry into 7 October to prevent other families suffering as his has.He said: “There needs to be an investigation to understand how this happened, in order to do everything possible that it won’t happen again. So many people were killed, injured, traumatised.”Benjamin Netanyahu, the prime minister, has fiercely opposed an independent state commission of inquiry. Critics say he is afraid it would expose his own failings.In the immediate aftermath of the attacks, few people inside or outside Israel expected him to stay in power long, particularly as the country’s coalition governments have rarely served out their full terms.Netanyahu had for years championed a foreign and security policy based on the premise that Hamas was “contained” in Gaza, behind unbreachable layers of fortifications.The security officials who were in command that day have all stepped down yet, three years on, Netanyahu is still in power, having deflected all demands for his resignation.Yaakov Godo, a bereaved father, interrupted Netanyahu’s speech at the official commemoration event this year to accuse him of negligence.“You did not protect my son on 7 October, you did not protect 1,200 people murdered in one day. Shame!” he shouted, before being ushered away.View image in fullscreenThe back of Yocheved Lifshitz’s home in Nir Oz. She has become a vocal critic of Benjamin Netanyahu.Photograph: The GuardianBoth US and Israeli officials have said Netanyahu rejected ceasefire deals that could have halted the war in Gaza and brought many Israeli hostages home sooner. But criticising the prime minister means venturing into a vicious political debate where age and loss offer little protection.Yocheved Lifshitz, 88, was taken hostage from Nir Oz with her husband Oded, whose magnificent cactus garden blooms at the heart of the kibbutz. He died in Gaza, she survived and since her return she has been a vocal critic of Netanyahu.A candidate for Netanyahu’s Likud party, Itzik Bonzel, said last month that he wished he could turn back the clock and return her to Hamas captivity. He later apologised, blaming grief for his son who died fighting in Gaza, but Lifshitz denounced it as a proxy attack driven by the prime minister.Netanyahu, who is battling a corruption trial and could be more vulnerable legally if he loses power, is pushing to intensify Israeli attacks on Gaza and his coalition partners are calling for ethnic cleansing and annexation ofPalestine.View image in fullscreenThe graves of Oded Lifshitz and Alex (Alexander) Dancyg, who were abducted by Hamas on 7 October.Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The GuardianThe war Israel launched in response to 7 October has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, the majority of them civilians, including about 20,000 children.Netanyahu has also waged a years-long campaign to dismantle institutions protecting democracy inside Israel’s 1967 borders. Palestinians under Israeli military rule in the occupied West Bank do not have the rights of Israeli citizens.Many Israelis opposed to this rightwing vision of perpetual war in a state with diminished institutions consider this election the most critical since Israel was founded in 1948, among them Margalit.Nir Oz, like many communities targeted by Hamas, had its roots in the leftwing Zionist movement, and although the brutality of 7 October pushed some to the right, others saw their pain as bitter proof that war alone cannot offer long-term security.“I don’t believe we can ignore the fact that Palestinians live here,” Margalit said. “We have to find a way we can live here with them and be secure. I don’t have an answer, I just know we are here to stay and they are here to stay. Maybe we need someone from the outside.”Explore more on these topicsIsraelGazaPalestineBenjamin NetanyahuMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: US, Israeli and European far-right figures to gather for conference in Israel | Far right (US) | The Guardian
description: Trump’s counter-terrorism ‘czar’, Sebastian Gorka, was scheduled to speak at conference but White House says he will no longer attend
Author: Jason Wilson
Headline: Trump’s counter-terrorism ‘czar’, Sebastian Gorka, was scheduled to speak at conference but White House says he will no longer attend
Content: Delegates at the National Conservatism Conference in Brussels, on 16 April 2024.Photograph: Simon Wohlfahrt/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDelegates at the National Conservatism Conference in Brussels, on 16 April 2024.Photograph: Simon Wohlfahrt/AFP/Getty ImagesFar right (US)US, Israeli and European far-right figures to gather for conference in IsraelTrump’s counter-terrorism ‘czar’, Sebastian Gorka, was scheduled to speak at conference but White House says he will no longer attendJason WilsonTue 6 Oct 2026 08.21 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 10.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA National Conservatism (NatCon) conference beginning today in Jerusalem advertises a talk from the Trump administration’s anti-terrorism czar alongside speeches from far-right Israeli politicians, European figures who have faced disciplinary action over alleged antisemitism, and Christian nationalist and far-right figures from the United States.The Jerusalem event is perhaps the most significant recent gathering to feature large contingents of Israeli nationalists alongside Christian nationalists and far-right European nationalists from a milieu sometimes shadowed by accusations of antisemitism.Sebastian Gorka, a senior White House official whose May anti-terrorism strategy promised to target and neutralise groups “whose ideology is anti-American, radically pro-transgender, and anarchist”, was scheduled to speak at the Jerusalem event, and his presence is still advertised on the website.But when the Guardian contacted the White House for comment on Gorka’s attendance at the conference, a spokesperson advised that he would no longer be attending due to a scheduling conflict, and that he had condemned Hamas’s 7 October attack on Israel.View image in fullscreenSebastian Gorka at the AmericaFest 2024 conference, sponsored by conservative group Turning Point in Phoenix, Arizona, on 20 December 2024.Photograph: Cheney Orr/ReutersFrom Israel, the program lists Bezalel Smotrich, the finance minister,self-declared “fascist homophobe”andinternationally sanctionedextremist, and Rabbi Shmuel Eliyahu, who in 2023calledfor an atom bomb to be dropped on Gaza and was earlierorderedto face disciplinary proceedings for racist incitement against Palestinians.The Guardian contacted both men for comment.From Europe come Hans-Georg Maaßen, who onceledGermany’s domestic intelligence agency but in 2023 faced anexpulsion attemptby his then party, the CDU, for “statements in the language of the milieu of antisemites and conspiracy ideologues”, and Austria’s Harald Vilimsky, whose far-right Freedom party has been subject to apolicy of non-engagementby Israel’s own government.According to Israeli media reports, Vilimsky has played a key role in building a rapprochement between the Freedom party – whose first two leaders after its founding in 1956 were former SS officers – and Tel Aviv. He has visited the country repeatedly and in Januaryreportedly leda European delegation to the country that was received by Benjamin Netanyahu, the Israeli prime minister, despite criticism from Austria’s own Jewish community.In a statement, Maaßen wrote: “I firmly reject the claim that I made ‘statements in the language of the milieu of antisemites and conspiracy ideologues’. This deliberately vague wording was never a concrete accusation but a politically motivated label, designed to damage my reputation and to discredit critics of the political mainstream of the time,” Vilimsky was also contacted for comment.View image in fullscreenHans-Georg Maaßen, former head of the Germany domestic intelligence service takes part in a constituency meeting of the Christian Democratic Union (CDU) district associations in Suhl, eastern Germany, on 30 April 2021.Photograph: Jens Schlueter/AFP/Getty ImagesThe American contingent includes William Wolfe, aself-describedChristian nationalist who hascalledfor “mass deportations, denaturalizations, and remigration” to preserve a white Christian majority, and Jonathan Keeperman, the publisherunmaskedby the Guardian in 2024 as the man behind the far-right internet persona “L0m3z”.Keeperman did not address questions sent to him when asked for comment. Wolfe did not respond directly to questions on his attendance at NatCon, instead sending personal insults.Dr Brendan McGeever, co-director of Birkbeck University’s Institute for the Study ofAntisemitism, said: “Many attendees at NatCon view Israel not just as an ally but as an embodiment of the exclusionary ethnostate they wish to establish. National Conservatism sees in Israel a blueprint for the realization of a white, Christian nation built on racialized exclusion, while far-right Israeli attenders at NatCon often argue that partnering with white Christian nationalists is the best way to protect Israel. It is racism that binds these forces together.”Attenders will also share a stage with high-profile conservatives including the Heritage Foundation president,Kevin Roberts, and former deputy national security adviserVictoria Coates, who is now vice-president at Heritage’s Davis Institute for National Security and Foreign Policy.The Guardian contacted Heritage with questions about their attendance at NatCon.Last October RobertsdefendedTucker Carlson after the broadcaster gave a friendly interview to the white nationalist and Holocaust denier Nick Fuentes, saying in a video that “the venomous coalition attacking him are sowing division”. He latercalledthe phrase “a terrible choice of words”, and said he and Heritage would speak out against antisemitism. In July a Heritage spokesperson said the thinktank’s “record opposing antisemitism is long, consistent and public”. In May, Heritageelectedthe Israeli nationalist and rightwing intellectual Yoram Hazony to its board.View image in fullscreenHeritage Foundation president Kevin Roberts introduces former vice-president Mike Pence during an event to promote his new book at the conservative thinktank on 19 October 2022 in Washington.Photograph: Chip Somodevilla/Getty ImagesRoberts and Wolfe are among the NatCon Jerusalem attenders singled out last month by the evangelical conservative commentator Erick Erickson, in abroadsideagainst “a group of white guys” who “have subtly inserted themselves into conservative institutions and church organizations” and who “to varying degrees … embrace white nationalism, antisemitism”.Erickson’s principal target was the shampoo tycoon and would-be “warlord” Charles Haywood, the subject of extensiveprevious reportingin the Guardian, but he also singled out Heritage fellowScott Yenor, another Jerusalem speaker. He was supported in his efforts by other NatCon attenders, including the writer Rod Dreher.The Guardian contacted Haywood and Erickson for comment.Matthew Taylor, a senior visiting fellow at the Georgetown Center for Faith and Justice and author of thenew book Defying Tyrants, said: “I think they were trying to find a way to kind of carve out a version of Christian nationalism that could synchronize with kind of European and Israeli politics … and I think what they’re discovering is kind of the impossibility of that.”He added: “[Hazony is] running up against the limits of that project because the reality is that you can’t simply stir up abstract Christian nationalism. One side of the Christian nationalist coalition is very aligned with Israel, is very Christian Zionist, the other side is leaning hard into this antisemitic impulse.”The gathering is the latest in a series of NatCon conferences held in the United States and abroad since 2019 by theEdmund Burke Foundation, whosefounderis Hazony.The conferences are high-profile gatherings of the international national conservative movement, which scholars describe as the most influential strand of ananti-liberal “New Right”.Past NatCons have featuredJD Vance,Viktor Orbán, Giorgia MeloniandNigel Farage, and have drawn accusations of racism and extremism since a speaker at the first Washington conferencearguedfor an immigration policy of “more whites and fewer nonwhites”. Conference organizer Hazony,reportedlysaid at that time that the speaker’s views were “legitimate and should be heard and debated”. In 2024 a Brussels mayororderedpolice to shut the event down before a courtoverturnedhim.The Guardian contacted Hazony for comment.Gorka islistedfor a 7 October plenary titled “The Meaning of October 7”, alongside Israel’s diaspora affairs minister, Amichai Chikli, and the former Polish president Andrzej Duda. The Guardian previouslyreportedon a video in which Gorka offered Israeli leaders advice on Hamas: “Kill every single one of them. God bless Israel. God bless Judeo-Christian civilisation.”In August 2024 Smotrichsaidof Gaza: “Nobody will let us cause 2 million civilians to die of hunger, even though it might be justified and moral, until our hostages are returned.” Britainsanctionedhim on 10 June 2025, acting with Australia, Canada, New Zealand and Norway. It held him responsible for “inciting, promoting and/or supporting” abuses, “in particular acts of aggression and violence against Palestinian individuals in the West Bank”.Rabbi Eliyahu, who for decades has served as chief rabbi of Safed, a public office in Israel, remarked of Palestinians in Gaza in a lecture his office posted to YouTube in November 2023, “Drop an atom [bomb] on them? It’s an option,” hesaid. The disciplinary hearing Israel’s high courtorderedin 2020 wasreportedlynot held until June 2024, and its outcome kept from the public.The conference’sco-sponsorsinclude the Sovereignty Movement and Regavim, the organisation Smotrichfounded. TheultranationalistIsraeli television news outlet Channel 14saysit is producing the event with Hazony’s foundation and his Herzl Institute. The conference website does not currently list the channel as a partner.The Guardian contacted Channel 14 for comment.Onepanelis titled “Immigration and Cultural Replacement”. Maaßen’s talk is billed as “Why Elites Embrace Mass Migration as a Tool of Cultural, Racial, and Political Transformation”. A fellow panelist, Nathan Pinkoski of theCenter for Renewing America, wrote the introduction to a 2025editionof The Camp of the Saints, a novel Dreher at one timecalled“racist”. Dreherappearsto have since softened that view.The Guardian contacted Pinkoski for comment.Vilimskyreportedlytold a Budapest conference in April 2024: “We do not want Mohammed to become the most common name in our countries.” He is listed for a NatCon plenary on 7 October.Gideon Sa’ar, the foreign minister, wholast monthwelcomed a speech by the FPÖ leader, Herbert Kickl, at a Strasbourg event Vilimsky organised with Likud, as making possible “a substantive, open and sincere dialogue” despite the ongoing disengagement, is listed for the conference dinner on 6 October.Wolfetolda Texas audience in February: “My boys all look like me. And I want my children to grow up in a country where they’re not minorities.” He hascalledErickson’s essay “a call for the assassination of a group of conservative Christians”. His conferencebiosays he served at the state department and the Pentagon in the first Trump administration.As previously reported in the Guardian Haywood’sprivate foundationgave the Edmund Burke Foundation, which organizes the NatCon conferences, $25,000 for “general operations” in the year to June 2023, itstax filingshows.Hazony’s former communications director was among the Jewish conservatives whocriticisedhim in January, after heblamedan “antisemitism-industrial complex” for failing to make the case against Tucker Carlson. He has sincerefusedCarlson a speaking slot in Jerusalem, and on 28 Septembercalledthe broadcaster’s show “the leading clearinghouse for antisemitism on the political Right in America”.Taylor, the religion scholar, said: “[Hazony is] still trying to play an older game of drawing boundary lines and saying, oh, there is an antisemitic far right that is the fringe that we have to cut off … But Tucker Carlson is not [fringe]. Tucker Carlson is about as mainstream today in rightwing politics as you can get.”The Guardian contacted the Carlson Network’s press office for comment.McGeever, the antisemitism scholar, wrote: “Yoram Hazony may express bewilderment about this surge of antisemitism, but it is baked into the very political alliances he has forged. His allies have repeatedly promoted ideas about ‘globalist elites’ and ‘secret cabals’ which utilize the same structural logic of antisemitic conspiracy theories.”The conferencerunsfrom 6 to 8 October at Jerusalem’s International Convention Center.Explore more on these topicsFar right (US)Trump administrationUS politicsThe far rightAntisemitismIsraelChristianitynewsShareReuse this content

title: Badenoch denies plan for ‘British Iron Dome’ – after Tories use phrase in press release | Kemi Badenoch | The Guardian
description: Leader also says party is ‘not out of the woods’ and she would rather have another election than form coalition with Reform
Author: Jessica Elgot
Headline: Leader also says party is ‘not out of the woods’ and she would rather have another election than form coalition with Reform
Content: Kemi Badenoch is due to give a speech to close the Conservative party conference on Wednesday.Photograph: Paul Ellis/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenKemi Badenoch is due to give a speech to close the Conservative party conference on Wednesday.Photograph: Paul Ellis/AFP/Getty ImagesKemi BadenochBadenoch denies plan for ‘British Iron Dome’ – after Tories use phrase in press releaseLeader also says party is ‘not out of the woods’ and she would rather have another election than form coalition with ReformJessica ElgotDeputy political editorTue 6 Oct 2026 17.15 EDTFirst published on Tue 6 Oct 2026 04.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKemi Badenoch has denied she compared a new air defence system proposed by the Conservative party to Israel’s Iron Dome, despite using the term in her press release and a newspaper article.The Tory leader said the party’sproposed “Britannia Shield”would not be comparable to the missile defence system in Israel, which is primarily designed to counter short-range attacks.The party has proposed allotting £1bn a year towards building the system, though the former army general Richard Barrons told Times Radio the cost of a system similar to Israel’s would be upwards of £100bn.Don’t mention the Iron Dome: comedy genius Kemi on warpath at Tory conference | John CraceRead moreIn a round of interviews at the Conservative party conference in Birmingham, Badenoch also admitted her party was “not out of the woods” despite what appeared to be the most unified and optimistic gathering in years. The Tories are still polling below their 2024 election defeat.“We are feeling chipper because we are going back to first principles,” she told the BBC. “We’re not out of the woods yet.”She added that “people at conference aren’t happy because we’re about to win an election. We’re happy because we know who we are.”She also said she would rather have another general election than do a deal with Reform UK to form a government, as senior party figures attacked their rightwing rivals with a ferocity that appeared to make the chances of any pact more remote.In her own conference speech on Wednesday, Badenoch is expected to announce plans to cut – but not abolish – inheritance tax, which is levied at 40% on all estates with property worth more than £500,000.She is expected to say the country is “running out of money”, adding: “Almost everything else flows from this. Our national debt currently stands at nearly £3tn and we are adding more than £100bn every year.“Last year, four in every five pounds borrowed by the government was spent on debt interest alone. That’s like taking out a second mortgage just to pay the interest on your first mortgage.“This is crazy. Unless we start creating more value, unless we start growing our economy, something is going to break.”The Tories have promised to cut employers’ national insurance from 15% to 7.5% for people aged 21-24 in an attempt to drive down the youth unemployment rate. Badenoch is expected to say she will fund the £2.3bn scheme through welfare cuts.However, she admitted it could be “difficult” to reverse Labour’s planned changes to the pensions triple lock once they had been brought in, as it emerged her party could head into the next election without a social care plan.In several interviews, the Tory leader was forced to clarify her party’s “iron dome” defence policy, as she tried to distance herself from using the term. She told Times Radio it was a “semantic argument” and that the new system would protect Britain from increasing threats.She told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme that the description had come from newspapers – though the Conservative party press release described the system as “in essence a British Iron Dome”.In a piece byBadenoch in the Sun, which illustrated its front page with an image of Israel’s Iron Dome, she wrote: “Modelled on Israel’s ‘Iron Dome’, Britannia Shield will invest £10bn over 10 years in the radar, missiles and technology needed to detect these threats and stop them before they reach British soil.”But Badenoch told Today that was not the aim. “We are not building the Iron Dome. We are doing what other European countries are doing: Greece, Benelux countries – Belgium and the Netherlands – and Germany. We are designing something specific for the kind of threat that we face here.”The shadow defence secretary, James Cartlidge, likened the phrase “iron dome” to the vacuum cleaner brand name Hoover when asked why Badenoch had denied theConservativeswere proposing an Iron Dome-style system.View image in fullscreenPart of Israel’s Iron Dome air defence system near Jerusalem.Photograph: Menahem Kahana/AFP/Getty ImagesAsked on Times Radio if the aim was to be able to intercept any attack over the entire country, Badenoch said: “It should, but it needs to protect critical national infrastructure … Critical national infrastructure protects the entire country. If we lose even one thing, the entire country is in a real problem, and that’s what we mean.”Tories unite behind Badenoch, but road to recovery remains longRead moreOn Today, asked whether she was ready for an election, Badenoch said she believed polls would improve but admitted the party was still unpopular because of the previous government’s record, even though her personal popularity had improved.“I think people still associate the Conservative party with the things they didn’t like about the previous government,” she said. “I need to work hard to change that … these things take time. I am the leader and I need to show that this party is different from the party that the people said no to two years ago.“I am confident that when that election is called, people will see that the Conservative party has the best offer. We have a strong team, we have a plan and we’re all about common sense.”A Labour source said: “It’s no surprise Kemi Badenoch wants to forget how the Tories hollowed out our armed forces.“But hoping her half-baked defence promise based on fantasy numbers will be forgotten just hours after it was made shows how unserious she is about our country’s security. The Tories can never be given responsibility for keeping Britain safe again.”Explore more on these topicsKemi BadenochConservativesConservative conference 2026Defence policynewsShareReuse this content

title: Chancellor plans major intervention to help poorer UK households with rising energy bills | Energy bills | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Officials working on further radical changes that would change how much energy companies could charge customers
Author: Kiran Stacey
Headline: Exclusive: Officials working on further radical changes that would change how much energy companies could charge customers
Content: The bulk of the £1bn the chancellor is planning to spend helping energy consumers will likely to go towards increasing the discount given to households on certain benefits.Photograph: Danny Lawson/PAView image in fullscreenThe bulk of the £1bn the chancellor is planning to spend helping energy consumers will likely to go towards increasing the discount given to households on certain benefits.Photograph: Danny Lawson/PAEnergy billsChancellor plans major intervention to help poorer UK households with rising energy billsExclusive: Officials working on further radical changes that would change how much energy companies could charge customersKiran StaceyandJessica ElgotTue 6 Oct 2026 15.27 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJohn Healey is planning a major intervention to cut energy bills for poorer households in this month’s budget, after ministers became alarmed atforecasts that showbills rising by hundreds of pounds in January.The chancellor is working on plans to spend more than £1bn to help energy consumers, the bulk of which is likely to go towards increasing the discount given to households on certain benefits.Sources say final decisions have not been made, but Healey is set to rebuff a call from the energy secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh to spend billions more on removing levies from bills altogether.Energy officials are working up more radical changes to bills, however, which could be implemented after the budget and would change how much companies could charge customers, rather than subsidising their bills.If approved, the energy discount will form a major plank of the budget, which government sources say will be low-key but focused on reducing voters’ cost of living.Labour figures uneasy about Healey’s ‘underpowered’ approach to budgetRead moreThe chancellor is facing a cash crunch as he looks for money to fund an additional £4.7bn in defence spending and rebuild his fiscal buffer, which has been eroded by higher borrowing costs.He is likely to raise taxes to pay for the additional spending, and is rumoured to be looking at higher bank taxes in particular.Government sources had previously insisted the VAT cut to electricity bills which Andy Burnham announced soon after becoming prime minister would be the last support to be offered this year.View image in fullscreenChancellor John Healey has been considering submissions from the energy department for how to ease the pressures on households in the coming months.Photograph: Ian Davidson/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.But they have become increasingly concerned byforecasts showingthat the Iran war will push the energy price cap up by as much as £442 in January – entirely eroding the impact of the VAT cut.As a result Healey has been considering submissions from the energy department on how to ease the pressures on households in the coming months.The most likely solution is understood to be increasing the warm homes discount – a £150 discount to energy bills offered to households on certain benefits.Healey is understood to be considering increasing this by a further £100, which would be funded by taxpayers, rather than bill-payers as the existing discount is.Fahnbulleh, meanwhile, has been pushing for more sweeping action to reduce bills for all consumers by as much as £120 by removing all levies.Under the energy secretary’s proposals, the levies, which fund renewable energy and efficiency schemes, would be paid for through taxation instead.Shetold the Guardianlast week: “If we want a system that is resilient, if we want a system that can cope, if we want a system that ultimately can deliver the diversity of energy that we want, what is the fairest way in which we pay for it?“That is both across the exchequer versus our bill-payers, and then within our bill-payers. So we have to ask that question. Every other country is asking that question, and ultimately we’ve got to come to a fair deal.”Removing levies from bills would reduce inflation, but would cost as much as £3.2bn and would be difficult for the government to unwind should energy costs come down in the future.Officials in the energy department are working on more radical proposals for after the budget, meanwhile, including proposals to reduce tariffs for poorer households or those that use less energy.Burnham told the Labour conference last week: “British businesses and bill-payers pay some of the highest energy costs in Europe. Within 10 years, I want those costs to be in line with our neighbours.“This means reforming a broken energy market so it better serves the public interest.”A so-called “social tariff” would force energy companies to charge poorer households less for each unit of electricity they consume than richer ones.Creating such a scheme, however, would involve a large amount of data collection from tax authorities, the Treasury and energy companies – an exercise likely to take far longer than the next few weeks.An alternative plan, known as a “rising block tariff”, would also vary the tariffs that energy companies can charge, but by consumption levels rather than income.The idea,which was proposedby the New Economics Foundation (NEF) thinktank when Fahnbulleh ran it, would charge consumers less for a set amount of “essential” use and more once their consumption crossed that level.Healey urged to offer energy support in budget as bills rise 4%Read moreAlex Chapman, head of economic and environmental policy at NEF, said: “A serious price spike is coming, and without action, bills will exceed the peak of the last crisis. The government must use the budget to put in place both targeted support for the most vulnerable and, critically, a safety net for all.”He added: “Repeated crises have exposed the flaws in our privatised energy system – these can only be fixed by fundamental reform. This means capturing the benefits of cheap renewables and offering every household a ‘block’ of essential energy at a truly protected and affordable price.”Alfie Stirling, economist and director of policy at the Joseph Rowntree Foundation, said: “Energy support for this winter needs to tick three boxes. It needs to support the majority of households; within this, it needs to target the most support towards those in greatest need; and – as far as possible – it needs to actually lower the price, thereby bringing down inflation.“The UK does not yet have the right toolkit to respond effectively to energy price shocks – building better tools is now a critical priority for our future security and living standards.”A spokesperson for the Treasury said: “As has always been the case, decisions on tax are a matter for the chancellor to set out at fiscal events, rather than routinely commenting on rumour, speculation or proposals.”Explore more on these topicsEnergy billsEnergy industryConsumer affairsHousehold billsUK cost of living crisisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Senior academics set out key questions Cambridge must answer over Jason Arday’s death | University of Cambridge | The Guardian
description: Letter from more than 40 signatories says university has backed away from promised thorough review of events before death
Author: Richard Adams
Headline: Letter from more than 40 signatories says university has backed away from promised thorough review of events before death
Content: Academics say it is not clear how Cambridge’s proposed review will answer difficult questions about its involvement in events leading up to Arday’s death.Photograph: Chris Radburn/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAcademics say it is not clear how Cambridge’s proposed review will answer difficult questions about its involvement in events leading up to Arday’s death.Photograph: Chris Radburn/AFP/Getty ImagesUniversity of CambridgeSenior academics set out key questions Cambridge must answer over Jason Arday’s deathLetter from more than 40 signatories says university has backed away from promised thorough review of events before deathRichard AdamsEducation editorTue 6 Oct 2026 14.44 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 17.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSenior Cambridge academics have criticised the university’s plans to investigate Prof Jason Arday’s death as inadequate, and said those responsible for “serious failures of leadership” should face consequences.In a letter to Chris Smith, Cambridge’s chancellor, the academics said “it is not yet clear” how the proposed review will answer difficult questions about the university’s involvement in the events leading up to Arday’s death, including its handling of the criticism Arday suffered after his appointment as professor of sociology of education in 2023.Ardaydied at his home in Londonon 14 August, nine days after he resigned amid allegations of plagiarism and inconsistencies in statements about his career.Cambridge University asks former chief crown prosecutor to open Arday reviewRead moreAninquest will be heldto determine the cause of death.Arday’s family said he was subjected to a campaign of sustained abuse for more than three years.Now, a letter signed by more than 40 professors, associate professors and fellows raises concern that Cambridge has backed away from initial promises by Deborah Prentice, the university’s vice-chancellor, to carry out a “thorough and transparent” examination of the circumstances that led to Arday’s appointment and treatment.Rather than reviewing the “lessons learned”, the group wants the investigation to pinpoint the crucial advice given and decisions made during Arday’s hiring and subsequent career.“The investigation must establish who authorised and directed the university’s public promotion of Professor Arday; what assessment was made of the risks that accompanied it; who authorised any legal or other communications with journalists investigating the story; what the university knew as racist and ableist abuse and media hounding escalated; and how responsibility for Professor Arday’s protection was allocated and exercised across the university,” the letter says.View image in fullscreenJason Arday’s family have said he was subjected to a campaign of sustained abuse for more than three years.Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianThe signatories included Cahir O’Kane, a professor of genetics; Caroline Bassett, a professor of digital humanities; Clair Wills, the King Edward VII professor of English literature; and Clément Mouhot, a professor of mathematical sciences.Cambridge last monthannounced a two-part review, with part one to beled by Nazir Afzal, a former chief crown prosecutor for north-west England, focusing on the support given to Arday immediately before his death.The university has not yet named a chair for part two of the review, which it said would be “a broader review of institutional processes and practice” and only consider “the wider context” of Arday’s period at Cambridge, including general appraisals of recruitment and support available to academics facing media scrutiny.Jason Arday accuser given three-month teaching ban but can continue researchRead moreThe group behind the letter, which was also sent to Cambridge’s governing council, said the “scope and investigative character” of the second part of the review would be crucial in settling the decisions, structures and processes involved.They wrote: “To this end, it is vital that the university establishes a clear chain of responsibility for the institutional decisions made in the period following Professor Arday’s appointment, through the events leading to his death and the university’s subsequent responses.“The university should state clearly how responsibility will be acted upon if the review establishes serious failures of leadership or responsibility … Serious findings must have consequences for the individuals and offices responsible.“At the same time, individual accountability cannot substitute for the institutional changes required where failures arose from structures of decision-making, scrutiny or governance.”TheUniversity of Cambridgewas approached for its response to the letter.Cambridgepublicised Arday’s appointmentat the age of 37 as the youngest black person ever appointed to a professorship at the university, saying he would “inspire more people from under-represented backgrounds into higher education, building on the university’s many initiatives in this area”.Arday denied the accusations of plagiarism but on 5 August Cambridge said it would open an investigation into his academic qualifications. Arday resigned hours later.Explore more on these topicsUniversity of CambridgeJason ArdayUniversity administrationUniversitiesHigher educationAcademicsUniversity leadershipnewsShareReuse this content

title: Labour figures rule out working with Greens after ‘Zionism is racism’ vote | Labour | The Guardian
description: Minister says they could not see parties cooperating, while official says coalition should be formally ruled out
Author: Aletha Adu
Headline: Minister says they could not see parties cooperating, while official says coalition should be formally ruled out
Content: Green party leader Zack Polanski stopped short of endorsing or criticising the motion.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAView image in fullscreenGreen party leader Zack Polanski stopped short of endorsing or criticising the motion.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPALabourLabour figures rule out working with Greens after ‘Zionism is racism’ voteMinister says they could not see parties cooperating, while official says coalition should be formally ruled outAletha AduandPeter WalkerTue 6 Oct 2026 14.26 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSenior Labour party figures said it was very unlikely their party would cooperate with the Greens in the future after theyadopted a policytreating Zionism as a form of racism.OneLabourminister said they could not foresee how the two parties could work together, while a government official said Labour should formally rule out a future coalition or other arrangement.There is also pressure within theLiberal Democratsfor them to end existing arrangements with Zack Polanski’s party, with some senior Lib Dems calling on the party to end its coalition with the Greens in Southwark, south London.Green members voted at the party’s conference on Sunday to adopt a binding policy that says Zionism should be treated by the party as racism, and which calls for a single Palestinian state in place of Israel.After the vote, Bridget Phillipson, the Labour chair, called the move “shameful”, saying it highlighted how vital it had been for her party to tackle antisemitismunder the leadershipof Jeremy Corbyn.While Phillipson’s statement was backed by her fellow ministers, there was debate as to whether Labour should go further and formally rule out any ties with the Greens, for example if a future general election delivered a hung parliament.A source linked to the Jewish labour movement said Labour should “absolutely” rule out governing with the Greens, arguing the policy raised serious questions about whether its treatment of Jewish members could breach equality law.It follows months of speculation of possible cooperation between the parties. Polanski said earlier this year that the Greens could consider an electoral pact with Labour under Andy Burnham or Angela Rayner, while ruling out one under the former prime minister Keir Starmer.Labour views the Zionism motion, and the criticism that has followed, as a means to simplify its political argument against the Greens at a time when Polanski’s party has increasingly sought to attract disillusioned Labour voters on the party’s left.A big test of this will come on Thursday, with voting in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, where Polanski is seeking to win Starmer’s former seat from Labour.The Greens have poured huge resources into the contest, with Polanski telling the Guardian that it is “really on a knife-edge”. Despite the Greens’ campaigning efforts, helped by their massively increased membership, Labour is considered the favourite to win.The Lib Dems and Greens already govern together in Southwark after May’s local elections, with the Greens as the senior partner.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFollowing the Zionism motion, both Southwark partiesreleased a“joint administration statement against antisemitism”. Without mentioning the new Green policy, it said they would “continue to work with Jewish community organisations to make sure they know they have a place in Southwark”.It brought a scathing response from some senior Lib Dems. Tagging Victor Chamberlain, the Lib Dem deputy leader of Southwark, Sarah Ludford, a peer and former MEP for the party,wrote on Xthat she did not understand “how you think this greenwash is an adequate response to the Greens’ antisemitic ‘Zionism is racism’ motion, from which I believe you should entirely distance yourselves”.Another Lib Dem peer, Lynne Featherstone, who was formerly an MP, replied to a post by Chamberlainto say: “I would ditch them. Grow a pair!”The policy was adopted at theGreen partyconference in Brighton on Sunday by 1,022 votes to 813, despite being opposed by four of the party’s five MPs.Polanski, who left the Green conference early on Friday to campaign, stopped short of endorsing or criticising the motion. In a statement on Monday night after the European Greens and German Greens distanced themselves from the policy, Polanski said antisemitism and criticism of the Israeli state “are and must always be completely distinct”. Polanski said he remained proud of the party’s stance on Palestinian rights.Explore more on these topicsLabourZack PolanskiGreen partyLiberal DemocratsAntisemitismJudaismnewsShareReuse this content

title: LA and San Diego residents ‘horrified’ by Trump suggesting Iran bomb them | Los Angeles | The Guardian
description: As Angelenos bemoan ‘sad situation’, those in San Diego say remark a ‘disservice’ to town with multiple naval bases
Author: Roque Planas
Headline: As Angelenos bemoan ‘sad situation’, those in San Diego say remark a ‘disservice’ to town with multiple naval bases
Content: Aerial photograph of the Jefferson Park neighborhood in Los Angeles, California.Photograph: halbergman/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAerial photograph of the Jefferson Park neighborhood in Los Angeles, California.Photograph: halbergman/Getty ImagesLos AngelesLA and San Diego residents ‘horrified’ by Trump suggesting Iran bomb themAs Angelenos bemoan ‘sad situation’, those in San Diego say remark a ‘disservice’ to town with multiple naval basesRoque PlanasandSam Levinin Los AngelesTue 6 Oct 2026 19.45 EDTFirst published on Tue 6 Oct 2026 18.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump’s extraordinary implication that Iran could “take out” Los Angeles and San Diego have sparked condemnation across the political spectrum. As residents of the two major west coast cities awoke on Tuesday toanother sweltering dayin a record-breaking heatwave, the president’s comments sent blood boiling even higher.Jessica, a 28-year-oldLos Angeleshair stylist, was scrolling through social media early on Tuesday morning and was shocked to see that Trump had just suggested Iran should decimate her home town.Trump suggests Iran could ‘take out’ Los Angeles or San DiegoRead moreFor Jessica, who declined to be identified by her full name because she fears for the safety of her Mexican-born parents, the comments marked a new low for a president who had already spent years attacking immigrant families like hers.“I was just thinking what the fuck is wrong with him?” she said while waiting for a Waymo outside grocery store in LA’s Koreatown neighborhood. “He hates us. He hates LA. He hates any Democratic state ... It’s just a really sad situation.”In southernCalifornia, Trump’s unprecedented musing before a cheering crowd at a Nebraska rally on Monday night – that perhaps a foreign power should decimate two of the country’s best-known cities – has been met with reactions ranging from deep hostility to dismissive incredulity. Gavin Newsom, the state’s governor, called the remarks “dangerous – if not treasonous – putting a target on two of our biggest cities and one of America’s largest naval hubs”.Perhaps most of all, California residents see it as a sign of the president’s fixation on tearing down west coast progressivism and diversity, most visibly through the deployment of national guard troops in Los Angelesduring a series of brutal ICE raidsin 2025.During a bustling lunch service at Grand Central Market, a food hall in downtown LA, tourists and residents milled between taco stands and dumpling stalls. Many had yet to hear of the president’s threats, until asked by a reporter. One of those who had was Jens Midthun, a downtown resident who often stops at the market for coffee.View image in fullscreenTrump suggested Iran could ‘take out’ LA and San Diego at a rally.Photograph: Harry How/Getty Images“Trump has tried to paint Los Angeles as a dystopia despite it being a wonderful place,” said Midthun, sipping an iced coffee under a shaded outdoor table as the temperature approached the triple digits. (Midthun serves as the president of the downtown LA neighborhood council, but was speaking only on behalf of himself.)“It reminded me that the president is obsessed with us – obsessed with California, obsessed with Los Angeles,” Midthun said. “We try not to think about him and yet, here he is with Los Angeles’s name right there in his mouth.”Trump’s remarks have sparked a particularly strong reaction in San Diego, which is home to roughly a quarter-million veterans and has one of thelargestconcentrations of military personnel in the US.“His statement was so irrational, it’s hard to explain exactly what he was saying, but it sounded like he was willing to give us up,” said Gil Field, communications director for San Diego Veterans for Peace, a group that opposes the war. “It’s horrible and we’re horrified.”The military supports nearly 357,000 local jobs in the region, representing $61.3bn of San Diego county’s economy, according to areportreleased last year. Defense spending accounts for 22% of San Diego’s gross regional product and the area is home to multiple naval bases and Marine Corps stations, withone out of fouractive-duty marines based in San Diego.“This is a military town, so you’ve got bipartisan objections to his comments,” said Field, who noted that there were always concerns thatSan Diegocould be targeted in war due to the heavy military presence. “So for him to say this about San Diego is particularly galling. He did San Diego a disservice.”Jim Desmond, a Republican naval veteran running for a congressional seat in San Diego, also offered a pointed rebuke.View image in fullscreenNavy ships are lined at the Naval Base San Diego.Photograph: The San Diego Union-Tribune/Getty Images“I served to protect Americans, not write off American cities as an acceptable price of war. Our job is to keep Americans safe, stand up to our enemies, and make sure a threat like that never becomes reality,” Desmondsaid on X. “No American city is expendable, and no American family should ever be treated as collateral damage.”Back in Los Angeles, far from the negative fantasies that Trump spins in his speeches, Midthun sees an economic powerhouse and vibrant cultural center sandwiched between the beach and the mountains, and enriched by some of the largest diaspora communities from across the world – South Korea, Mexico, El Salvador, Armenia and even Iran.“The president keeps talking about us, and talking about us,” Midthun said. “He’s got a lot of issues to solve. He should work on those issues instead of obsessing over the beautiful, great people of Los Angeles.”Explore more on these topicsLos AngelesDonald TrumpSan DiegoCaliforniaWest CoastUS-Israel war on IrannewsShareReuse this content

title: Disney accuses Trump officials of ‘blatant violations’ of constitution amid FCC battle | ABC | The Guardian
description: Lawyers tell judge ABC being unfairly targeted as US regulator seeks review of network’s local TV station licenses
Author: Jeremy Barr
Headline: Lawyers tell judge ABC being unfairly targeted as US regulator seeks review of network’s local TV station licenses
Content: Lawyers in court said ABC faces a ‘chilling effect’.Photograph: Mario Anzuoni/ReutersView image in fullscreenLawyers in court said ABC faces a ‘chilling effect’.Photograph: Mario Anzuoni/ReutersABCDisney accuses Trump officials of ‘blatant violations’ of constitution amid FCC battleLawyers tell judge ABC being unfairly targeted as US regulator seeks review of network’s local TV station licensesJeremy Barrin WashingtonTue 6 Oct 2026 16.12 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 16.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLawyers for Disney accused theTrump administrationof “blatant violations of the US constitution” and censorship on Tuesday in the first court hearing over the Federal Communications Commission’s early review of the media giant’s eight local television station licenses.District judge Loren AliKhan seemed unswayed by government arguments that the order to force Disney’sABCto apply years early to renew local television station licenses was tied to an investigation into parent company Disney’s hiring practices.ABC, Disney and its station groupfiled suit against the FCC in August, seeking to block the US media regulator from taking any further steps to punish or pressure the network in connection to the order.In its lawsuit, ABC argued that the FCC’s actions – taken at the behest of the Donald Trump-appointed chair, Brendan Carr – were actually intended to chill the network’s speech, which the president and Carr have argued is tilted against the administration.In legal filings and during Tuesday’s hearing, the network cited past threats by the president and the FCC chairman that jeopardized the licenses of television networks, including ABC on several occasions, for editorial purposes.“These are blatant violations of the US constitution,” the prominent trial lawyer Beth Wilkinson, arguing on behalf of ABC, told the judge during the approximately two-hour hearing.She said ABC faced a “chilling effect” that has affected – and will continue to impact – its editorial decision-making, as the network steers clear of political bookings and any other programming decisions that could spark further ire from the Trump administration and Carr. “That chilling effect has been happening and will happen every day,” she said, causing “irreparable harm” to the network and its ability to broadcast independent news for the benefit of the American people.ABC has said it has stopped booking politicians on the daytime talkshow The View and chose to air a July speech by Trump on its streaming platform so as not to antagonize the president. “Our editorial decisions are being affected right now,” Wilkinson said, noting the significance of decisions about how to cover next month’s pivotal midterm elections. “We are watching everything we do … We have already altered our conduct because of the fear of retaliation.”She also noted that ABC recently chose to air a Jimmy Kimmel-conducted interview with Texas US Senate candidate James Talarico on YouTube, rather than television, “because the FCC has no control over YouTube”.Dimitar P Georgiev, representing the FCC defendants, argued that “there is no reason to believe the early renewal order has prompted changes to the plaintiffs’ editorial decisions”. He also argued that the US district court for the District of Columbia was not the proper jurisdiction for the case, saying that ABC could instead appeal any adverse decision to the US court of appeals for the District of Columbia.ABC is seeking a decision from the judge to enjoin the FCC from taking any further actions against the network’s licenses. “We are asking to stop pure retaliation, putting us in a process that we should never have to be in,” Wilkinson said.In what Wilkinson called a “fatal admission”, Georgiev said the license renewal process “is not about the licenses”, but is instead a “tool” to expedite the commission’s review of ABC for potential violations of federal equal opportunities regulations. The lawyer also said the FCC could choose to end the license review process early if ABC is able to satisfy its document requests.Considering that the FCC opened its employment practice investigation into Disney last year, with requests for documents ongoing since then, the judge asked: “Why is it only in the summer that you determined that their responses were woefully inadequate?”She also questioned why the commission required the company to submit renewal applications for all eight of its stations simultaneously.And she noted past comments by Carr about the network’s licenses, including a remark in July,when he had said ABC’s decisionnot to carry the president’s speech that month on its linear channel could factor into the license investigation.“It strikes me with all the comments that this was merely over a discovery dispute, what made this so different that you needed to call for an early license renewal?” Judge AliKhan asked lawyers for the FCC, whom she asked for a list of some of the other enforcement actions the commission could have taken short of calling up the network’s licenses early.And she noted that there was “some daylight” in the FCC’s arguments, considering that the diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) inquiry was handled by the commission’s enforcement bureau, while the license order was made by the media bureau.The judge ended the hearing without issuing an order, saying she would take the matter “under advisement”.Explore more on these topicsABCTrump administrationUS television industryUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: S&P 500 and Nasdaq surge to record highs after AI chipmaker rally | Stock markets | The Guardian
description: S&P tops 7,800 for first time in history as investors optimistic despite signs of instability in US economy
Author: Lauren Aratani
Headline: S&P tops 7,800 for first time in history as investors optimistic despite signs of instability in US economy
Content: A trader on the stock exchange floor.Photograph: Brendan McDermid/ReutersView image in fullscreenA trader on the stock exchange floor.Photograph: Brendan McDermid/ReutersStock marketsS&P 500 and Nasdaq surge to record highs after AI chipmaker rallyS&P tops 7,800 for first time in history as investors optimistic despite signs of instability in US economyLauren ArataniTue 6 Oct 2026 16.28 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 16.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe S&P 500 andNasdaqclosed at a record high after a rally around AI chipmakers and a dip in US treasury yields.At market’s close, the S&P 500 was up 0.58%, topping 7,800 for the first time in its history. The tech-heavy Nasdaq index rose 0.45%, while the Dow, which is slightly down from its record high in August, climbed 0.49%.Investors appeared optimistic after recent developments for chipmakers including Marvell Technology, Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom that showed growth in the markets for the chips used to power AI.Wall Street has also grown more optimistic that the US Federal Reserve will leave interest rates unchanged at its next board meeting in October. Job figures from September showed underwhelming growth in the labor market, and multiple Fed officials have said the next interest rate increase can probably wait.The optimism in the stock market, largely coming from continuing investment in AI, has defied other signs of instability in the US economy and global politics.The US bond market, typically seen as one of the safest investment vehicles, has been in turmoil in recent weeks. US bond yields, or the return an investor receives when a bond matures, reached recent highs amid concerns over high inflation and interest rates. The yield for 10-year US treasury bonds on Monday reached 5.349%, the highest since April 2022, before dipping back down on Tuesday.For American consumers, higher energy prices continue to be a major pain point. While gas prices have dipped over the last week, prices are still about $1.20 a gallon onaveragehigher than a year ago. Diesel, which is used to fuel trucks, buses and trains, has also gone down from record high but is still over 40% higher than a year ago.The economy is expected to be a top issue in the upcoming midterm elections, with many voters expressing frustration over high prices. Donald Trump, who has been stumping for Republican candidates across the country, has been trying to paint a different picture for voters.At a rally in Nebraska on Monday night, Trumpsaidthat “our nation is doing better now than it’s ever done” and that gas prices would fall below $1.85 a gallon “in no time”.Explore more on these topicsStock marketsNasdaqnewsShareReuse this content

title: Misuse of AI is brands’ top reputational threat, new survey says | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: The findings come after warnings from tech leaders that AI placed in the wrong hands could trigger larger threats such as nuclear war or bioweaponry destruction
Author: Ramon Antonio Vargas
Headline: The findings come after warnings from tech leaders that AI placed in the wrong hands could trigger larger threats such as nuclear war or bioweaponry destruction
Content: People protest outside OpenAI's office in New York City on 21 September.Photograph: Julius Constantine Motal/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPeople protest outside OpenAI's office in New York City on 21 September.Photograph: Julius Constantine Motal/The GuardianAI (artificial intelligence)Misuse of AI is brands’ top reputational threat, new survey saysThe findings come after warnings from tech leaders that AI placed in the wrong hands could trigger larger threats such as nuclear war or bioweaponry destructionRamon Antonio VargasTue 6 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 12.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMisusingartificial intelligence(AI) is the top threat to companies’ reputations – more so than being accused of putting children in the way of mental, emotional or physical harm and issues exposed by the US-Israel war on Iran, among other brand risks, according to a new survey of more than 150 public affairs leaders.Those findings in the new edition of the quarterly Reputation Risk Index, released on Tuesday, came on the heels of other perhaps more dire warnings from leading tech figures that AI in the wrong hands couldprecipitateexistential threats on a mass scale such as nuclear war or destruction by bioweaponry.Theindex’s publisher, the Global Risk Advisory Council, acknowledged that misuse of AI is not a particularly new concern in its area of focus, having been identified as a top worry repeatedly since thefirst editionof the survey in April 2025.But the council said what was new was its attaching an advisory to its latest survey advising business leaders to “take immediate and decisive action to mitigate potential long-term brand damage” with respect to AI, as the technology has “become a clear and present danger to public confidence for many corporations”.“As AI is rapidly deployed for productivity gains, we have also seen diminishing public trust in the technology, elevating the need for businesses to take measures to protect their brands,” council chair Isabel Casillas Guzman said in a statement. “In this environment, AI use or overuse can quickly damage a company’s standing with customers, investors, or other key stakeholders, making it essential for companies to deploy preventive tactics now.”The creators of the council and the Reputation Risk Index – the Washington DC-based public affairs firm Global Situation Room – said such tactics include removing or reducing the use of AI content and relying on humans for customer service.The Global Situation Room said that the Reputation Risk Index released on Tuesday surveyed former heads of state, government ministers and senior executives from more than 20 countries in five continents who were invited to participate after establishing their credentials in responding to crises.Respondents to that survey collectively perceived the technology to have shown great promise in creating “organizational efficiency” – while simultaneously “accelerating safety and data concerns, hacks, fraud, straining privacy protections, upending the workforce, and dragging companies into court as lawsuits increasingly link AI products to real-world harm”.Meanwhile, actions or accusations of putting children at risk of mental, emotional or physical harm also ranked highly behind misused AI – along with infringing individuals’ sensitive information, according to the index results published on Tuesday.Unethical or illegal behavior used to gain a strategic advantage or profit and, separately, poor strategic or operational decisions resulting in reduced financial or public standing rounded out the top five, according to the index.The index noted that its preceding edition released in July identified supply chain issues, divisive political stances and other factors associated with thewarthat the Trump’s administration started in Iran alongside Israel as the leading risk to companies’ reputations. But those surveyed indicated that those anxieties had eased as the conflict dragged out – and perhaps despite it remaining unresolved since it was launched in February.“The geopolitical shock … hasn’t gone away, but its first, sharpest reputational blow has faded, and the conflict has slipped out of the top tier [of concerns] even as it grinds on,” Guzman said in a “message from the chair” included in the index.Guzman put out her message two days after Donald Trump’s administration named a new AI czar: the director of national intelligence, Jay Clayton. The president said in a social media post that Clayton would oversee an entity coordinating “the federal government’s engagement with consumers, public interest groups, religious organizations, critical infrastructure providers, and” AI tech companies.Clayton had previously told federal lawmakers that AI was a “gamechanger” but also posed “a threat”.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)US politicsUS-Israel war on IrannewsShareReuse this content

title: Paramount completes $111bn acquisition of Warner Bros to form new media empire Skydance | Business | The Guardian
description: David Ellison and ex-Mattel CEO Ynon Kreiz to oversee both film studios, HBO Max, CNN and CBS News as co-executives
Author: Gaya Gupta
Headline: David Ellison and ex-Mattel CEO Ynon Kreiz to oversee both film studios, HBO Max, CNN and CBS News as co-executives
Content: The Paramount water tower in Los Angeles, California.Photograph: Mario Tama/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Paramount water tower in Los Angeles, California.Photograph: Mario Tama/Getty ImagesBusinessParamount completes $111bn acquisition of Warner Bros to form new media empire SkydanceDavid Ellison and ex-Mattel CEO Ynon Kreiz to oversee both film studios, HBO Max, CNN and CBS News as co-executivesGaya GuptaTue 6 Oct 2026 10.14 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 17.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleParamountcompleted its $111bn acquisition ofWarner Bros Discoveryon Tuesday, consolidating some of the world’s most recognizable studios and news outlets after a bidding war with Netflix and months of legal turmoil.The new company, now called Skydance, will have David Ellison, the son of a billionaire tech mogul, at its helm, with the former CEO of Mattel, Ynon Kreiz, as co-executive. They will oversee Paramount and Warner Bros’ movie studios, HBO Max, CBS News and CNN.“Today is a historic day, not just for Skydance but for our entire industry,” Ellison said in a statement. “From the start, our ambition was to bring these two storied studios together and create a stronger competitor, with the talent, resources, and reach to tell great stories in every genre, on every platform, for audiences everywhere. Now that ambition is a reality.”The consolidation of Paramount and Warner Bros combines two of the last five legacy studios in Hollywood, which includes Disney, Universal Pictures and Sony Pictures.Mark Thompson will remain chief executive at CNN after Paramount saleRead moreThough the merger was approved in June, California, New York and 10 other statessuedParamount over concerns that the move would “extinguish” competition and lead to fewer movie theaters in theaters and at home.As part of thesettlement agreementreached last month, Skydance is required to release a minimum of 30 films each year and more than 180 television shows. CBS News and CNN will also berequiredto maintain independent editorial boards.A trustee will monitor Skydance’s compliance with the terms of the settlement. Rob Bonta, the California attorney general, said he would be prepared to go to court if the company ever fails to comply.“This settlement is not a vote of support for this merger; it’s not a blessing of the broader merger,” he said on 21 September, when the settlement was announced. “Broadly speaking, we believe further consolidation in markets that are essential to American economic life doesn’t serve the American economy, consumers or competition well.”The merger has also raisedconcernsabout Ellison’sinfluenceover CNN after his overhaul of CBS News. Ellison is the son of Larry Ellison, the co-founder of Oracle who was a Trump megadonor in the 2024 presidential election. The elder Ellison’s net worth is $193bn, according toBloomberg.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhen David Ellison’s Skydance CorporationacquiredParamount last year, he appointedBari Weiss, a former New York Times opinion writer who launched an “anti-woke” media outlet, as the head of CBS News, despite her lack of television experience. Since then, the television network has faced accusations of bias toward the Trump administration, though Ellison has defended his stewardship of both CBS and now, CNN.On Monday, CNN’s CEO, Mark Thompson,announcedthat he would remain in his role under its new parent company, saying that he had spoken with Ellison and Skydance leadership and that he has “real confidence that they both understand and will fully support the principle and practice of the kind of independent news that CNN has always stood for”.Explore more on these topicsBusinessMedia businessParamount+Warner BrosUS televisionUS television industryTelevision industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: Harry Kane doubles up on landmark night as England cruise past Czechia | Nations League | The Guardian
description: England won 3-0 against Czechia in the Nations League at Wembley, Harry Kane scoring twice to mark his record-equalling 125th cap
Author: David Hytner
Headline: England won 3-0 against Czechia in the Nations League at Wembley, Harry Kane scoring twice to mark his record-equalling 125th cap
Content: Harry Kane jumps for joy after doubling England’s lead on his 125th senior appearance.Photograph: Adam Davy/PAView image in fullscreenHarry Kane jumps for joy after doubling England’s lead on his 125th senior appearance.Photograph: Adam Davy/PANations LeagueHarry Kane doubles up on landmark night as England cruise past CzechiaDavid Hytnerat WembleyTue 6 Oct 2026 16.50 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 18.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was a night that belonged to Harry Kane. Yet another one. It began with him being shown a replay of his first England goal during a pre-match interview with ITV – the header against Lithuania in 2015, just 79 seconds after he came on as a substitute for his debut. It ended with him reflecting on two more in what was a supremely comfortableNations Leaguevictory over Czechia. Some things never change.It remains a numbers game for Kane. They are getting bigger and ever more impressive. On the occasion of his 125th cap, the one that took him level with Peter Shilton at the top of the all-timeEnglandlist, he moved to an astonishing 91 goals. Nobody will be surprised if he reaches the century. The only question appears to be when.England know how to beat the game’s smaller fry. Under Thomas Tuchel, they have played 16 matches against teams ranked outside the world’s top 20. They have won 15 and drawn one – against Ghana at the World Cup. They have conceded only once – against the Democratic Republic of the Congo, also at the World Cup.Czechia, who are ranked No 50, were never in the contest.Harry Kane wins record-equalling 125th England cap, drawing level with Peter ShiltonRead moreKane is similarly inevitable. The captain even claimed the assist for the breakthrough goal with a cross into the corridor of uncertainty that spooked Vladimir Coufal so severely he shot into his own net. Kane’s passing was very good.
