When he was withdrawn in the 82nd minute, he left to a great ovation.The victory meant that England virtually guaranteed their progress into the Nations League quarter-finals and, perhaps more importantly, saw them close out this elongated window with plenty of optimism. One of the main goals was to put as much distance as possible between themselves and the World Cup semi-final defeat against Argentina. It was mission accomplished.Kane will break the caps record when England host Croatia in November and that will be the night when he is truly feted. As an aside, he would want to do it at Wembley rather than in Madrid against Spain where England’s next-but-one game will be staged. Was that why he was so keen to play in all four of the matches during this window? It might have been a part of it.Then again, Kane always wants to play. He was one of only three England players to start each of the matches in this series. The others were Manchester City’s Marc Guéhi and Elliot Anderson. Was the City manager, Enzo Maresca, happy about that? Probably not. Does he have bigger problems at the moment? Yes.Kane’s act of drawing level with Shilton was the box-office detail. His name was on everybody’s lips; his face on the big screen before kick-off. He was pictured alongside Shilton when his name was read out with the teams. The Wembley crowd roared.Kane was at the heart of the opening goal, providing the teasing cross from the right and it was some finish from the player just inside the six-yard box. One that Kane would have been happy to call his own. The problem from a Czechia point of view was that it came from their right-back. Coufal could feel Eberechi Eze at his back as he faced towards his own goal, albeit the England winger was not that close. Coufal stretched and everybody had the time to have the same thought: you do not have to do this. Coufal did it. He could not check his momentum and steered firmly past his goalkeeper.View image in fullscreenCzechia’s Vladimir Coufal scores an own goal to put England ahead.Photograph: Adam Davy/PATrent Alexander-Arnold, who Tuchel recalled at right-back, was involved in the buildup and he caught the eye, especially when surging up and inside. He repeatedly got into advanced areas and there was one moment in the first half when he stormed into the No 9 position on to an Anderson pass. He just could not bring it under his spell. Alexander-Arnold had extended Lukas Hornicek with a whipped free-kick at the outset.Jude Bellingham was excellent. Of course he was. There were fizzed passes from him that took the breath, getting England into dangerous positions, including one for Morgan Rogers in the 25th minute that the Chelsea attacker wasted. There were those strutting runs and it was Bellingham, as much as anybody, who advertised the fact that England were going to break through.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnderson should have made it 2-0 after a Bellingham lay-off; Kane sparked the move and Alexander-Arnold’s cross drove it. The second goal arrived before half-time and it had to be Kane. It would have been all about the buildup were it not for the identity of the scorer. Anderson’s lofted ball up the inside right was a beauty and Rogers’ first-time cross on the half-volley was even better, cut unerringly towards you-know-who in the middle. Kane was unmarked. Hornicek was helpless.Kane wanted more. As usual. He got it. As usual. There was the moment shortly after the restart when he unloaded from the edge of the area and watched the shot kiss the top of the crossbar. Hornicek was beaten. Then he was for real.View image in fullscreenHarry Kane’s header puts England 3-0 up at Wembley.Photograph: Adam Davy/PAIt was Lewis Hall – impressive at left-back – who swung over the corner, which came after Hornicek kept out an audacious Bellingham flick. Only Jiri Slama knows why he gave Kane so much room in front of goal. It was always going to end badly for the Czechia defender. Kane rose and the header had too much power for Hornicek.There was the minor irritation for Tuchel when Myles Lewis-Skelly got himself booked in the 53rd minute for pulling back Pavel Sulc. The midfielder will be suspended for England’s next game and it was certainly not a great idea for him to get in the face of Michal Sadilek shortly afterwards. Sadilek had fouled Rogers and was booked. It was a needless risk from Lewis-Skelly.England toyed with Czechia in the second half with Eze running through some of his party tricks. It was Kane who provided the substance.Explore more on these topicsNations LeagueEnglandCzechiaHarry Kanematch reportsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I will not be moving on’: sale of WNBA’s Connecticut Sun leaves Native fans facing cultural loss | Connecticut Sun | The Guardian
description: The Mohegan Tribe made the Sun the first Native-owned franchise in pro sports. Fans say the team’s move echoes centuries of erasure and displacement
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The Mohegan Tribe made the Sun the first Native-owned franchise in pro sports. Fans say the team’s move echoes centuries of erasure and displacement
Content: After 24 seasons, the WNBA’s Sun played their final game in Uncasville, Connecticut, last month.Photograph: Brian Babineau/NBAE/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAfter 24 seasons, the WNBA’s Sun played their final game in Uncasville, Connecticut, last month.Photograph: Brian Babineau/NBAE/Getty ImagesConnecticut Sun‘I will not be moving on’: sale of WNBA’s Connecticut Sun leaves Native fans facing cultural lossThe Mohegan Tribe made the Sun the first Native American-owned franchise in pro sports. Fans say the team’s move to Houston echoes centuries of erasure and displacementFrankie de la CretazTue 6 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 06.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen the Connecticut Sun played their final WNBA game last month, fans at Mohegan Sun Arena came together in an act of collective celebration and grief. The beloved franchise was leaving after 24 seasons,soldto a new ownership group in Houston, in a process so controversial that the state of Connecticut is considering legal action. The end of the Sun is a loss for the entire New England region, which is now without a WNBA team.The Sun entered the league in 2003 and brought professional women’s basketball to Connecticut, which is considered the “Basketball Capital of the World” – at least, according to signs along the state’s highways. The Sun were the first independently owned WNBA team, and the first Native American-owned pro sports franchise.The story of the Mohegan Tribe, which bought the Sun in 2003, often gets lost in conversations about the team. But it shouldn’t, Native fans told the Guardian. You can’t understand the birth or the death of the team without understanding Native history and the ways cultural and historical harm still reverberates today.“We are sovereign nations and sovereignty is so important to us, and that’s something that’s been continually challenged and disputed and really disregarded throughout history,” says Natalie Welch, a member of the Eastern Band of Cherokee tribe and the program director of MBA in sport and entertainment management at Seattle University. “This whole situation, sadly, seems like another disregarding of sovereignty, and is really belittling to the Mohegan Tribe.”The Mohegan Tribe, whose ancestral lands are along the Thames River in southeastern Connecticut, fought hard to gain its sovereign status. Its land was taken by white settlers during colonization. The tribe applied for federal recognition in 1978, which was finally granted in 1994. The following year, the Connecticut governor signed a bill authorizing the state to return 240 acres of the tribe’s original ancestral lands to the federal government, to be held in trust for the Mohegan Tribe. Over the years, the tribe has bought more of its land back, acquiring hundreds of acres. It currently has more than 2,400 registered members.The Mohegan Sun Casino and the arena inside it are located on the tribe’s reservation in Uncasville, named for a pre-colonial tribal leader, Sachem (Chief) Uncas. Shortly after the tribe received its sovereign status and land, it decided to pursue gaming as a way to “return the tribe to economic self-sufficiency”,according to the tribe. The casino opened in 1996, and many tribal members work there.“Before the casino was built, that land was also not ours,” says Haley Kerwin, a Mohegan tribal member and Sun fan whose father works at the casino. “It was ours, and then it was taken away, it was something that we had to fight to get back. The reason that we were able to open the casino there, the reason that my dad was able to get a job and start a family, is because of the work that the members of our tribe have done to not let us be erased.”View image in fullscreenBeth Regan, chairwoman of the Mohegan Tribe’s council of elders, watches the Sun’s final home game on 24 September.Photograph: Jessica Hill/APThe Mohegan Tribe chose to invest in the WNBA at a time when it was not financially popular to do so. When the league began in 1997, the NBA collectively owned the teams, and each WNBA team was run by its NBA counterpart in its city. After a rapid expansion process that saw the league double in size over its first four seasons from 1997 to 2000, it restructured in 2002. The NBA teams had to decide for themselves whether they wanted to operate their W counterparts. Four WNBA teams folded in the wake of that change – the Portland Fire andthe Miami Solceased to exist (the Fire would return as an expansion franchise this year), while the Utah Starzz moved to San Antonio and the Orlando Miracle were bought by the Mohegan Tribe for $5m and became the Connecticut Sun.“Basketball is really big in Native communities, but I think what’s so special is that theWNBAhas always been a majority-Black women, and so for the Mohegans to come in as a business and invest in something that people didn’t think would exist 30 years later, much less be thriving, I just think it’s a really great display of investment in community,” says Shea Vassar, a Sun fan and a registered member of Cherokee Nation.Val Ackerman, the WNBA’s president at the time, says the significance of bringing the first Native-owned pro sports team to the league wasn’t really part of the consideration around the awarding of the franchise. The area was already a women’s basketball stronghold. An hour north was UConn, where coach Geno Auriemma was building a dynasty; when the Sun entered the WNBA, the Huskies had just won their third national title in four years. There were multiple bidders in the state, but ultimately the Mohegan Tribe won out because they had a built-in arena with just over 9,000 seats – the perfect size for the fanbase.“We saw [having the first Native-owned team] as a positive, but that wasn’t why we did it,” Ackerman says. “It was really the other factors. It was this very unique setup in a part of the country where we knew women’s basketball had a great following, and we knew they were great operators because they also have a lot of other events they bring into the building there.”From day one, the tribe played a huge role in the public image and branding of the team. In a world where sports franchiseshave adopted Native imageryfor team names or mascots that many consider racist, having an identity that was Native-informed was significant. Kerwin, who grew up going to Sun games with her family, interned for the team’s content department for the 2022 and 2023 seasons. She was proud to help shape the public narrative and bring a Mohegan perspective to the team’s social presence.In 2021, when the WNBA debuted its “Rebel Edition” uniforms, the Sun’s set highlighted and honored Mohegan culture. The 2024 and 2026 versions continued that trend. On the front, instead of having the word “Sun” on the jersey, it said “KEESUSK”, which means “sun” in the Mohegan language. Symbols on the waistband corresponded to the four dome directions in Mohegan Tribal culture – east, south, west, north. Along the neckline, arms, and trim of the shorts, dots represented the “Trail of Life”, or the Mohegan belief that,“We walk as a single spirit on the Trail of Life. We are guided by 13 generations past and responsible for 13 generations to come.”View image in fullscreenDuring the 2024 playoffs, Marina Mabrey and DiJonai Carrington wore jerseys with the word Keesusk, which means “sun” in the Mohegan language.Photograph: Erica Denhoff/Icon Sportswire/Getty ImagesVassar was drawn to the Sun specifically because of their Native ownership. “I wanted to get into the WNBA but being in Oklahoma, I wasn’t sure which team I wanted to root for,” she says. Vassar’s dad went to UConn and his side of the family still lives in Connecticut, so when she found out that the Sun were owned by the Mohegan Tribe, she instantly knew they would be her team: “Having that entry point to theConnecticut Sunjust felt like magic.”When players joined the Sun, they were educated on Mohegan beliefs and traditions. Members would come to practices and games and offer traditional blessings for the team. Point guard Charlisse Leger-Walker played her rookie season this year with the Sun, and she cherished the opportunity to spend the first season of her career playing for a Native-owned team. She is an Indigenous New Zealander of Māori heritage from the Te Whakatōhea and Ngāti Porou iwi (tribes).“It just really hits a different part of my identity and connects me back to my roots, without it actually being my roots,” Leger-Walker says. “Coming into the league and everything is so new, that [connection] almost feels familial in a sense. It’s something I’ll definitely remember throughout my career.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly for the 2026 WNBA seasonSign up toWNBA 30A limited run women’s basketball newsletter dedicated to the league’s historic 30th season.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionKerwin spoke with Sun players Brittney Griner and Saniya Rivers during this season’s Indigenous Peoples Night game, and offered them wampum, beads that carry significant ceremonial significance to the Mohegan Tribe.“Wampum is an honor to be gifted, and I was just going to vaguely say that it was ‘a Mohegan thing’ when handing it to them,” Kerwin says. But the pair surprised her by already knowing about the significance of wampum and understanding the honor it was to receive it. “Them already knowing and they remembered what it means, that’s something that means something to them now, too. That is something really special, that a part of the tribe will also be with all the players that will go on to their new teams.”The handling of the Sun sale was roundly criticized, but for Native fans of the league, it hit particularly hard. They say it brought up centuries of disenfranchisement and erasure. The Mohegan Tribe was selling the teamto reduce debt and focus on their core gaming operations. As the league grew, the Sun’s lack of a dedicated practice facility for players was becoming a detriment. The state of Connecticut looked into ways to keep the franchise, includinga bid from a Hartford-based ownership groupand an effort tobring in minority ownershipvia state funds and private investment to build the Sun a practice facility in Hartford and keep games at Mohegan Sun Arena. The league rejected those options.View image in fullscreenSaniya Rivers signs autographs prior to the Sun’s final game in Uncasville.Photograph: Jessica Hill/APIn 2025,the Mohegan Tribe secured a deal with a Boston ownership group for $325m to move the Sun from Connecticut but keep them in New England. Thenthe WNBA stepped inand said that the Boston ownership group could not buy the team, as they had not put a bid in for an expansion team during the previous round.Instead, the tribe would reach an agreement to sell the team for $300m to an ownership group in Houston, which had pursued a franchise in recent rounds of expansion but missed out. Not only did the tribe get less money for the team, but the new ownership group was led by Tilman Fertitta, the owner of the NBA’s Houston Rockets and Donald Trump’s ambassador to Italy. Some politicianscalledthe sale “rigged” and called for antitrust investigations into the league.Despite a season plagued by injuries, where the Sun went 11-33 and finished second to last in the standings, their final home game on 24 September was a triumph. The crowd of diehard Connecticut fans celebrated as their team defeated the Toronto Tempo 95-81. The Sun’s final season was spent honoring their legends, from franchise icon Alyssa Thomas to 2021 MVP Jonquel Jones. The concern for all fans – but especially Native fans familiar with having their stories erased – is that the franchise’s rebrand once it moves to Houston (wherethe Comets identitywill be resurrected) will mean a loss of 24 seasons of history.Many fans of the Sun, whether they were Native or not,were drawn to the teambecause of its independent ownership and the fact that their monetary support was going back to a Native tribe. To them, the move to Houston is about so much more than just location. It’s also about values. For a tribe that fought long and hard to be granted tribal sovereignty, the decision being taken out of their hands can feel like a violation of that sovereignty.“To me, it really harkens back to the fact that for Native people, land is so important and place is so important,” Welch says. “To have this team in this area and to see the success that they saw and build this fanbase and then completely leaving them with nothing. It’s so tied to the continued erasure and displacement of Native people.”“That erasure of the Sun’s history intertwined with the tribe’s history is anxiety-inducing,” Kerwin adds. “If I’m being honest, I just don’t want people to stop talking about them. I fear people are going to move on very quickly, and I will not be moving on any time soon, if ever.”Explore more on these topicsConnecticut SunWNBAUS sportsBasketballNative AmericansfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Philadelphia Eagles great Lane Johnson abruptly retires citing ‘mental health’ | Philadelphia Eagles | The Guardian
description: The six-time Pro Bowl right tackle says he is stepping away after 14 seasons to focus on his mental health and spend more time with his family
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: The six-time Pro Bowl right tackle says he is stepping away after 14 seasons to focus on his mental health and spend more time with his family
Content: Lane Johnson walks off the field after the Philadelphia Eagles’ victory over the Dallas Cowboys at Lincoln Financial Field in November 2023.Photograph: Mitchell Leff/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenLane Johnson walks off the field after the Philadelphia Eagles’ victory over the Dallas Cowboys at Lincoln Financial Field in November 2023.Photograph: Mitchell Leff/Getty ImagesPhiladelphia EaglesPhiladelphia Eagles great Lane Johnson abruptly retires citing ‘mental health’Two-time All-Pro won two Super Bowls with EaglesJohnson says family priorities have changed36-year-old started 171 games for PhiladelphiaGuardian sportTue 6 Oct 2026 16.32 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 16.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLane Johnson, the Philadelphia Eagles’ decorated right tackle and a cornerstone of the franchise for nearly a decade and a half, announced his retirement from the NFL on Tuesday after 14 seasons.The 36-year-old, a two-time first-team All-Pro and six-time Pro Bowl selection, said in a statementon social mediathat he had hoped to play one final season but had decided to step away to prioritize his mental health and spend more time with his family.“I deeply wanted to gut it out for one more year; to take the field with my brothers for one last season,” Johnson wrote. “But after a lot of reflection, I’ve realized that my personal and family priorities in my life have changed.”Johnson added that it was “critical that I focus on my mental health”, saying he owed it to his teammates, coaches, the organization and Eagles supporters to be fully committed if he continued playing.“Right now my heart is telling me that it’s time to say goodbye to football,” he wrote.Allow Instagram content?This article includes content provided byInstagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueJohnson thanked Philadelphia, Eagles owner Jeffrey Lurie, the organization and his teammates while reflecting on a career in which he became one of the NFL’s most formidable offensive linemen.“I have given it my all for 14 years, season after season putting my body to the max and tirelessly working my craft to not only live up to the legacy of the guys that came before me, but to set a new standard of success for the best franchise in all of sports,” he wrote.The announcement comes two days after Johnson was a surprise inactive for the Eagles’ loss to the Los Angeles Rams because of a personal matter. He also missed four practices during training camp for personal reasons and, after returning, acknowledged that this season would “probably” be his last.Johnson, taken by the Eagles with the fourth overall pick in the 2013 draft, retires as one of the most accomplished offensive linemen in team history. He spent his entire NFL career in Philadelphia, starting 171 regular-season games at right tackle and helping the Eagles make three Super Bowls appearances with two wins.Explore more on these topicsPhiladelphia EaglesNFLUS sportsShareReuse this content

title: Coco Gauff says ‘insane’ wave of racist abuse followed disputed point at China Open | Tennis | The Guardian
description: Coco Gauff said she received an ‘insane’ amount of racist comments on social media following a controversial point in her China Open win against home player Sun Xinran
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Coco Gauff said she received an ‘insane’ amount of racist comments on social media following a controversial point in her China Open win against home player Sun Xinran
Content: Coco Gauff after defeating Sun Xinran at the China Open.Photograph: Robert Prange/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCoco Gauff after defeating Sun Xinran at the China Open.Photograph: Robert Prange/Getty ImagesTennisCoco Gauff says ‘insane’ wave of racist abuse followed disputed point at China OpenAmerican stopped rally after being distracted in match‘You can dislike me or disagree … without being racist’Associated PressTue 6 Oct 2026 04.28 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 16.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCoco Gauff said she received an “insane” amount of racist ­comments on social media ­following a ­controversial point in her China Open match against the home player Sun Xinran.Gauff stopped a rally after ­electronic advertising boards ­lining the court flickered during a point late in the first set of her 7-5, 6-1 third-round victory over Sun, a 16-year-old who recently won the US Open junior title.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDaniil Medvedev disqualified from China Open semi after hitting fan with ballRead more“Hey everyone, you can dislike me or disagree about what happened without being racist,” Gauff said in a reply on X. “The amount of racist comments/dms I’ve received in the last few hours is insane. Lastly, I’m not a cheater or a thief.”Sun appeared about to win the point when Gauff stopped playing. The chair umpire then ordered the point to be replayed. Gauff, a two-time grand slam champion ranked No 4, went on to take control of the match on Monday.“I think it’s weird I’m ­getting hate for ­following the rules. ­Xinran is [an] incredible talent and player, I ­apologised for the situation at the end of the match and she ­completely understood,” Gauff added in another post.Sun, who was given a wildcard entry by tournament organisers and was making her WTA Tour debut, appeared distraught after the loss. Gauff, who reached the fourth round of Wimbledonas a 15-year-old in 2019, sympathised with Sun. “I did not like to see her so emotional as I’ve been there and I really ­understand what it is like but this is just the ­beginning of an incredible career,” Gauff said. “It was an honour to share the court in front of her home crowd.”Explore more on these topicsTennisCoco GauffnewsShareReuse this content

title: Cristiano Ronaldo accuses Portugal coach Jorge Jesus of broken promises | Cristiano Ronaldo | The Guardian
description: Cristiano Ronaldo has accused the Portugal head coach, Jorge Jesus, of twice breaking his word, saying a failed agreement to publicly explain ⁠his omission against Norway
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Cristiano Ronaldo has accused the Portugal head coach, Jorge Jesus, of twice breaking his word, saying a failed agreement to publicly explain ⁠his omission against Norway
Content: Cristiano Ronaldo sits on the bench during the Nations League game between Norway and Portugal in Oslo.Photograph: Paulo Novais/EPAView image in fullscreenCristiano Ronaldo sits on the bench during the Nations League game between Norway and Portugal in Oslo.Photograph: Paulo Novais/EPACristiano RonaldoCristiano Ronaldo accuses Portugal coach Jorge Jesus of broken promisesForward says he will be available after punishmentRonaldo insists coach ‘had broken his word to me’ReutersTue 6 Oct 2026 15.48 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCristiano Ronaldo has accused the Portugal head coach, Jorge Jesus, of twice breaking his word, saying a failed agreement to publicly explain ⁠his omission against Norway drove him out of the camp but insisting he remained available after any punishment.In a lengthy statement, the 41-year-old gave his ⁠account of the dispute ⁠that promptedhis ​departure from Copenhagenbefore Portugal’s Nations League match against Denmark last week.Ronaldo’s break with Portugal is sad, fitting, and long overdue | Jonathan WilsonRead moreRonaldo said Jesus had agreed a plan under which the forward would ⁠miss the Norway and Denmark matches to manage his fitness. However, on the day of the Norway game, the coach told him he would play for 30 ⁠minutes.“Everyone knows the rest. I warmed up from half-time onwards, watched the minutes tick by and wasn’t called ​on,” Ronaldo said. “The manager had broken his ‌word to me.”Portugal’s captain and ‌all-time leading scorer said a subsequent meeting with Jesus, attended by his club side Al-Nassr’s sporting ‌director Simão Coutinho, produced an agreement for the coach to clarify events at his next press conference.According to Ronaldo, an eight-point document was prepared saying he had never demanded playing time, had respected Jesus’s decisions and that the coach asking him to warm up without bringing him on had been a mistake. Ronaldo said the agreed notes did not require Jesus to apologise to him ‌but said the coach’s public remarks bore no resemblance to their private discussion.“It was the second time he had broken his word to me,” Ronaldo said. “I decided ​to leave the training camp without waiting for any further broken promises.”The statement provided Ronaldo’s account but on Sunday, after Portugal’s win over Norway, Jesus denied he had made any agreement with the player but left the door open for his return.The Portuguese Football Federation (FPF) did not immediately respond to a request for ⁠comment about Ronaldo’s statement.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRonaldo apologised for failing to greet supporters after the Norway ​match and for leaving his ​teammates, accepting that his captaincy made ​his conduct more serious. “The consequences of my actions must be assessed and punished ​by the Portuguese Football ‌Federation,” he said.Despite ​the rupture, Ronaldo said ​he was not limiting his international ambitions to a farewell appearance. “If I’m physically fit, playing for my club – scoring goals, I hope – after serving whatever suspension is imposed on me, I’ll be available, as I’ve always been until now, to compete and win for our national team,” he added.Explore more on these topicsCristiano RonaldoPortugalNations LeaguenewsShareReuse this content

title: Djokovic ends title drought with China Open triumph while Alcaraz claims glory in Japan | Tennis | The Guardian
description: Novak Djokovic capped a remarkable week with his first tournament for nearly a year at the China Open, while Carlos Alcaraz won the Japan Open for his first title since February
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Novak Djokovic capped a remarkable week with his first tournament for nearly a year at the China Open, while Carlos Alcaraz won the Japan Open for his first title since February
Content: Novak Djokovic of Serbia poses with the trophy at the China Open in Beijing.Photograph: Hermann Chu/Eurasia Sport Images/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenNovak Djokovic of Serbia poses with the trophy at the China Open in Beijing.Photograph: Hermann Chu/Eurasia Sport Images/Getty ImagesTennisDjokovic ends title drought with China Open triumph while Alcaraz claims glory in JapanSerb victorious after De Minaur retires injuredAlcaraz beats Lehecka for first title since FebruaryPress AssociationTue 6 Oct 2026 09.35 EDTFirst published on Tue 6 Oct 2026 07.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNovak Djokovic capped an outstanding week at the China Open with his first title for nearly a year. The 39-year-old profited from the retirement of his final opponent, Alex de Minaur, after only one game of the second set to win a seventh title in Beijing and maintain his record of never having lost at the tournament.The 7-6, 0-1 victory means Djokovic has won at least one title in each of the past 21 years, while he now has 102 tour level trophies overall. Both men reached the final without having to complete their matches on Monday – Djokovic thanks to the much-publiciseddisqualification of Daniil Medvedev, while De Minaur’s opponent Hubert Hurkacz pulled the plug because of injury.Coco Gauff says ‘insane’ wave of racist abuse followed disputed point at China OpenRead moreDjokovic edged a very tight first set on a tie-break before the two men each took a medical timeout, but it came as a big surprise when De Minaur abruptly shook hands after winning the opening game of the second set. The Australian, who returned to court with strapping on his left thigh, said in his on-court interview: “I want to say sorry to all the amazing fans that came to watch this match. I didn’t want to finish like this.”When Djokovic lost in the opening round of the US Open amid ongoing physical struggles, the sporting obituaries were being prepared, but the Serb has shown once again that writing him off would be premature.Djokovic, who also defeated the top seed, Alexander Zverev, during his run, said: “It’s been 11 years since I played here last. I always have high expectations for myself and always want to visualise myself with the trophy, but particularly here in Beijing, the place where I’ve never lost.“I was also quite aware that reality’s a little bit different these days. This year has been quite challenging for me, lots of ups and downs and physical and health issues, so I was just trying to find a good feeling on the court.“I know that when I’m feeling well and striking the ball well I can still compete at the highest level. This week has been an evidence to that. I’m very proud. This trophy means much more than one trophy, one tournament.”Earlier,Carlos Alcarazdefeated Jiri Lehecka in the final of the Japan Open to win his first individual title since February. Playing only his third tournament since returning from four and a-half months out with a wrist injury, Alcaraz recovered from a shaky start to defeat the Czech Lehecka 7-6, 6-4.Carlos Alcaraz takes first title since February with victory in Japan Open final – videoIt is a second title in a row in the Japanese capital for Alcaraz, who showed patchy form at times but finished strongly. The Spaniard told Sky Sports: “I’m really happy to be able to lift a trophy again. It’s been a while and obviously it’s extra special after my injury.“It was a tough week that I didn’t find my best tennis, my best level, but I did find the good solutions and I think that’s what matters in the end. I would say today was the best match of the week, or at least more consistent the level that I played, so I’m just really, really happy.”Meanwhile, Jannik Sinner confirmed on Tuesday that he will be out for the rest of the year due to an injured knee.“On ‌the advice of his ‌medical team, Jannik Sinner will follow a course of treatment for inflammation in his knee,” his ‌team said in a statement. “The decision has been ​made to have the treatment now to give Jannik the necessary ⁠time to recover before beginning ​preparations ​for 2027. As ​a result, Jannik ​will ‌be unable ​to ​compete again during the 2026 season.”Explore more on these topicsTennisCarlos AlcaraznewsShareReuse this content

title: Sturm warning rocks Pocognoli as abject Scotland turned over by Slovenia | Nations League | The Guardian
description: Sébastian Pocognoli’s start as Scotland manager took a turn for the worse as Slovenia completed a 2-1 comeback win at Hampden Park
Author: Ewan Murray
Headline: Sébastian Pocognoli’s start as Scotland manager took a turn for the worse as Slovenia completed a 2-1 comeback win at Hampden Park
Content: Danijel Sturm completes Slovenia’s second-half comeback at Hampden Park.Photograph: Ian MacNicol/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDanijel Sturm completes Slovenia’s second-half comeback at Hampden Park.Photograph: Ian MacNicol/Getty ImagesNations LeagueSturm warning rocks Pocognoli as abject Scotland turned over by SloveniaEwan Murrayat Hampden ParkTue 6 Oct 2026 16.50 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe nature of this Scotland defeat felt far more significant than the fact it arrived at all. Sébastien Pocognoli is already in tricky territory, just four games into his tenure as Scotland head coach. Slovenia comprehensively outplayed the fragile hosts at Hampden Park, which leaves Pocognoli staring at a third-placed finish in a softNations Leaguesection. Brave new dawn or beginning of an error?Scotland were defensively disorganised. Their attacking play was timid. Long before full time, the 39-year-old Belgian had the look of a coach throwing darts blindly at a board. And missing. Wastefulness fromSloveniaprevented Scottish embarrassment.Cristiano Ronaldo accuses Portugal coach Jorge Jesus of broken promisesRead moreA scathing assessment arrived from theScotlandcaptain, Andy Robertson, who admitted his team were “outfought”. Robertson added: “They looked a lot fresher, a lot more hungry.”Pocognoli was more circumspect. “We didn’t play the game we wanted to,” he said. “We were not at the level we expect to be. I will not say everything is perfect or everything is bad but we need to improve many things. We have enough quality.”A pre-match presentation to Robertson, who reached the 100-cap mark duringScotland’s win in North Macedoniaon Saturday, carried wider meaning. Gordon Strachan and Alex McLeish, Robertson’s first two Scotland managers, were joined on the Hampden pitch by Steve Clarke. This marked a swift and welcome return to the national stadium for Clarke, who departed the Scotland job in unsatisfactory circumstances following failings at the World Cup. Clarke, bashful by nature, took as significant a bow as was ever likely before supporters.Scotland find themselves in a post-Clarke state of flux. He was the manager who made this country relevant on the wider stage once again. There was, however, widespread criticism that Clarke’s team lacked ambition. Pocognoli has been charged with not only maintaining at least decent results but also delivering an alternative brand of football. It is a fanciful quest, perhaps.The first quarter mirrored the opening half whenthese teams met in Ljubljana. Scotland looked uncertain. Slovenia were perfectly comfortable, not only in a defensive sense but when springing into attack. Adam Gnezda Cerin should have afforded the visitors a 13th-minute lead but failed to connect with appropriate force, allowing Jack Hendry to boot clear when just three yards from his own goal. This venue, which should be an asset to Scotland, was eerily quiet.Ryan Christie raised the mood. That the goal was horribly ugly mattered not a jot to the Scottish contingent. A short free-kick was played wide to Ben Gannon-Doak, whose deflected cross was headed on to a post by Hendry. Modern football’s madness means Oli McBurnie will be credited with an assist for the header with which he was undoubtedly trying to score. The ball instead landed at the feet of Christie, who tapped home from close range.View image in fullscreenRyan Christie gives Scotland the lead from close range.Photograph: Robert Perry/EPARobertson demonstrated his ongoing value before the break. Zan Vipotnik seemed certain to equalise before the Tottenham full-back’s rescue act, courtesy of a sliding block. Ominously for Scotland, Danijel Sturm had totally bamboozled their three-man defence when supplying Vipotnik.It was impossible to argue Slovenia were not worthy of their equaliser, which arrived 11 minutes after half-time. It came from a Scotland throw-in, where possession was cheaply conceded. Sturm played through the centre and towards Aljosa Matko, who brushed Luis Binks aside as if the Brøndby defender was not even there. The Scotland goalkeeper Angus Gunn, as is something of a theme, was weak in trying to deal with Matko’s shot. Sturm should have sent Slovenia in front two minutes later but saved the blushes of a hilariously open Scotland defence by shooting over. This had to be alarming for Pocognoli.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSlovenia were swaggering around their hosts. Pocognoli switched to a back four for the first time in this elongated international window shortly before Matko was denied his second goal of the night by an offside flag. The decision was not at all debatable.View image in fullscreenScotland’s Sébastian Pocognoli looks away in horror on the touchline.Photograph: Ian MacNicol/Getty ImagesNeither was the goal which took Slovenia ahead. This time Matko turned supplier, having rampaged down the right flank and crossed for the onrushing Sturm. Gunn was left with no chance as Sturm slammed the ball past him. Pocognoli was now subjected to Tartan Army boos.Findlay Curtis and Josh McPake had penalty claims rejected for Scotland. Desperation had indeed become the order of the day. McPake was at least lively, having stepped from the bench. Too many of his teammates either underperformed or are not cut out for this level. It is up to Pocognoli to source answers, and sharply. This is no patient football domain.Explore more on these topicsNations LeagueScotlandSloveniamatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Fifa reportedly allowed DR Congo into World Cup despite ineligible player in qualifying | World Cup 2026 | The Guardian
description: Fifa allowed the Democratic Republic of the Congo to compete at this summer’s World Cup despite reports suggesting an internal investigation found that the country had fielded an ineligible player in qualifying
Author: Paul MacInnes
Headline: Fifa allowed the Democratic Republic of the Congo to compete at this summer’s World Cup despite reports suggesting an internal investigation found that the country had fielded an ineligible player in qualifying
Content: Lionel Mpasi played a key role for the Democratic Republic of the Congo at this summer’s World Cup.Photograph: Daniel Becerril/ReutersView image in fullscreenLionel Mpasi played a key role for the Democratic Republic of the Congo at this summer’s World Cup.Photograph: Daniel Becerril/ReutersWorld Cup 2026Fifa reportedly allowed DR Congo into World Cup despite ineligible player in qualifyingNigeria filed complaint over ineligible players in playoffFifa investigators aware of situation before tournamentPaul MacInnesTue 6 Oct 2026 14.12 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFifa allowed the Democratic Republic of the Congo to compete at this summer’sWorld Cupdespite reports suggesting an internal investigation found that the country had fielded an ineligible player in qualifying.The player in question, the goalkeeper Lionel Mpasi, starred for his nation at the tournament, including againstEngland in the last 32. Mpasi, who was born in France and played forLes Bleusat youth level, had never completed the process of switching nationalities, Fifa reportedly found. No punishment was levied against the Congolese federation, Fecofa.Lionel Messi has completed football and can bid Argentina farewell with prideRead moreThe news willagain raise questionsover the Fifa president, Gianni Infantino, with a series of governance scandals having brought heightened scrutiny on his position. Fifa’s investigative teams are independent and the president has no input into their proceedings. Fifa is understood to have denied that Infantino played a part in the decision-making process over Mpasi, but his name is likely to remain in focus owing to a former university associate, Véron Mosengo-Omba, being elected unopposed as president of Fecofa this May.The Nigerian Football Federation submitted a complaint over the DRC apparently fielding ineligible players during a World Cup playoff tie between the nations, which the DRC won on penalties, in November.According to reporting by the New York Times and Le Monde,Fifainvestigators were aware of Mpasi’s situation before the DRC defeated Jamaica in a final intercontinental playoff round in March. Faced with a series of possible responses, including banning the DRC from the playoffs, Fifa chose to reject the Nigeria complaint on the grounds it had not been submitted within the necessary timeframe.Nigeria appealed against the decision and government representatives have suggested they could seek financial compensation for their loss, with a member of the national sports commission , which regulates Nigerian sport, telling ESPN: “Nothing has been decided yet, but we will seriously consider seeking compensation from Fifa for all of the economic losses this has cost Nigeria.”Concacaf, the North and Central American and Caribbean confederation, which includes Jamaica among its members, said it “takes player eligibility matters very seriously and expects the applicable regulations and procedures to be applied consistently and fairly in all competitions”. In a statement it asked that any “concerns regarding player eligibility” be “thoroughly reviewed and addressed through Fifa’s appropriate governance and disciplinary bodies”.Fifa, Concacaf, Caf, the Nigeria Football Federation and Fecofa, were all approached for comment.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOn Tuesday the Norwegian football federation confirmed it had submitted a three-pronged complaint to Fifa over its governance, including the decision tooverturn a red cardawarded to the USA’s Folarin Balogun after a telephone intervention by Donald Trump. The other instances cited by the NFF are the Fifa peace prize and the abandoned plan to sell a share in the World Cup to investors, known as theFifa Forward Enterprise scheme.“Each of these cases must be assessed based on the facts of each individual case,” said the president of the NFF, Lise Klaveness. “At the same time, the cases point to a more fundamental question: has Fifa’s position, authority or influence been used in a way that was not appropriate, and if so, did the mechanisms that were supposed to prevent this function work as they should?”Explore more on these topicsWorld Cup 2026FifaDemocratic Republic of the Congo football teamGianni InfantinoWorld CupFootball politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Too nice: do Arsenal lack the grit and tenacity to end WSL title drought? | Arsenal Women | The Guardian
description: Renée Slegers’ team have the technical ability to succeed, but doubts remain over the nastiness needed to rival Manchester City and Chelsea
Author: Tom Garry
Headline: Renée Slegers’ team have the technical ability to succeed, but doubts remain over the nastiness needed to rival Manchester City and Chelsea
Content: Arsenal fell 10 points behind the WSL leaders Manchester City after a 4-2 defeat on Sunday.Photograph: Molly Darlington/WSL/WSL Football/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenArsenal fell 10 points behind the WSL leaders Manchester City after a 4-2 defeat on Sunday.Photograph: Molly Darlington/WSL/WSL Football/Getty ImagesArsenal WomenToo nice: do Arsenal lack the grit and tenacity to end WSL title drought?RenéeSlegers’ team have the technical ability, but doubts remain over the nastiness needed to rival Manchester City and ChelseaTom GarryTue 6 Oct 2026 12.55 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 14.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleArsenal, 10 points adrift of the Women’s Super League leaders, are poised to undertake a “big review” of their season during this international break to try to determine where things have gone so horribly wrong – again – in the early stages. After their4-2 loss at Manchester Cityon Sunday, it felt as if the agenda needs to include an unusual but potentially critical question: is this team nasty enough to win a WSL title?The technical ability throughout the world-class squad Arsenal have assembled could hardly be higher but the levels of grit, resilience and tenacity need examining in a group that appears unable to match Chelsea and Manchester City when it comes to the mental aspects of a title race. Arsenal last won the WSLin 2019.WSL talking points: heat cranks up on Arsenal but Putellas and Diani shineRead moreWhen speaking to sources close to the Arsenal players, it is common to hear of the squad being like a “family”, very supportive of each other and full of “great people”. Those admirable traits, and a general sense the club is full of nice characters, often come across when watching games or during player interviews. Arsenal have built a team of good eggs; polite, courteous and professional individuals who people would be glad to call friends. In the vast majority of scenarios in life this is, quite obviously, a good thing. But are they too nice to beat City?It is quite hard to imagine many of the Arsenal squad raising their voices in anger. It is equally hard to recall the last time anybody at the club engaged in so-called “housery”; perhaps not sinceKatie McCabe’s hair pullagainst Chelsea in last season’s Champions League quarter-final. The irony is that McCabe is one of the senior, influential players who left this summer – in her case to join Chelsea – and McCabe, regardless of what fans might think of her, is someone Arsenal could rely on to roll up her sleeves and get stuck in, to raise her game in a hostile atmosphere and be combative.Last term, no Arsenal players – not even McCabe – registered in Stats Perform’s list of the top 20 WSL players for percentage of duels won. Only one Arsenal player has been shown a red card in a WSL game since 2021-22. Admirable discipline, yes, but are they lacking that fire in the belly?This season, the team appear to be without a dogged, refuse-to-lose type of character in the mould of Lucy Bronze, whose never-say-die attitude has frequently come to England’s aid in crucial moments at major tournaments; or the gritty battling spirit of Erin Cuthbert, who has helped Chelsea lift seven league titles; or – to take an Arsenal example – a leader such as Gabriel Magalhães, a rock for others to lean on during tough games.It is possible to be successful without a Roy Keane in your squad and Arsenal do have Leah Williamson, who has led England to two European titles, so it would be wrong to imply there is no leadership in this group. Leaders can step up in different ways but recently RenéeSlegers, when praising her senior players’ reactions to theirdisappointing draw in Paris, mentioned there had been “lots of hugs” and praised how supportive everybody had been for each other. That sounds like the sort of unified workplace culture millions would envy, but to win titles sometimes you need to fall out, yell, be angry and demand higher standards.View image in fullscreenOnly one Arsenal player has been shown a red card in a WSL game since 2021-22.Photograph: Molly Darlington/WSL/WSL Football/Getty ImagesOn Friday I asked Slegers whether Arsenal had enough of a nasty edge to win the league, and she replied defiantly: “I think so, and nastiness or that grittiness, that can express itself in different ways, and I think we have certain ways in which we express that and [in] which we can do that. But of course, with our performances where we haven’t been at our best, you maybe don’t see those moments as much which we can bring, but we’re convinced that we can bring that to games as well, in our way, the Arsenal way, because it’s definitely there.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThat was not evident on Sunday in the little – but important – moments, such as shortly after Arsenal had twice taken a lead they would surrender. City seemed unfazed and carried the resolve of a team who had no doubt they would win.Part of the way that belief has been instilled into the defending champions was evidenced in a clip, released by Sky Sports, of Andrée Jeglertz’s pre-match team talk, which he concluded with the words: “The most important thing: we are Manchester City, we are playing at home and we are winning this game.” The matter-of-fact, defiant instruction was not easy to imagine hearing in this Arsenal dressing room with any real conviction right now, not from the players and not from Slegers, who has many excellent qualities as coach, and is, by all accounts, an intelligent, detail-oriented coach of whom the players are very fond.In decades to come, all the nice characteristics this Arsenal squad demonstrate will no doubt stand them in good stead in the real world, with their friendships, but the cliche “nice guys finish last” is starting to feel increasingly appropriate for this amiable side.Explore more on these topicsArsenal WomenWomen's Super LeagueWomen's footballfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Cameron Green injury opens door to Nic Maddinson ahead of first South Africa Test | Australia cricket team | The Guardian
description: Andrew McDonald insists Nic Maddinson’s Test squad call-up should be no shock, with the left-hander edging closer to replacing the injured Cameron Green
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Andrew McDonald insists Nic Maddinson’s Test squad call-up should be no shock, with the left-hander edging closer to replacing the injured Cameron Green
Content: Nic Maddinson is tipped to replace the injured Cameron Green for Australia in the first Test against South Africa in Durban.Photograph: Josh Chadwick/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenNic Maddinson is tipped to replace the injured Cameron Green for Australia in the first Test against South Africa in Durban.Photograph: Josh Chadwick/Getty ImagesAustralia cricket teamCameron Green injury opens door to Nic Maddinson ahead of first South Africa TestAustralia all-rounder fails to overcome abdominal strainMaddinson or Cooper Connolly to fill No 5 spot in Durban openerAustralian Associated PressTue 6 Oct 2026 18.29 EDTFirst published on Tue 6 Oct 2026 17.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndrew McDonald insists Nic Maddinson’s Test squad call-up should be no shock, with the left-hander edging closer to replacing the injured Cameron Green in Durban.Green has been officially ruled out of Australia’s side for the opening Test against South Africa, after failing to overcome the abdominal strain suffered in last week’s final ODI.Sandpaper made Australia the story in 2018 while South Africa’s achievement faded into irrelevanceRead moreAustralia are confident the allrounder will return in the three-Test series, but do not expect to have him bowling given he was also managing a shoulder issue.That has left the tourists with a call to make between Maddinson and Cooper Connolly, with a dry Kingsmead pitch ahead of Friday a major consideration.Maddinson’s Test squad call up following a one-day cup century and Josh Inglis’s fractured finger was a feelgood story, given he beat testicular cancer last year.But it was also met with surprise and strong criticism from the likes of Matthew Hayden, with the 35-year-old’s last Test in December 2016 and most recent first-class appearance 18 months ago.Maddinson did average 52.37 in the Sheffield Shield from December 2018 to March 2024, before a difficult 2024-25 summer while feeling run down prior to his cancer diagnosis.“From 2018 to 2024, he was one of the leading players in Shield cricket,” McDonald said. “Anyone that’s been on the radar or there or thereabouts, they don’t drop off automatically.“If Nic comes in, he can bat at the top, he can bat in the middle. We feel like he’s got some good craft against spin and quality pace. He’s been at this level before. It may not have been obvious for others, but we felt like he was the player that we needed, in particular with Josh Inglis going out, in terms of his flexibility.”Maddinson was not picked on Australia’s recent A-tour of India with McDonald reasoning there was a balance of also taking players for the future. But he has played six first-class games for Australia A since his last Test.Sam Harper was also called up as another replacement for Inglis, but the Victorian is more filling the role of a reserve wicketkeeper.“We’re going to get challenged with spin and tours to the subcontinent we’ve had in the past, Nic’s been well and truly in our thoughts for those,” McDonald said.“Lost in all of that has been Sam Harper’s story as well with his battles. He missed a lot of cricket with that heavy concussion early in his career. That should be the story. It should be exciting for those guys coming into the Test squad, as opposed to potentially negativity around the selection.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMcDonald indicated Travis Head would still open rather than move to No 5 to replace Green, while Alex Carey will also remain at No 6.The potential of a dry Kingsmead also looms, with the expectation spin could become an increasing factor through the Test.Australia have Matt Kuhnemann in their squad, but have traditionally been hesitant to play a second tweaker ahead of one of their three frontline quicks outside of Asia.“It would have to be quite compelling for us to shift into two spinners,” McDonald said, suggesting they were “open to all options”.McDonald also suggested Connolly’s ability to bowl spin would not be a major factor for selectors.“It would be factored in, but ultimately when you bat in the top-six or the top-seven, runs are the critically important piece to that,” he said.“We have got some other spinning all-round options, if you want to call it, or part-time bowlers in the top-order there that can pick up some overs if we need be.”Explore more on these topicsAustralia cricket teamSouth Africa cricket teamCricketAustralia sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Jude Bellingham hails 125-cap Harry Kane as England’s best-ever player | Harry Kane | The Guardian
description: Harry Kane was described as England’s best ever player by Jude Bellingham after the 3-0 Nations League victory over Czechia
Author: Jacob Steinberg
Headline: Harry Kane was described as England’s best ever player by Jude Bellingham after the 3-0 Nations League victory over Czechia
Content: Jude Bellingham congratulates Harry Kane after his second goal.Photograph: Catherine Ivill/AMA/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJude Bellingham congratulates Harry Kane after his second goal.Photograph: Catherine Ivill/AMA/Getty ImagesHarry KaneJude Bellingham hails 125-cap Harry Kane as England’s best-ever playerCaptain scores twice in 3-0 win over CzechiaKane equals Peter Shilton’s appearance recordJacob Steinbergat WembleyTue 6 Oct 2026 18.25 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJude Bellingham called Harry Kane England’s best-ever player after the captain equalled Peter Shilton’s record of 125 caps during Tuesday’s3-0 win over Czechiain the Nations League.Kane, who is only nine off a century of international goals after scoring twice in another fine display, was the star attraction as the Wembley crowd watched Thomas Tuchel’s side close on a spot in March’s quarter-finals. England’s record goalscorer showed why he is in the running for the Ballon d’Or and the way the Bayern Munich striker passed another milestone earned him rave reviews from Bellingham.Harry Kane doubles up on landmark night as England cruise past CzechiaRead more“There’s not much more you can say that hasn’t already been said,” the midfielder said. “From my perspective first and foremost he is an unbelievable human being, as a captain and a man.“He is the bestEnglandplayer to ever wear the shirt and it is an honour to play with him. He is pretty unmatched. He is scoring goals for fun, he goes deep and he gets tackles in. He is only getting better.”Kane, who made the opening goal when he crossed for Czechia’s Vladimir Coufal to put into his own net, said making his 125th appearance for his country goes down as one of the biggest achievements of his career.“I think it’s right up there,” the 33-year-old said. “There are so many milestones throughout your career. This is even beyond my wildest dreams. To be joint at 125 is an extreme privilege. I love coming to every England camp. Tonight was a special night. It’s not about me, it’s about the team. To help the team with a couple of goals and a good team performance, it’s been the perfect night for me.”The former Tottenham forward will break Shilton’s record when England, who are second in Group A3 with two games left, host Croatia next month. He has no intention of slowing down.“I’m not going to be around for ever and I still hope that’s a long way away,” Kane said. “I hope there’s still more to go. I guess only time dictates that. I still feel like I’ve got room to improve.“I’ve just come back off my best season ever and right now I feel in an even better place. I’m not going to stop. I’m going to keep pushing and see where it takes me. Maybe in 10 years or so, we’ll see where that ceiling is at.”Kane, who made clear that he would swap all of his individual accolades for a major trophy with England, laughed at the thought of chasing down the overall record of international goals: Cristiano Ronaldo’s tally of 146 for Portugal.“Maybe that’s the ceiling we’re talking about,” he said. “We’ll see … it’s 50 odd goals, an awful long way away, but who knows? I’m in great shape.“I’ve said before about players who have played well into the late 30s, still at the highest level, and even into the 40s. As long as I feel I can help the team I’ll be around. The moment I feel like I can’t, I won’t. That’s just the way I am.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThe joint record holders on Wembley’s big screen.Photograph: Nigel French/Getty Images/AllstarKane also thought about whether the appearance record matters more than reaching 100 goals.“I got asked this question by a few of the staff before the game,” he said. “The 100 goals is maybe a more exclusive club and being a striker, it would be an incredible club to be a part of.“Obviously I’m getting closer to the 100 now. I’m in the 90s. I try not to think about it too much. It’s like being a cricketer in the nineties – the more you think about the 100, you don’t always get there. I’m just going with the flow right now.”Tuchel, who said that Kane “deserves the stage, the praise”, feels that England have progressed since finishing third at the World Cup. “I think it’s necessary to move on,” the manager said.“We didn’t go out in the group stage – it sometimes feels like that but we didn’t. There were some question marks but we are trying to build something. When there was a bit of criticism, I said we don’t start completely new because we can build together. Now we take the next step.”Explore more on these topicsHarry KaneEnglandCzechiaNations LeagueThomas TuchelnewsShareReuse this content

title: Harry Kane wins record-equalling 125th England cap, drawing level with Peter Shilton | Harry Kane | The Guardian
description: Harry Kane made a record-equalling 125th appearance for England’s men against Czechia at Wembley, drawing level with Peter Shilton
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: Harry Kane made a record-equalling 125th appearance for England’s men against Czechia at Wembley, drawing level with Peter Shilton
Content: Harry Kane with Jordan Pickford during the pre-match ceremomy.Photograph: Charlotte Wilson/Offside/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenHarry Kane with Jordan Pickford during the pre-match ceremomy.Photograph: Charlotte Wilson/Offside/Getty ImagesHarry KaneHarry Kane wins record-equalling 125th England cap, drawing level with Peter ShiltonStriker starts against Czechia at WembleyJoint-top of England men’s list and behind seven womenGuardian sportTue 6 Oct 2026 13.32 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 17.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHarry Kane made a record-equalling 125th appearance for England on Tuesday night against Czechia at Wembley, drawing level with Peter Shilton.Kane, who made his debut in March 2015, was selected to start his fourth international game in 13 days. It draws the striker level with Shilton as the most-cappedEnglandmen’s player.Seven women have made more England appearances, with the list topped by Fara Williams, who played 172 times. Kane has scored an England record 89 goals, including four in this window. Before kick-off, Kane said: “It’s always special [walking out at Wembley] and the excitement of what’s to come. It’s a special night but we’ve got to focus on the job and hopefully finish off with a win.”Graphic showing England men’s most-capped playersShilton, the former goalkeeper, made his appearances from 1970 to 1990, his caps reduced by a period when he and Ray Clemence were rotated. Clemence won 61 caps from 1972 to 1983.Shilton, who played for England from 1970 to 1990, congratulated Kane in a video message on social media — and said the former Tottenham striker could set an appearance record that “might never be beaten.”“Because you’re still going strong, Harry,” the 77-year-old Shilton said. “You’re still playing well and scoring goals. And I know how much dedication and hard work you actually put into achieving this.”Kane will hope to move ahead of Shilton when England play at home to Croatia in their next game, on 12 November.Explore more on these topicsHarry KaneEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

Headline: How will the USA and Canada fare today? Here is what to know, including kick-off time, TV channels and live stream options
Content: Mauricio Pochettino are looking to close out the international window with four wins from four.Photograph: Taylor Nickerson/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenMauricio Pochettino are looking to close out the international window with four wins from four.Photograph: Taylor Nickerson/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockSoccer watching and streaming guideSoccerInternational friendly match today: How to watch USA v Canada, TV channels & live stream Wednesday 6 OctoberHow will the USA and Canada fare today? Here is what to know, including kick-off time, TV channels and live stream optionsGraham RuthvenTue 6 Oct 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 15.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBasking in the glow ofa 3-0 win over Mexico on Saturday, the US men’s national team are in a good place right now. A fourth straight win would make this window a resounding success for Mauricio Pochettino and his players.Canada, however, have won their last two encounters with the USMNT, and are fresh from back-to-back victories over Chile and Peru. Jesse Marsch’s side have good reason to believe they can leave Minnesota with a third successive win.While this rivalry lacks the ferocity of the one between Mexico and the USA, Canada have more than proven themselves as a member of Concacaf’s elite in recent times with Marschalways keen to make a pointto US Soccer after being passed over for the national team job.Here is your complete guide on how to watch Tuesday’s international friendly fixture, including kick-off times, broadcast networks, and online streaming options.USA v CanadaTime (ET):8pmStadium:Allianz Field (St Paul, Minnesota)How to watchUnited States:FS2,Stream on FuboCanada:Stream on FuboWhat to watch forPochettino’s youthful revolutionhas re-energised the USMNTafter the 2026 World Cup with prospects such as Cavan Sullivan, Julian Hall and Diego Kochen all showing why they deserve to play an important role in the national team’s next cycle.After three games in little over a week, Pochettino is expected to rotate his team. This makes it difficult to predict the lineup that will take to the field on Tuesday. Nonetheless, the USMNT won’t be short of players hoping to make a good impression.Marsch says Canada “can beat just about anybody.” However, the visitors must ensure the transition moments fall in their favor otherwise the US could blow away another opponent, after scoring 11 times in their last three outings.Player to watch:Cavan Sullivan,USA- The 17-year-old was the star man (boy?) for the USMNT against Mexico, scoring his first international goal just a few days after making his first international start.
