title: ‘We’re not going to go away’: the mom fighting for social media reform after her son’s suicide | Documentary films | The Guardian
description: A new documentary follows Kristin Bride as she takes on Congress after the death of her 16-year-old son who was cyberbullied
Author: Vivian Ho
Headline: A new documentary follows Kristin Bride as she takes on Congress after the death of her 16-year-old son who was cyberbullied
Content: Kristin Bride in a still from Your Attention Please.Photograph: Yahna Harris/Attention RebellionView image in fullscreenKristin Bride in a still from Your Attention Please.Photograph: Yahna Harris/Attention RebellionDocumentary films‘We’re not going to go away’: the mom fighting for social media reform after her son’s suicideA new documentary follows Kristin Bride as she takes on Congress after the death of her 16-year-old son who was cyberbulliedVivian HoTue 6 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 12.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt this point in time, going anywhere without your smartphone feels almost like leaving behind a limb. Whether it’s for directions, distraction or the discourse on social media, our phones have become both a necessity and a crutch in our everyday lives, with our bodiesliterally evolvingaround the glow of the screen.But no matter how much we think we need all the bells and whistles of the attention economy, the attention economy actually needs us more than we need it.This is the overarching message of the documentary Your Attention Please, available to rent or own on 6 October. The film explores the human cost of our technology addiction – as well as the very human efforts to combat it – driving home how social media companies likeMetaandTikTokbenefit financially in rewiring our brains in order to keep us scrolling.“We’re dealing with a business model that encourages extreme behaviors because those have been proven to be more attention-grabbing,” director Sara Robin says in an interview.The documentary follows Kristin Bride in herfight for social media reform, traveling to Capitol Hill to push for legislation and testifying before Congress. Bride was thrust into online safety advocacy after her 16-year-old son, Carson, was cyberbullied and took his own life in 2020 – even after she thought she took all the right steps to safeguard him from the dangers of the internet.“We waited until Carson was through middle school to give him his first very old iPhone with no apps on it, and we had really hoped that it would stay that way,” she says. “But when he got to 10th grade, he begged for Snapchat because that was the way that all the kids were connecting … he didn’t make it to 11th grade.”But social media is not just dangerous for kids, which the documentary makes a point of highlighting through interviews with experts like the former US surgeon generalVivek Murthy, who has called for tobacco-style warning labels on social media platforms, as well asFrances Haugen, the Facebook whistleblower who will be portrayed by Mikey Madison inThe Social Reckoningout this week.Robin likes to quote Cal Newport, a computer science professor at Georgetown University, in describing social media as “designed to feel as if you are slipping into a warm bath”. “You go on there and then you forget why you got on there and you forget what you’re doing while you’re on there and then two hours have passed,” she says. The bath in this analogy, however, is actually more a pot – and we are the frogs being slowly boiled alive without realizing it.“In a time where social media is still designed to actively disrupt our lives, it’s really up to us now to say: ‘My goal today is to get more out of social media than it will get out of me,’” Robin says. “That’s quite hard to do. But I think in the interim, when we’re still dealing with these, highly addictive, very imperfect platforms that are designed to exploit our attention, that’s to an extent what we have to do while we’re transitioning to something healthier.”View image in fullscreenA still from Your Attention Please.Photograph: Yahna Harris/Attention RebellionWhile both Bride and Robin hope the documentary will make people confront their phone addictions and social media usage, they also see it as a call to action – whether in Bride’s continued fight to get Congress topass the Kids Online Safety and Privacy Actor in being part of a cultural shift to get off your phone. The documentary features interviews with the founders of the Offline Club in Amsterdam, where attenders must check their phones at the door before events, and with the principal and a teacher of Brockton high school in Massachusetts, where students are required to keep their devices locked in secure pouches for the entire school day, as examples of how this is possible.“We’re not anti-tech – we’re pro-better tech and we’re pro a more balanced relationship with tech,” Robin says. She acknowledges the irony that with the promotion of the film, she is more on social media than she’s ever been before. “A lot of the conversation critical of the attention economy is happening on these attention economy platforms,” she says.But she is not denying that social media has been a society-changing tool in how it has allowed people to connect and organize and self-promote – it’s just that the companies behind these platforms have designed their algorithms to keep its users on there as long as possible, beyond their original purpose. “If monetary value trumps everything else, then we naturally land in a situation where the human being is forgotten,” Robin says.The way to combat this on an individual level is to be intentional with your usage. “Be very clear what you’re looking to get out of the platform,” Robin says. “Go in and do that. Know the moment you open it, it’ll throw the most distracting thing at you. Pull yourself back out. Do the thing that you intended to do, and then get out.”On a larger scale, the fight will be even more challenging. Bride says two years later that she is back to where she was in the documentary with theKids Online Safety and Privacy Act– the bill stalled after passing in the Senate in 2024. Seeing Donald Trump buddying up with the tech billionaires behind these platforms has been particularly disheartening, Bride says.“But how can we not keep fighting?” Bride says. “We’re not going to go away, and we’re going to keep being loud and vocal.”Your Attention Please is streaming on Documentary+ and is also available on VOD nowIn the US, you can call or text the988 Suicide & Crisis Lifelineat 988 or chat at988lifeline.org. In the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsDocumentary filmsSocial mediaFacebookMetaDigital mediaSocial networkingTikTokfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Silver Pines review – a stylish, neo-noir detective drama | Games | The Guardian
description: Abandoned shops, ruined apartment buildings and rotting sewer networks make up a dark landscape in which you play a private eye searching for a missing singer-songwriter
Author: Keith Stuart
Headline: Abandoned shops, ruined apartment buildings and rotting sewer networks make up a dark landscape in which you play a private eye searching for a missing singer-songwriter
Content: A game to sit back and wallow in … Silver Pines.Photograph: Wych Elm Games, Team 17View image in fullscreenA game to sit back and wallow in … Silver Pines.Photograph: Wych Elm Games, Team 17GamesReviewSilver Pines review – a stylish, neo-noir detective dramaPC, PS5, Switch 2; Wych Elm Games, Team 17Abandoned shops, ruined apartment buildings and rotting sewer networks make up a dark landscape in which you play a private eye searching for a missing singer-songwriterKeith StuartTue 6 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 09.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn a weird deserted town miles from anywhere, a troubled detective searches for a missing musician and the girl he may or may not have murdered. It could be a Silent Hill game or a lost David Lynch movie from the 1990s – in fact, it’s neither. And also both. If that whets your appetite, stick around, there’s plenty more to come.Developed by Scandinavian studio Wych ElmGames, Silver Pines is a dark Metroidvania-style adventure, where you play as shambling private eye, Red Walker, exploring a 2D universe of abandoned shops, ruined apartment buildings and rotting sewer networks. Officially, everyone has left because of an incoming storm, but very quickly you learn that something much darker is afoot. Someone has hired you to find singer-songwriter Eddie Velvet, but you don’t know why; your only contact with your client is via the payphones dotted around town, where you can also save your progress – as long as you have a dollar to pay for the call. Each location is filled with clues and puzzles – a weird newspaper story pinned to the wall, a strange statue that needs a missing piece – and through these artefacts you unlock new rooms and descend further into the mystery.View image in fullscreenVery quickly you learn that something much darker is afoot … Silver Pines.Photograph: Wych Elm Games, Team 17This format will be incredibly familiar to anyone who has played a point-and-click adventure in the last 30 years; it’s not doing anything wildly original with the formula. And when the monsters inevitably emerge, you find yourself fighting them off with knives that break easily, and pistols that have to be painstakingly re-loaded with limited ammo, reminding you that you’re in survival horror territory, too.But what makes this game much more than an amalgam of familiar adventure tropes is its brilliant sense of style, it’s considered pace and it’s wonderfully constructed mythology. Using rotoscoping to create the lead character’s animation, he looks like some film noir drunk sloping around in the darkness, fumbling with clues. Each location is loaded with detail, from strange paintings, to battered furniture and fizzing neon signs, while parallax scrolling is used to brilliant effect, allowing you to see forthcoming locations in the distance as you wander the streets. Each room is beautifully constructed, so that as you move, the light coming from filthy windows or an old reading lamp sends slivers of shadow creeping over the walls. This is a design team that really understands the aesthetics of film noir, a fact underscored by the soundtrack a sleazy jazz club combo of Angelo Badalamenti and Vangelis.Silver Pines trailerAs you progress, new areas of the town open up, and you meet a few weird inhabitants that stuck around despite the incoming weather emergency, among them a cynical police chief and a brooding femme fatale. The puzzles can be obtuse, but thorough exploration often yields the answers you need: could you squeeze through that air duct? Could you climb that apparently impassable wall? Sometimes the answer is yes. Combat is always tense and panicked, especially the boss battles, where you’ll be floundering about with different weapons and ammunition as some Lovecraftian monstrosity pummels you. But then, this is very true to the earliest survival horror titles, where the inability to actually move, shoot and/or avoid incoming blows was part of the drama – you were always a victim and never a super cop. Besides, you can turn the difficulty right down if it’s the story you want to experience.As I played, I discovered countless references to 80s and 90s neo-noir culture – from Blue Velvet to Twin Peaks (you drink coffee to increase your stamina), from the X-Files to Alan Parker’s hellish Angel Heart. It was a pleasure to explore every broken-down movie theatre, oily car garage and sweat-stinking interrogation room, collecting weird trinkets and working out how they’d all fit together – then exploring them again (and again) when the answers failed to show up. Silver Pines is a game to sit back and wallow in, like a private eye, kicking off his wingtip shoes and pulling that bottle of bourbon from the bottom drawer as rain trickles down the window and sodium street lights paint the walls a sickly shade of yellow.Silver Pines is out 8 OctoberExplore more on these topicsGamesPCNintendo Switch 2PlayStation 5reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Artificial review – Luca Guadagnino takes on OpenAI in muddled tech satire | New York film festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: The origin story of Sam Altman’s company is reimagined as a campy comedy starring Andrew Garfield
Author: Owen Myers
Headline: The origin story of Sam Altman’s company is reimagined as a campy comedy starring Andrew Garfield
Content: Andrew Garfield as Sam Altman and Yura Borisov as Ilya Sutskever in Artificial.Photograph: Courtesy of NeonView image in fullscreenAndrew Garfield as Sam Altman and Yura Borisov as Ilya Sutskever in Artificial.Photograph: Courtesy of NeonFirst look reviewNew York film festival 2026ReviewArtificial review – Luca Guadagnino takes on OpenAI in muddled tech satireNew York film festival:The origin story of Sam Altman’s company is reimagined as a campy comedy starring Andrew GarfieldOwen MyersTue 6 Oct 2026 12.58 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 13.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn the day thatLuca Guadagnino’s film aboutSam AltmanandOpenAIpremiered, Vanity Fair released acover storyon Altman. Alongside glossy portraits from Annie Leibovitz, the world’s pre-eminent portrait photographer, the story describes him as the Oppenheimer of his day, evoking the image of a man leading humanity towards its own inevitable demise at the hands of sentient robots. Altman doesn’t seem to be grappling with much existential angst about the whole thing though: in aninterviewalso released this week, he said that we should be prepared to accept “bad things” in return for the benefits of AI.Club Kid review – Jordan Firstman’s heartfelt comedy is irresistibleRead moreHow much worse can things get? AI agents have alreadygone rogue, hacking into government systems and “bruteforcing” UN databases.Last year, a young woman usedChatGPTas a therapist before she killed herself (the software helped her write her suicide note). Studies show that using AI is probably leading us all towards something called cognitive surrender, which does not seem like the best use of your one wild and precious life.Artificial is a stylish and blunt satire that is unambiguous in its perspective: that Sam Altman is an amoral manipulator who might be dead inside. That goes some way towards explaining why Amazon MGM Studiospulled outof distributing the film in June (Jeff Bezos’s company has a $50bn investment in OpenAI). I found it to be more of an op-ed than a movie, with little insight into what makes Altman and the tech elite tick. Neither does it have much to say about the world – glossy magazines included – that has welcomed them with open arms.In 2003, a young math prodigy named Ilya Sutskever (Yura Borisov, the heartbeat of the film) visits Prof Geoff Hinton (Mark Rylance) in his office hoping for a job with the man known as the godfather of AI. “Have you ever considered the link between knowledge and patience?” Hinton serenely asks his young charge. You can almost feel Guadagnino is turning to the audience and giving us a big stage wink.Nine years later, Sutskever and Hinton’s technology is starting to work “much the way your mind does”, with an ability to differentiate between cats and dogs, but Sutskever is growing increasingly impatient with what he sees as Hinton’s conservative ambitions for the technology. It’s at this point that Elon Musk (Ike Barinholtz) introduces Sutskever to Sam Altman (Andrew Garfield), who is fresh from selling his Loopt app, a kind of proto-Find My Friends, for $40m.You Can See Everything review – Nathan Fielder’s Elizabeth Holmes doc is a modern masterpiece of deceitRead moreThese guys are total dweebs, peppering each other with puerile jokes while doing shots in upscale restaurants as servers grimace and pray for a tip. Everyone is starting to want what these guys are selling, and one prospective investor speculates that AI will soon be able to reverse climate change and cure cancer. When talking about the technology, Sutskever’s eyes light up. “All pain, all loneliness will cease,” he says, as knowingly over-the-top haunted house music plays. “We will be free.”The film’s dramatic tension rests in the opposing poles of thought represented by Sutskever, a delusional optimist, and the self-motivated hubris of Altman. As we move into the recent past, cracks and fissures appear in their partnership as OpenAI’s self-learning technology begins to first outsmart humans at video games, and then becomes a different beast entirely. Garfield is brilliantly slimy, nailing Altman’s evolution from demon twink to a narcissistic grifter with a victim complex that climaxes with him being fired as the CEO ofOpenAIand then rehired five days later. “They’re being very mean to me,” he pouts in one scene after his board airs one of its many legitimate concerns over the ethics of his product.View image in fullscreenYura Borisov, Luca Guadagnino, Andrew Garfield and Ike Barinholtz at the Artificial premiere at the New York film festival on Monday.Photograph: Michael Loccisano/Getty Images for FLCArtificial is the most outwardly comedic Guadagnino film to date, with a script by the New Yorker essayist Simon Rich. The humor can be frustratingly broad, and it often feels like Barinholtz is impersonating Mike Myers doing Musk on Saturday Night Live than the Tesla founder himself (Rich is a former writer on SNL). Garfield seems to be playing Altman, who is an out gay man, as more effete than he actually is, which is strange as there are plenty of reasons to laugh at the tech oligarch that don’t involve him being light in his loafers. At other times, the script is satisfyingly savage. After being questioned over safety concerns by his associate Mira Murati (Monica Barbaro), Altman snaps, “I didn’t invent teen suicide, Mira.”A Statement review – outstanding climate change dramedy about a 1980 meetingRead moreI could have done without some Artificial’s clangingly obvious visual metaphors, such as a random shot of a unhoused person wearing VR goggles, or the sudden plunge into a simulator-like sequence of a car accelerating over a foggy Golden Gate Bridge (we get it, we’re taking a reckless leap into the unknown). The film comes with a score by Damon Albarn, and the Blur frontman contributes one original composition that an ASPCA advert would reject for being too on-the-nose with lyrics like, “In a corrupt world, we’ll sing the saddest song.”It’s tech oligarch season at the movies, with films aboutElon Musk, Elizabeth Holmes and Mark Zuckerberg also due for release over the next few months as film-makers try to respond to the zeitgeist in real time. “We opened Pandora’s box,” Altman says in a standout monologue towards the end of the film. “Countries will fall, industries will collapse, and we get to be the ones to usher people into this new world.”It’s a grim prophecy that gets lost in Guadanigno’s tonal jumble of a film, which has a certain self-satisfaction in telling us that dystopia is upon us. I couldn’t help but crave a leaner, meaner version of this movie. Despite some genuinely chilling moments, Artificial shows the limits of holding up a mirror to the world.Artificial is screening at the New York film festival and wil be released in the US on 25 December, in Australia on 21 January and in the UK on 27 JanuaryExplore more on these topicsNew York film festival 2026First look reviewSam AltmanOpenAIAI (artificial intelligence)ComputingElon MuskLuca GuadagninoreviewsShareReuse this content

title: JD Vance and Ted Cruz are fighting for control of the GOP. The problem? Neither is called Trump | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: Having seemingly written off the midterms, the Republican bigwigs are making their pitches for 2028. But the current commander-in-chief could be looking closer to home, writes Arwa Mahdawi
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: Having seemingly written off the midterms, the Republican bigwigs are making their pitches for 2028. But the current commander-in-chief could be looking closer to home, writes Arwa Mahdawi
Content: Best of enemies … Ted Cruz and JD Vance at a conservative conference in 2023.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBest of enemies … Ted Cruz and JD Vance at a conservative conference in 2023.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesOpinionUS midterm elections 2026JD Vance and Ted Cruz are fighting for control of the GOP. The problem? Neither is called TrumpArwa MahdawiHaving seemingly written off the midterms, the Republican bigwigs are making their pitches for 2028. But the current commander-in-chief could be looking closer to homeTue 6 Oct 2026 10.46 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 17.15 EDTShareThe US midterm elections are a month away and it’s looking rough for the Republicans. I wouldn’t discountdevious schemesbehind the scenes, but, on the face of it, the president and his entourage seem to be flailing. Donald Trump is desperatelydangling moneyin front of voters andpromising “a big surprise”. Meanwhile, the vice-president, JD Vance, and the GOP senator Ted Cruz seem more concerned with fighting over who will be Trump’s heir than with the midterms.If the polls are to be believed,Vance is the frontrunnerfor the Republican presidential nomination in 2028. But while he may have great name recognition, Vance is also unlikable. According to theCNN analyst Harry Enten, he is one of the least popular vice-presidents in history. He’s also apparentlymade enemies within his own party, largely because of his scepticism about the Iran war. His detractors include Cruz, who toldMS Nowin August that Vance wasn’t a shoo-in for the nomination. The party, Cruz said, was still figuring out the best candidate and needed “to decide who we are, what do we believe”.These remarks did not go unnoticed by the ever-observant vice-president. “It is really obvious to me that, at this very moment, Ted Cruz is running for president,” Vance said in an interview with NBC Newson Friday. “At this moment, I’m not. I’m trying to help elect Republicans.”Cruz, in turn, denied he was thinking about 2028 yet and suggested Vance may have a chip on his shoulder. “In my experience, people engage in political bomb-throwing when they’re feeling insecure,” Cruztold Politicoon Saturday. “So he’s welcome to make whatever comments he likes.”Yes, please continue making whatever comments you like, JD! In fact, I’d strongly suggest you take it up a notch and remind people of Cruz’s greatest hits. There was the time he fled to Cancún on holiday when his state, Texas, was facingdeadly, record-breaking freezing temperatures, for example. And the time his official Twitter account “liked” apornographic tweet(apparently it was “a staffing issue, and it was inadvertent”). And there’s the longstanding joke, which started with a meme in 2013, that Cruz is theZodiac killer. Obviously, this was baseless, but it went viral because apparently it is believable. Indeed, a2016 pollfound that 10% of voters in Florida thought Cruz was the Zodiac killer and an additional 28% said they were not sure.That said, Vance should be careful about what he dishes out: he’s been the subject of a few memes himself. Who can forget the (completely unfounded) viral rumours about the vice-presidenthaving sexual relations with a couch?While Vance and Cruz may be butting heads now, I suspect they’ll eventually kiss and make up. They are pragmatists, which is a polite way to say soulless opportunists. They had similar journeys when it comes to Trump, for example. In 2016,Cruz called Trump, who nicknamed him Lyin’ Ted, a “serial philanderer” and a “pathological liar”. Around the same time, Vance wondered if Trump was“America’s Hitler”andcalled him“the most-raw expression of a massive finger pointed at other people”. Now, of course, it’s a very different story. Vance is veep and Cruz has become such a staunch Trump ally that the president calls himBeautiful Ted.With the news as grim as it is, you’ve got to find satisfaction where you can. And it’s certainly satisfying to watch Vance (who absolutely does not fornicate with furniture) and Cruz (who is definitely not the Zodiac killer) feud. Ultimately, though, it may turn out that we don’t have to worry about either man come 2028. MS Now’s Rachel Maddow thinks the president may follow the authoritarian playbook and install a family member as his successor.“If he wants [his family] to not end up in jail or prosecuted or having their … gains investigated … he’s got to make sure that the next president is also a Trump,” Maddow opined on arecent podcast. Potus himselfhas said“there could be” a Trump dynasty and seemed to suggest his daughter-in-law Lara may be his successor. Take a seat on a comfy couch for this one, JD: you’re going to have a tough time trumping a Trump.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines USGet the most important US headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionArwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Sorry, but I’m bringing my iced coffee to the job interview | Tayo Bero | The Guardian
description: What, exactly, about the drink is so distracting? The viral debate raises bigger questions about who defines ‘professionalism’
Author: Tayo Bero
Headline: What, exactly, about the drink is so distracting? The viral debate raises bigger questions about who defines ‘professionalism’
Content: ‘These discussions are a reminder of the deep chasms that exist generationally and culturally when it comes to notions of professionalism and how we’re supposed to show up in public life.’Photograph: vasa/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘These discussions are a reminder of the deep chasms that exist generationally and culturally when it comes to notions of professionalism and how we’re supposed to show up in public life.’Photograph: vasa/AlamyOpinionUS work & careersSorry, but I’m bringing my iced coffee to the job interviewTayo BeroWhat, exactly, about the drink is so distracting? The viral debate raises bigger questions about who defines ‘professionalism’Tue 6 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTShareThe greaticed coffee debateof 2026 is the latest submission to the young-people-just-don’t-get-it discourse and, of course, it’s as polarizing as ever.Recruiters say youshouldn’t bring iced coffee to interviews, while young people are (rightly) asking: what’s the big deal? It’s one of those conversations that makes me cringe, given just how eagerly it springs up from the generational divide plaguing mainstream culture. And as usual, gen Z are cast as the entitled morons who want to live life with no rules or responsibilities, all to the detriment of the millennials and gen X-ers who have to deal with them.Iced-coffeegate blew up on social media after the president of a recruiting firm shared a TikTok saying the drink “looks a little too casual” to hiring managers. With thousands of outraged responses across TikTok and Twitter/X, I was stunned to see so many people up in arms about someone bringing a coffee to an interview. Per one of my favorite comments: “It’s an iced coffee, not a bomb!”Still, these discussions are a reminder of the deep chasms that exist generationally and culturally when it comes to notions of professionalism and how we’re supposed to show up in public life. As I scrolled through endless posts lamenting how terrible youth culture is, I wondered seriously: what is it about an iced coffee that feels so distracting or unprofessional?Then again, so much of this is tied up in the cultural symbolism and associations we create with the world around us. Iced coffee? So gen Z. But what if it was a warm coffee, in a nice, grown-up looking travel mug? Or what if it was just water? See how silly and arbitrary it all is?But let’s put the iced coffee to the side.The bigger picture is that for the most part, rules of professionalism are rooted in racist constructs. From Eurocentric dress and hair codes to the weaponization of “what’s appropriate to say at work” to suppress dissenting discourse and discourage non-conformity, “professionalism” is and has always been about social control. These unknowable norms are mostly code for whiteness, and are regularly and violently weaponized against racialized, disabled, poor, young or otherwise minoritized people.An HBCU has banned durags and bonnets. That reinforces anti-Blackness | AD CarsonRead moreUnfortunately, much of how we are able to show up in publicoverallis also guided by workplace rules – a clear sign of the death grip that capitalism has on us. Workplaces function as enforcement agents of white supremacy in the office, in ways that inevitably spill over into our lives outside it. As oppressive dress codes limit religious expression, and hair discrimination pushes Black women to alter their natural hair textures, the workplace has become the arbiter of how we are allowed to exist.Even higher institutions are complicit in pushing the importance of professionalism. Just a few months ago, Tuskegee University, a historically Black institution, announced a new dress code prohibiting students from wearing bonnets and durags in class or any official campus spaces.Their reasoning?Well, in anemail tothe student body, the Tuskegee president, Dr Mark Anthony Brown, said the new rules were intended to “prepare [students] with a solid foundation for the workforce.“Employers are less forgiving and too often presentation may overrule stellar preparation,” he wrote.We spend far too much time policing irrelevant things like iced coffees, while gen Z languishes in a punishing job market amid the steadily rising cost of living. And as long as we remain beholden to professionalism culture and its shackles, we’ll continue the generational culture wars while young people bear the cost.Tayo Bero is a Guardian US columnistExplore more on these topicsUS work & careersOpinionCoffeeRaceWork & careerscommentShareReuse this content

title: Rightwing ‘great replacement’ fears mask tech’s real great replacement | Jason Stanley | The Guardian
description: While adherents to the racist theory condemn a shadowy global elite, Silicon Valley is working toward the replacement of humans with AI
Author: Jason Stanley
Headline: While adherents to the racist theory condemn a shadowy global elite, Silicon Valley is working toward the replacement of humans with AI
Content: ‘The fear that white workers will be replaced by non-white workers is masking the reality that all workers are being replaced bynon-humanworkers.’Photograph: Posed by model; d3sign/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘The fear that white workers will be replaced by non-white workers is masking the reality that all workers are being replaced bynon-humanworkers.’Photograph: Posed by model; d3sign/Getty ImagesOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)Rightwing ‘great replacement’ fears mask tech’s real great replacementJason StanleyWhile adherents to the racist theory condemn a shadowy global elite, Silicon Valley is working toward the replacement of humans with AITue 6 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 10.36 EDTShareAcross the world, “great replacement” theory has been employed again and again asthe political foundation for fascism. Some of its fundamental tenets, such asthe viewthat “whites are a dying minority”, have been amplified by tech billionaires and their platforms.According to the version of this theory most employed in Europe and the United States, white replacement theory, white populations are being “replaced” by non-white populations, a replacement engineered by a shadowy global elite. For example, the need for skilled labor is supposedly being used by global elites as an excuse to bring in non-white immigrants to replace white workers.Great replacement theory – a phenomenon Ibram X Kendi extensively documents inhis recent book, Chain of Ideas – is the governing ideology of Europe’s far-right parties. It also serves as a justification for the US’s remorseless and violent politics of mass deportation or “remigration”, the term introduced by the far-right Austrian nationalistMartin Sellnerin a 2024 book of that title. While a powerful international far right promotes this theory, arealgreat replacement is happening: of humanity with artificial intelligence.We don’t need to panic about AI. We need to hold its creators accountable when things go wrong | John QuigginRead moreAlternative für Deutschland (AfD) is Europe’s most prominent extreme far-right party, whose central platform is, essentially, remigration. Elon Musk is avocal supporterof this party, havinggiven a speech remotely at the AfD campaign launchin January 2025, stating: “You have to go all out to convince people to vote for AfD.” AfD’sparty program for Saxony-Anhaltexplicitly uses the concerns of the fake great replacement theory to justify implementing the real one. Point 28 of its agenda for “Immigration and Remigration” begins:double quotation markAn AfD-led state government will develop a strategy for Saxony-Anhalt focused on technological upgrading, digitalization, and AI. This strategy is intended to help alleviate bottlenecks in the local labor market. Furthermore, it aims to avoid the immigration of skilled workers from culturally dissimilar backgrounds.AfD proposes “financial support for technological upgrading, digitalization, and the use of AI by small and medium sized enterprises through the establishment of a dedicated funding program” as well as other kinds of support for companies to adopt AI. Again, this is not listed as part of AfD’seconomicprogram – that is another section. Replacement of human jobs by AI is rather part of itsimmigrationprogram – that is, its program motivated specifically by its central ideology of great replacement theory.Palantir’s multibillionaire CEO, Alex Karp, while rejecting AfD’s Russia-friendly politics, has argued thatAI will make mass migration obsolete, by obviating the need for skilled immigration into western countries.At the same time as the global far right is promoting fear about non-white populations replacing white populations, tech companies are engineering the mass replacement of humanity by AI.The panic about the replacement of white populations by non-white populations distracts attention from thisrealgreat replacement.The global elitearein fact in a conspiracy to replace people. But the global elites in this instance are not liberals or Jews or Marxists or Islamists – they are the heads of giant companies. And their productions threaten not the replacement of white people by non-white people – they threaten to replaceallpeople with AI agents.On 18 April, Palantirposteda 22-point summary of Alex Karp and Nicholas Zamiski’s book The Technological Republic: Hard Power, Soft Belief, and the Future of the West. Point 21 was:double quotation markSome cultures have produced vital advances; others remain dysfunctional and regressive. All cultures are now equal. Criticism and value judgments are forbidden. Yet this new dogma glosses over the fact that certain cultures and indeed subcultures … have produced wonders. Others have proven middling, and worse, regressive and harmful.According to this ideology, what makes for a superior culture are the skills and crafts it nurtures, and the productions (the “wonders”) that are the result of these skills.If the goals of its creators are met, AI will replace human skills, and with it, human skilled production – indeed, even human cognitive skill by the cognitive labor of AI agents. And if you are in the game of ranking cultures, and in the business of replacing human production with AI production, you are going to logically end up with the view that humanity itself should ultimately be discarded.Things are changing behind the scenes, so you must decide: do you want human civil servants or AI bots? | The civil servantRead moreTranshumanism is the view, popular among the Silicon Valley tech elite, that humans can be technologically augmented to give rise to a superior species, the “transhuman” (Elon Musk’s company Neuralink is devoted tomerging humanitywith AI).Transhumanism can be viewed as a contemporary version of eugenics, the project of using genetics and selective breeding to engineer supposedly “superior” humans, an endeavor central to Nazism.But I believe almost as popular as transhumanism among the Silicon Valley elite isAI successionism– the view that humans should give way to AI agents. With that handover, the center of moral concern should also change, fromhumanwelfare to the welfare of AI agents. It is not hard to imagine the creators of this new species wanting to survive in remote bunkers or outer space, with the knowledge that they have, like gods, been the agents of such a succession.The fear that white workers will be replaced by non-white workers is masking the reality that all workers are being replaced bynon-humanworkers. Similarly, the fear of the replacement of European civilization by foreign civilization is masking the threat of the replacement ofallhuman civilization with an artificially designed one.The global promotion of the fascist great replacement theory, the replacement of white workers by non-white workers, and the supposed displacement of “white civilization” is nothing other than a distraction from the real threat of agenuinegreat replacement, of humans by AI agents.Jason Stanley is the Bissell-Heyd chair of American studies at the Munk School at the University of Toronto. He is the author of Erasing History: How Fascists Rewrite the Past to Control the FutureExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionElon MuskPeter ThielRaceWork & careerscommentShareReuse this content

title: Deion Sanders created Prime Time so he could get paid. Why deny college athletes the same chance? | College sports | The Guardian
description: The Hall of Famer says his successful college career helped him and his family thrive. Now he appears to be backing legislation that would help others
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The Hall of Famer says his successful college career helped him and his family thrive. Now he appears to be backing legislation that would help others
Content: Deion Sanders moved from playing to the media to coaching.Photograph: David Ballering Ii/ADM Newswire/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenDeion Sanders moved from playing to the media to coaching.Photograph: David Ballering Ii/ADM Newswire/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockCollege sportsDeion Sanders created Prime Time so he could get paid. Why deny college athletes the same chance?Andre GeeThe Hall of Famer says his successful college career helped him and his family thrive. Now he appears to be backing legislation that would help othersTue 6 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 06.03 EDTShareLast week, journalist Rob Parkercalled Deion Sanders a “sellout”fortaking part in an advertpromoting the Protect College Sports Act (PCSA). The “sellout” label is harsh, but reflects how disappointing it is for many people to see Sanders stumping for a bill that will hurt athletes.The major points of contention around the PCSA, which the Senatepassedlast week and now awaits approval from the House, are a ceiling of around $49m that schools can direct to athletes, as well as a new transfer rule that would, except in a few specific circumstances, restrict players to one “free” transfer (if they move schools again, they’d have to wait a year to play for their next team). Former NFL player Domonique Foxworthhas saidthat “the core of [the PCSA] is about reestablishing the power the NCAA had in the past – that the court system determined was illegal”.Sanders takes a different approach. In his pro-PCSA ad, he notes, “As a coach and father, I’m helping the next generation find their spotlight. That’s why I support the Protect College Sports Act. It gives student-athletes a chance to shine on and off the field, strengthens historically Black colleges and universities, and keeps both men’s and women’s sports strong.”That feels like a vague word salad used to shroud his true intentions. Sanders, like PCSA booster Nick Saban and other coaches, appears to be trying to take back control from players. Student-athletes have more freedom than ever with name, image and likeness (NIL) deals and the transfer portal. In June,Sanders told reporter Baker Machadothat, “I do believe that college athletes should be compensated for their name, image and likeness. But it’s not about name, image and likeness right now. It’s just about pay-per-view.” Four years earlier, when he was coach at Jackson State, he had lamented that NIL deals turn NCAA athletes into “professionals”, saying “you don’t have staffs large enough and equipped enough to handle a young man with money.” The PCSA would not end or cap NIL, but it would mean players would have to prove the deal was worth approximately what a figure of the same standing would earn for a similar endorsement. Deals would need to be proven to have a genuine commercial purpose, something that could end deals that effectively pay students athletes to play.Sanders’s comments echoSaban’s assertionthat NIL “created an environment with no control, no guardrails”. The former Alabama coach added: “Now you’ve got transfers that are out of control. You’ve got salaries that are out of control. You’ve got budgets that are out of control.”But Saban said nothing about coaches’ salaries being out of control; he made more than $121mduring his 17-year tenure at Alabama. Sanders, who earns $10m a year, is the highest-paid head coach in the Big 12. Meanwhile Colorado’s athletic department hada $27m deficitin the last fiscal year, partly due to Sanders’s huge salary. While the PCSA has a “Lane Kiffin rule” that keeps coaches from jumping teams in the same season, there’s no cap on coaching salaries or buyouts. The players are the reason why the NCAAgrosses more than $1bn in revenuea year, but this act unfairly targets athletes’ earnings potential.It’s disappointing to see Sanders, who is idolized by Black athletes after his brilliant football career, appear to be such a hypocrite. In his 2011 NFL Hall of Fame induction speech, the former cornerback was candid about his mother’s financial woes when he was growing up. He added that his brash “Prime Time” persona came from economic necessity: “Cornerbacks, running backs, linebackers, defensive backs weren’t paid a lot. And in my dormitory room at Florida State, I created this image … You could love him or you could hate him, but he was Prime Time.” He now laments that NIL has turned theNCAAinto “a business”, but “Prime Time” was a business decision. Does he expect anyone to believe that he would have passed on an endorsement deal to support his mother when he was at college?Sanders’s stance reminds me of Michael Jordan, then owner of the Charlotte Bobcats,reportedly advocatingfor NBA players to get just 47% of the league’s basketball-related income during the 2011 lockout. (The final figure ended up being 51.2% for the 2011-12 season.) Years before, he told then-Washington Wizards owner Abe Pollin, “If you can’t make it work economically, you should sell the team,” during the 1998 lockout. (Jordan didn’t take his own adviceuntil 2023when he sold his majority stake.) The reverence for Sanders among athletes isn’t far off the respect paid to Jordan. That’s why it was particularly disappointing to see Jordan, and now Sanders, lose solidarity with their peers once they became part of the management machine. Deion “Prime Time” Sanders made a braggadocious 1994 rap song called Must Be the Money. But “Coach Prime” wants to rein in player compensation.In May,Sanders made his intentions clear: “At Colorado … I want to win. I want to win it all. It ain’t no negotiation. No side steppin’. That’s my No 1 goal.” The NIL boom has hampered those efforts at Colorado, who lack the finances of the biggest football programs. Recruitment at Colorado, who have lost three straight games, has proved difficult for Sanders. In April, Sports Illustrated’s Andrew Hugheswrote that,“The Buffs no longer spend enough to truly be relevant on a national scale.”Whatever Sanders’s stated reasons, the bill could also benefit him competitively. Sanders says he is pro-PCSA to “help the next generation”, but complicating NIL salaries and restricting transfers benefits him as a coach more than it helps athletes. Sanders can accept as many transfers as he wants, but the players would no longer be able to move freely without restriction themselves. If a post-PCSA NCAA results in less player movement, and “blue blood” programs can’t just buy up every top prospect, Sanders will be able to better leverage his Hall of Fame bona fides as a recruiter, and could theoretically have more continuity on his roster. All of these developments serve his No 1 goal. But it’s a shame that he appears so focused on wins that he’d work against the very student-athlete he used to be.At Jackson State, Sanders’s star power gave him a recruiting edge no coach could compete with. Travis Hunter, the top-ranked high school player in the country, signed with the school towards the start of Sanders’s reign. His success at Jackson State proved five-star recruits would go to HBCUs. Then, he abruptly left for the brighter lights (and bigger paycheck) of Colorado.He could be content like other former NFL stars who have become college coaches at HBCUs. Michael Vick (Norfolk State), DeSean Jackson (Delaware State) and Marshall Faulk (Southern University) are unlikely to lead their teams to national championships, but they’re getting the chance to be mentors to young men while staying competitive in their respective conferences. It seems like that happy medium won’t satisfy Sanders, though. That’s why he left another HBCU, Jackson State, to take the Colorado job in 2023.The chase for success has him stumping for what amounts to a federally protected salary-cap and employment framework imposed without collective bargaining. With the PCSA, a power circle of legislators, leading figures at college institutions and influential boosters would collectively roll back players’ labor rights without a single NCAA athlete having a meaningful representative role in the act’s framework. The changes will disproportionately work against Black players, who make up 66% of the football rosters at ACC, SEC and Big 12 conferences.In a letter to Congress opposing the PCSA and opposing attacks on Black voting rights, NAACP president Derrick Johnsonwrote, “Public institutions cannot depend upon Black athletes to fill their stadiums, secure television contracts, attract donations, and build nationally recognized brands, then claim neutrality when the political rights of those athletes, their families, and their communities are under attack.”Sanders is dead wrong for working against those rights. Instead of using his voice to tell the pro-PCSA faction that the NCAA wouldn’t make a dime without its athletes and shouldn’t be trying to police their movement, he is doing their bidding. Why would he betray young Black athletes like this? Must be the glory.Explore more on these topicsCollege sportsCollege footballNCAAUS sportscommentShareReuse this content

title: Trump is fueling a culture of misogynistic impunity  | Robert Reich | The Guardian
description: The allegations against seven men at Cornell University come amid a climate of belligerent sexism
Author: Robert Reich
Headline: The allegations against seven men at Cornell University come amid a climate of belligerent sexism
Content: ‘An implicit promise of the 2024 Trump campaign was to restore patriarchy to America.’Photograph: Syndi Pilar/Sopa Images/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘An implicit promise of the 2024 Trump campaign was to restore patriarchy to America.’Photograph: Syndi Pilar/Sopa Images/ShutterstockOpinionDonald TrumpTrump is fueling a culture of misogynistic impunityRobert ReichThe allegations against seven men at Cornell University come amid a climate of belligerent sexismTue 6 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 10.44 EDTShareLast month, a young womanfiled a lawsuitagainst Cornell University,alleging thattwo years ago the university had failed to protect her from being raped by seven men at a fraternity house near the university campus. She also sued the fraternity.The lawsuit has plunged the university into a crisis and invited criticism of the district attorney, Matthew Van Houten, who decided there wasn’t enough evidence to bring criminal charges against the seven men.At this point, we can only guess why neither Cornell nor Van Houten did more in response to the young woman’s allegations. But there’s little question that we’re living through a time when men feel some impunity when it comes to attacking women.Violence against women is hardly new. Nor is the impunity that some men feel in attacking them.But the man now occupying the White House has contributed to a lower and more dangerous standard for what men can do to women with impunity.Trump wasfound in civil courtto have sexually abused the writer E Jean Carroll. He has repeatedly insulted the physical appearance of femalejournalists,politicians and public figures. He was caught on a hot microphone boasting about using his fame to forcefully kiss and grope women without consent, stating that being a star allows men to “do anything” and “grab ’em by the pussy”.When women have spoken out against him, Trump has resorted to smear campaigns, as he did with Carroll,Stormy DanielsandHillary Clinton. When women have stood up to him, he has exploded in anger against them, as he did withMegyn Kelly,Rosie O’Donnell,Kamala HarrisandAlexandria Ocasio-Cortez.His administration is the most belligerently misogynistic of any in memory. It has openly equatedtestosterone levelsto strength, conducted acage match on the White House lawnas part of its celebration of America’s 250th anniversary,firedseniorfemaleofficials, andaccusedthe Democratic party of being run by “a bunch of childless cat ladies”.Nor do I think it irrelevant that Trump, JD Vance and Trump’s erstwhile pal Elon Musk inhabit what’s been termed the “manosphere” – a place where the main events are dominance and submission. The wholepointis to humiliate weak men and to subjugate women.An implicit promise of the 2024 Trump campaign was to restore patriarchy to America. Fifty-four per cent of men supported Trump in that year’s election.After Trump’s re-election, sexist and abusive attacks on women – such as “your body, my choice” and “get back in the kitchen” – surged across social media, according to ananalysisfrom the Institute for Strategic Dialogue.A remarkable number of Trump’s cronies are sexual harassers and predators. Trump was introduced at the Republican national conventionby Dana White, chief executive of the Ultimate Fighting Championship, who was oncecaught on tapeslapping his wife in a nightclub.JD Vancehas claimedmen in America are “suppressed” in their masculinity.Before becoming Trump’s defense secretary, Pete Hegseth paid off a woman whoaccused him of sexual assault. (Hegseth’s own motheraccusedhim of abusing women, though she later disavowed her words. He has denied the claims.) And as secretary, Hegseth has championed “high-T” men andblocked promotionsof female officers.One of Elon Musk’s companies, SpaceX, reportedly paid $250,000 to a flight attendant who said Musk had exposed himself to her, though he denies the allegation. In alawsuitfiled last year, former employees accused him of “treating women as sexual objects to be evaluated on their bra size”.After kissing Trump’s derriere, Mark Zuckerberg, the third-richest person in the US, called formore “masculine energy”because the corporate world was becoming “culturally neutered”. Hetold Joe Rogan: “Having a culture that celebrates the aggression a bit more has its own merits that are really positive.”The Trump regime celebrated toxic masculinity bysmoothing the wayfor Andrew and Tristan Tate to be released from Romania to the United States. The Tate brothers had been accused of luring women to Romania and then forcing them to work as pornographic webcam performers. Britain isalso investigatingthe Tate brothers for rape and human trafficking. (US marshalsarrested the Tate brothersin Miami on 18 July, following an extradition request from the United Kingdom. They’ve denied all charges.)“I’m a Trump fan because I’m a man,”Tate has said. “You have to support Trump if you’re a man.”Trump’s authoritarian manosphere is organized around a hierarchy topped by heroic male warriors. Winning is all about getting other males to submit to the dominant male.Womenare relegated to subservient roles.Anything that challenges the traditional heroic male roles of protector, provider and controller of the family is considered a threat to the social order. LGBTQ+ people are believed to weaken the heroic male. Hence, Trump’s executive order declaring that the US governmentwill recognizeonly a person’s sex assigned at birth, limit the definition of a “male” or “female” to their reproductive cells, andpotentially withholdfederal funding from programs that acknowledge transgender people or “gender ideology”.I don’t want to oversimplify a complex social phenomenon or engage in the same kind of gender stereotypes that the manosphere promotes. Male domination is hardly the only characteristic that unites Trump, Vance, Hegseth, Kennedy, Musk and the tech bros. Misogyny is not unique to authoritarian men.Nor do I presume to know what happened at the Cornell fraternity house two years ago. But I don’t think it unreasonable to see it related to a climate of distrust bordering on hate, fostered by Trump and his administration against people who seem weak or feminine.Robert Reich, a former US secretary of labor, is a professor of public policy emeritus at the University of California, Berkeley. He is a Guardian US columnist and his newsletter is atrobertreich.substack.com. His new book, Coming Up Short: A Memoir of My America, isout now in the USandin the UKExplore more on these topicsDonald TrumpOpinionGenderWomencommentShareReuse this content

title: I witnessed the Pinochet regime’s fall. It offers hope – and a warning – for the US | Ariel Dorfman | The Guardian
description: November’s midterms bring parallels with a moment in October 1988. But Pinochet’s exit wasn’t the end of his influence
Author: Ariel Dorfman
Headline: November’s midterms bring parallels with a moment in October 1988. But Pinochet’s exit wasn’t the end of his influence
Content: ‘Ridding Chile of its strongman saved it for democracy, but did not undo the vast damage he did to the country.’Photograph: Fernando Lavoz/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘Ridding Chile of its strongman saved it for democracy, but did not undo the vast damage he did to the country.’Photograph: Fernando Lavoz/NurPhoto/ShutterstockOpinionChileI witnessed the Pinochet regime’s fall. It offers hope – and a warning – for the USAriel DorfmanNovember’s midterms bring parallels with a moment in October 1988. But Pinochet’s exit wasn’t the end of his influenceTue 6 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 11.27 EDTShareA malignant, monomaniacal president, deeply unpopular, faces an election that could restrict his power and end his domination of his country.It is true that, to influence the outcome, he counts on a supine supreme court and his ability to legislate through executive decrees, as well as an onslaught of fake news accusing his opponents of being unpatriotic communists, true that he has colossal financial support from an entrenched oligarchy that has thrived thanks to his rightwing neoliberal policies, true that he has gone out of his way to limit the freedom of those who vote and true that he has absolute command of the armed forces.None of this seems sufficient to deter an electorate that is tired of his reign and determined, despite widespread intimidation, to make itself heard. Even as the polls indicate a rout, the delusional strongman, emboldened by sycophants and fawning courtiers too afraid to inform him of the facts, refuses to accept that the upcoming referendum will go against his divinely inspired will.Donald Trump in 2026?Vance wants voters to ‘give us another chance’. But he is cornered | Sidney BlumenthalRead moreIn fact, I was also describing the dictator of Chile, the GenAugusto Pinochet, in October of 1988, when he insisted that he would win a plebiscite which would decide whether he remained as head of state for another eight years (and probably well beyond) or whether a transition to democracy should begin. On 5 October of that year, the military autocrat, who had misgoverned Chile since ousting the democratically elected president Salvador Allende in a 1973 coup, resoundingly lost, with 55.9% of his compatriots telling him to retire.He did not go easily.I was there, that night, as the results poured in verifying that the regime was being repudiated, I was there when the vote count was suspended and an informational blockade was established at 10pm; I was there, in front of the presidential palace in Santiago, when, at around 1am of 6 October, the air force general Fernando Matthei, a member of the junta, recognized publicly that the “no” vote had clearly won, thwarting an auto-coup that Pinochet was contemplating at that very moment.These events have a significant bearing on the United States as the 3 November midterms approach and with them, a dire uncertainty: can the majority of Americans, by winning both chambers of Congress, constrain the ravings and corruption of a wannabe autocrat who is as unhinged today, and contemptuous of the law, as Pinochet was back then?That Chilean October should serve, at this existential moment, as a way to encourage and inspire those who won’t let their voices be silenced. No matter how much supremacy, no matter how many resources deployed by a deranged chief executive, no matter the fear and funds and lies at a powerful ruler’s disposal, he can be beaten if courageous people are resolute and smart enough.And Chile, in effect, subsequently transitioned to democracy, electing a center-left president in 1990 and, since then, an uninterrupted series of presidents of different ideological strains and policies.But that October 1988 milestone in Chile also entails warnings for those who believe it is possible to limit Donald Trump’s authoritarian tendencies.Just as Pinochet intended to disavow the results that were ousting him, the current occupant of the White House could try to do something similar – maneuvers that would far outdistance his violent and illicit attempts to annul his loss in the 2020 elections.Only heightened civilian and institutional vigilance, the daily epic of everyday people resisting – and patriotic armed forces unwilling to obey illegal dictatorial orders – can guarantee, as in Chile, that such a potential assault on democracy will fail.That will not be enough. Ridding Chile of its strongman saved it for democracy, but did not undo the vast damage he did to the country. He kept mutilating it grievously during the year and a half left in his mandate and then for another eight years as a threatening commander-in-chief of the army.But more insidious was how he permanently changed Chilean society. Not just the dismantlement of the welfare state created by decades of struggle, replaced by a savage capitalism that did not care how much pain it inflicted or who was left defenceless. Worse perhaps was how the spreading of fear and mistrust affected the psyche of the country, sickened its soul.Indeed, despite major advances in reversing Pinochet’s long legacy, his shadow still looms over Chile.Despite the dictator’s appalling record of disappearances, torture, exile and persecutions, José Antonio Kast,an admirer of Pinochetwhowould like to pardonthe agents of the dictatorship imprisoned for gross violation of human rights, is now Chile’s president.Hisvictory in December of 2025can be partly explained by an economically distressed populace falling for his rabidly anti-immigrant platform and vows to deal with a narco crime wave that has shaken the country. Nonetheless, the fact that a whopping 56% of voters were willing to turn a blind eye to Kast’s denial of past atrocities is a cause for long-term concern and, in my case, of mourning.It is disturbing to witness the erosion, perhaps the funeral, of the dream that once was Chile, a land of solidarity and thirst for justice and dignity that enthralled me when I arrived there as a lad of 12 in the winter of 1954. So strong was that enthrallment that I never doubted, during the eternal night of the dictatorship, that it would resurrect and, in effect, on 5 October 1988, thanks to so many Chileans who suffered and fought for it, that fearless, hopeful country proved it was alive, an indispensable stepping stone towards an indefinite future.Something went wrong.Maybe that is why I force myself to wonder, in this other promising and foreboding October, if we are aware in this other country, the United States, that is also mine, how much long-lasting harm have the Trump years wrought?I ask this because back in October 1988, the democratic militants of Chile, carried away by the glorious illusion that the dawn of a new era was upon us, did not then fully deal with the vexing question of how such a monster could have arisen in our midst.Donald Trump’s Maga cult is finally crumbling | Arwa MahdawiRead moreIt was a public and private task, both intellectual and emotional, that enough Chilean men and women, given the triumphant return of a Pinochet fanatic to lead their country, have still not sufficiently grappled with collectively: what mistakes did we originally make to facilitate the existence of such a despicable and enduring regime and, most crucially, what could we have done better, what must we do better in the coming years?My adopted US homeland should be wary of making the same mistakes.Though the electorate at this moment is sensibly focused on achieving a victory that will grant some reprieve and solace, such an urgency should not postpone the need for an overdue reckoning with the dark imperfections in our history and national character that generated the conditions for the republic to be in such dire peril.Those conditions, enabled by those who enabled Trump and ignored his danger, his nastiness, his serial mendacity, will probably endure well beyond the day (if it comes) when he leaves the White House. We will be left to contend with the worst traits of the US’s past that he exalted and exacerbated: the imperial arrogance, the nativism and misogyny, the ecological degradation, the assault on minority and workers’ rights, the myth of exceptionalism.That is the somber lesson that Chile yesterday and today whispers to us from afar. Only a profound and painful self-examination of our identity, what the splendid guardians of this experiment that started 250 years ago are demanding, can help to stave off the ominous possibility that years from now the country will be facing a repetition of the current terrifying crisis.By then, it may be too late.Ariel Dorfman is the Chilean American author of Death and the Maiden and the novels The Suicide Museum and Allegro, and the forthcoming collection of stories, What She SawExplore more on these topicsChileOpinionAmericasTrump administrationUS midterm elections 2026Donald TrumpAugusto PinochetUS politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: Angus Taylor’s immigration plan misses the target – on politics and on policy  | Abul Rizvi | The Guardian
description: The most surprising aspect of the Coalition’s policy is that in six pages of detail there is not a single mention of the labour market
Author: Abul Rizvi
Headline: The most surprising aspect of the Coalition’s policy is that in six pages of detail there is not a single mention of the labour market
Content: ‘Massive fluctuations in net overseas migration are never good policy. Business and government agencies need stability and predictability to plan and invest.’Photograph: Bianca de Marchi/AAPView image in fullscreen‘Massive fluctuations in net overseas migration are never good policy. Business and government agencies need stability and predictability to plan and invest.’Photograph: Bianca de Marchi/AAPOpinionAustralian immigration and asylumAngus Taylor’s immigration plan misses the target – on politics and on policyAbul RizviThe most surprising aspect of the Coalition’s policy is that in six pages of detail there is not a single mention of the labour marketTue 6 Oct 2026 18.47 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 19.18 EDTShareUnder pressure to match One Nation’s most recent iteration of its immigration policy of negative net overseas migration (Nom) for three years in a row, Angus Taylor has announced theCoalition’s new Nom targetwill be 100,000 in its first two years from 2028-29, rising to 130,000 then 160,000 by 2032. That sits conveniently between Labor’s target and One Nation’s.The most surprising aspect of the Coalition’s announcement is that in six pages of policy detail, for which the opposition should be commended, there is not a single mention of the labour market.There is no chance a Nom figure of 100,000 a year over two years can be delivered if the labour market remains at around its current state. That is, an unemployment rate of 4.6%, and a participation rate of 67% with about 325,000 job vacancies. The Coalition would be overwhelmed by pressure from the business community to increase its target.In my experience, the Coalition can never stand up to the business community on immigration levels. It was why it stomped on the immigration accelerator after the lifting of Covid lockdowns by introducing unprecedented reductions in immigration standards that Taylor now says need to be increased. The Coalition kept urging the Labor government to increase immigration levels in the second half of 2022.Labor was too slow to act on the blowout in Nom in 2022-23 and is now paying the price for pretending it didn’t need to be managed.Coalition’s migration plan risks breaching India free trade agreement and damaging economy, advocates warnRead moreThe Coalition may point to Canada successfully reducing Nom from well over 1 million in 2023-24 to less than 200,000 in 2025-26. That was driven by a very weak labour market with unemployment about 7% and a falling participation rate in most of 2025. In that weak labour market,Canada massively cut student and temporary worker numbers.It smashed university budgets. But Nom in Canada is now rising strongly as its labour market strengthens.Massive fluctuations in Nom are never good policy. Business and government agencies need stability and predictability to plan and invest. That includes the housebuilding industry which, without massive government support, will be reluctant to increase housebuilding against the background of an ongoing competition for huge cuts to immigration levels.That is not to say there aren’t aspects to the Coalition’s announcement that may be necessary. Reducing the humanitarian program from 20,000 to 10,000 is sensible when you consider we are now struggling to provide adequate settlement services to this highly vulnerable cohort. The finding that90% of refugee kids live their first year in povertyis not the sign of generosity but of policy failure.It also makes sense to reduce the number of temporary graduate visa holders in Australia as well as the number on bridging visas.But the claim that the policy will “virtually eliminate bridging visas” from more than 400,000 currently to 20,000 is arrant nonsense. A very large portion of the bridging visa backlog is onshore applications for not just student visas but also parent visas, partner visas and asylum. While some of the Coalition’s and Labor’s tightening of onshore visa applications will help reduce the flow of applications into bridging visas, the bulk of the backlog will remain.At more than 270,000, there are too many temporary graduates in Australia chasing too few permanent residence places. Labor should have done more to address this. However, the Coalition’s policy of trying to reduce this to 10,000 is going too far.Temporary graduates are a key feeder group into skilled temporary visas, the regional visa, state and territory-nominated visas and the skilled independent visa. The Coalition is not proposing to cut any of these – indeed, it is proposing to increase skilled temporary visas by over 100,000. If that is the case, it will need to find more people directly from overseas to fill these visa places. More people coming directly from overseas would increase Nom, not reduce it. It would also require a reduction in standards, not the increase Taylor is promising.Taylor’s hardline immigration plan drags Australian politics further to the right – and it’s all upside for One NationRead moreThe Coalition is proposing to reduce annual student commencements to 245,000 from the government’s national planning level (NPL) of 295,000 in 2026 and 2027. But under Labor’s own policy, with eye-wateringly high levels of student visa refusals, the 295,000 will not be delivered. Essentially, Labor and the Coalition are very close on student visa policy. It’s One Nation’s policies that are more likely to smash the international education industry, forcing taxpayer-funded bailouts of universities and/or huge job losses.The permanent migration program is to be held at 185,000 a year. That contributes about 75,000 a year to Nom, which the Coalition seems to have not considered.The Coalition says the number of New Zealand citizens in Australia will increase by 45,000 to 776,600. That would require both continuation of a strong labour market as well as a major contribution of NZ citizens to the Nom of about 35,000 a year. That is because between 20,000 and 30,000 New Zealanders become Australian citizens annually – thus are no longer counted as NZ citizens in Australia.The large annual contribution to Nom from working holidaymakers is to continue. In 2024-25, that was well over 50,000 which could fall marginally but would largely continue in a strong labour market.With a strong labour market, there will also be high numbers of Australian citizens returning and fewer leaving although the net contribution to Nom would remain negative.On its own calculations, the Coalition would not come close to delivering its Nom target of 100,000 in years one and two. Those are political targets, not policy targets.Abul Rizvi is a former deputy immigration­ ­secretaryExplore more on these topicsAustralian immigration and asylumOpinionMigrationCoalitionAngus TaylorcommentShareReuse this content

title: Kemi Badenoch is the most rightwing leader in Tory history. Isn’t it time she got some actual scrutiny? | Owen Jones | The Guardian
description: Farage’s scandals have allowed Badenoch to get her party back in the race. But her programme would be no less ruinous for our country, says Guardian columnist Owen Jones
Author: Owen Jones
Headline: Farage’s scandals have allowed Badenoch to get her party back in the race. But her programme would be no less ruinous for our country, says Guardian columnist Owen Jones
Content: Kemi Badenoch prepares to give an interview at the Conservative party conference in Birmingham on Tuesday.Photograph: Oli Scarff/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenKemi Badenoch prepares to give an interview at the Conservative party conference in Birmingham on Tuesday.Photograph: Oli Scarff/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionKemi BadenochKemi Badenoch is the most rightwing leader in Tory history. Isn’t it time she got some actual scrutiny?Owen JonesFarage’s scandals have allowed Badenoch to get her party back in the race. But her programme would be no less ruinous for our countryTue 6 Oct 2026 14.04 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 19.57 EDTShareThe Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, will march on to the conference stage in Birmingham feeling buoyed. “Kemi’s soaring,”coos the Sun, and that sums up the prevailing wisdom. More than four in 10 Britonsthink she is doing wellas Tory leader, compared with a third who think otherwise. As Nigel Farage’s stock has plummeted thanks to scandals over a £5m personal gift anddonations from crypto billionaires, the polling suggests that the Conservatives could regain the mantle of Britain’s main rightwing force.Yet Badenoch has been the beneficiary of circumstance. Her tenure as opposition leader has been defined by Keir Starmer’s project imploding almost as soon as it gained power. When Reform UK enjoyed its seismic polling lead, the Tory plight was double-edged: they were starved of attention, but that inevitably resulted in a lack of scrutiny, too. It has been easy for Badenoch to appear formidable while her opponents have disintegrated.With the Conservatives now back in the race, the spotlight falls on Badenoch. Let us consider the absurdity of her proposed air defence system. Our would-be prime ministerdenied comparing it to Israel’s Iron Dome, despite the term appearing in both a press release and a newspaper article under her own name. This amateurishness is one thing, but even on its own terms, her proposal is a mess. It will “protect the whole United Kingdom, our sovereign territories and British bases overseas”, she claims, which would be impossible for the £10bn over 10 years she is proposing to spend on it.The former British general Richard Barrons suggestssuch a systemwould cost more than £100bn.What does this say about Badenoch’s sense of priorities? The actual urgent national security threat Britain faces is not volleys of missile attacks, but the climate emergency. There were estimated to be thousands of excess deaths from heatwaves this summer, while ourintelligence serviceswarn of serious disruption to our food supply from 2030. YetBadenoch has committed to repealing the Climate Change Actand claimed that net zero by 2050 is “impossible” without bankrupting Britain. This not onlycontradicts the conclusionof the government’s statutory climate scientific advisers, but Badenoch herself. As a Treasury minister in 2021,she told parliamentthat it would cost less than 2% of GDP, largely from “increased investment in growth markets of the future”. Even three former Tory prime ministers have criticised Badenoch’s shift against net zero –including the former rightwing pin-upBoris Johnson.Then there’s her economic agenda.A year ago, Badenoch declared that she sought to become Britain’s version of Argentina’s far-right president, Javier Milei. His government has imposed devastating cuts to pensions,universitiesandpublic healthcare, while poverty isonce more surging. Badenoch proposes welfare cuts worth £23bn, and misleads the public as she does so. In May,she declared: “For the first time ever, the total welfare bill is now higher than total receipts from income tax.” This has been the case since 2011, and as the UK Statistics Authority notedin a letterrebuking her, this was misleading for other reasons: the gap had actually narrowed in recent years, and most of the welfare bill goes to pensioner benefits, including the state pension.What would £23bn in cuts mean? They would includestripping workers with indefinite leave to remainof social security – people who have lived here for years, worked and paid taxes. That would not only be an injustice to them – consider that there isalready a staffing crisisin sectors such as social care that immigration restrictions are worsening. She wouldreinstate a two-child benefit capthat would drive hundreds of thousands of children into poverty. Most of the rest would fall on the shoulders of sick and disabled people, including those receiving support while they work.Consider this too: while we still live with the consequences of the 2008 financial crash,Badenoch proposes endingthe ringfence for big banks separating retail and investment activities, and reducing their capital requirements.What of her authoritarianism? Badenoch hasdeclared free speechto be “the birthright of every citizen”, yet has advocated a blanket ban on pro-Palestinian protests. The justification is conflating opposition to genocide with threats to Jewish people, but this is a Tory leader who, when asked about Gaza,said that“Israel is fighting a proxy war on behalf of the UK”. Withdrawal from the European convention on human rights and repealing the Human Rights Act would strip citizens of crucial protections against an overbearing executive and abuses of state power. Badenochadvocates an ICE-style mass deportationapparatus with sweeping powers of surveillance – directly mimicking an institution across the Atlantic that snatches people from the street and kills migrants and US citizens alike.Her attitude to the rights of minorities, meanwhile, is underlined by her commitment toscrap the public sector equality dutyin its entirety. As a minister in 2021, shebacked it, saying it helped ensure “that fairness is at the heart of everything we do”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionYet the average punter knows little about Badenoch. The increasing extremism and scandals of Farageism have allowed her to appear somehow more reasonable and stable in comparison. But Badenoch is easily the most rightwing Tory leader in the party’s history. Her programme is a wishlist of rightwing zealots – one which would be ruinous to our social fabric. Yet few have bothered to look under the bonnet. The danger is that Britain discovers what Badenoch really stands for only when she is close enough to power to put it into practice.Owen Jones is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
