title: Pedro Sánchez is a master of the political comeback. But calling a snap election in Spain may be a gamble too far | Paolo Gerbaudo | The Guardian
description: A thriving economy, a model green transition, social advances – Spain’s PM shouldn’t be in trouble. Yet he is, and it’s a lesson for progressives everywhere, says sociologist Paolo Gerbaudo
Author: Paolo Gerbaudo
Headline: A thriving economy, a model green transition, social advances – Spain’s PM shouldn’t be in trouble. Yet he is, and it’s a lesson for progressives everywhere, says sociologist Paolo Gerbaudo
Content: Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, attends a press conference at the Moncloa palace, Madrid, on Tuesday.Photograph: Juan Medina/ReutersView image in fullscreenSpain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, attends a press conference at the Moncloa palace, Madrid, on Tuesday.Photograph: Juan Medina/ReutersOpinionSpainPedro Sánchez is a master of the political comeback. But calling a snap election in Spain may be a gamble too farPaolo GerbaudoA thriving economy, a model green transition, social advances – Spain’s PM shouldn’t be in trouble. Yet he is, and it’s a lesson for progressives everywhereTue 6 Oct 2026 10.57 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 12.48 EDTShareTo progressives across the west, Spain has been arare glimmer of hopein a world where far-right parties are increasingly entering government. Under Pedro Sánchez, who became prime minister in 2018, the country has combined a post-Covid economic boom with a bold green energy transition programme, anda pro-immigration stance with a principled opposition to the war agenda of Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu. Yet, at the end of next month, this rare beacon of democratic progress could fall.OnMondaySánchez called asnap generalelection, set for 29 November, after two decrees to address the country’s housing crisiswere voted downin the lower chamber by politicians from rightwing parties. Speaking from the staircase of the Moncloa palace,Sánchez admittedthat his government had not achieved all it had set out to do. “Many injustices remain to be corrected … particularly regarding inequality in public services and access to housing,” he said, adding: “To do more, we need to renew and expand public support.”Sánchez attempted to pass the legislation after tens of thousands took to the streets to protest against the housing crisis,setting up camps reminiscent of thecountry’s 15-M anti-austerity movementand the global Occupy movement of 2011. But this explosion of popular anger has been long in the making. According to Spain’s national public opinion research institute Centro de Investigaciones Sociológicas (CIS), housing has been thecountry’s top preoccupationsince the end of 2024, as a growing number of people struggle to pay rent.It shouldn’t take the eviction of an 87-year-old to get Spain’s housing crisis fixed | María RamírezRead moreIn the latest gamble of his long career as master of the political comeback, Sánchez hopes to ride the wave of popular mobilisation to turn public attention away from theCeuta immigration crisisof July, which rightwing opponents exploited as a demonstration of the government’s failures, and focus attention on the housing crisis, an issue where the left holds stronger political ground.But this time it will be hard to convince Spaniards that with a new lease of life, the progressive coalitiongovernment will solve an issue it had promised to address a long time ago.Sánchez’s troubles provide useful lessons for progressives all over the world about the difficulties of translating policy achievements into a solid base of political support.They are also a reminder that – as championed by New York’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani – addressing the affordability crisis rather than promising abstract economic growth is of more significance to voters.In the US midterm election campaign, Republicans are struggling because ofrising prices at the gas pump, while in Brazil, rightwing challengerFlávio Bolsonaro justrode to an impressive resultin the first round of the presidential elections partly due to discontent with living conditions and household pressures. In Spain, Sánchez’s government is facing similar concerns about affordability, which are obfuscating an otherwise impressive macro-economic performance.Indeed, seen from the outside, Sánchez’s Spain may appear to be a dazzling political success. The country, which in the 2010s was derided as part of theEuropean Piigs– a term coined to mock Portugal, Ireland, Italy, Greece and Spain as the eurozone’s weakest economies –has become an economic powerhouse. In the years after the Covid pandemic, Spain’s GDPgrew at a rate of around 3%, while France, Germany, the UK and Italy grew at a miserly 1% or less.Spain is also held up as a model of successful green transition, with renewables now generating close to60% of the country’s power, which has also kept energy bills low and helped insulate the country from the energy shocks caused by international crises. Spain, enabled by significant Chinese investment, is also surprisingly becoming the leading European hub for electric car production, to thedismay of some of the country’s traditional allies.To these economic and environmental achievements add the significant social improvements achieved under Sánchez, exemplified by the rise in the minimum wage from€736 to €1,184 per month since 2018.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionYet despite these measurable successes, Sánchez’s centre-left coalition is nowtrailing the right by about 7 percentage pointsin national polling. That’s partly because while minimum wages have increased, median wages have remained relatively stagnant. But it is real estate that Sánchez’s government has been judged as failing to deliver: during its eight years in power, house prices have risenby an estimated 50%, with rents rising by over 40%.As climbing the housing ladder becomes prohibitive, a growing number of young people in Spain are forced to pay extortionate rents. This is acutely felt in large urban areas, where the presence of tourists and digital nomads further increases rents, forcing out local residents; this is enabled by private equity firms, who purchase entire blocks to expel local inhabitants in orderto create Airbnbs. Sánchez’s government has repeatedly promised to take action on these issues, but its measures have been thwarted by political gridlock or otherwiseproven indecisive, partly due to fear of alienating homeowners and antagonising international finance.If Spain’s centre-left coalition falls, the country could be left with an alliance of the mainstream conservative Partido Popular and the far-right party Vox. It would be the most rightwing Spanish government since Francisco Franco’s dictatorship.The lesson for progressives everywhere is clear: economic growth and ambitious reform will count for little unless working people feel the benefits in their daily lives.Paolo Gerbaudo is a senior researcher at the faculty of political science and sociology of Complutense University in Madrid and a lead researcher at the Alameda InstituteExplore more on these topicsSpainOpinionPedro SánchezThe far rightEuropecommentShareReuse this content

title: While British children go hungry, we waste 1.1bn meals a year. Bring on the redistribution revolution | Charlotte Hill | The Guardian
description: Food businesses and the government must make redistribution a key policy to address food insecurity. We know the surplus food is out there, says Charlotte Hill, chief executive of the food redistribution organisation Felix
Author: Charlotte Hill
Headline: Food businesses and the government must make redistribution a key policy to address food insecurity. We know the surplus food is out there, says Charlotte Hill, chief executive of the food redistribution organisation Felix
Content: Heaps of rejected carrots and potatoes that do not meet the criteria for class 1 supermarket vegetables, Curlew farm, Burscough, Lancashire.Photograph: MediaWorldImages/AlamyView image in fullscreenHeaps of rejected carrots and potatoes that do not meet the criteria for class 1 supermarket vegetables, Curlew farm, Burscough, Lancashire.Photograph: MediaWorldImages/AlamyOpinionFood wasteWhile British children go hungry, we waste 1.1bn meals a year. Bring on the redistribution revolutionCharlotte HillFood businesses and the government must make redistribution a key policy to address food insecurity. We know the surplus food is out thereCharlotte Hill is chief executive of the food redistribution organisation FelixTue 6 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 17.15 EDTShareHow often does this happen? You open the fridge and find some ingredient you meant to use but didn’t get round to, and even though it’s still edible you think perhaps it’s just easier to throw it away. In the UK it’s estimated that an average household wastes aboutthree meals a week, or 156 meals a year.Household fridges are one thing. But across the food sector, more than 1bn meals’ worth of easily accessible surplus food iswasted each year in the UKfor the same reason: because it is easier to throw it away. That equates to470,000 tonnes– enough to feed every child in the UK three meals a day for a month. When so many people are struggling to afford food, that is a staggering amount – and what’s even more shocking is that it is good quality and nutritious.We hear a lot about grocery stores and restaurants throwing out perfectly edible food, but they are just a small part of the problem. The vastmajority of food waste, about 850m meals, comes from farms, followed by food manufacturing facilities with 178m meals, another 71m from the hospitality and food service sector, and finally 12m meals from the retail sector.When I say easily accessible, I mean this is food we have the capacity to rescue and get to people. The organisation I head, Felix, is a food rescue charity. We recover edible surplus food that would otherwise go to waste and get it to more than 8,000 organisations that do amazing work to feed people in need. This food sustains lunch clubs for older people where friendships are forged and isolation is addressed. It supports food pantries, where families can access a weekly bag of shopping for just a few pounds. And it can provide meals in homelessness shelters and refuges. But with food insecurity rising, so too is the need for the food we recover. So we must rescue more of that billion-meal surplus.In our food system, unavoidable surplus food is generated at every stage of the supply chain. On farms, unpredictable weather, grading standards and mismatches between harvest volumes and buyer orders contribute to the enormous quantities of edible produce without a home. But we are working with farmers to ensure this food is getting to people’s plates; almost half the food we gave out last year was fresh fruit and vegetables.In manufacturing, production overruns, packaging changes and quality control measures create surplus that cannot be sold through normal channels. But there are bright spots – and an incredible example is the food manufacturer Premier Foods. When their noodle nests don’t pass quality control, we take them and use a partner organisation to repack and label them. We are doing a similar project with 2 Sisters Food Group, a huge manufacturing company that uses late-night surplus factory capacity to repack breaded chicken with minor visual defects.We are also working with supermarkets such as Asda, Co-op, Ocado, Sainsbury’s, Tesco and Waitrose. They give us a huge amount of stock that we get straight back out to every part of the UK.So many companies are doing their bit, but the reason many are not is economics. It is cheaper for a business to waste food than to give it to people: the corporation tax system does not reward food donation in the same way it does a financial one. In addition, public subsidies for alternative disposal routes – such as turning food waste into animal food or biogas – provide profit. This creates a market that actively pulls surplus away from human consumption. We must change this.That is why Felix has started the Redistribution Revolution. Felix, City Harvest, Community Shop, The Bread and Butter Thing, His Church, Feeding Britain, Neighbourly and the wider Felix and Xcess Networks have formed the Food Redistribution Partnership UK, working together to rescue more food. Backed by the government, we have launched a national programme to redistribute surplus food that aims to triple the amount of food we redistribute over the next decade. According to our research, about 1% of all excess food in the UK food system is redistributed by charities.France redistributes about twice that, while the US does three times more.Our revolution needs food businesses to make redistribution the default route for all surplus food, and view it as an opportunity for social good. We need philanthropists to invest in the infrastructure required to store and move the food. And we need the government to change the tax system and make it more financially viable for companies to get food to people.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFinally, we need donations and volunteers to help us rescue and deliver more food.We know surplus food is out there, and while it is very important to recognise that redistribution is not a systemic solution to poverty, we are certain that good food is going to waste. Rescuing it can be a powerful way to alleviate the symptoms of food insecurity, and to support organisations that are helping people tackle the challenges in their lives.Charlotte Hill is chief executive of the food redistribution organisation FelixExplore more on these topicsFood wasteOpinionFood povertyFood banksVoluntary sectorPovertyFarmingcommentShareReuse this content

title: Burnham’s surprise EU-turn could deliver the Tories from a generational mess | Gaby Hinsliff | The Guardian
description: Badenoch would never have reopened the door on Brexit, but now that the PM has, it suits the Conservatives to let him walk through it, says Guardian columnist Gaby Hinsliff
Author: Gaby Hinsliff
Headline: Badenoch would never have reopened the door on Brexit, but now that the PM has, it suits the Conservatives to let him walk through it, says Guardian columnist Gaby Hinsliff
Content: An effigy outside parliament in 2019 depicting Tory politicians Theresa May, Boris Johnson, Michael Gove and David Davis.Photograph: Facundo Arrizabalaga/EPAView image in fullscreenAn effigy outside parliament in 2019 depicting Tory politicians Theresa May, Boris Johnson, Michael Gove and David Davis.Photograph: Facundo Arrizabalaga/EPAOpinionBrexitBurnham’s surprise EU-turn could deliver the Tories from a generational messGaby HinsliffBadenoch would never have reopened the door on Brexit, but now that the PM has, it suits the Conservatives to let him walk through itTue 6 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 07.59 EDTShareThere’s no way on earth it should have worked, but somehow he may have got away with it. Last week, the actorRichard E Grantbecame the first contestant on The Traitors – a show whose only unbreakable rule is never to let anyone know you’re the murderer – to gleefully announce within minutes of being selected that yes, haha,it’s him!Yet even then many of his fellow contestants seemed to like him too much to recoil.And that, roughly speaking, is now Andy Burnham’s Brexit strategy. After years of Labour politicians – not least Burnham himself,in the Makerfield byelection, without which he would not now be prime minister – trying to hide their real feelings about Brexit, Burnham has decided just to tell the truth and hope people roll with it. Leaving hasn’t worked, he said bluntlylast week in Liverpool, and Britain should consider the alternatives. If you’re a leaver who suspects him of being out to unwind Brexit – well, yes, he is. This bold strategy seemingly surprisedmuch of his own cabinet, an early lesson in how he likes to work for those who hadn’t studied his Manchester operation closely enough. But the oddly muted initial response to what would once have been a seismic shock suggests it’s wrongfooting some opponents, too.Nigel Farage has been the only one to react withunfettered glee. Reform’s next manifesto is basically now written for him: save Brexit, stop the boats and don’t vote for Restore because it can’t win.Things are more complicated for the Lib Dems and Greens, who, having pitched themselves as the only real pro-Europeans on the left, are now stuck with trying to take credit for pushingLabourinto doing the right thing. But it’s the party currently holding its conference in Birmingham that faces the most interesting dilemma.Kemi Badenoch doesn’t mention Brexit much these days – only elected after the referendum, she seems to regard the generational Conservative trauma of that period as history now – and it gets only brief mentions inThe Right Way, the 95-page personal essay she says would form the bedrock of a Tory government. In his platform speech on Monday, the shadow chancellor, Andrew Griffith, chose to focus on accusing Burnham of supposedly dragging Britain back to the 1970s, rather than back to 2015. On this they echo much of what’s left of the Tory vote, who are more interested in tax, the costs of doing business, small boats and what exactly Labour has againstlabradors in pubsthan in relitigating the Brexit deal. Yet the Conservatives are stillpromising to reverseany Labour unravelling of Brexit, regardless of how that affects the economic growth Badenoch simultaneously insists is everything to her.It makes no intellectual sense, which arguably didn’t bother previous Tory leaders. But it’s a mistake for one pitching herself as a rigorous thinker, approaching power with the same robustly worked-through theory of the world as Thatcher in the 1970s.Growth is now Badenoch’s rationale for everything, fromscrapping the Environment Agency– accused of being a drag on developers, although that’s precisely what some rural Tory voters like about it – togiving parents earning over £100,000 free childcare(on the grounds that, currently, high earners will cut their working hours rather than lose that nursery place). It’s her defence for some potentially unpopular choices, her alpha and omega. Yet by ignoring the ongoing damage Brexit is doing to trade and GDP, Badenoch is chopping her self-professed growth mission off at the knees.In her 1976 essayThe Right Approach, which Badenoch’s treatise consciously echoes, Margaret Thatcher declared that her party “has always been outward-looking, while concerned with the security, the economic interests and the honour of Britain”, and lambasted Labour’s lack of enthusiasm for the then European Community. The context now is obviously different, but Thatcher in 1976 was still a pragmatist arguing for Europe “to concentrate on what is practical and what is attainable”, where Badenoch in 2026 is an ideologue. The Tory brand remains toxic despite its leader’srelative popularitymostly because voters got sick of endless Brexit-related drama consuming Westminster, while none of the practical benefits materialised. There’s no point dangling policies such as free childcare for bankers over the remain-voting former Tory shires without acknowledging all that. But if she can’t bring herself to do so, then Badenoch’s next best bet is to let Burnham rescue her party from a dead end of its own making.Though they would never have opened this door, in truth it suits the Tories to let Burnham walk through it, while blaming him for whatever goes wrong. If he can construct some mythical EU deal boosting trade and prosperity while remaining acceptable to an electorate convulsed with anxiety about immigration – a big if – then future governments will owe him. If he can’t, Badenoch can just join the chorus of condemnation. But it’s not in Tory long-term interests to strangle this at birth.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionReaders who couldn’t care less about Tory long-term interests, meanwhile, should care thatEuropewon’t re-enter tortuous Brexit negotiations until it’s clear they could survive a change of government in Britain. If not a referendum, that means at least tacit cross-party acceptance that the country could do better. Badenoch doesn’t even have to say yes to a rethink. All she has to do, for once, is not say no.Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsBrexitOpinionKemi BadenochAndy BurnhamConservative conferenceConservative conference 2026ConservativesEuropean UnioncommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘My poetry won me asylum’: Cecilia Vicuña on exile life in ‘sad’ Britain after Pinochet’s coup | Art and design | The Guardian
description: Five decades after convincing judges she’d be killed if she returned to Chile, the artist is back with a politically charged retrospective in the country she grew to love
Author: Nadia Khomami
Headline: Five decades after convincing judges she’d be killed if she returned to Chile, the artist is back with a politically charged retrospective in the country she grew to love
Content: ‘My stories want to live again’ … Vicuña with Quipu Menstrual at her new Whitechapel exhibition.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘My stories want to live again’ … Vicuña with Quipu Menstrual at her new Whitechapel exhibition.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianArt and design‘My poetry won me asylum’: Cecilia Vicuña on exile life in ‘sad’ Britain after Pinochet’s coupFive decades after convincing judges she’d be killed if she returned to Chile, the artist is back with a politically charged retrospective in the country she grew to loveNadia KhomamiTue 6 Oct 2026 10.28 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 17.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCecilia Vicuña was 24 when she first arrived in London. She had come from Santiago on a British Council scholarship to study at the Slade School ofArt, and her stay was supposed to be so brief that she didn’t even unpack her suitcase.Then, in September 1973, General Augusto Pinochet’s military coup overthrew Chile’s democratically elected president, Salvador Allende. Vicuña was one of a handful of Chilean students in London immediately expelled from their universities and expected to leave Britain. At a Home Office hearing, her pro-bono lawyers argued that she would be killed if she returned to Chile, and showed the judges her recently published art and poetry book, Saborami, which documented the aftermath of the coup. The judges granted her asylum.“It’s really one of the main stories of my life,” Vicuña says now. “How my poetry came to protect my wellbeing.”We meet on Zoom, with Vicuña in her apartment in New York, where she has lived since 1980. Wearing a knitted hat, she speaks softly and sagely, like a shaman offering advice – small and fragile, but with big, existential ideas about life and art.More than half a century since her arrival in London, Vicuña, now 78 and one of Latin America’s most renowned artists, poets and feminist activists, is returning – specifically to Stepney Green, where she lived as a young artist – for her first major UK exhibition, at theWhitechapel Gallery. She has mixed feelings. “In a way, I’m going back to relieve my original experience,” she says.View image in fullscreenSpeaking to things lost … aprecariofrom 1967.Photograph: © 2026 Cecilia Vicuña/Artist Rights Society (ARS), New York Courtesy the artist and Lehmann MaupinThe London Vicuña encountered in the 1970s was very different from the image of “swinging London” exported around the world. “When you walked down the streets, people were extremely poor,” she says. “People had to put a penny to heat their little apartments. There was a feeling of sadness, of not being able to realise one’s full potential.”But she began meeting exiles from failed revolutions across Africa, the Middle East, Greece and Latin America, found a thriving art community, and published her first book in London after it had been censored in Chile. “I grew to love it,” she says. “But I also understood that true creative energy was on the other side of the continent.”The new exhibition, Living Threads, brings together six decades of Vicuña’s work across painting, textile, photography, installation and film. It also returns to her political life as a young artist speaking at trade union gatherings on the top floor of English pubs. A room is dedicated to Artists for Democracy, which Vicuña co-founded in 1974 with Guy Brett, David Medalla and John Dugger in solidarity with Chile and other liberation struggles worldwide, bringing together never-before-seen documents, photographs and printed materials.“There have been a few attempts to tell this story without my presence,” she says. “The story has been told as if I was a visitor to the organisation.”View image in fullscreenPerformance protest … Nudo de tres, 1969-1970.Photograph: © 2026 Cecilia Vicuña/Artist Rights Society (ARS), New York Courtesy the artist and Lehmann MaupinHer involvement began after artist Conrad Atkinson invited her to an ICA discussion about artists’ rights and sales. Shocked that people were discussing money while artists were being killed in Chile, Vicuña stood up to speak. Brett, Medalla and Dugger, sitting at the back, sent her a note afterwards. “I proposed that we should found an organisation for democracy,” she says.“England was the first country to acknowledge Pinochet as the new leader of Chile,” she adds. “This violent overthrow of democratic government was celebrated by Britain.” Yet the same country had granted her the legal protection to stay: “The place where the defence of the law was powerful enough to grant me that.”The exhibition also brings back a painful part of that period: the work Vicuña lost. During her exile, she left pieces with friends in London, Chile and Bogotá; one trunk contained 400 sculptures, eventually thrown away.“I was so devalued as a person, as an artist,” she says. “To be a dark little South American woman, even in Latin America, is to be in a position of pain, disrespect and inappreciation.” Some have since been recreated from memory and photographs – not reconstruction, she says, but something closer to reincarnation. “It’s the stories and images that want to live again.”View image in fullscreen‘Will greater visibility of women translate to women being valued as equals? We will see’ … Llaverito (Blue Lady) / Ladilla, Crab, 2019 after a lost original 1979 work.Photograph: © 2025 Cecilia Vicuña Courtesy of the artist and Lehmann MaupinThat idea of disappearance runs through the two forms Vicuña is best known for. She began making what she callsprecariosin the 1960s from sticks, feathers, leaves, stones, bones and debris – deliberately fragile, impermanent works, a response to standing as a 17-year-old on a Chilean beach, in the shadow of an oil refinery built over an ancestral burial ground, suddenly aware of the relationship between sea, wind and objects. The only survivingprecariofrom her London years is in the show.“To preserve and disappear are not opposite things,” she says. “Awareness of disappearance is what needs to be preserved. It’s the belief that life itself is poetry, and poetry is life. Disappearance is regeneration.”Herquipus, meanwhile, are made from knotted and unspun fibre, drawing on an ancient Andean system of recording and communication. Vicuña has spent decades reimagining the form, including in Quipu Menstrual, a towering installation in deep red that will be shown at Whitechapel.Her work has increasingly turned towards ecology. She has worked with water for more than 50 years, and she describes the current situation in Chile as both devastating and potentially transformative.“Latin America is the most destroyed of all continents: 95% of its biodiversity has been destroyed already, because people continue to vote for leaders who open the gates to this violent extraction. They call them resources, but it’s not resources. It’s life.” But she points to hope: “Reports show that young Chileans see their future as professional defenders of the land. That, to me, is the most beautiful sign that this shift is still possible.”double quotation markI think, in truth, democracy was never really practised in the westThe current shift to the right in Chile, she argues, doesn’t simply repeat 1973. Back then, she says, those seeking justice, democracy and freedom of expression were the majority and were “violently crushed by foreign intervention. Now, people are willingly choosing to be aligned with the forces that deny global warming and deny people’s rights, women’s rights, the rights of nature.”I ask her if democracy has become more fragile. “I think, in truth, democracy was never really practised in the west.” She points to Allende’s Chile as one example of participatory democracy, and argues that many indigenous societies offered earlier models that were destroyed by colonisation.The internet, she adds, was another squandered chance: a tool for universal access to knowledge that became a place of surveillance and misinformation. “Each chance that the people of this planet have had to open up to the potential of democracy a destructive force comes in to stop it.”View image in fullscreen‘My work was acknowledged for the first time as a work that had meaning and importance’ …Vicuña at her Whitechapel show.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianShe sees artificial intelligence through a similar lens. Her concern is that AI is controlled by private companies for profit, while governments have failed to regulate what she sees as an existential threat.“Now AI has been trained to train itself, and as soon as that happens, it started to behave in a destructive way. Powerful people are saying the existential threat to humanity is a hoax. I have the feeling most people in the world don’t feel it’s a hoax at all. So where is the democratic will of this planet? Is it crushed or prevented?”Vicuña spent decades operating relatively under the radar before a burst of institutional recognition began with her inclusion in Documenta in 2017, aged 69 – she was the youngest artist in a group that included women in their 80s and 90s. “It was the event that changed my life,” she says. “My work was acknowledged for the first time as a work that had meaning and importance.” The museum told her visitors came looking for “the red thing” – herquipu. Since then she has won the Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement at the Venice Biennale, received a Guggenheim survey, and completed a Tate Modern Turbine Hall commission.That 2022 work, Brain Forest Quipu, featured huge mobiles of fraying wool, knotted rope and debris mudlarked from the Thames, an elegy to lost language and wilful destruction;the Guardian’s five-star reviewcalled it the most moving Turbine Hall commission in years.She sees the greater visibility of women, and of Latin American, Asian and African artists, in major museums as a genuine shift – but remains cautious. “Will that translate to women being valued as equals? We will see.”For now, she is returning to the neighbourhood where the young artist she once was became an exile and activist. The Whitechapel exhibition brings together works that survived, works that disappeared, and works that have been remade. “I do hope it will be healing,” she says.Cecilia Vicuña: Living Threads is at theWhitechapel Gallery, London, from 7 October until 14 FebruaryExplore more on these topicsArt and designSculptureWhitechapel GalleryArtInstallationPaintingExhibitionsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The 90s: Art and Fashion review – this isn’t an exhibition, it’s a magazine spread | Art | The Guardian
description: The Young British Art of the 1990s was brash and macabre but also intelligent and emotional. This breathlessly superficial show reduces it to a stylish pose
Author: Jonathan Jones
Headline: The Young British Art of the 1990s was brash and macabre but also intelligent and emotional. This breathlessly superficial show reduces it to a stylish pose
Content: Great Deeds Against the Dead, 1994, by Jake and Dinos Chapman.Photograph: Jake and Dinos Chapman/Jake and Dinos Chapman. All Rights Reserved, DACS ImagesView image in fullscreenGreat Deeds Against the Dead, 1994, by Jake and Dinos Chapman.Photograph: Jake and Dinos Chapman/Jake and Dinos Chapman. All Rights Reserved, DACS ImagesArtReviewThe 90s: Art and Fashion review – this isn’t an exhibition, it’s a magazine spreadTate Britain, LondonThe Young British Art of the 1990s was brash and macabre but also intelligent and emotional. This breathlessly superficial show reduces it to a stylish poseJonathan JonesTue 6 Oct 2026 05.54 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 14.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJake and Dinos Chapman were dismissed by some even in the 1990s as overgrown adolescents selling shock for its own sake, and yet it is their work that brings this dismally shallow show closest to a moment of depth. Their sculpture Great Deeds Against the Dead, based on a print of Napoleonic war atrocities by Goya, is a display of dismembered, bleeding nude corpses hung on a tree. It asks questions about war and art, the representation of pain, whether art can have a moral purpose. The best British art of the 1990s was like that, coming on as brash, vulgar, macabre, yet also unexpectedly intelligent and emotional. Unfortunately this show is neither.You’d thinkTate Britainwould want to do justice to a decade in which these Millbank premises played a starring role, staging the Turner prize in the years when bisected cows, concrete houses and elephant dung got the nation arguing. At the start of the 1990s no one thought Britain was a leader in contemporary art. By the millennium, we were better known for new art than new novels.View image in fullscreenHarmless … Two Similar Swimming Forms in Endless Motion (Broken), 1993, by Damien Hirst.Photograph: Damien Hirst and Science Ltd/DACS ImagesA show that spectacularly revisited fin-de-siecle British art would be an interesting proposition. Instead former Vogue editor Edward Enninful has been invited to stage his personal fantasy version of that decade, mixing up art and fashion, with the emphasis very much on fashion. There’s more about Isabella Blow than Rachel Whiteread, who is represented by an early cast of the inside of a hot-water bottle. Damien Hirst has a couple of small, harmless-looking sharks balanced on a circular rail. There’s no chance of understanding from this how his early work seemed to confront the tiger shark’s maw of death. Perhaps his 1990s art can still move, or perhaps it has become silly with time, but there is not enough of it to even begin to decide.This is not a real exhibition. It’s a magazine spread. Not only are there style mags in the show, its design has the breathless superficiality of a glossy layout bigging up its glib theme, in this case “The 90s”, in a glamorous sweep of strikingly juxtaposed images. But setting fashion photography alongside works of conceptual art is a terrible idea. If you take the fashion images seriously you reduce the art to another stylish pose. If, like me, you care about the art, the fashion looks pretty vacant.Juergen Teller’s 1996 photograph Kristen McMenamy No 3 is hung next to Sarah Lucas’s 1997 work Chicken Knickers. Teller’s picture depicts its subject naked and smoking with a lipstick heart drawn on her containing the word “Versace”. What is it saying other than “Buy Versace”? Now look at Lucas’ photograph of a raw chicken stuck to someone’s knickers. It’s funny – a great deed against a dead chicken from an artist with a genius for estrangement, as a Lucas sculpture of a “Bunny” on a chair with thin stockinged legs reminds you.View image in fullscreenA genius for estrangement … Chicken Knickers, 1997, by Sarah Lucas.Photograph: Tate Photography/Courtesy the artist and Sadie Coles HQ, LondonTeller is exposed as just a clever stylist whose images lack poetry or meaning. His portrait of Kate Moss has none of the distance or mystery of Gary Hume’s painting of her with a shiny, metallic, mirroring face. Hume provides one of the few moments when fashion and art genuinely overlap – but as pop art, his Kate is more a baleful, Richard Hamilton-like comment on celebrity than a celebration of Cool Britannia.Not that the show has much to say about that wider pop cultural fizz. There’s an entire room full of party pics depicting the club scene, but surely another point of the 90s was that mainstream British pop was revived – I guess Enninful is too sophisticated to find space for Oasis or Blur, let alone Fat Les.Instead we get couture. You can obviously see Alexander McQueen as an artist. But honestly. The room dealing with “body horror” is dominated by his costumes that are just mannered and pretentious. If they express anything it might be a hatred of women whom he forced to go on catwalks in suits of wire and steel bouquets. In the same room pompous, awful images shot by Sean Ellis for The Face take up an entire wall. It’s next to these that Jake and Dinos look so profound.View image in fullscreenPompous, awful images … The Dark Knight Returns, by Sean Ellis for the Face, 1998.Photograph: © Sean EllisOther fine artists don’t fare so well. Helen Chadwick gets two tokenistic eerie photoworks while the death-obsessed art of Hamad Butt, shown beautifullyat the Whitechapelnot so long ago, is squeezed to the end of the gallery. Chris Ofili is namechecked with No Woman, No Cry; Tracey Emin gets one neon. Other artists are noticeable by their absence, from Jeremy Deller to Mat Collishaw to the late and missed Christine Borland.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toArt WeeklyYour weekly art world round-up, sketching out all the biggest stories, scandals and exhibitionsEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHard parties, cheap rents and horrible flats: how 90s art and fashion redefined British cultureRead moreOr am I wrong? Does Young BritishArtfully deserve the dismissive treatment that Tate, which did so well out of these artists, gives it? Perhaps it really was a load of codswallop. But even if you don’t share my belief that some of the art of that time is powerful and enduring, surely it deserves enough space to be seen and judged.After just seven rooms it suddenly ends. I hoped what I’d seen was a prologue to more art, bigger art, with enough space to appreciate it. But no. That’s it. You leave as dissatisfied as you might after flicking through a 30-year-old copy of The Face in a dentist’s waiting room.The 90s is atTate Britain, London, from 8 October 2026 until 14 February 2027Explore more on these topicsArtTate BritainExhibitionsMuseumsPhotographyreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Bel review – a tearful, heartbreaking tribute to a spellbinding singer  | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: Beldina Odenyo was on the verge of stardom when she took her own life in 2021. In this beautiful documentary, her grief-stricken sister Leah attempts to finish her album – and her journey will make you cry again and again
Author: Chitra Ramaswamy
Headline: Beldina Odenyo was on the verge of stardom when she took her own life in 2021. In this beautiful documentary, her grief-stricken sister Leah attempts to finish her album – and her journey will make you cry again and again
Content: Beldina Odenyo in 2017.Photograph: BBC/Hopscotch Films/Andrew CawleyView image in fullscreenBeldina Odenyo in 2017.Photograph: BBC/Hopscotch Films/Andrew CawleyTV reviewTelevision & radioReviewBel review – a tearful, heartbreaking tribute to a spellbinding singerBeldina Odenyo was on the verge of stardom when she took her own life in 2021. In this beautiful documentary, her grief-stricken sister Leah attempts to finish her album – and her journey will make you cry again and againChitra RamaswamyTue 6 Oct 2026 18.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn 2021, the Kenyan-Scottish singer-songwriter Beldina Odenyo was on the brink of major stardom. That October, aged 31, she headlined a gig at Edinburgh’s Usher Hall, delivering an instantly legendary performance; barefoot, cloaked and bone-shaking in its intensity. Everyone in that concert hall knew they were witnessing something extraordinary that night. Two weeks later, Odenyo took her own life.This tender and grief-stricken documentary, which opens a year after her death, is directed with remarkable care by Louise Lockwood. What emerges is a sensitively drawn portrait of a visionary artist haunted by trauma, formed through her teenage video diaries, the words of those who loved her, the handful of exquisite songs she left behind – kept in a folder on her hard drive named “passable demos” – and the determination of her older sister, Leah McAleer, to keep her astonishing voice alive. A deeply painful venture that she understands is itself a product of her insurmountable grief.“All of this is a futile attempt to bring her back,” says McAleer while listening to Odenyo’s songs in the studio, her sparse guitar-playing sent through an amplifier to sound as though she’s in the room. Earlier, she put it even more starkly: “I need to finish her album.”View image in fullscreenExtraordinary … Bel’s last performance at  Edinburgh’s Usher Hall in 2021.Photograph: BBC/Hopscotch Films/Euan RobertsonAnd what an album it is, propelled by musical genius, the poles of suffering and survival between which Odenyo was buffeted, and her tremendous voice. “I love music,” says the often cocky, often crying 15-year-old at the start of Bel, in one of the charismatic video diaries delivered from her bedroom in the ex-mining village of Kirkconnel, Dumfries and Galloway, to her future fans. “I want to be a musician. I want to be famous, to show the world my skills …” she laughs, “and just rock their socks off.” In another video she notes: “I’m quite mad as a person. I don’t give a fuck, to be honest.”Odenyo was born in Kisumu, western Kenya, and for the first few years of her life lived with her mother and siblings. She met her father for the first time at around the age of six or seven. “A few weeks later,” she says in an interview, “I was in Scotland.” McAleer’s memory of what happened and why Odenyo was taken from her mother by her father is equally fractured – neither family spoke about the devastating loss that reverberated through her life. “My father came back [from Kenya] with a small child,” says McAleer. “I just remember the shock … and her pristine white dress. She didn’t cry. She didn’t speak for three days.” All this silence and shock was channelled into her music, and that once-in-a-generation voice.View image in fullscreenLeah and Bel circa 1998.Photograph: BBC/Hopscotch Films/Leah McAleerBel is also a close study of mental illness, its healing but also precarious relationship with creativity, and the devastating impacts of exile and racism. In Kirkconnel, where Odenyo was the only black kid in her school, “she was set on fire once,” says her best friend, Frances. “She had a chain wrapped around her neck … it was horrific physical abuse.” In Glasgow, during a mental health episode in which an ambulance was called by a friend because she was self-harming, the police arrived first. Odenyo said they broke down her door, threw her down the stairs, and demanded to know if she had HIV because “people from where you’re from do”. By the time lockdown hit she was living alone in Paisley, increasingly isolated, ill and vulnerable. It was then that she uploaded those “passable demos” to her computer.It’s a harrowing watch, which brings me to tears over and over again, brimming with voices traumatised by her suicide. The poet Jackie Kay was blown away by Odenyo’s self-possession: “Bel didn’t feel the need to smile or ingratiate herself with an audience.” Ex-boyfriend and fellow musician Lewis Semple remembers first hearing her sing in Glasgow: “Her voice fucking blew me away. I was shaking in my seat.” For venue booker Joe Rattray, she was “someone who makes a place cooler”. For Scottish singer-songwriter Kathryn Joseph whose sublime song The Bird was covered by Odenyo at that Usher Hall gig, “she was someone who understood humans … and pain.” At the end of Bel, footage from the Usher Hall gig plays again. Then Odenyo’s voice cuts out. A long, painfully apt silence ensues alongside stills of her flat, her musical equipment, her cables, her glasses. It’s beautifully done.In many ways Bel belongs to McAleer, a dignified and humane presence throughout. She was clearly a mother figure to Odenyo – they were “adultified children” who “grew up fast” is how she puts it – and speaks with incredible articulacy and self-awareness considering the immediacy of her grief. At Odenyo’s graveside in Kenya, where she wanted to be buried close to her mother and where the documentary ends, McAleer plays her album, which she’s worked tirelessly to release independently, and confesses: “I feel on a very deep level I let her down.” Which couldn’t be further from the truth: Bel is a memorial to her love.Ultimately, though, it’s Odenyo’s music that most powerfully tells her story. She performed as Heir of the Cursed, a name that came to her in a dream and turned out to be a translation of the Tetela name of the assassinated Congolese leader Patrice Lumumba. These few heartbreaking, sometimes foreshadowing songs, into which Odenyo poured all that she could not say, are played throughout the film. Watch it. Then go and listen to her phenomenal music.Bel aired on BBC Four and is on iPlayer now.In the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123, or emailjo@samaritans.orgorjo@samaritans.ie. In the US, you can call or text theNational Suicide Prevention Lifelineon 988, chat on988lifeline.org, ortext HOMEto 741741 to connect with a crisis counsellor. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. title: Artificial review – Luca Guadagnino takes on OpenAI in muddled tech satire | New York film festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: The origin story of Sam Altman’s company is reimagined as a campy comedy starring Andrew Garfield
Author: Owen Myers
Headline: The origin story of Sam Altman’s company is reimagined as a campy comedy starring Andrew Garfield
Content: Andrew Garfield as Sam Altman and Yura Borisov as Ilya Sutskever in Artificial.Photograph: Courtesy of NeonView image in fullscreenAndrew Garfield as Sam Altman and Yura Borisov as Ilya Sutskever in Artificial.Photograph: Courtesy of NeonFirst look reviewNew York film festival 2026ReviewArtificial review – Luca Guadagnino takes on OpenAI in muddled tech satireNew York film festival:The origin story of Sam Altman’s company is reimagined as a campy comedy starring Andrew GarfieldOwen MyersTue 6 Oct 2026 12.58 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 13.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn the day thatLuca Guadagnino’s film aboutSam AltmanandOpenAIpremiered, Vanity Fair released acover storyon Altman. Alongside glossy portraits from Annie Leibovitz, the world’s pre-eminent portrait photographer, the story describes him as the Oppenheimer of his day, evoking the image of a man leading humanity towards its own inevitable demise at the hands of sentient robots. Altman doesn’t seem to be grappling with much existential angst about the whole thing though: in aninterviewalso released this week, he said that we should be prepared to accept “bad things” in return for the benefits of AI.Club Kid review – Jordan Firstman’s heartfelt comedy is irresistibleRead moreHow much worse can things get? AI agents have alreadygone rogue, hacking into government systems and “bruteforcing” UN databases.Last year, a young woman usedChatGPTas a therapist before she killed herself (the software helped her write her suicide note). Studies show that using AI is probably leading us all towards something called cognitive surrender, which does not seem like the best use of your one wild and precious life.Artificial is a stylish and blunt satire that is unambiguous in its perspective: that Sam Altman is an amoral manipulator who might be dead inside. That goes some way towards explaining why Amazon MGM Studiospulled outof distributing the film in June (Jeff Bezos’s company has a $50bn investment in OpenAI). I found it to be more of an op-ed than a movie, with little insight into what makes Altman and the tech elite tick. Neither does it have much to say about the world – glossy magazines included – that has welcomed them with open arms.In 2003, a young math prodigy named Ilya Sutskever (Yura Borisov, the heartbeat of the film) visits Prof Geoff Hinton (Mark Rylance) in his office hoping for a job with the man known as the godfather of AI. “Have you ever considered the link between knowledge and patience?” Hinton serenely asks his young charge. You can almost feel Guadagnino is turning to the audience and giving us a big stage wink.Nine years later, Sutskever and Hinton’s technology is starting to work “much the way your mind does”, with an ability to differentiate between cats and dogs, but Sutskever is growing increasingly impatient with what he sees as Hinton’s conservative ambitions for the technology. It’s at this point that Elon Musk (Ike Barinholtz) introduces Sutskever to Sam Altman (Andrew Garfield), who is fresh from selling his Loopt app, a kind of proto-Find My Friends, for $40m.You Can See Everything review – Nathan Fielder’s Elizabeth Holmes doc is a modern masterpiece of deceitRead moreThese guys are total dweebs, peppering each other with puerile jokes while doing shots in upscale restaurants as servers grimace and pray for a tip. Everyone is starting to want what these guys are selling, and one prospective investor speculates that AI will soon be able to reverse climate change and cure cancer. When talking about the technology, Sutskever’s eyes light up. “All pain, all loneliness will cease,” he says, as knowingly over-the-top haunted house music plays. “We will be free.”The film’s dramatic tension rests in the opposing poles of thought represented by Sutskever, a delusional optimist, and the self-motivated hubris of Altman. As we move into the recent past, cracks and fissures appear in their partnership as OpenAI’s self-learning technology begins to first outsmart humans at video games, and then becomes a different beast entirely. Garfield is brilliantly slimy, nailing Altman’s evolution from demon twink to a narcissistic grifter with a victim complex that climaxes with him being fired as the CEO ofOpenAIand then rehired five days later. “They’re being very mean to me,” he pouts in one scene after his board airs one of its many legitimate concerns over the ethics of his product.View image in fullscreenYura Borisov, Luca Guadagnino, Andrew Garfield and Ike Barinholtz at the Artificial premiere at the New York film festival on Monday.Photograph: Michael Loccisano/Getty Images for FLCArtificial is the most outwardly comedic Guadagnino film to date, with a script by the New Yorker essayist Simon Rich. The humor can be frustratingly broad, and it often feels like Barinholtz is impersonating Mike Myers doing Musk on Saturday Night Live than the Tesla founder himself (Rich is a former writer on SNL). Garfield seems to be playing Altman, who is an out gay man, as more effete than he actually is, which is strange as there are plenty of reasons to laugh at the tech oligarch that don’t involve him being light in his loafers. At other times, the script is satisfyingly savage. After being questioned over safety concerns by his associate Mira Murati (Monica Barbaro), Altman snaps, “I didn’t invent teen suicide, Mira.”A Statement review – outstanding climate change dramedy about a 1980 meetingRead moreI could have done without some Artificial’s clangingly obvious visual metaphors, such as a random shot of a unhoused person wearing VR goggles, or the sudden plunge into a simulator-like sequence of a car accelerating over a foggy Golden Gate Bridge (we get it, we’re taking a reckless leap into the unknown). The film comes with a score by Damon Albarn, and the Blur frontman contributes one original composition that an ASPCA advert would reject for being too on-the-nose with lyrics like, “In a corrupt world, we’ll sing the saddest song.”It’s tech oligarch season at the movies, with films aboutElon Musk, Elizabeth Holmes and Mark Zuckerberg also due for release over the next few months as film-makers try to respond to the zeitgeist in real time. “We opened Pandora’s box,” Altman says in a standout monologue towards the end of the film. “Countries will fall, industries will collapse, and we get to be the ones to usher people into this new world.”It’s a grim prophecy that gets lost in Guadanigno’s tonal jumble of a film, which has a certain self-satisfaction in telling us that dystopia is upon us. I couldn’t help but crave a leaner, meaner version of this movie. Despite some genuinely chilling moments, Artificial shows the limits of holding up a mirror to the world.Artificial is screening at the New York film festival and wil be released in the US on 25 December, in Australia on 21 January and in the UK on 27 JanuaryExplore more on these topicsNew York film festival 2026First look reviewSam AltmanOpenAIAI (artificial intelligence)ComputingElon MuskLuca GuadagninoreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘We got that bad guy and took him down!’ Jaclyn Smith on the fun, friendship and frustration of Charlie’s Angels | Television | The Guardian
description: It’s 50 years since Smith joined TV’s bikini-clad crime fighters alongside Farrah Fawcett and Kate Jackson. She talks about the love she found on set, the harassment she endured off it and the drug-taking she did her best to ignore
Author: Emine Saner
Headline: It’s 50 years since Smith joined TV’s bikini-clad crime fighters alongside Farrah Fawcett and Kate Jackson. She talks about the love she found on set, the harassment she endured off it and the drug-taking she did her best to ignore
Content: ‘Pretty clothes, pretty locations, fast cars … come on, it was just having fun’ … Jaclyn Smith.Photograph: Randee St NicholasView image in fullscreen‘Pretty clothes, pretty locations, fast cars … come on, it was just having fun’ … Jaclyn Smith.Photograph: Randee St NicholasTelevisionInterview‘We got that bad guy and took him down!’ Jaclyn Smith on the fun, friendship and frustration of Charlie’s AngelsEmine SanerIt’s 50 years since Smith joined TV’s bikini-clad crime fighters alongside Farrah Fawcett and Kate Jackson. She talks about the love she found on set, the harassment she endured off it and the drug-taking she did her best to ignoreTue 6 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 07.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor a TV show that only ran for five years, Charlie’s Angels packs a punch like a bikini-wearing big-hair-flicking private investigator. “We never thought we’d be talking about it 50 years later,” says Jaclyn Smith, the only original Angel to make it to the end of the show’s run. Smith, 80, has now written a memoir, I Once Knew a Guy Called Charlie – she is not, you gather, the type of actor to want to distance herself from her defining project.As I read her book, and speak to her over Zoom, she comes across as sensible, hardworking and optimistic. Also lucky: loving and supportive parents, agents who seem to appear from nowhere and offer her work, an early hit show, a gift for making friends and getting over heartbreak. Even when she was diagnosed with breast cancer more than 20 years ago, terrifying as it was, it was caught early and successfully treated. Her positive outlook seems to extend to the excesses of US TV in the 1970s and 80s (drug use on set only gets a brief mention); her three ex-husbands get off fairly lightly; and any difficulties – her OCD, the men who stalked her at the height of her fame – are not dwelled on.View image in fullscreenThe original Angels …(from left)Jaclyn Smith, Kate Jackson and Farrah Fawcett in 1976.Photograph: THA/AlamySmith wanted to be a dancer. By the late 50s, she was attending a dance school in Houston, where she grew up, which was run by Patsy Swayze (mother of Patrick, who would go on to be a successful actor, but was then around seven and, Smith says, “an absolute doll”). She describes an idyllic childhood – happily married parents and a Methodist minister grandfather who was a steady and reassuring presence. Her dad was a dentist and “gave me my work ethic”; her mother was a “goddess of love – she just made you feel No 1”. Smith recalls: “Whatever I am happened in that secure family they provided for me – morals, ethics, values.” Downtime was spent at the family farm in Texas: “Two hundred acres with the San Marcos river running through it. It was life at its best.”But her childhood was also when her compulsive behaviour started. “It became sort of a form of prayer for me – it’s probably the way my brain works – but that all came about protecting loved ones,” she says. She would pray obsessively, thinking it would keep her grandfather safe; later, she would do the same when her two children were born, and she says it still flares up in times of stress.View image in fullscreen‘I didn’t walk on the wild side ever.’Photograph: Randee St NicholasAfter leaving school, Smith convinced her parents to allow her to go to New York to train as a dancer. Her father insisted she live at thewomen-only Barbizon hotel, one-time home to Sylvia Plath, Grace Kelly and Joan Didion among many other notable women. “There were such strict rules there,” she says. “You couldn’t wear slacks in the lobby. I was in hose and a dress and a pair of heels. And boys could not go above the mezzanine.”It must have been exciting to have been a young dancer in New York in the late 60s? “Very competitive,” says Smith. But also a lot more accessible than it is now. “There were open calls for Broadway shows, whereas today you have to have a social media following, an agent, a manager, everything. When I started, you’d read about auditions, and it would be a mass cast call, and maybe you’d make it, maybe you wouldn’t.”Offers for roles in shows started coming in, and Smith – beautiful, classy – was also in demand for lucrative advertising work. While her peers were protesting, taking drugs or embracing early 70s counterculture, Smith married the actor Roger Davis – famous, she writes, for his role in Dark Shadows, the “daytime vampire-themed soap opera”.“I just didn’t get into it,” she says of New York’s bohemian scene. “Did I go to a discotheque and dance? Yeah, I loved it, but no, I didn’t walk on the wild side ever. I was a hard worker.”Perhaps also a little square. When she turned up to audition for Hair, she wore a blue leotard, with pink tights and hair in a neat bun. Smith laughs at her naive Texas primness when trying to convince producers she could be in a taboo-breaking hippie musical: “I looked like I had come from another planet.”Sexual harassment was usual. “I experienced it. I think every actress does,” says Smith. “You can walk away. You can say, ‘Hey, I don’t need that movie. I don’t want it if this is what it requires.’” Were there ever expectations that certainthingswere expected? “Yeah, there was some of that, but you can say no. I think I was never, ever desperate about a career. Maybe that’s because where I came from with my parents, and I knew I could make my own way.” She says she would have been offered a bigger part in one early film if she’d done a nude scene (she refused), and was dropped from another after she got married. Because she was expected to be single, or available? “I guess. But I wanted to be cast not because I was single, but because I was right for the part.”Her first marriage didn’t last; neither did her second to another actor, Dennis Cole. But her career zipped along – small parts in successful series such as the police drama McCloud, and TV movies. She got her first regular job opposite Robert Wagner in the crimefighting caper Switch. It was Wagner who recommended her to producers Aaron Spelling and Leonard Goldberg, who were putting together a new show featuring three female detectives.View image in fullscreenSmith with her fourth husband, Brad Allen, at a Farrah Fawcett Foundation benefit gala in October 2022.Photograph: Rick Kern/Getty Images for Farrah Fawcett FoundationSmith was the last to be cast in Charlie’s Angels, as calm and empathetic Kelly Garrett, and was offered the lowest fee – $3,000 an episode, compared with her original co-stars Farrah Fawcett ($5,000) and Kate Jackson ($10,000). Jackson was a more established star, but Smith demanded to be paid at least the same as Fawcett, whom she reasoned had done a similar level of work to her. “My agent said, ‘Are you sure? We have a good feeling about this series.’ I stood my ground, and I got it.” She would have walked away, she says. “It wasn’t about money. It was the fact that we’d done the same thing, and I thought that was only fair.” (By the fifth season, Smith was earning $100,000 an episode.)The show was an instant hit when it was first broadcast in 1976. “I was excited because I knew it was different – three women instead of three men, chasing danger instead of being rescued from danger.” It was often ridiculous – the three private investigators, working for a mysterious Charlie who only appeared via speakerphone, would go undercover to catch criminals as, Smith writes, “stewardesses, beauty pageant contestants, singers, magicians’ assistants, Ice Capades skaters, football players, jewel thieves, Keystone Cops, toy makers, tennis champions and exotic dancers”. In one episode, Kris Munroe (played by Cheryl Ladd, replacing Fawcett, who left after the first season), wrestles an alligator.View image in fullscreenOn the cover of Time magazine in 1976.Photograph: Patti McConville/AlamyPeople questioned why they had to do all of this looking like supermodels, or criticised the show for objectifying women. “I thought it was silly,” Smith says. “We were not controlled by Charlie. We were working hard, courageous, we went about our job. Usually women on TV then were nurses, mothers, wives. We went into a territory that only men occupied. We got that bad guy and took him down. Also, it was fun and it was escapism. Pretty clothes, pretty locations, fast cars, thin girls taking down a 200lb man … come on. It was just having fun.”Did she ever think they shouldn’t be in bikinis so often? Smith laughs. “I think we did say to Aaron, ‘We don’t want to be in a bikini unless we’re near water.’” But it looks so innocent, she says, “compared to today. Our characters were loyal, chaste, involved in the friendship part of it … we never really had love affairs. It was always the sisterhood.”The original three Angels got on instantly, says Smith, even though inevitably the media tried to create rumours of rivalries and conflict. “Definitely no jealousies,” says Smith. “We loved one another. It was a fellowship, a sisterhood, a team.” They became lifelong friends (Jackson is godmother to Smith’s daughter). “We held each other up during breast cancer, during different things.” Although Fawcett only did one season, Smith says, “I adored Farrah. What you saw was what you got. She was beautiful, had fun, liked to laugh and had great humour.” Fawcett died in 2009, but “we were close until the end of her life”.Having two co-stars go through the strain of becoming famous overnight helped them all, she says. The show had to employ bodyguards for the three Angels, and Smith was a victim of stalking. “I had many restraining orders after Charlie’s,” she says, describing one man who climbed over a security fence during a shoot and claimed to be her husband. He later turned up at her house. “When you’re in someone’s living room every week, I guess they feel they know you.”View image in fullscreenSmith in the 1981 film Jacqueline Bouvier Kennedy.Photograph: Walt Disney Television Photo Archives/ABCBy the fifth and final season, Smith, the only original lead, wasn’t finding it as fun. It was the 1980s and the Angels had to be even more glamorous. Drugs, especially cocaine, were also on set, she writes, “with some people using it constantly”. It took her time to realise, she says. “I was innocent to drugs, but then you tune in to it because people slow down and can’t perform.” Was it common for big TV shows to have drug use? “I think it was,” she says, but she doesn’t approve of it. “It just takes out your spark.” She stayed distant from it all. “I just went about my business, then went to my trailer, and as long as we got our show, everything was fine.”Charlie’s Angels ended in 1981. Smith would later have cameos in the 2000 film reboot, starring Cameron Diaz, Lucy Liu and Drew Barrymore, and the2019 follow-up film. After the show ended, she believes she was typecast as glamorous, but frivolous.View image in fullscreen‘When you’re in every someone’s living room every week, they feel they know you.’Photograph: THA/AlamyBy 1981 she was in her mid-30s and had to fight to play the first lady in the TV biopic Jacqueline Bouvier Kennedy. “They didn’t want a Charlie’s Angel playing Jackie Kennedy,” she says. She is of the generation of actresses who struggled to find decent roles past 40, but by then Smith had two young children – with the cinematographer Tony Richmond, her third husband.As well as parenting, she had a lucrative fashion line and interiors brand, one of the earliest celebrity branding successes. Life, she says, has “been a pretty smooth ride. Yeah, there’s been things along the way, mainly marriages.” Smith has been with Brad Allen, a heart surgeon, since 1991. She spent decades trying to recreate her parents’ happy marriage. “Finally got it,” she says.Her memoir is already out in the US and, doing signings, Smith has loved meeting women who grew up with Charlie’s Angels. “Did the show give women a chance to break out of their mould, to be brave, to be independent? I like to think that.”I Once Knew a Guy Named Charlie by Jaclyn Smith (Simon & Schuster, £20). To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com.
