title: A medieval manuscript has confounded scholars for centuries. Have they been reading it wrong all this time? | Culture | The Guardian
description: Researchers argue incorrect binding of Voynich manuscript radically changes ideas about its drawings and indecipherable text
Author: Philip Oltermann
Headline: Researchers argue incorrect binding of Voynich manuscript radically changes ideas about its drawings and indecipherable text
Content: Folded page from the Voynich manuscript.Photograph: Universal History Archive/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFolded page from the Voynich manuscript.Photograph: Universal History Archive/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesCultureA medieval manuscript has confounded scholars for centuries. Have they been reading it wrong all this time?Researchers argue incorrect binding of Voynich manuscript radically changes ideas about its drawings and indecipherable textPhilip OltermannEuropean culture editorTue 6 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt has been called the world’s most mysterious manuscript: a medieval set of pages filled with botanical drawings, astronomical diagrams, pictures of nude women and indecipherable text. Claimed at various times to be a book in a lost language, a musical score, an instruction manual or just an elaborate hoax, the so-called Voynich manuscript’s true meaning has defied cryptographers and codebreakers for centuries.Now, new research offers an explanation for why a scholarly consensus over this enduring puzzle has been so hard to come by: not only because its truth is so profoundly mysterious – but because everyone has been reading its pages in the wrong order.In an article published in peer-reviewed journal Digital Medievalist, Colin Layfield and Lisa Fagin Davis argue that the manuscript’s folded sheets may have originally been piled on top of each other as “singulions” – like a stack of Christmas cards – but were mis-bound in a more typical “nested” arrangement at some point in the mid to late 15th century.View image in fullscreenA page from The Voynich manuscript.Photograph: Photo 12/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesWhile their finding does not immediately de-code the script, written in what has commonly become known as “Voynichese”, the authors say their finding radically changes our idea of the manuscript’s function.“There are a lot of people who wanted the Voynich to have been created by one mad genius working in their attic in medieval London or wherever,” said Davis. “In fact, the evidence suggests we’re talking about a more communal object, perhaps a set of booklets through which information was passed down from one generation to the next – the ‘lone genius’ idea is kind of out of the door.”The manuscript’s unknown provenance has piqued scholarly interest ever since it surfaced in book collectors’ records in the 17th century. When it was bought in 1912 by Wilfrid Voynich, a Polish revolutionary and book dealer with a shop on London’s Soho Square, it was thought to be a scientific diary written by the 13th-century polymath Roger Bacon. Others have credited the codex to Leonardo da Vinci.Voynich manuscript misboundRecent chemical analyses of the manuscript, which is held at Yale University, have carbon-dated its parchment to between 1404 and 1438, ruling out these famous authorships.Some scholars have argued that the text of the Voynich Manuscript is nothing more than gibberish intended as a hoax or a forgery, thoughrecent linguistic analysishas found it more likely that it is written in a natural, if yet unidentified, language.In 2019, a biology research assistant at the University of Bristol,claimed that the manuscript was written in a “calligraphic proto-Romance” language, but the findings were later disputed, and the university subsequently removed a reference to the claims from its website.For their article “Singulion Structure and the Voynich Manuscript”, Layfield and Davis used a numerical analysis tool to compare blocks of text and found that many of the attached pages scored highly for coherence even when there were many intervening pages, suggesting the manuscript had been mis-bound.View image in fullscreenA page from the Voynich manuscript, an illustrated codex hand-written in an unknown writing system.Photograph: GL Archive/AlamyThere were also visual clues suggesting the pages were supposed to be read in a different order. In the current binding, some illustrations of streams or pipes run into the gutter – the blank space along the inner margins where pages are bound – but don’t fully match with the pictures on the opposite page. “Once you treat them as loose pages stacked together, all these artistic anomalies suddenly join up”, said Layfield, a senior lecturer in information systems at the University of Malta.“Our hypothesis fixes a lot of problems with the structure of the manuscripts in a really elegant way”, said Davis, an expert on medieval handwriting.She said the only other known medieval manuscripts she has found preserved in a singulion arrangement were Qurans from north Africa, which were likely meant to be handed out as small booklets for instruction purposes.“I think it’s likely we are looking similarly at an object that was made by a community that wanted to pass its knowledge forward,” said Davis, adding that her hypothesis was supported by paleographical analysis suggesting the manuscript was written by up to five different scribes.View image in fullscreenThe quality control operator of the Spanish publishing outfit Siloe Luis Miguel works on cloning the illustrated codex hand-written manuscript Voynich in Burgos in 2016.Photograph: César Manso/AFP/Getty ImagesSome of the drawings in the manuscript resemble the female reproductive system, while others hint at herbal lore and astrology. “When you put all of this together, it starts to feel like a book of women’s folk knowledge that’s being preserved,” she said. “But you cannot prove that yet.”As to the mystery of the manuscript’s language, Davis said it wasn’t out of the question that there would have been other manuscripts written in Voynichese.“The problem is that so few manuscripts have survived from the middle ages, because they weren’t bound. The irony is that whoever mis-bound this manuscript still did us a huge favour by ensuring its survival.”Explore more on these topicsCultureEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: V/H/S/Mixtape review – murderous puppets pull the strings in mixed bag of gory music-themed mini-movies | Movies | The Guardian
description: Metal band Gwar host this instalment of the horror series, which serves up darkly humorous movie morsels that would struggle to frighten a toddler
Author: Leslie Felperin
Headline: Metal band Gwar host this instalment of the horror series, which serves up darkly humorous movie morsels that would struggle to frighten a toddler
Content: They’re no muppets … puppets seek revenge on studio executives in Renee Zhan’s short film Dance, Dance, Dance, Dance, featured in V/H/S/MixtapeView image in fullscreenThey’re no muppets … puppets seek revenge on studio executives in Renee Zhan’s short film Dance, Dance, Dance, Dance, featured in V/H/S/MixtapeMoviesReviewV/H/S/Mixtape review – murderous puppets pull the strings in mixed bag of gory music-themed mini-moviesMetal band Gwar host this instalment of the horror series, which serves up darkly humorous movie morsels that would struggle to frighten a toddlerLeslie FelperinTue 6 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe latest in the long-running horror-feature series is, as per usual, a decidedly diverse ragbag of shorts, strung together with the thinnest of connective tissue. The theme this go-round seems to be music and sound, so it sort of makes sense that hosting duties for the interstitial bits fall to the goofy metal bandGwar, its assorted members met here cracking Halloween dad jokes in their trademark extravagant outfits.The five mini movies vary significantly in length as well as quality. Flying Lotus’s stop-motion exercise Another Cabin posits a young boy in a rural cabin living with a mean old grannie who tries to push him forward when a tentacled demon tears the roof of the house in search of a snack. The characters’ resemblance to the cast of early 2000s series The PJs is slightly jarring, given this is such a different register, but the brevity works in its favour. In contrast Renee Zhan’s Dance, Dance, Dance, Dance, the opener, drags on a bit, but has a reasonable gags-to-gore ratio in its tale of murderous puppets taking revenge on visiting studio execs who would dare to “reimagine” some ageing IP best left dormant. The funniest gag is the bright major-scale title song the puppets (designed by Jim Henson’s Creature Shop) sing about how all things must die.Venerable cinematographer turned director Ernest Dickerson (who filmed several key Spike Lee films including Do the Right Thing and Malcolm X) turns the unsurprisingly beautifully shot and designed but thinly written amuse-bouche The Music of Mr Sze. This features Jihad Brent as an aspiring film-maker who becomes bewitched by the violin melodies emanating from the bedsit of his upstairs neighbour (Alex Hsu), a story that escalates into a fantasia of trippy but borderline incomprehensible imagery.Far more straightforward narratively but repetitive, Death Tone (directed by RZA) stars Neela Jolene as the daughter of a famed music producer who follows her late father’s instructions – and dips into his narcotic supply – to make the perfect song, featuring the screams of agony from a range of random victims. RZA is clearly having a jolly chuckle to himself over gags that might crack them up in the sound booth, but they don’t travel as well as he seems to think. Somewhere in the middle of this package David Moreau’s Heartbeat is a snoozy riff on a theme from Edgar Allan Poe, about obnoxious YouTubers who get trapped in a Bulgarian military base.Throughout the practical effects are over the top, rubbery and absurd; so much so they would struggle to frighten a toddler, but with its unpleasantly warped humour it’s not really for kids anyway.V/H/S/Mixtape is on Shudder and AMC+ from 9 OctoberExplore more on these topicsFilmHorror filmsFlying LotusComedy filmsComedyreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Craft review – cult high-school horror a reminder of the fearless 90s | Movies | The Guardian
description: The 30th-anniversary rerelease of this classic tackles the sensitivities of teenage anxiety with energy and confidence
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: The 30th-anniversary rerelease of this classic tackles the sensitivities of teenage anxiety with energy and confidence
Content: Dark side of high-school comedies … The Craft. Robin Tunney (left), Fairuza Balk (centre left), Rachel True (centre right), Neve Campbell (right)Photograph: AJ Pics/AlamyView image in fullscreenDark side of high-school comedies … The Craft. Robin Tunney (left), Fairuza Balk (centre left), Rachel True (centre right), Neve Campbell (right)Photograph: AJ Pics/AlamyMoviesReviewThe Craft review – cult high-school horror a reminder of the fearless 90sThe 30th-anniversary rerelease of this classic tackles the sensitivities of teenage anxiety with energy and confidencePeter BradshawTue 6 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 04.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe chrysalis of 80s and 90s high-school comedy finally gave us a veritable butterfly of fear in this cult girl-power classic from 1996, co-written and directed by Andrew Fleming, now rereleased for its 30th anniversary. It’s a movie to compare with Heathers or Mean Girls but with a supernatural edge, a flourish of scariness where the comedy or sexiness might otherwise go – and it incidentally delivers a very disturbing “René Magritte mirror” visual stab worthy of any straight-ahead chiller.Robin Tunney plays Sarah, a shy, studious teen from San Francisco who suffers from depression and buried guilt about the fact that her mother died in childbirth, and from lingering resentment at her new stepmother, with whom her dad has bought her to Los Angeles for a fresh start at a new school. Something about this new arrival intrigues a clique nicknamed “the bitches of Eastwick”, led by badass goth Nancy (Fairuza Balk); she rules over her two disciples Rochelle (Rachel True) and Bonnie, played by Neve Campbell, that same year to become a scary-movie hall-of-famer for the fledgling Scream franchise.The Craft trailerThey are devoted to “the craft” of being a witch and it is plain that Sarah too is one of their number: she has somehow alchemised her pain and fear into dark superpowers, far in excess of anything the other three can manage. Inevitably, the forces unleashed get out of control: the group find that they can kill people and take revenge on who they want; just as inevitably, a power struggle for dominance develops between the black-lipsticked Nancy and the more wholesome Sarah.A pouting blond princess named Laura (Christine Taylor) finds that, after making a racist remark to Rochelle, her hair starts falling out in a brutally explicit sequence in the swimming pool changing room. Sexist creep Chris (played by Scream stalwart Skeet Ulrich) is magicked into a humiliating submission to Sarah after spreading vengeful rumours about her. Nancy discovers that she can walk on water after a dark ceremony on the beach and the appearance on the sand of dead sharks is a tribute to her new eminence. But there appears to be white magic too: the burn marks on Bonnie’s back are magically cured after the girls invoke the assistance of a certain higher (or lower) power.The Craft has got its own energy and confidence, as well as a kind of 90s fearlessness that went with not knowing, or perhaps not caring, about the sensitivities surrounding young people’s anxieties that are a more central part of today’s conversation. It was the dark side to 90s high school comedies like Clueless or 10 Things I Hate About You, and it’s interesting to see easygoing Breckin Meyer in an early, unsympathetic role.The Craft is in UK and Irish cinemas from 9 October.Explore more on these topicsFilmHorror filmsThrillersreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Lost Children of Tuam review – deeply serious retelling of Ireland’s devastating tragedy  | Movies | The Guardian
description: Monica Dolan is superb as the amateur historian who uncovered the horror of mass graves at a mother and baby home in this Liam Neeson produced drama
Author: Cath Clarke
Headline: Monica Dolan is superb as the amateur historian who uncovered the horror of mass graves at a mother and baby home in this Liam Neeson produced drama
Content: Hard to look away … Monica Dolan, who plays Catherine Corless in The Lost Children of Tuam.Photograph: Element PicturesView image in fullscreenHard to look away … Monica Dolan, who plays Catherine Corless in The Lost Children of Tuam.Photograph: Element PicturesMoviesReviewThe Lost Children of Tuam review – deeply serious retelling of Ireland’s devastating tragedyMonica Dolan is superb as the amateur historian who uncovered the horror of mass graves at a mother and baby home in this Liam Neeson produced dramaCath ClarkeTue 6 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe children were never lost; if a baby goes missing, the police get called, social services become involved. The babies born at the mother and baby home run by nuns in the town of Tuam in County Galway were discarded: up to 796 tiny bodies thrown away, some in an old sewage tank. The amateur historianwho uncovered the horrorof the mass graves at the St Mary’s mother and baby home is Catherine Corless, superbly played here by Monica Dolan. Produced by Liam Neeson, and based on a2017 New York Times article, The Lost Children of Tuam is a painful, devastating film. It feels scraped clean of anything unnecessary that might trivialise, fiction-ise or movie-ise what happened at St Mary’s, home to thousands of unmarried women and children between 1925 and 1961.‘She never accepted no’: Liam Neeson on dogged heroine behind Tuam mass baby grave filmRead more“It gets me out of the house,” Corless says when she starts a course in local history. She turns detective after becoming interested in the children from St Mary’s, and what she uncovers is that babies died at a rate of nearly one a fortnight at the home – from whooping cough, measles, malnutrition and other childhood illnesses. Eventually, she obtains nearly 800 death certificates, but cannot find burial records for the babies. There are no graves.It is usual to say that a film like The LostChildrenof Tuam is a difficult watch – but in fact it’s the opposite: hard to look away. Dolan is excellent as Corless, who does most of her research at her kitchen table, and is ill at ease in the spotlight when the media finally picks up the story. Just as compelling are the actors playing the survivors – neglected and abused by nuns as children, now in their late middle age. Some only appear for a matter of moments, but their faces stayed with me. It’s a deeply serious film; there’s no exhilaration at the end, no comforting sense of closure, just pain.The Lost Children of Tuam is in Irish cinemas now and UK cinemas from 9 OctoberExplore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsIrelandLiam NeesonChildrenreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Celibidache was a musical visionary, an uncompromising perfectionist – and my father  | Classical music | The Guardian
description: The legendary conductor was acclaimed for his dazzling music-making, and infamous for his hatred of recordings. His son, writer of a new film about him, remembers a loving yet intransigent and demanding father
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The legendary conductor was acclaimed for his dazzling music-making, and infamous for his hatred of recordings. His son, writer of a new film about him, remembers a loving yet intransigent and demanding father
Content: Convinced that music can only be experienced live… Sergiu Celibidache (1912-1996) conducting in the early 1980s.Photograph: INTERFOTO/AlamyView image in fullscreenConvinced that music can only be experienced live… Sergiu Celibidache (1912-1996) conducting in the early 1980s.Photograph: INTERFOTO/AlamyClassical musicCelibidache was a musical visionary, an uncompromising perfectionist – and my fatherThe legendary conductor was acclaimed for his dazzling music-making, and infamous for his hatred of recordings. His son, writer of a new film about him, remembers a loving yet intransigent and demanding fatherSerge CelibidacheTue 6 Oct 2026 04.27 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 04.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMy father, Sergiu Celibidache, loved children more than anything because they are free and true to themselves. And yet, he once made a young boy wet himself when he dared to ask for an autograph, shouting at the poor child as if he had committed a federal crime because he knew there was a black market selling his signature behind his back.I grew up a privileged child with presents from all around the world. I was spoiled – to the despair of my mother, who always tried to keep my feet on the ground. But the gifts were part of my father’s way of making up for his long absences – he was often away touring with his orchestras.View image in fullscreenI missed him terribly when he was away on tour… Serge with his father Sergiu Celibidache,  in the 1970s.Photograph: Serge CelibidacheAs a young boy I had very little understanding that my father was a world-renowned conductor. I always missed him terribly when he was away, and yet he was nonetheless always very present in my life, and we were close. He was generous and attentive. There were frequent speeches about the less privileged and our duty to do something for them, and he was always eager to share stories of his picturesque childhood in Iași,Romaniaand his many adventures after leaving home to pursue music, without any support from his family.Those tales – some of which would eventually become part of The Yellow Tie – were fascinating. And he was such a good storyteller that I could hardly wait for my bedtime stories whenever he was around.But as much as I had a generous and entertaining father I also had an intransigent and demanding one.Whatever the school activity, whatever the situation at home, he expected me to be the best version of myself. If I received a disappointing grade or disrespected my mother in any way, I would have to explain myself. I was not to begin a sentence unless I knew where it was leading. If the structure of your thought was not clear, silence was a much better choice, he said.My father could not accept doing anything half heartedly. You had to be completely immersed in whatever you were doing at that very moment, fully invested in the “now”. Looking back, I remember the joy he found in preparing food for the four St Bernards at our country house, or in feeding the wild ducks at the river with such patience and dedication. So much life invested in the simplest activities. And he expected me to treat life as he did: with that drive, that indestructible belief in God and in oneself, and that absolute dedication.double quotation markHe considered it his duty to pass knowledge on to the next generation, but he was a highly demanding teacher who spared no one’s feelings.This pursuit of perfection was present throughout our daily lives. Even if only on a subconscious level, the pressure was constant for all of us – family, friends, colleagues and students. Oh, the poor students! As much as he was a phenomenal musician, my father’s approach to teaching remains questionable to this day. “Teaching is the most noble activity to which one can dedicate oneself,” he said; he loved it and considered it his duty to pass knowledge on to the next generation, in the manner of Socrates.Yet he was a highly demanding teacher who spared no one’s feelings. I remember one masterclass in Paris, at the Schola Cantorum. I was filming the session in which experienced students were invited to conduct the student orchestra in front of a live audience. Almost none of the trainee conductors escaped his harsh criticism – for an unjustified and perhaps overly expansive gesture or – God forbid – a forgotten background musical phrase. Sometimes, he would even ridicule them, to the audience’s amusement and their evident humiliation. I hid behind my camera, thanking God I had decided not to pursue a musical career. But I also knew that he loved them as he loved me, and wanted them to become the best versions of themselves. His intentions were pure but did his methods work? It’s debatable.View image in fullscreenBen Schnetzer as Celibidache in The Yellow TiePhotograph: Adi MarineciHis uncompromising perfectionism mixed with a deep sense of integrity led him to develop, over time, a profound disdain for recordings, which were, in his view, a dangerously false representation of live music experienced in a concert hall. Refusing lucrative offers from the four corners of the globe, he remained faithful to his conviction that music can only be experienced live.With no recordings of my father available, my thirst for knowledge drove me to discover the classical repertoire through the recorded music of the conductor who, judging by the music store shelves lined with his name seemed, at the time, to be the most widely acclaimed – Karajan. In my quest to absorb the masterworks, I was turning to the ultimate commercial recording figure as a substitute for a conductor who rejected recordings entirely! Still, I eased my conscience, remembering my father saying that when they first met in Berlin, Karajan was a genuine talent. (What happened later is another story …)As a small act of provocation, I would occasionally play a piece louder than necessary to provoke a reaction from my father. I found it difficult to accept that he would not make “his music” available to everyone – that he would not leave behind something of his extraordinary musical vision. In fact it infuriated me. So much so that, upon my return from NYU, I did exactly what you see in the film: I played a bootleg recording of one of his performances and pretended to him it was by a new conductor I’d discovered ... Needless to say, that conversation didn’t end well.double quotation markI grew up in awe of my father, but I did not agree with all that he did. That distance helped me approach a biopic about himI believed that even if a recording was not authentic music in his sense of the word, it would still have been the memory of a musical moment – and that, in itself, had value. I was so convinced of this that I agreed to let some of the orchestras he conducted in his later years record his concert performances without his knowledge. It was never about money, but about the genuine value of the documents themselves. He knew nothing about it, and, of course, I could not tell him. But today, I feel blessed that these “memories” exist.I grew up in awe of my father, but I did not agree with all that he did. That distance helped me find the courage to approach a biopic about his life. The goal was never to put him on a pedestal. The opening scene – where Japanese record company executives offer him a lucrative recording deal alongside a concert tour – does more than just show his aversion to recorded music. It introduces him as an impetuous and unpredictable man who wasn’t afraid of confrontations.View image in fullscreenHis is a truly inspirational story… Serge with his father Sergiu Celibidache.Photograph: Serge CelibidacheI and my co-writer James Olivier tried to remain faithful to the man we knew. The Yellow Tie is not only a story about music, love and integrity. It is a story about sacrifice, survival and identity. Beyond my father’s devastating exile from his familial roots, his is a deeply inspirational true story about an immigrant trying to succeed in a country that is largely hostile.All I can hope is that my father’s story may inspire those who sometimes struggle to find and define their own path. If he could do it against all odds, perhaps we can too.Serge Ioan Celibidachi is the director and co-writer of The Yellow Tie, in UK cinemas from Friday 9 October.Read Peter Bradshaw’s reviewExplore more on these topicsClassical musicRomaniaEuropefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Fine scenery, historic towns and great pubs: a weekend walk on the Shropshire Way | Walking holidays | The Guardian
description: A new series of rambles cuts the 185-mile trail into bitesize portions reachable by train, with urban beavers the Devil’s Chair tor and some delicious food along the way
Author: Jane Dunford
Headline: A new series of rambles cuts the 185-mile trail into bitesize portions reachable by train, with urban beavers the Devil’s Chair tor and some delicious food along the way
Content: Linley Beeches on Linley Hill in Shropshire.Photograph: Simon Whaley Landscapes/AlamyView image in fullscreenLinley Beeches on Linley Hill in Shropshire.Photograph: Simon Whaley Landscapes/AlamyWalking holidaysFine scenery, historic towns and great pubs: a weekend walk on the Shropshire WayA new series of rambles cuts the 185-mile trail into bitesize portions reachable by train, with urban beavers, the Devil’s Chair tor and some delicious food along the wayJane DunfordTue 6 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 05.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFew pubs boast a more idyllic setting. As I emerge from the woods after a 15-mile hike,The Bridges, on the banks of the Onny River, in the rolling south Shropshire hills, glistens in the late afternoon sun. Inside it’s all wooden beams, with light streaming through stained glass and huge bunches of homegrown flowers adding splashes of colour. There’s time for a pint before general manager Sam Thompson shows me to my room in the recently converted stables.I’m here exploring part of the 185-mile (297km) Shropshire Way, on a two-day Heart of the Hills hike – one of the county tourist board’s newRail-Ready Short Breaks. Designed for people who don’t have time to tackle the whole route, the itineraries focus on loops that are easy to access by train, with illustrated PDF downloads, GPX files, accommodation suggestions and highlights of what to do along the way. My route will take me from Shrewsbury to Bishop’s Castle via Ratlinghope – about 27 miles, perfect for a weekend.View image in fullscreenThe Bridges pub in Ratlinghope.Shrewsbury itself is worth lingering in – the historic market town is crammed with independent shops and restaurants (I lovedCsonsfor its creative small plates) and impressive Tudor architecture. But I’m most intrigued to learn that beavers have been reintroduced here by the council and theShropshire Wildlife Trust. The first kit in the county in 400 years was born late last year and the Trust’s Tom Freeland shows me around the site, the Old River Bed nature reserve, just two miles north of the town centre. A boardwalk crossing wetlands allows an up-close view of the rewilding project. Although we don’t spy the elusive creatures (we see heron and plenty of moorhen), there’s still lots to learn. “It’s been a great success in inspiring the community to find out more about our local wildlife,” says Tom. Nature talks and guided tours of the beaver enclosure are in the pipeline, too.View image in fullscreenShrewsbury Square, Shropshire.Photograph: Nik Reates/AlamyBack at my base, the 16th-centuryLion + Pheasant townhouse hotel, I dine on pan-roasted trout in the beamed restaurant (there’s a popular wine and tapas bar on site too) and the next morning set off to walk the first leg to Ratlinghope. Crossing the River Severn, the city soon peters out and quiet country lanes lead to Lyth Hill Country Park where expansive views open up across Shropshire.It’s a steady climb to Wilderley Hill, past fields of rape, bright patches of yellow in a sea of green, and I stop under an oak tree to picnic. There’s no one around, just the songs of wren and chaffinch filling the air. The landscape changes on the approach to Ratlinghope as the route traces a brook, crosses wooden bridges and winds through pretty woodland. Just off the path lies the 12th-century St Margaret’s Church, the burial place of 19th-century farmer Richard Munslow, the last known “sin-eater”, whose job it was to eat bread and drink ale over corpses to absorb their sins.double quotation markThe Bridges is such a lively, friendly place I’m tempted to move nearby for the pub aloneI enjoy a drink instead in the pretty beer garden at The Bridges. The seven immaculate, minimalist rooms are round an adjacent courtyard – and guests have access to a lounge above the pub, too. The food in the bar includes Guinness rarebit and duck terrine, while the light-filled restaurant focuses on organic fare from the owners’ regenerative farm on the Linley Estate and the Welsh Marches. I feast on huge radishes with anchoïade, and hake with fennel, capers and crispy polenta. Breakfast the next morning – homemade granola and poached rhubarb – is equally delicious. It’s such a lively, friendly place I’m tempted to move nearby for the pub alone. They’ll even drive locals home if they’ve had one too many, Sam tells me.Blue skies and gentle sunshine greet me for day two of the hike, a 12-mile yomp across rugged moorland and pastures to Bishop’s Castle. The pub lies on the edge of the Long Mynd, a heath and moorland plateau, but I’m heading north to the Stiperstones, a national nature reserve with a wild, dramatic ridge of quartzite rock formations that pierce the ground. I climb higher, passing Devil’s Chair tor, watching skylarks and buzzards soar overhead.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThe Devil’s Chair on the Stiperstones Ridge, Shropshire.Photograph: Vincent Lowe/AlamyIt’s a beautiful walk. After several hours, a magnificent avenue of Linley Beeches line the descent into Bishop’s Castle, a charming town of half-timbered houses.Bank House B&B, a Georgian renovation with an oak-panelled drawing room and five antique-filled rooms, is my home for the night. I pop into thePoetry Pharmacywhere prescriptions are poems chosen to spark specific emotions, to be “taken” when required (I leave with a bottle of Joy). Although little remains of the medieval castle that once stood here and gives the town its name, the grandCastle Hotel, with its pretty gardens and welcoming restaurant, is worth a visit.With more time, I could, of course, carry on and add another loop of the trail. But the train back home beckons – Craven Arms station is a short bus or taxi ride away – and I leave feeling pleased to have dipped my toe into a small segment of theShropshireWay. As far as rambling weekends go, it’s ticked all the right boxes, and whetted my appetite to discover more.The trip was provided byVisit Shropshireand train travel from London to Shropshire was byVisit England.The Bridgeshas rooms from£120a night. title: How to maximise the umami in mushrooms | Fungi | The Guardian
description: Whether you sizzle, sweat, wet-fry or oven-cook, enhancing the savoury flavour of your mushrooms will depend on the variety, says our panel of fun guys
Author: Anna Berrill
Headline: Whether you sizzle, sweat, wet-fry or oven-cook, enhancing the savoury flavour of your mushrooms will depend on the variety, says our panel of fun guys
Content: To bring out the flavour inFuchsia Dunlop's mushroom mapo tofu, cut it into 5mm cubes, then fry on a high heat for two to three minutes, until ‘tinged with gold’.Photograph: Patricia Niven/The Guardian. Food styling: Tamara Vos. Prop styling: Anna Willkins. Food styling assistant: Katie Smith.View image in fullscreenTo bring out the flavour inFuchsia Dunlop's mushroom mapo tofu, cut it into 5mm cubes, then fry on a high heat for two to three minutes, until ‘tinged with gold’.Photograph: Patricia Niven/The Guardian. Food styling: Tamara Vos. Prop styling: Anna Willkins. Food styling assistant: Katie Smith.Kitchen aideFungiHow to maximise the umami in mushroomsWhether you sizzle, sweat, wet-fry or oven-cook, enhancing the savoury flavour of your mushrooms will depend on the variety, says our panel of fun guysAnna BerrillTue 6 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHow do I cook mushroomsat homeso they have the umamiyou get in restaurant dishes?John, by emailFor Chantelle Nicholson, chef-patron ofApricityin London, boosting the savoury side of ’shrooms comes down to three main things. First, they hold a lot of water, so “you need to cook that out of them, so heat is super-important, as are fat and salt”. Tomás Gormley, chef-owner ofCardinalin Edinburgh, adds that he can “almost guarantee” that John isn’t using enough of the latter: “As a rule, I use 1.5% of the weight of whatever I’m seasoning. With mushrooms, especially, season early, before they hit the pan, to draw out their moisture. That resulting mushroomy water then cooks the mushrooms while it’s reducing and concentrating the flavour.”But there are so many varieties of mushrooms out there, and they all behave in different ways, so John needs to be using the right ones for the job. “If you’re making a soup, puree or paté, field, portobello or button mushrooms are fine,” Nicholson says. “But if you’re looking for a delicious sauteed mushroom, say, ideally you need something with less water content – chestnut, shiitake or blue/grey oyster mushrooms. Heat oil in a pan, then add the shredded or sliced mushrooms, and season with fine salt straight away.” Nicholson would be inclined to toss in a bay leaf and some thyme or sage, too, and maybe a smashed clove of garlic. “Cook over a high-ish heat until lightly golden, then add a bit of butter and keep cooking until golden. If you want to enhance the flavour even further, a splash of dry sherry works really well.”That said, Buttons Mira, author ofThe Mushroomery, throws her ’shrooms into a dry frying pan: “That’s right, no oil or fat! I put a lid on top and let them sweat out that rich, umami flavour.” Alice Zaslavsky, author ofWeeknights with Alice, deploys a similar tactic: “Cooking mushrooms the traditional way in fat can inhibit the intensification of umami and lock in too much moisture, which is why I’ve taken to wet-frying my mushrooms.” She first lets them bubble away in a little water “spliced with condiments: umami-rich soy sauce and/or Worcestershire sauce work well”, until all the liquid evaporates. “Only then do I add oil and/or butter to lift off the flavour in the base of the pan and encourage caramelisation for extra depth and sweetness.”Heading out of the frying pan and into the oven, a properly roasted mushroom can also be meaty and deeply flavoured: “That makes them super-nutty and delicious,” says Mira, who then uses them in pastas and risottos. The best way to do this is, again, with high heat, salt and oil, Nicholson says: “I’d also suggest using chestnut mushrooms over button mushrooms, and quartering them – hard herbs, such as thyme, bay or rosemary, will help as well.”Just like the rest of us, though, sometimes those mushrooms need a bit of a helping hand: “Up the umami potential by doubling down on the right kind of mushroom,” Zaslavsky says, which in her book includes sprinkling over dried shiitake or porcini in powdered form: “Both offer a deep, savoury aroma and flavour that helps enhance milder varieties.” Magic mushrooms, indeed.Got a culinary dilemma? title: Jose Pizarro’s recipe for poached pear and almond tart with PX caramel | Food | The Guardian
description: This tart uses the richness of red vermut to bring together the sweet and the nutty for a flavour explosion
Author: José Pizarro
Headline: This tart uses the richness of red vermut to bring together the sweet and the nutty for a flavour explosion
Content: Jose Pizarro’s poached pear and almond tart with PX caramel.Photograph: Ola O Smit/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.FoodJose Pizarro’s recipe for poached pear and almond tart with PX caramelThis tart uses the richness of red vermut to bring together the sweet and the nutty for a flavour explosionJosé PizarroTue 6 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn Spain, vermut is traditionally enjoyed as an aperitif, while pedro ximénez is often poured at the end of a meal, alongside dessert or a piece of cheese, say. In this tart, however, they come together to tell the story of the Spanish table in the form of pudding. We have a wonderful tradition of fortified wines, and while lighter sherries often hog the limelight, vermut and pedro ximénez deserve just as much attention. They’re both made from wine, but each brings something completely different to a dish. Here, vermut, which is infused with herbs and spices, gently perfumes the pears, while PX, with its rich raisin, fig and caramel notes, introduces a flavour that’s impossible to resist.Poached pear and almond tart with PX caramelPrep15 minCook1 hr 50 minChill30 min+Serves10-12750ml bottle red vermut– I likeLustau Vermut Rojo, but any vermut rojo will do, or standard red vermouth3 tbsprunny honey1 vanilla pod, split and seeds scraped outPared zest of 1 orange4 just-ripe medium-sized dessert pears(williams or comice, say), peeledCream or creme fraiche, to serveFor the pastry225g plain flour,plus extra for dusting110g cold unsalted butter50g caster sugar2egg yolksFor the filling100mlpedro ximénez2 tbsp caramel sauce(Sainbury’s does a good one), or dulce de leche1 pinchflaky sea salt125g unsalted butter, softened125g caster sugar, plus 2 tbsp extra for the glaze2 mediumeggs125g ground almonds1 tbsp plain flourPut the vermut, honey, vanilla pod and seeds, orange zest and 300ml water in a pan just big enough to hold the pears snugly. Bring to a simmer, then add the pears and leave to poach gently for 20-25 minutes, until glassy-looking and just tender to the tip of a knife. Take off the heat and leave the pears to cool in the liquid.Meanwhile, in a food processor, pulse the flour, butter and sugar until they resemble breadcrumbs. Add the egg yolks and pulse again briefly to make a dough; if need be, add up to two teaspoons of water to help bring it together. Tip out on to a lightly floured surface, quickly shape into a ball, then press down into a flat disc. Wrap in baking paper and chill for at least 30 minutes.Roll out the pastry on a lightly floured surface, then use it to line a greased deep, fluted 23cm tart tin; the pastry will be very soft, so if it breaks, just press it back together with your fingertips. Return to the fridge to chill again.In a small pan, bring the PX to a simmer, then reduce until there’s only about two tablespoons of sticky liquid left. Tip into a bowl, blend with the caramel sauce and a pinch of salt, then spread the PX mix all over the base of the tart case, and chill again.Heat the oven and a baking sheet to 190C (170C fan)/375F/gas 5. Lift the cooled pears out of the poaching liquid, pat dry, then cut in half lengthways and scoop out the cores. Turn each pear half on to its flat side, then cut a few times across its width without slicing all the way through. Press down gently to fan out the slices, then pat dry again.Whisk the softened butter and caster sugar until light and fluffy, then work in the eggs, almonds and flour. Spread this evenly over the caramel layer in the tart case, then neatly top with the pear halves pointy ends in, and gently press them into the almond layer.Bake for 45 minutes on the heated tray, then cover with foil so the pastry doesn’t brown too much and bake for 15 minutes more, until set all the way through.Meanwhile, put 300ml of the pear poaching liquid in a pan, add two tablespoons of sugar, bring slowly to a boil, then reduce to a glossy, sticky glaze.Leave the tart to cool for 10 minutes, then remove from its tin and put on a rack. Once it’s just warm, brush the vermut glaze over the top and serve with cream or creme fraiche.Explore more on these topicsFoodDessertAutumn food and drinkFruitSpanish food and drinkBakingCakerecipesShareReuse this content
